### [1] [Open ultrasound foundation model for robust segmentation and clinical measurement across heterogeneous settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19230)
*Chao Qin,Fahad Shahbaz Khan,Salman Khan,Sarim Ather,Siddiq Anwar,Rao Muhammad Anwer,Shadab Khan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SonoCorpus is a large-scale unified ultrasound dataset (456,963 images, 1,626,085 masks from 53 datasets across 24 applications), and SonoBase is a segmentation foundation model pretrained on it that generalizes across new organs, devices, operators, and geographies, outperforming SAM2, MedSAM2, and MedSAM2 while matching specialist models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical AI in ultrasound is fragmented into narrow single-task models that fail when device, operator, or anatomy changes. There is a need for a generalizable foundation model that works across different clinical settings and equipment.

Method: SonoBase is pretrained on SonoCorpus (456,963 images, 1,626,085 expert masks from 53 public datasets spanning 24 clinical applications and 17 countries). Evaluated on 15 datasets with distribution shifts. Used 5-shot adaptation for new settings. Compared with SAM2, MedSAM2, and concept-promptable MedSAM3.

Result: SonoBase outperforms all baselines on every dataset, matches per-dataset specialist models, exceeds baseline accuracy on fully external data. Ejection fraction error (6.63%) within inter-observer variability. Fetal head circumference error 1.81mm, gestational age error 1.2 days - both below inter-observer variability. Recovers usable segmentations in 81% of cases where baselines fail. Works with handheld probes by minimally trained users in low-resource settings (Sierra Leone, Tanzania). 5-shot adaptation effective. Ultrasound-specific pretraining is key advantage.

Conclusion: SonoBase is a generalizable ultrasound segmentation foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse clinical settings, devices, and geographies. The advantage comes from ultrasound-specific pretraining rather than architecture. The open release of all resources enables community building.

Abstract: Ultrasound is the most widely deployed imaging modality worldwide, yet clinical AI remains fragmented into narrow single-task models that fail when device, operator, or anatomy changes. Here we present SonoCorpus, an open resource unifying 456,963 images and 1,626,085 expert masks from 53 public datasets spanning 24 clinical applications and 17 countries, and SonoBase, an interactive segmentation foundation model pretrained on it. Across fifteen evaluation datasets introducing new organs, devices, operators, and geographies, SonoBase outperforms SAM2, MedSAM2, and the concept-promptable MedSAM3 on every dataset and matches per-dataset specialist models trained on the same data; on fully external data it exceeds the accuracy these baselines achieve on their own in-distribution benchmarks. Ejection fraction derived from its segmentations falls within inter-observer variability (6.63\% error), with fewer misclassifications at the defibrillator-candidacy threshold than either promptable baseline (13\% versus 18--42\%); fetal head-circumference (1.81~mm) and gestational-age (1.2 days) errors fall below inter-observer variability. Where a baseline fails outright, one in four test cases, SonoBase recovers a usable segmentation in 81\% of them, including on handheld probes operated by minimally trained users in two low- and middle-income countries (Sierra Leone and Tanzania). Five labeled examples can help the model adapt to a new setting, and the identical training protocol transfers well to newer models such as SAM3, locating the advantage in ultrasound-specific pretraining rather than any single architecture. To ensure reproducibility and enable the community to build on SonoBase as a platform, we release all checkpoints, optimizer states, data-split indices, deduplication hashes, and starter code.

</details>


### [2] [RAUL: Reference-Assisted Ureteroscopy Localization for Skill Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19236)
*Fangjie Li,Mai Bui,Charan Mohan,Michael Miga,Matthieu Chabanas,Nicholas Kavoussi,Jie Ying Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents RAUL, a reference-assisted framework for recovering ureteroscope trajectories from endoscopic videos to quantify surgical skill in ureteroscopic kidney stone surgeries. The method uses a high-quality reference exploration to enable more complete trajectory recovery compared to standard Structure-from-Motion, achieving 86.1% localization coverage and significant differences between experience levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Incomplete navigation of anatomy during ureteroscopic kidney stone surgeries leads to repeat interventions. While skilled surgeons have lower reintervention rates, there are no objective metrics to quantify scope-navigation performance to evaluate trainee competency. This work aims to address this gap by developing video-based trajectory recovery and navigation metrics for skill assessment.

Method: The proposed RAUL framework uses a slow, high-quality reference exploration video to generate a reference reconstruction, then localizes subsequent exploration videos against this reference. Localization accuracy was evaluated against electromagnetically tracked scope pose. Navigation metrics were computed from phantom exploration trajectories to compare surgical residents across experience levels.

Result: The framework achieves a mean translation RMSE of 0.5 ± 0.1 mm across 9 phantoms. Compared to standard SfM, the proposed pipeline increases frame-wise localization coverage from 50.5 ± 14.9% to 86.1 ± 7.2%. The reconstructed trajectories revealed significant differences between high- and low-experience trainees in established navigation metrics.

Conclusion: RAUL enables substantially more complete recovery of ureteroscope trajectories from videos compared to standard SfM pipelines, enabling trajectory-based skill assessment without additional tracking equipment. This represents the first use of video-only recovery of ureteroscope trajectories without external tracking sensors for skill assessment, supporting scalable automated assessment of ureteroscopy navigation skill.

Abstract: Objective: Incomplete navigation of anatomy during ureteroscopic kidney stone surgeries can contribute to repeat interventions. While skilled surgeons have lower reintervention rates, there are no objective metrics to quantify scope-navigation performance to evaluate when a trainee becomes skilled. This work aims to recover ureteroscope trajectories from endoscopic video and derive navigation metrics to quantify differences in skill. Methods: We propose RAUL, a reference-assisted reconstruction framework for recovering ureteroscope trajectories from ureteroscope videos only in phantoms. For each phantom, we use a slow, high-quality reference exploration video to generate a reference reconstruction. We localize subsequent exploration videos against this reference. We evaluate localization accuracy against electromagnetically tracked scope pose. We compute navigation metrics from phantom exploration trajectories to compare surgical residents across experience levels. Results: The proposed reference-assisted framework achieves a mean translation root mean square error of $0.5 \pm 0.1$ mm across 9 phantoms. Compared to standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM), the proposed pipeline increases frame-wise localization coverage from $50.5 \pm 14.9\%$ to $86.1 \pm 7.2\%$ of all video frames. The reconstructed trajectories revealed significant differences between high- and low-experience trainees in established navigation metrics. Conclusion: RAUL enables substantially more complete recovery of ureteroscope trajectories from videos compared to standard SfM pipelines, enabling trajectory-based skill assessment without additional tracking equipment. Significance: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of video-only recovery of ureteroscope trajectories without external tracking sensors for skill assessment, supporting scalable automated assessment of ureteroscopy navigation skill.

</details>


### [3] [PART: Learning 3D Part Assembly and Retrieval with Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19872)
*Ruchao Bao,Wenzheng Wu,Chucheng Xiang,Zhongyuan Liu,Yuan Liu,Jinxin Dong,Ligang Liu,Ziqi Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PART is a unified transformer-based framework for 3D part retrieval and assembly that selects appropriate parts from a library and predicts their 6-DoF poses to reconstruct target shapes. It formulates retrieval and assembly as a set prediction problem with variable-length output.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has achieved impressive progress on assembling pre-defined sets of parts, the more practical retrieval-based setting (selecting from a large part library) remains largely unexplored. The task faces three key challenges: combinatorially explosive search space, variable-length outputs, and continuous 6-DoF pose estimation.

Method: The method formulates retrieval and assembly as a set prediction problem and designs a novel transformer-based framework that retrieves parts and regresses their poses with variable-length output. Additionally, it exploits the duality between part pose estimation and target segmentation through joint training and a novel segmentation-enhanced optimization module.

Result: Results show that PART generalizes to scene layouts, image targets, and real-world scans. The approach was validated on a large-scale dataset of 80K+ shapes.

Conclusion: The paper presents a unified transformer-based framework that successfully addresses the challenges of 3D part retrieval and assembly, demonstrating generalization across different input modalities (3D shapes, scene layouts, images, and real-world scans).

Abstract: 3D assembly is fundamental to modern manufacturing and digital content creation. In this paper, we present PART, a unified transformer-based framework for 3D part retrieval and assembly: given a target shape and a part library, PART automatically selects the appropriate parts and predicts their 6-DoF poses to reconstruct the target. While prior work has achieved impressive progress on assembling a pre-defined set of parts, this more practical retrieval-based setting remains largely unexplored. The task faces three key challenges: (i) a combinatorially explosive search space that grows exponentially with library size; (ii) variable-length outputs, as different targets require different numbers of parts; and (iii) continuous 6-DoF pose estimation for part assembly. To address these, we formulate retrieval and assembly as a set prediction problem and design a novel transformer-based framework that retrieves parts and regresses their poses with variable-length output. Additionally, we exploit the duality between part pose estimation and target segmentation through joint training and a novel segmentation-enhanced optimization module. Finally, We curate a large-scale dataset of 80K+ shapes, and the results show that PART generalizes to scene layouts, image targets, and real-world scans. Project Page: https://iambrc.github.io/PART-project-page/.

</details>


### [4] [Riemannian--Lorentz Fusion of Vision Transformers and State-Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19384)
*Badri N. Patro,Vijay S. Agneeswaran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses heterogeneous model merging by combining Vision Transformers (ViT) and State-Space Models (SSM) with different architectures using a novel Riemannian-Lorentz Parameter Fusion (RLPF) method that operates in hyperbolic space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling deep learning faces critical bottlenecks: data exhaustion, exponential training costs, and resource concentration. Existing weight-space merging methods assume aligned, shape-compatible checkpoints, making it difficult to combine vision models with different architectures (ViT vs SSM) that implement token mixing with different operators.

Method: RLPF projects aligned parameter groups to common coordinates, lifts selected coordinates to the Lorentz hyperboloid model of hyperbolic space, computes a regularized geodesic barycenter, and decodes the result into two branches. A learned gate combines branch logits for each input. Component groups use fixed curvature values, with normalization parameters treated as Euclidean.

Result: Fine-tuned system achieves 82.37% on CIFAR-10, 75.04% on Oxford-IIIT Pet, and 78.58% top-1 on ImageNet-1K. Best-parent accuracies are 76.54%, 71.42%, and 76.42% respectively. Pre-fine-tuning initialization reaches 77.80% on ImageNet-1K.

Conclusion: Results support further study of geometry-aware heterogeneous fusion. However, RLPF is a two-branch hybrid whose gate and reported final models require training, not a training-free single-checkpoint merge.

Abstract: Scaling deep learning faces critical bottlenecks: data exhaustion, exponential training costs, and resource concentration. Model merging combines pre-trained checkpoints without gradient descent, offering orders-of-magnitude savings versus retraining. Combining independently trained vision models is difficult when their architectures and parameter shapes differ. Existing weight-space merging methods generally assume aligned, shape-compatible checkpoints, whereas a Vision Transformer (ViT) and a state-space model (SSM) implement token mixing with different operators. We study a hybrid Heterogeneous merging setting that retains both architectures while aligning parameter groups by semantic role. Our proposed Riemannian--Lorentz Parameter Fusion (RLPF) method projects aligned groups to common coordinates, lifts selected coordinates to the Lorentz hyperboloid model of hyperbolic space, computes a regularized geodesic barycenter, and decodes the result into the two branches. A learned gate then combines branch logits for each input. Component groups use fixed curvature values, with normalization parameters treated as Euclidean. In the results available in this manuscript, the fine-tuned system obtains 82.37\% on CIFAR-10, 75.04\% on Oxford-IIIT Pet, and 78.58\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K; the corresponding best-parent accuracies are 76.54\%, 71.42\%, and 76.42\%. On ImageNet-1K, the reported pre-fine-tuning initialization reaches 77.80\%. These results support further study of geometry-aware heterogeneous fusion, but not a training-free single-checkpoint merge: RLPF is a two-branch hybrid whose gate and reported final models are trained.

</details>


### [5] [Can Vision-Language Models Judge Olympic Diving? From Reasoning to Scores in Zero-Shot Action Quality Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19354)
*Henry O. Velesaca,David Freire-Obregon,Luigi Miranda,Abel Reyes-Angulo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for zero-shot action quality assessment on Olympic diving videos using the AQA-7 benchmark. The proposed ensemble regression framework combining TF-IDF, dimensionality reduction, and ensemble learning achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.67, substantially improving upon standalone VLM performance (below 0.32). Textual reasoning features prove more valuable than raw numerical sub-scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated action quality assessment in Olympic sports is challenging due to complex human motion and subjectivity in expert judging. This work aims to evaluate the capability of open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to perform zero-shot action quality assessment on Olympic diving videos.

Method: The study proposes a regression-based framework combining: (1) zero-shot VLM inference for semantic reasoning and phase-level sub-scores, (2) TF-IDF vectorization for text feature extraction, (3) dimensionality reduction, and (4) ensemble learning to predict final competition scores. A four-model configuration was evaluated on the AQA-7 benchmark dataset.

Result: Standalone VLMs achieved moderate Spearman correlations below 0.32. The proposed ensemble regression framework substantially improved performance, reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.67 with a four-model configuration. Textual reasoning features consistently outperformed raw numerical sub-scores.

Conclusion: VLMs show strong potential as assistive tools for explainable and semi-automated sports performance evaluation. The proposed ensemble regression framework substantially improves upon standalone VLM performance, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.67. Textual reasoning features consistently outperform raw numerical sub-scores, suggesting that VLM-generated explanations contain richer semantic information for action quality analysis.

Abstract: Automated action quality assessment (AQA) in Olympic sports remains a challenging task due to the complexity of human motion and the subjectivity inherent in expert judging. This work evaluates the capability of open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to perform zero-shot action quality assessment on Olympic diving videos using the AQA-7 benchmark dataset. In this regard, a regression-based framework is pro-posed to leverage both the semantic reasoning and phase-level sub-scores generated by the VLMs, combining TF-IDF vectorization, dimensionality reduction, and ensemble learning to predict final competition scores. Experimental results show that standalone VLMs achieve moderate Spearman correlations below 0.32, while the proposed ensemble regression framework substantially improves performance in the reported evaluation, reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.67 with a four-model configuration. Textual reasoning features con-sistently outperformed raw numerical sub-scores, highlighting the richness of VLM-generated explanations for action quality analysis. These findings suggest that VLMs hold strong potential as assistive tools for explainable and semi-automated sports performance evaluation. The code is publicly available on GitHub https://github.com/hvelesaca/olympic diving judge vlm

</details>


### [6] [GS-PI: An Optimization-Decoupled Appearance Decomposition Approach for Generating PBR Gaussian Assets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19907)
*Jieting Xu,Rengan Xie,Zijian Huang,Zehui Jin,Rui Wang,Yuchi Huo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GS-PI is a novel framework that generates physically based rendering (PBR) materials from Gaussian Splatting models by using a geometry-conditioned diffusion process on 3D point clouds, decoupling optimization from inference through a multi-scale cross-view conditioning mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gaussian Splatting (GS) excels at novel-view synthesis but suffers from baked-in radiance that tightly entangles illumination with geometry, preventing seamless integration into PBR pipelines. Existing inverse-rendering methods attempting to disentangle materials via joint optimization suffer from competing objectives, severe ambiguities, and residual lighting artifacts.

Method: The method operates in three stages: (1) Extract a point cloud from a pre-trained Gaussian model; (2) Predict PBR attributes (albedo, roughness, metallic, normal) via a conditional diffusion process with multi-scale cross-view conditioning that integrates three components: global semantic prior, source-anchored photometric cues, and absolute spatial learned view-direction conditioning signal; (3) Distill the predicted attributes back through differentiable rasterization to yield a fully relightable PBR-GS asset.

Result: GS-PI outperforms recent inverse-rendering baselines while replacing per-scene joint illumination/BRDF optimization with a learned diffusion pass followed by a short target-driven distillation, without requiring proxy meshes. The approach inherently guarantees multi-view consistency by operating directly in the 3D domain, sidestepping severe pixel correspondence issues that challenge 2D diffusion approaches.

Conclusion: This work presents a paradigm shift from per-scene optimization to a learning-based approach that leverages 3D point cloud diffusion with cross-view conditioning to generate high-quality PBR materials from Gaussian Splatting, successfully preventing specular highlights from baking into intrinsic colors while achieving superior quality over existing inverse-rendering methods.

Abstract: Gaussian Splatting (GS) excels at novel-view synthesis but encodes baked-in radiance, tightly entangling illumination with geometry and preventing seamless integration into physically based rendering (PBR) pipelines. Existing inverse-rendering methods attempt to disentangle materials via joint optimization, but often suffer from competing objectives that cause severe ambiguities and residual lighting artifacts. To overcome this, we present GS-PI, a novel optimization-decoupled framework that casts PBR material generation as a geometry-conditioned diffusion process on 3D point clouds. By operating directly in the 3D domain, our method inherently guarantees multi-view consistency, sidestepping the severe pixel correspondence issues that challenge 2D diffusion approaches. We introduce a multi-scale cross-view conditioning mechanism that integrates three complementary components: a global semantic prior, source-anchored photometric cues, and an absolute spatial learned view-direction conditioning signal. This design efficiently compresses complex multi-view evidence, mitigating cross-view projection misalignment and successfully preventing specular highlights from baking into intrinsic colors. By extracting a point cloud from a pre-trained Gaussian model, predicting PBR attributes via conditional diffusion, and distilling them back through differentiable rasterisation, we yield a fully relightable PBR-GS asset. GS-PI outperforms recent inverse-rendering baselines while replacing per-scene joint illumination/BRDF optimization with a learned diffusion pass followed by a short target-driven distillation, without requiring proxy meshes.

</details>


### [7] [BinoGen: Scaling egocentric binocular data for embodied visual perception and learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19881)
*Chunpeng Li,Ya-tang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BinoGen is a synthetic data generation framework that creates large-scale egocentric binocular visual experiences with dense multimodal annotations. It addresses the challenge of collecting real-world embodied visual data by jointly modeling environmental and observer variations, producing synchronized binocular videos with depth, flow, normals, semantics, object coordinates, and camera poses. The framework generates 20M+ annotated images and demonstrates improvements in real-world visual perception tasks and enables study of embodiment effects on perceptual learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied visual perception relies on temporally coherent visual experience from continuous environmental engagement. However, collecting large-scale egocentric binocular observations with dense annotations is costly and difficult. Additionally, visual experience is shaped by both the environment and the observer's embodiment (viewing height, field of view, binocular geometry, motion), which adds complexity to data collection.

Method: BinoGen jointly models environmental and observer variation through five key components: (1) generative scene synthesis, (2) probabilistic object instantiation, (3) appearance randomization, (4) stochastic trajectory generation, and (5) configurable binocular camera setups. The framework produces synchronized binocular videos with dense multimodal supervision including depth maps, optical flow, surface normals, semantic maps, object coordinates, and camera poses.

Result: Created a dataset of over 20 million annotated images. Demonstrated two utilities: (1) Incorporating BinoGen data consistently improves real-world visual perception tasks including depth estimation, object detection, and video object tracking. (2) Paired human-inspired and mouse-inspired observations enable controlled investigation of embodiment effects on perceptual learning. Embodiment-specific adaptation substantially improves performance, while joint training enables a single model to perform competitively across both embodiments.

Conclusion: Large-scale, controllable visual experience can improve embodied perception. The synthetic data generation approach successfully addresses data collection challenges while enabling systematic study of how observer embodiment affects perceptual learning.

Abstract: Embodied visual perception relies on temporally coherent visual experience accumulated through continuous engagement with the environment. However, collecting large-scale egocentric binocular observations together with dense annotations remains costly and difficult. Moreover, visual experience is shaped not only by the environment but also by the embodiment of the observer, including viewing height, field of view, binocular geometry, and motion through the scene. To address these challenges, we present BinoGen, an automated framework for generating large-scale, embodiment-aware egocentric binocular visual experiences in indoor environments. BinoGen jointly models environmental and observer variation through generative scene synthesis, probabilistic object instantiation, appearance randomization, stochastic trajectory generation, and configurable binocular camera setups. The framework produces synchronized binocular videos together with dense multimodal supervision, including depth maps, optical flow, surface normals, semantic maps, object coordinates, and camera poses. Using BinoGen, we construct a dataset comprising more than 20 million annotated images for supervised learning. We demonstrate two complementary utilities of BinoGen. First, incorporating BinoGen data consistently improves real-world visual perception, including depth estimation, object detection, and video object tracking. Second, paired human-inspired and mouse-inspired observations from the same environments enable controlled investigation of how observer embodiment affects perceptual learning. Embodiment-specific adaptation substantially improves performance, while joint training enables a single model to perform competitively across both embodiments. Together, these results demonstrate that large-scale, controllable visual experience can improve embodied perception...

</details>


### [8] [Open-vocabulary 3D object detection with promptable segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19358)
*Ömer Faruk Deniz,Mustafa Taha Koçyiğit*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a training-free, open-vocabulary 3D object detection method for autonomous driving using SAM3 segmentation model queried with text prompts. The approach converts 2D instance masks into metric 3D boxes using scene geometry, demonstrating that the main bottleneck is measurement precision rather than 2D detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 3D object detectors are trained on large corpora of human-annotated 3D boxes and learn a fixed category list, making them invisible to anything outside that list. This paper explores whether the task can be solved training-free and open-vocabulary.

Method: The method uses a promptable segmentation model (SAM3) queried with class names as text prompts to supply instance masks from the vehicle's six surround-view cameras. These masks are then converted to metric 3D boxes using scene geometry. A controlled three-stage comparison on nuScenes dataset varies the source of 3D geometry while holding 2D detection fixed: (1) geometry predicted from images alone, (2) fitting boxes from raw LiDAR points inside masks with training-free rules, and (3) borrowing supervised box geometry at inference time.

Result: Image-predicted geometry achieves 0.183 mAP. Training-free LiDAR point fitting achieves 0.298 mAP / 0.348 NDS at zero labeling cost. Using supervised box geometry lifts detections to 0.413 mAP / 0.555 NDS, identifying the largest deficit as measurement precision rather than 2D detection. A camera-witness rule improves a supervised LiDAR-only detector from 0.596 to 0.630 mAP (half the gain of fully supervised camera fusion). SAM3 finds 84% of in-range objects with correctly named masks; failures are due to misnaming or geometric difficulty, not unseen classes.

Conclusion: The largest deficit in the training-free pipeline is measurement precision rather than 2D detection capability. The approach demonstrates that open-vocabulary, training-free 3D detection is feasible, with SAM3 achieving 84% coverage of in-range objects. The method shows potential for improving supervised detectors through camera fusion without any training.

Abstract: Three-dimensional object detection for autonomous driving is dominated by detectors trained on large corpora of human-annotated 3D boxes. Such a detector learns a fixed category list, and everything outside it is invisible. This paper asks whether the task can be solved training-free and open-vocabulary. A promptable segmentation model (SAM3), queried with class names as text prompts, supplies instance masks in the vehicle's six surround-view cameras, and the masks are turned into metric 3D boxes using the geometry of the scene. The core is a controlled three-stage comparison on nuScenes in which 2D detection is held fixed and only the source of 3D geometry changes. Geometry predicted from images alone reaches 0.183 mean average precision (mAP) under the official protocol; fitting boxes from raw LiDAR points inside the same masks with training-free rules reaches 0.298 mAP / 0.348 nuScenes detection score (NDS) at zero labeling cost; borrowing supervised box geometry at inference time lifts the same detections to 0.413 mAP / 0.555 NDS, which locates the pipeline's largest deficit in measurement precision rather than 2D detection, while class confusion and confidence calibration survive that substitution. Reversing the direction, a three-state camera-witness rule built from the same masks improves a supervised LiDAR-only detector from 0.596 to 0.630 mAP, roughly half the gain of fully supervised camera fusion, with no training. A coverage analysis shows that SAM3 finds 84% of in-range objects with a correctly named mask; the classes that fail in the official metric are misnamed or geometrically unforgiving, not unseen.

</details>


### [9] [SplashSplat: Reconstructing Splashing Liquids from Real-World Multi-View Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20818)
*Peiyu Liu,Dingxi Zhang,Federico Tombari,Marc Pollefeys,Christina Tsalicoglou,Daniel Barath*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first synchronized multi-view dataset of real splashing liquids and presents SplashSplat, a novel 3D reconstruction method that combines SDF-based geometry, level-set velocity transport, and Lagrangian carrier advection with differentiable Gaussian splatting for high-fidelity liquid capture and reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current liquid reconstruction research focuses on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces because real splashes are extremely challenging: they last only fractions of a second, sheets tear into ligaments and droplets, appearance is view-dependent and nearly textureless, and they don't persist long enough to track. No synchronized multi-view dataset of splashing liquids currently exists.

Method: SplashSplat is built on a single principle: impose physical structure only where observations can constrain it. The method uses: (1) Per-frame liquid SDFs fused from manually refined per-view masks for geometry, (2) Level-set transport between consecutive SDFs to yield a coarse velocity field, (3) Lagrangian carriers advected along this flow, corrected against new observations and reseeded where coverage is lost, (4) Local Gaussians decoded for differentiable rendering.

Result: SplashSplat outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting methods on real captures and synthetic benchmarks, with physically more plausible motion and lower training cost. The same representation supports temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.

Conclusion: This work provides the first real splash dataset and a novel reconstruction method that achieves state-of-the-art results by combining physical constraints with flexible Gaussian splatting, enabling applications like temporal interpolation and style transfer.

Abstract: A splash lives for a fraction of a second: sheets tear into ligaments and droplets, appearance is view-dependent and nearly textureless, and little persists long enough to track. Reconstruction research has consequently focused on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces. To our knowledge, no synchronized multi-view dataset of splashing liquids exists. We therefore introduce a benchmark of 20 real scenes, from coherent streams to violent splashes, captured by seven synchronized, calibrated 4K cameras at 60 fps, with manually refined per-view liquid and container masks and fixed evaluation splits. We further present SplashSplat, built on a single principle: impose physical structure only where the observations can constrain it. Per-frame liquid SDFs fused from the masks provide the geometry, level-set transport between consecutive SDFs yields a coarse velocity field, and Lagrangian carriers advected along this flow, corrected against each new observation and reseeded where coverage is lost, decode local Gaussians for differentiable rendering. SplashSplat outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting methods on our real captures and on a synthetic benchmark, with physically more plausible motion and a lower training cost. The same representation supports temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.

</details>


### [10] [LinePilot Digitizer: Line-Plot Recovery with Manual and Automatic Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19377)
*Fengbo Ma,Rayan Akhtar,Aakash H. Joshi,Xiaoting Li,Haijian Sun,Zhen Xiang,Xianyan Chen,Yiping Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LinePilot Digitizer is a tool for recovering numerical data from line plots, featuring three calibration modes (standard, enhanced, OCR). The authors introduce DigitizerBench, the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating digitizers, and demonstrate that LinePilot achieves state-of-the-art performance with the lowest FPC-NRMSE and highest usability across different benchmark configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recovering numerical data from line plots is challenging due to the need for accurate axis calibration and reliable curve extraction. Existing tools lack systematic evaluation, and no dedicated benchmark exists for assessing digitizer performance. This work addresses the need for standardized evaluation and improved digitization accuracy.

Method: The authors developed LinePilot Digitizer combining continuous color-based curve recovery with three calibration modes: LinePilot (standard), LinePilot (enhanced), and LinePilot (OCR). They created DigitizerBench, the first dedicated benchmark using an orthogonal design spanning signal, rendering, and plot-structure factors, with both automatic and human-guided evaluations. Performance was measured using FPC-NRMSE, which penalizes missing, unusable, or catastrophically inaccurate outputs.

Result: On DigitizerBench-Full, LinePilot (OCR) achieved the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.672) and highest trusted usability (38.2%). On DigitizerBench-Lite, LinePilot (enhanced) achieved the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.081), 100% output success, and highest trusted usability (93.3%). The orthogonal benchmark design enabled factor analysis to identify key performance-influencing factors.

Conclusion: The three calibration modes of LinePilot provide a practical trade-off between automation, user control, and accuracy within a shared curve-recovery workflow. The introduced DigitizerBench benchmark enables systematic evaluation and factor analysis of digitizer performance.

Abstract: Recovering numerical series from line plots requires accurate axis calibration and reliable curve extraction. We present LinePilot Digitizer (LinePilot), which combines continuous color-based curve recovery with three calibration modes: LinePilot (standard), LinePilot (enhanced), and LinePilot (OCR). We also introduce DigitizerBench, the first dedicated benchmark for systematically evaluating digitizer performance, using an orthogonal design spanning signal, rendering, and plot-structure factors with complementary automatic and human-guided evaluations. We evaluate performance using failure-penalized capped normalized root-mean-square error (FPC-NRMSE), which assigns unit loss to missing, unusable, or catastrophically inaccurate outputs. On DigitizerBench-Full, LinePilot (OCR) achieves the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.672) and highest trusted usability (38.2%) among the tested automatic pipelines. On DigitizerBench-Lite, LinePilot (enhanced) achieves the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.081), 100% output success, and highest trusted usability (93.3%). The orthogonal benchmark design further enables factor analysis to identify the factors that most significantly affect digitizer performance. Together, the three calibration modes provide a practical trade-off between automation, user control, and accuracy within a shared curve-recovery workflow.

</details>


### [11] [WZPlanner: Safe End-to-End Path Planning for Autonomous Driving in Work Zones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19393)
*Nishad Sahu,Changzhong Qian,Guangzhou Cai,Shounak Sural,Ragunathan,Rajkumar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WorkZonePlan is a dataset and model for autonomous vehicle navigation in work zones, featuring 149K+ synthetic and 5K+ real-world multimodal samples with 3D annotations, plus 228 evaluation routes. BoundaryFormer (BF) and BF++ are transformer-based models that jointly predict lane/work zone boundaries and driving trajectories, with BF++ achieving driving scores of 63.0 (Camera) and 64.4 (Camera+LiDAR) compared to 59.3 for SimLingo and 26.1 for TransFuser++.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Work zones alter lane geometry through temporary traffic controls absent from on-board maps, challenging AV perception and planning. Additionally, public datasets with structured geometric supervision for work zones are scarce, limiting generalization.

Method: WAVE (Work-zone-focused AV data generation in Virtual and rEal Environments) is a semi-automated pipeline for dataset creation. BoundaryFormer (BF) uses slot attention for joint boundary prediction. BF++ introduces Camera and Camera+LiDAR variants with metric ground-plane encoding, typed boundary/trajectory queries, long-range point anchors, image-space curve refinement, and conservative gated LiDAR fusion.

Result: On 211 evaluation routes, BF++-Camera achieves 63.0 Driving Score and BF++-Camera+LiDAR achieves 64.4, outperforming SimLingo (59.3) and TransFuser++ (26.1). BF++ is 40x smaller than SimLingo and 10x+ smaller than TF++.

Conclusion: Jointly predicting lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectories is a promising direction for safer AV operation in work zones. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Nishad-Sahu/WZPlanner.

Abstract: Work zones alter lane geometry through temporary traffic controls and closures that may be absent from on-board maps, challenging autonomous vehicle (AV) perception and planning. Generalization is also limited by scarce public datasets with structured geometric supervision. We present WorkZonePlan, a dataset comprising 149K+ synthetic and 5K+ real-world multimodal samples with 3D annotations for lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectory options. It also provides 76 closed-loop CARLA scenarios replayed under three weather conditions, yielding 228 Bench2Drive-format evaluation routes. We introduce WAVE (Work-zone-focused AV data generation in Virtual and rEal Environments), a semi-automated pipeline for creating the dataset, and BoundaryFormer (BF), a transformer-based model that jointly predicts lane and work zone boundary polynomials and driving trajectories. BF uses slot attention for boundary prediction. Ablations show that a separate trajectory decoder using boundary slot features substantially improves trajectory prediction over a slot-attention-only approach. Building on this finding, BF++ offers Camera and Camera+LiDAR variants with metric ground-plane encoding, typed boundary/trajectory queries, long-range point anchors, image-space curve refinement, and conservative gated LiDAR fusion. On the 211 routes common to all four models at the evaluation freeze, BF++-Camera and BF++-Camera+LiDAR achieve Driving Scores of 63.0 and 64.4, respectively, compared with 59.3 for SimLingo and 26.1 for TransFuser++ (TF++). BF++ is 40 times smaller than SimLingo and more than 10 times smaller than TF++, while achieving higher Driving Scores. These results support jointly predicting lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectories as a promising direction toward safer AV operation in work zones. Code and dataset: https://github.com/Nishad-Sahu/WZPlanner.

</details>


### [12] [RGS: Reflection-aware Gaussian Splatting via Learning Geometry Continuity for Reflective Objects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19421)
*Xiaobiao Du,Yida Wang,Cheng Bi,Kun Zhan,Xin Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Reflection-aware Gaussian Splatting (RGS), a physically-based deferred rendering framework that addresses surface collapse issues in reflective regions when using 3D Gaussian Splatting for novel view synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods suffer from surface collapse issues on reflective regions, leading to inferior geometry and low-quality specular highlights in novel view synthesis.

Method: The method incorporates two key techniques: (1) a cross-view shape consistency regularization that uses a 3D foundation model as geometric prior combined with cross-view constraints to regularize geometry surfaces, and (2) a reflection-aware densification strategy designed to capture specular variations across various views.

Result: RGS produces smoother geometric surfaces on reflective regions while reducing geometric hollows, enabling high-quality novel view rendering of reflective objects.

Conclusion: The proposed RGS framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in rendering high-quality reflective objects, demonstrating consistent improvement over existing methods.

Abstract: Gaussian Splatting has significantly improved the quality of novel view synthesis with explicit Gaussian representation. However, we observed that existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods (3DGS) often suffer from surface collapse issues on reflective regions, and thus produce inferior geometry and low-quality specular. In this work, we propose a physically-based deferred rendering framework, named Reflection-aware Gaussian Splatting (RGS), that can accurately model specular regions and improve novel view synthesis performance. Specifically, we found that a powerful 3D foundation model can provide a strong 3D geometric prior to foster correct geometric modeling. Based on this, we propose a cross-view shape consistency regularization to regularize the geometry surface with the large model prior and cross-view constraints. In this manner, our RGS can produce smoother geometric surfaces on reflective regions while reducing geometric hollows. To further improve rendering results on reflective regions, we present a reflection-aware densification strategy that is designed to capture specular variations across various views. With this strategy, our RGS is able to render novel views of objects in higher quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate our method consistently renders high-quality reflective objects, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [13] [Seeing Abnormal from Normal: Glomerular Abnormality in Representations of Normal Renal Morphology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19444)
*Greta Hasko,Rachit Saluja,Tianyu Shi,Leiyue Zhao,Yuechen Yang,Daniel Reisenbuechler,Tianyuan Yao,Zhenhao Guo,John Cannon,Haichun Yang,Yuankai Huo,Yuling Chi,Lorraine Gudas,Mert R. Sabuncu,Yihe Yang,Ruining Deng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A novel framework (NoRDeC) for detecting glomerular pathologies using one-class anomaly detection with a frozen pretrained U-Net backbone, eliminating the need for labeled abnormal examples during training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-grained glomerular pathology evaluation requires distinguishing multiple abnormality types, but supervised methods need labeled examples of all categories—impractical for rare subtypes. One-class anomaly detection offers a solution by modeling normal data and scoring deviations.

Method: NoRdeC combines Mahalanobis normal-reference scoring with layer-wise representation analysis. Uses frozen residual U-Net backbone from Omni-Seg (pretrained on normal renal primitives). Evaluates different backbone layers and aggregation strategies (Center-70). Compares with PaDiM and PatchCore. Uses centered kernel alignment (CKA) for representation analysis.

Result: Layer 4 with Center-70 aggregation achieved pooled AUROC of 0.926±0.013. NoRDeC outperformed in 6 of 7 abnormality categories and in pooled analysis. CKA revealed subtype-dependent changes in inter-layer relationships not captured by anomaly scores alone.

Conclusion: A frozen renal feature extractor can support both detection and representation-level characterization of glomerular abnormalities without training on abnormal examples, enabling detection of previously unseen pathology subtypes.

Abstract: Fine-grained evaluation of glomerular pathology must distinguish normal glomeruli from abnormalities such as global and segmental glomerulosclerosis, obsolescent, ischemic, solidified, disappearing, and atubular glomeruli. Supervised classification requires labeled examples of every category, which is impractical when subtypes are rare or absent from the training cohort. One-class anomaly detection offers an alternative by modeling normal data and scoring deviations, allowing previously unseen abnormalities to be detected. We use the frozen residual U-Net backbone of Omni-Seg, pretrained to segment structurally normal renal primitives without abnormal-subtype labels. We propose NoRDeC (Normal-Reference Detection and Characterization), a framework combining Mahalanobis normal-reference scoring with layer-wise representation analysis to determine whether and where glomerular pathology is encoded, how spatial aggregation affects detection, and whether abnormalities alter inter-layer relationships differently. Using glomerular images from two institutions, we evaluate backbone layers and aggregation strategies, compare NoRDeC with PaDiM and PatchCore, and analyze representations using centered kernel alignment (CKA). Layer 4 with Center-70 aggregation achieved a pooled AUROC of $0.926\pm0.013$. NoRDeC achieved the highest AUROC in six of seven abnormality categories and in the pooled analysis, while CKA suggested subtype-dependent changes in inter-layer relationships not captured by anomaly scores alone. The normal-reference model is fitted using only normal glomeruli; abnormality labels are used for configuration selection, evaluation, and grouping in the representation analysis. These results show that a frozen renal feature extractor can support both detection and representation-level characterization of glomerular abnormalities without using abnormal examples to fit the detector.

</details>


### [14] [Efficient Unified Multimodal Understanding (EUMU): Winning Solution for the MUMU Track at the 8th LSVOS Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19451)
*Dayoung Kil,Seong-heum Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EUMU is a winning solution for the MUMU Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge, designed to jointly perform multi-concept image tagging, open-vocabulary object detection, and image captioning in a single efficient model. It leverages a pretrained multimodal model with task-aware inference refinement where task outputs serve as cross-task cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The MUMU Challenge requires a single efficient model to jointly perform three distinct vision-language tasks: multi-concept image tagging, open-vocabulary object detection, and image captioning, while satisfying strict resource constraints.

Method: EUMU builds on a shared pretrained multimodal model, utilizing its prompt-based capabilities for detection and captioning. Lightweight prediction heads are trained on shared visual features for quality, scene, and event tagging. The key innovation is task-aware inference refinement - cross-task cues where detection outputs refine captions, caption outputs improve detection recall, and combined cues refine scene/event predictions.

Result: EUMU achieves a final challenge score of 17.3409 with 239.169M parameters, 23.947 GFLOPs, and 4.5 GB peak inference memory.

Conclusion: EUMU successfully unifies three vision-language tasks within a single efficient model through shared visual features and cross-task inference refinement, demonstrating that task interdependence can be leveraged to improve overall performance under resource constraints.

Abstract: The Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding (MUMU) Challenge requires a single efficient model to jointly perform multi-concept image tagging, open-vocabulary object detection, and image captioning. We present Efficient Unified Multimodal Understanding (EUMU), the winning solution for the MUMU Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge. EUMU builds on a shared pretrained multimodal model, using its prompt-based capabilities for detection and captioning and training lightweight heads on shared visual features to predict quality, scene, and event tags. Rather than treating the three tasks independently, EUMU applies task-aware inference refinement by reusing task outputs as cross-task cues. For detection, caption cues help recover objects missed by the initial detection. For captioning, detection cues help refine the caption to better reflect the detected objects. For tagging, image statistics refine quality predictions, while caption and detection cues refine scene and event predictions. This design unifies all three tasks within a single model while satisfying the challenge's resource constraints. EUMU contains 239.169M parameters, requires 23.947 GFLOPs, uses 4.5 GB of peak inference memory, and achieves a final challenge score of 17.3409. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Dayoung-Kil/EUMU.

</details>


### [15] [ParticleSplat: Self-supervised Object-centric Latent Particle Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19463)
*Lyuxing He,Daniel Guo,Elizabeth Terveen,Deepak Pathak,David Held,Tal Daniel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ParticleSplat is a self-supervised object-centric learning method that extends the 2D Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework to 3D by leveraging 3D Gaussian Splatting. It represents scenes as latent particles in 3D space, enabling unsupervised object mask learning and controllable 3D scene editing, with improved performance on robotic manipulation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key limitation of DLP is its inherently 2D nature, which prevents explicit 3D spatial and geometric reasoning critical for downstream tasks such as robotic manipulation. The authors exploit the structural similarity between latent particles and 3D Gaussian primitives to address this gap.

Method: The method introduces a 3D latent particle space trained with a novel view synthesis objective. It jointly encodes multiple views with camera poses into a shared 3D object-centric latent space, then transforms particles into particle-aligned 3D Gaussians whose composition reconstructs the full scene.

Result: The formulation inherently learns object masks without supervision and supports controllable 3D scene editing, such as moving objects by modifying particles in the latent space. The learned 3D representation improves downstream performance on robotic manipulation tasks.

Conclusion: ParticleSplat successfully bridges 2D object-centric learning and 3D scene understanding, enabling unsupervised object decomposition, editable 3D representations, and improved robotic manipulation capabilities.

Abstract: We present ParticleSplat, a self-supervised object-centric learning method that decomposes scenes into a set of latent ''particles'' representing semantic entities through feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, which represents images as a set of particles with attributes such as position, scale, and visual appearance, we address a key limitation of DLP: its inherently 2D nature, which prevents explicit 3D spatial and geometric reasoning that are critical for downstream tasks such as robotic manipulation. Leveraging the structural similarity between latent particles and 3D Gaussian primitives, we introduce a 3D latent particle space trained with a novel view synthesis objective. Our model jointly encodes multiple views with camera poses into a shared 3D object-centric latent space, then transforms particles into particle-aligned 3D Gaussians whose composition reconstructs the full scene. On simulated and real-world datasets, we show that this formulation inherently learns object masks without supervision and supports controllable 3D scene editing, such as moving objects by modifying particles in the latent space. We further establish that the learned 3D representation improves downstream performance on robotic manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [16] [SCOUT: Sim-to-Real Text-Based Person Retrieval by Embedding-Space Prediction over Frozen Video Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19483)
*Abdarahmane Traoré,Andy Couturier,Éric Hervet*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SCOUT uses frozen encoders (V-JEPA video, EmbeddingGemma text) with a trainable predictor for text-based person retrieval under sim-to-real gap, achieving 84.25 mAP@10 on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 with only 95 GPU-hours vs. 16 GPU-days for fine-tuned cross-encoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the sim-to-real gap in text-based person retrieval using synthetic training data and real-image gallery, while questioning whether costly fine-tuned cross-encoders are necessary. The goal is to develop a frozen-encoder system that can compete with fine-tuned approaches.

Method: 1) Trainable predictor maps patch tokens from frozen video encoder (V-JEPA) to embedding space of frozen text encoder (EmbeddingGemma) under bidirectional InfoNCE objective; 2) Training-free alignment score to rank text encoders by geometry matching; 3) ExPLoRA adaptation for parameter-efficient video encoder tuning; 4) Training-free attribute-decomposed reranker using vision-language model; 5) Local-versus-public calibration for domain transfer.

Result: 1) Training-free alignment score ranks text encoders with Spearman ρ=1.0; 2) ExPLoRA and reranker add 2.2 points R@1; 3) Full system achieves 84.25 mAP@10, single frozen model achieves 60.63; 4) Total training cost ~95 GPU-hours vs. 16 GPU-days for fine-tuned cross-encoders.

Conclusion: Frozen-encoder systems can compete with fine-tuned cross-encoders for text-based person retrieval under sim-to-real gap. The geometry matching approach effectively selects text encoders without training. Precision-targeted interventions (ExPLoRA + reranker) significantly improve top-rank precision. The local-versus-public calibration study identifies which interventions transfer to real domain.

Abstract: Text-based person retrieval under a sim-to-real gap (synthetic training data, a real-image gallery) is usually tackled with costly fine-tuned cross-encoders. We ask whether a frozen-encoder system can compete. We present SCOUT, which casts cross-modal retrieval as prediction in embedding space. A trainable predictor maps the patch tokens of a frozen video encoder into the embedding space of a frozen text encoder under a bidirectional InfoNCE objective, and no encoder is fine-tuned in the base model. The video encoder is V-JEPA, the text encoder is EmbeddingGemma, and the predictor is initialized from a Qwen3.5-0.8B decoder. We make three findings. First, the best frozen text encoder is simply the one whose geometry best matches the video features. A training-free alignment score ranks three candidate text encoders in the same order as their retrieval accuracy on our held-out split (Spearman $ρ= 1.0$); a fourth, LLM-based encoder shows the rule is metric-dependent, holding for a neighborhood-overlap score ($ρ= 0.8$) but not for a linear probe ($ρ= -0.2$). Second, two precision-targeted levers, parameter-efficient ExPLoRA adaptation of the video encoder and a training-free attribute-decomposed reranker built on a vision-language model, improve the top-rank precision that otherwise limits the frozen system, adding 2.2 points of leaderboard R@1. Third, a local-versus-public calibration study explains which interventions transfer to the real domain. On AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 the full retrieve-fuse-rerank system reaches 84.25 mAP@10 on the final leaderboard, while a single frozen model submitted alone reaches 60.63. Our trained components cost about 95 GPU-hours. CMP, the dataset authors' fine-tuned cross-encoder that trains for sixteen GPU-days, is one fusion member of the full system, not an alternative. Code and annotations: https://github.com/abtraore/SCOUT-ECCV

</details>


### [17] [AMB3R-SLAM: Kilometer-scale SLAM with Hierarchical Backend](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19518)
*Hengyi Wang,Lourdes Agapito*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AMB3R-SLAM is a real-time monocular SLAM system that reconstructs kilometer-scale trajectories over 10k frames on a single consumer-grade GPU. It uses a lightweight front-end for low-latency tracking coupled with a hierarchical backend enforcing local, mid-level, and global consistency, while naturally handling dynamic scenes without relying on the static world assumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SLAM systems rely on bundle adjustment with the static world assumption, which limits their ability to handle complex dynamic scenes. There is a need for a system that can reconstruct large-scale trajectories in real-time on consumer hardware while gracefully handling dynamic environments.

Method: AMB3R-SLAM couples a lightweight front-end for low-latency online tracking with a hierarchical backend that progressively enforces local, mid-level, and global consistency. By avoiding bundle adjustment that relies on the static world assumption, the system naturally handles dynamic scenes. The method can be extended to leverage stereo, RGB-D, and LiDAR inputs.

Result: AMB3R-SLAM achieves strong camera tracking performance across 9 datasets, reducing absolute trajectory error (ATE) of previous state-of-the-art methods on VBR and Oxford Spires by over 70%. With additional LiDAR input, the model further reduces ATE to sub-meter level on KITTI and VBR datasets.

Conclusion: AMB3R-SLAM demonstrates that real-time kilometer-scale SLAM with robust dynamic scene handling is achievable on consumer-grade GPU. The hierarchical consistency enforcement and multi-sensor fusion capabilities enable state-of-the-art tracking performance with significant accuracy improvements.

Abstract: We present AMB3R-SLAM, a real-time monocular SLAM system capable of reconstructing kilometer-scale trajectories over 10k frames on a single consumer-grade GPU. Our model couples a lightweight front-end for low-latency online tracking with a hierarchical backend that progressively enforces local, mid-level, and global consistency. By avoiding bundle adjustment that relies on the static world assumption, our system naturally handles complex dynamic scenes out of the box. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be extended to leverage stereo, RGB-D, and LiDAR as additional inputs. AMB3R-SLAM achieves strong camera tracking performance across 9 datasets, reducing the absolute trajectory error (ATE) of previous state-of-the-art methods on VBR and Oxford Spires by over 70%. With additional LiDAR input, our model further reduces ATE to sub-meter level on KITTI and VBR datasets.

</details>


### [18] [PerSeM: Persistent Semantic Memory for Long-Horizon Open-Vocabulary UAV Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19542)
*Saurbh Singh Jamwal,Ganesh Ramakrishnan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PerSeM is a training-free persistent semantic memory framework for long-horizon open-vocabulary UAV mapping that associates frame-wise semantic observations with persistent 3D voxels and refines them through majority-based voting, history-preserving spatial refinement, trust-aware replay, and context-guided verification. It achieves substantial gains in semantic correctness and temporal stability over frame-wise predictions without requiring retraining or additional neural-network inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-vocabulary segmentation enables rich semantic perception for UAVs, but frame-wise predictions can remain temporally inconsistent across repeated observations and changing viewpoints, which is a critical limitation for long-horizon UAV mapping applications.

Method: PerSeM associates frame-wise semantic observations with persistent world-space voxels and constructs a majority-based semantic memory. This memory is conservatively refined through three mechanisms: (1) history-preserving spatial refinement, (2) trust-aware replay, and (3) context-guided verification. The framework is training-free and does not require retraining or additional neural-network inference.

Result: Experiments on Forest and UAVScenes benchmarks show that persistent 3D memory provides substantial gains in semantic correctness and temporal stability over frame-wise predictions. PerSeM provides consistent additional improvements across all five evaluated UAVScenes sequences. Analysis shows these gains are concentrated in semantically difficult and temporally unstable regions where majority-based memory is most likely to remain uncertain.

Conclusion: Persistent 3D aggregation provides a strong foundation for long-horizon semantic mapping. Conservative refinement of uncertain memory states can provide additional improvements without retraining or additional neural-network inference, making it a practical approach for real-world UAV applications.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary segmentation enables rich semantic perception for UAVs, but frame-wise predictions can remain temporally inconsistent across repeated observations and changing viewpoints. We present PerSeM, a training-free persistent semantic memory framework for long-horizon open-vocabulary UAV mapping. PerSeM associates frame-wise semantic observations with persistent world-space voxels and constructs a majority-based semantic memory, which is conservatively refined through history-preserving spatial refinement, trust-aware replay, and context-guided verification. Experiments on the Forest and UAVScenes benchmarks show that persistent 3D memory provides substantial gains in semantic correctness and temporal stability over frame-wise predictions. Beyond this strong persistent-memory baseline, PerSeM provides consistent additional improvements, improving both semantic accuracy and temporal stability across all five evaluated UAVScenes sequences. Analysis using regions identified independently of the final PerSeM predictions further shows that these gains are concentrated in semantically difficult and temporally unstable regions, where majority-based memory is most likely to remain uncertain. These results demonstrate that persistent 3D aggregation provides a strong foundation for long-horizon semantic mapping, while conservative refinement of uncertain memory states can provide additional improvements without retraining or additional neural-network inference.

</details>


### [19] [A Multi-Modal Generative Model for Tomato Disease Leaves Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19555)
*Khang Nguyen Quoc,Minh-Phuoc Tran,Gia-Han Truong,Luyl-Da Quach*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SOLAR is a multimodal generative model for tomato disease analysis that formulates disease understanding as a Visual Question Answering task, supporting six diagnostic QA tasks within a single model through a Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI approaches for plant disease treat understanding as isolated prediction tasks, failing to capture complementary relationships among symptom recognition, severity assessment, and diagnostic reasoning. Practical deployment requires integrating visual symptoms with semantic context for comprehensive, explainable understanding.

Method: SOLAR uses a Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-experts to align visual features with task-aware language representations, enabling contextually relevant answer generation across diverse diagnostic tasks. It formulates tomato disease analysis as a generative VQA task, supporting multi-task inference within a single model.

Result: Evaluated on 41,677 images with 216,209 QA pairs under both closed and open-ended QA settings, SOLAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art vision-only, vision-language, and task-specific models across all tasks, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and multimodal reasoning.

Conclusion: Generative multimodal modeling represents an effective direction for plant disease understanding, with SOLAR's success highlighting the potential of this approach for precision agriculture applications.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence for plant disease analysis has advanced from task-specific classifiers to multi-modal models capable of jointly interpreting visual and textual information. However, practical deployment in precision agriculture remains limited because most existing approaches treat disease understanding as isolated prediction tasks, failing to capture the complementary relationships among symptom recognition, severity assessment, and question-driven diagnostic reasoning. In tomato pathology, accurate interpretation of diseased leaves requires more than label prediction; it demands integrating visual symptoms with semantic context to support a comprehensive and explainable understanding. Here, we present SOLAR, a multimodal generative model that understands tomato disease spanning six question-answering tasks. SOLAR learns to align visual features with task-aware language representations by Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-expert, enabling it to generate contextually relevant answers across diverse diagnostic tasks. By formulating tomato disease analysis as a generative Visual Question Answering (VQA) task, SOLAR provides a flexible framework that supports multi-task inference within a single model while improving performance and cross-task knowledge sharing. We evaluate SOLAR on $41,677$ images, including $216,209$ Question-Answering (QA) pairs to understand tomato leaf disease under both closed and open-ended QA settings. Experimental results show that SOLAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art vision-only, vision-language, and task-specific models across all tasks, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and multimodal reasoning. These findings highlight the potential of generative multimodal modeling as an effective direction for understanding of plant disease. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/EnalisUs/SOLAR.

</details>


### [20] [Selective Cotton Boll Localization for Robotic Harvesting: Evaluation of Deep Learning Vision Models Under Field Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19592)
*Thevathayarajh Thayananthan,Xin Zhang,Isuru Laddusinghe Badu,Jonathan Harjono,Glen C. Rains,Beiwen Li,Leonardo M. Bastos,Nuwan K. Wijewardane,Vitor S. Martins*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This study develops and evaluates a deep learning perception framework for selective robotic cotton picking. It compares multiple YOLO-based detection and segmentation models, as well as foundation models like SAM, on a dataset of 1,008 field images. YOLOv12-m-seg achieved the best balance of accuracy and speed for segmentation, while GELAN-s excelled in detection. The framework was validated on a real robotic system (UR5e manipulator with ZED2i camera).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robotic cotton harvesting requires accurate perception to selectively identify and pick cotton bolls. Existing methods lack the efficiency needed for real-time field deployment, necessitating evaluation of modern deep learning approaches including the latest YOLO variants and foundation models.

Method: The study evaluated: (1) Detection models: YOLOv8 through YOLOv13 families with default configurations; (2) Direct segmentation models: YOLOv8-seg, YOLOv11-seg, YOLOv12-seg, SAM, SAMv2.1, FastSAM, and Grounded-SAM with RAM; (3) Detection-prompted segmentation: using GELAN-s bounding boxes to prompt SAM variants. Evaluation included mAP, precision, recall, F1-score, AP@0.5, FPS, and R² against manual annotations. Field validation used UR5e robotic manipulator with custom end-effector and ZED2i stereo camera.

Result: Best detection: GELAN-s achieved mAP 86.1%, precision 81.6%, recall 76.6%, F1 79.0%, with 42.3ms inference. Best direct segmentation: YOLOv12-m-seg achieved AP@0.5 of 83.7% with 20.4ms inference. Detection-prompted: GELAN-s + SAMv2.1 Tiny outperformed FastSAM and Grounded-SAM with RAM. Area-based R²: YOLOv12-m-seg achieved 0.966 vs 0.860 for GELAN-s + SAMv2.1 Tiny. Field experiments validated YOLOv12-m-seg for real-time detection, segmentation, and selective picking.

Conclusion: YOLOv12-m-seg provides an efficient perception model for robotic cotton harvesting with strong potential for field deployment, offering the best balance between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. The detection-prompted approach with SAM variants shows promise but doesn't outperform direct segmentation for this task.

Abstract: This study developed and evaluated a deep-learning-based perception framework for selective robotic cotton picking. The dataset contained 1,008 annotated field images collected using three cameras under varying natural lighting and weather conditions. Object-detection models from the YOLOv8 through YOLOv13 families were evaluated using their default configurations, while segmentation performance was assessed using YOLOv8-seg, YOLOv11-seg, YOLOv12-seg, the Segment Anything Model (SAM), SAMv2.1, FastSAM, and Grounded-SAM with the Recognize Anything Model (RAM). Among the detection models, GELAN-s achieved the most favorable balance between mean average precision (mAP) and inference speed, obtaining an mAP of 86.1%, precision of 81.6%, recall of 76.6%, and an F1-score of 79.0%, with an average inference time of 42.3 ms per image. Among the direct segmentation models, YOLOv12-m-seg provided the most favorable balance between AP@0.5 and FPS, achieving a segmentation AP@0.5 of 83.7% with an inference time of 20.4 ms per image. In the detection-prompted segmentation approach, bounding-box prompts generated by GELAN-s improved the localization of cotton bolls for SAM and SAMv2.1, while SAMv2.1 Tiny consistently outperformed FastSAM and Grounded-SAM with RAM. In the area-based evaluation against manually annotated segmentation masks, YOLOv12-m-seg achieved an $R^2$ value of 0.966, compared with 0.860 for GELAN-s + SAMv2.1 Tiny. Field experiments conducted using a UR5e robotic manipulator, a custom end-effector, and a ZED2i stereo camera further validated the effectiveness of the YOLOv12-m-seg model for real-time cotton boll detection, segmentation, and selective picking under varying confidence levels. These results demonstrate that YOLOv12-m-seg provides an efficient perception model for robotic cotton harvesting and has strong potential for field deployment.

</details>


### [21] [VGGT-GS SLAM: Uncalibrated Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Feed-Forward Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19628)
*Yuhang Han,Hao Wang,Jiaxi Cao,Xingyu Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VGGT-GS SLAM is a monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system for uncalibrated videos that combines feed-forward VGGT priors with submap differentiable bundle adjustment to jointly optimize camera poses, 3D Gaussian maps, and camera intrinsics/distortion parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) in uncalibrated settings - specifically, when camera intrinsics and distortion parameters are unknown. Traditional SLAM systems assume calibrated cameras, which limits their applicability in real-world scenarios with uncalibrated video input.

Method: The system uses feed-forward VGGT (Video Gaussian Gaussian Transformer) to obtain pose and depth priors, then performs submap differentiable bundle adjustment that jointly refines camera poses and 3D Gaussian maps. It optimizes submap-shared intrinsics and radial-tangential distortion through analytic calibration Jacobians. Additionally, Gaussian-native alignment (GNA) is introduced for camera-anchored scale refinement between sequential submaps and loop-closure verification.

Result: Experiments on standard indoor benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in localization accuracy and strong rendering quality under uncalibrated settings, establishing a strong baseline for uncalibrated Gaussian SLAM.

Conclusion: VGGT-GS SLAM represents a significant advancement in uncalibrated monocular SLAM by effectively combining 3D Gaussian Splatting with learned priors and joint optimization of geometric and camera calibration parameters, achieving both improved localization and rendering quality.

Abstract: We present VGGT-GS SLAM, a monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system designed for uncalibrated videos. Starting from feed-forward VGGT pose and depth priors, our system performs submap differentiable bundle adjustment that jointly refines camera poses and a 3D Gaussian map, while optimizing submap-shared intrinsics and radial--tangential distortion through analytic calibration Jacobians. To improve global consistency, we introduce Gaussian-native alignment (GNA) for camera-anchored scale refinement between sequential submaps and verification of loop-closure candidates. Extensive experiments on standard indoor benchmarks show consistent improvements in localization accuracy and strong rendering quality under uncalibrated settings, establishing a strong baseline for uncalibrated Gaussian SLAM.

</details>


### [22] [Instance Segmentation and Fine-grained Classification for Urban Buildings with Adaptive Region Dividing and Spatially-Supervised Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19631)
*Weiyuan Zhang,Qi Zhang,Hui Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses two key challenges in urban building understanding from large-scale point clouds: 1) dependency on predefined spatial blocks for training/evaluation, and 2) lack of fine-grained classification methods for urban buildings. The authors propose an adaptive region-dividing strategy that uses BEV projection and pretrained segmentation to create structure-aligned training blocks without manual design, plus a fine-grained classification model using point transformers with spatially-supervised contrastive loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for urban building analysis rely on predefined spatial blocks, which are rarely available in real-world applications, require additional preprocessing, and fragment complete building structures. Additionally, there is a lack of methods for fine-grained classification of urban buildings beyond instance-level understanding.

Method: 1) Adaptive region-dividing strategy: Project 3D point cloud onto BEV plane → use pretrained segmentation model to detect building regions → back-project bounding boxes to construct structure-aligned adaptive training blocks. 2) Fine-grained classification: Point transformer classifier encoding body and local context using geometric, color, and core-context information → class-balanced weighted cross-entropy for class imbalance → spatially-supervised contrastive loss assigning greater weight to spatially proximate same-category buildings.

Result: Extensive experiments on UrbanBIS and STPLS3D datasets demonstrate advantages over existing SOTA methods in both building instance segmentation and fine-grained classification.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully enables adaptive region partitioning without manual design and achieves superior performance in building instance segmentation and fine-grained classification, representing a practical approach for real-world urban building analysis.

Abstract: Accurate instance-level and functional understanding of urban buildings in large-scale point clouds is essential for digital city modeling and urban analysis. However, the extensive spatial coverage of urban scenes leads most existing methods to rely on predefined blocks for training and evaluation, although such partitions are rarely available in real-world applications and introduce additional preprocessing while fragmenting complete building structures. To address this issue, we propose an adaptive region-dividing strategy with unified scene-level evaluation. Specifically, the 3D point cloud is projected onto a bird's-eye-view (BEV) plane, where a pretrained segmentation model is used to detect building regions. The detected bounding boxes are then back-projected to the original point cloud to construct structure-aligned adaptive training blocks, enabling semantically guided dynamic partitioning without manual design. Furthermore, beyond instance-level understanding, few methods have explored fine-grained classification for urban buildings, and thus we also put forward a fine-grained classification model for urban buildings with a spatially-supervised contrastive loss. First, for each segmented building, a point transformer classifier jointly encodes its body and local context using geometric, color, and core-context information. Then, the class-balanced weighted cross-entropy is used to alleviate severe class imbalance. The proposed spatially-supervised contrastive loss further enhances inter-class discriminability by assigning greater weight to spatially proximate, same-category buildings, encouraging compact functional representations while separating easily confused categories. Extensive experiments on UrbanBIS and STPLS3D demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method in building instance segmentation and fine-grained classification compared to existing SOTA methods.

</details>


### [23] [Scientific Image Quality Assessment via Multi-modal Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19634)
*Yinuo Zhang,Bingshuo Liu,Zhiying Tu,Dianhui Chu,Qingbin Liu,Xi Chen,Jiang Bian,Xiaoyan Yu,Dianbo Sui*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for scientific image quality assessment that addresses both understanding (SIQA-U) and scoring (SIQA-S) tracks by integrating multimodal indexing with multi-route retrieval and fusion mechanisms.


<details>
