  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods struggle to evaluate complex scientific images effectively. This paper aims to enhance large language models' capability to assess scientific images by providing highly relevant reference cases through a retrieval-augmented approach.

Method: The framework constructs a multimodal index combining textual semantics with fine-grained visual features, and develops a multi-route retrieval and fusion mechanism to provide LLMs with relevant reference cases for evaluation.

Result: The framework effectively aligns with human expert judgment criteria and achieves 1st place in the SIQA-U track at the ICME 2026 Grand Challenges.

Conclusion: The proposed RAG framework successfully enhances LLM performance in scientific image quality assessment, demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented approaches for complex visual evaluation tasks.

Abstract: This paper proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for scientific image quality assessment, designed to simultaneously address both the understanding track (SIQA-U) and the scoring track (SIQA-S) of the SIQA challenge. We construct a multimodal index that integrates textual semantics with fine-grained visual features, and develop a multi-route retrieval and fusion mechanism to provide large language models with highly relevant reference cases, thereby enhancing their capability to evaluate complex scientific images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively aligns with the judgment criteria of human experts. Ultimately, our method achieves 1st place in the SIQA-U track of the SIQA challenge at the ICME 2026 Grand Challenges.

</details>


### [24] [Towards Active Cross-View Object Geo-Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19662)
*Shunyu Yao,Xiaohan Zhang,Zhuoran Yang,Haoqi Lai,Qi Ming,Xiaoxi Hu,Hui-Liang Shen,Si-Yuan Cao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ActiveGeo addresses the limitation of traditional cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) by enabling mobile agents to actively select viewpoints and determine when to stop, improving localization with minimal observations. The proposed ActiveMoPT framework uses three-stage training: Multi-View Prompt-Preserving Adaptation, Trajectory-Guided Policy Initialization, and Cost-Aware Policy Refinement. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV and zero-shot evaluation on ActiveGeo-858.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional CVOGL assumes a fixed query image, ignoring the ability of mobile agents to actively acquire more informative observations. This limitation prevents systems from optimizing viewpoint selection to improve localization accuracy while minimizing observation costs. The motivation is to develop an active framework where agents can sequentially select new viewpoints and determine when to stop, balancing localization accuracy with observation efficiency.

Method: The ActiveMoPT framework employs a three-stage training approach: (1) Multi-View Prompt-Preserving Adaptation enables the model to aggregate multiple query views while reusing the initial prompt; (2) Trajectory-Guided Policy Initialization uses supervised agent trajectories to learn viewpoint selection and initial stopping behavior; (3) Cost-Aware Policy Refinement employs GRPO (Gradient-based Reinforcement Policy Optimization) with a gain-cost reward to jointly optimize localization accuracy and observation efficiency.

Result: ActiveMoPT achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV using only 1.45 query views on average, substantially outperforming previous CVOGL approaches under zero-shot evaluation on ActiveGeo-858 (containing 858 scenes and 1,716 target annotations).

Conclusion: The ActiveGeo paradigm and ActiveMoPT framework successfully address the limitation of passive CVOGL by enabling active viewpoint selection. The three-stage training approach effectively balances localization accuracy with observation efficiency, achieving superior performance with minimal queries. The introduced ActiveGeo-858 dataset provides a valuable benchmark for zero-shot evaluation in active cross-view object geo-localization.

Abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) typically assumes a fixed query image, overlooking the ability of mobile agents to actively acquire more informative observations. To address this limitation, we introduce Active Cross-View Object Geo-Localization (ActiveGeo), where an agent sequentially selects new viewpoints and determines when to stop, aiming to improve localization with minimal observations. We further propose ActiveMoPT, an ActiveGeo framework with three-stage training. First, Multi-View Prompt-Preserving Adaptation enables the model to aggregate multiple query views while reusing the initial prompt. Second, Trajectory-Guided Policy Initialization uses supervised agent trajectories to learn viewpoint selection and initial stopping behavior. Third, Cost-Aware Policy Refinement employs GRPO with a gain-cost reward to jointly optimize localization accuracy and observation efficiency. We also construct ActiveGeo-858, a zero-shot test set containing 858 scenes and 1,716 target annotations. Experiments show that ActiveMoPT achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV using only 1.45 query views on average, and substantially outperforms previous CVOGL approaches under zero-shot evaluation on ActiveGeo-858.

</details>


### [25] [VideoResearcher: Self-Improving Tool Design for Long-Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19664)
*Dingqiang Ye,Dongdi Zhao,Kaishen Wang,Qingqiao Hu,Jingchen Sun,Yijun Liang,Yuqi Jia,Yiqiao Huang,Yunjie Tian,Jiaxing Zhang,Chuanyang Jin,Ke Zhang,Vishal M. Patel,Di Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VideoResearcher is a training-free multi-agent framework that autonomously designs, tests, and refines tools for long-video understanding, eliminating the need for costly manual engineering. It uses dual Solving and Evolving loops to iteratively improve tool capabilities without updating model parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video-agent systems require expensive manual design and trial-and-error. Existing self-improvement methods either refine low-impact prompts, recombine predefined micro-tools, or struggle with convergence in harness optimization. There is a need for a high-impact, training-free approach that can autonomously develop and refine tools for video understanding.

Method: VideoResearcher operates through dual Solving and Evolving loops: (1) analyzes tool-use trajectories to identify capability gaps, (2) coordinates specialized agents to develop and validate executable tools, and (3) reuses evolved tools to strengthen evidence acquisition in subsequent video reasoning. The system iteratively refines and validates tools without updating model parameters.

Result: VideoResearcher achieves state-of-the-art performance among self-improving agents and approaches the human-designed upper bound, demonstrating a training-free paradigm for long-video understanding that expands agent capabilities through autonomous tool development while reducing costly manual engineering.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully enables autonomous tool development for video understanding without training. It bridges the gap between self-improving agents and human-designed systems, offering a promising direction for reducing manual engineering costs while maintaining high performance in long-video understanding tasks.

Abstract: Video agents have made substantial progress in long-video understanding. Yet effective video-agent systems require costly, time-consuming manual design and trial and error. Current self-improvement methods either refine low-impact prompts, recombine predefined micro-tools, or struggle with convergence in harness optimization. To bridge this gap, we target high-impact video-tool with VideoResearcher, a training-free multi-agent framework that autonomously designs, tests, and refines tools for video understanding, like a human researcher. VideoResearcher operates through dual Solving and Evolving loops: it analyzes tool-use trajectories to identify capability gaps, coordinates specialized agents to develop and validate executable tools, and reuses evolved tools to strengthen evidence acquisition in subsequent video reasoning. Through iterative tool refinement and validation, it progressively strengthens evidence acquisition without updating model parameters. VideoResearcher achieves state-of-the-art performance among self-improving agents and approaches the human-designed upper bound, demonstrating a training-free paradigm for long-video understanding that expands agent capabilities through autonomous tool development while reducing costly manual engineering.

</details>


### [26] [Beyond Patch Removal: Persistent Adversarial Effects in Vision-Language-Action Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19669)
*Enhao Wu,Fusen Guo,Yuxin Cao,Ziyang Lyu,Lin Li,Wei Song*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a state-restoration protocol to separate and measure persistent effects of adversarial patches on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies after patch removal, demonstrating that only 36.2% of episodes remain recoverable compared to 87-90% in control conditions, and that a recovery adapter can improve recovery but requires timely intervention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of adversarial attacks on VLA policies focus on continuous attacks and fail to separate immediate action corruption from persistent state effects that remain after the patch is removed. This gap limits understanding of the true long-term impact of adversarial patches on robotic control systems.

Method: The authors introduce a state-restoration protocol that removes the adversarial patch at matched action-chunk boundaries and measures subsequent recoverability under the same remaining step budget. They use four control conditions: clean (no patch), random-patch, deviation-matched, and fixed-direction controls to distinguish adversarial effects from occlusion, action-error magnitude, and directional persistence. They also evaluate a recovery adapter trained on attack-induced states under controlled intervention latency.

Result: On OpenVLA-OFT with EDPA attacks, only 36.2% of LIBERO-Long episodes remain recoverable after five chunks, compared with 89.9% and 87.0% for the deviation-matched and fixed-direction controls. Similar persistent effects are observed on autoregressive OpenVLA. The recovery adapter improves recovery from 7.7% to 47.4% at one-chunk latency, but its benefit decreases substantially with delayed intervention.

Conclusion: Adversarial effects on VLA policies can persist significantly after patch removal, and timely intervention is critical for successful recovery. The persistent effects are distinct from control conditions, demonstrating a unique characteristic of adversarial attacks that goes beyond simple occlusion or action errors.

Abstract: Adversarial patches to Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies can cause both immediate action corruption and persistent state effects that remain after the patch is removed. Existing evaluations largely focus on continuous attacks and do not separate these two effects. We introduce a state-restoration protocol that removes the patch at matched action-chunk boundaries and measures subsequent recoverability under the same remaining step budget. Clean, random-patch, deviation-matched, and fixed-direction controls distinguish adversarial effects from occlusion, action-error magnitude, and directional persistence. We also evaluate a recovery adapter trained on attack-induced states under controlled intervention latency. On OpenVLA-OFT with EDPA attacks, only 36.2% of LIBERO-Long episodes remain recoverable after five chunks, compared with 89.9% and 87.0% for the deviation-matched and fixed-direction controls. Similar persistent effects are observed on autoregressive OpenVLA. The recovery adapter improves recovery from 7.7% to 47.4% at one-chunk latency, but its benefit decreases substantially with delayed intervention. These results show that adversarial effects can persist after patch removal and that timely intervention is critical for recovery.

</details>


### [27] [IMFD: End-to-end Multi-Face Forgery Detection through Instruction-based Large Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19693)
*Dasom Choi,Sangjun Moon,Hyeongchan Im,Jaeeon Park,Jingun Kwon,Hidetaka Kamigaito,Taro Watanabe,Manabu Okumura*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: IMFD is an instruction-based multi-face forgery detector that leverages LVLMs to jointly localize faces and predict forgery labels in a single-stage end-to-end framework. It integrates predicted face bounding boxes into instructions as visual cues to enhance detection performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional multi-face forgery detectors process each face independently, ignoring background context and inter-face relationships, leading to suboptimal performance. The rise of deepfakes on social media necessitates more effective detection methods.

Method: 1) Single-stage end-to-end framework using instruction-based LVLMs
2) Joint face localization and per-face forgery prediction
3) Integrate predicted face bounding boxes into instructions as visual cues for enhanced instruction grounding
4) Convert existing multi-face forgery datasets to instruction-based format for training and evaluation

Result: IMFD improves multi-face forgery detection by integrating face bounding boxes into instructions and consistently outperforms various state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: The proposed IMFD demonstrates that incorporating face bounding boxes as visual cues in instructions significantly enhances multi-face forgery detection, achieving superior performance over existing methods.

Abstract: The rapid increase of deepfakes has raised significant concerns due to their spread on social media. Traditional multi-face forgery detectors crop and verify each face independently, ignoring background context and inter-face relationships, which often yields suboptimal performance. To overcome these limitations, we leverage instruction-based Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), which can interpret entire images and follow complex textual instructions. We propose a simple yet effective single-stage multi-face forgery detector, called IMFD (Instruction-based Multi-face Forgery Detector), which is trained end-to-end to jointly localize faces and predict per-face forgery labels. Rather than treating face box prediction only as a joint objective, IMFD explicitly integrates predicted face bounding boxes into the instruction as visual cues that enhance instruction grounding and forgery detection. To support the training and evaluation of IMFD, we convert existing multi-face forgery datasets into an instruction-based format. Experimental results and analyses show that IMFD improves multi-face forgery detection by integrating face bounding boxes into the instruction, and consistently outperforms various state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [28] [Understanding and Exploiting Diagonal Attention Sparsity in Autoregressive Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19702)
*Daeun Kim,Junwha Hong,Changhun Oh,Yoonsung Kim,Yoonhyeong Lee,Jongse Park*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first systematic study of attention sparsity in autoregressive image generation, identifying unique properties like prefill-decode asymmetry and diagonal attention patterns. Based on these findings, a diagonal-aware sparse attention mechanism is proposed, achieving up to 3.1x throughput improvement with less than 2% quality degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive image generation faces decoding bottlenecks due to thousands of visual tokens requiring KV cache accesses during attention computation. While sparse attention works well for text-based LLMs, it was unclear whether its assumptions generalize to image generation workloads.

Method: The authors conducted systematic characterization of attention sparsity across diverse workloads and open-source models. They proposed a diagonal-aware sparse attention mechanism that selectively skips KV entries along the diagonal attention direction within a recent window. Implementation used FlexGen, FlashAttention-2, and custom kernels on GPU.

Result: The approach achieves up to 3.1x throughput improvement and 1.19x latency improvement with less than 2% quality degradation compared to dense inference.

Conclusion: The study reveals that attention sparsity in autoregressive image generation has distinct characteristics (prefill-decode asymmetry, concentration on prompt/local tokens, diagonal sparsity pattern) that differ from text-based LLM inference. The proposed diagonal-aware sparse attention effectively exploits these patterns to achieve significant efficiency gains while maintaining acceptable quality.

Abstract: Autoregressive image generation has emerged as a paradigm for multimodal AI systems due to its compatibility with transformer-based LLM serving infrastructures. However, generating thousands of visual tokens per request makes decoding increasingly bottlenecked by KV cache accesses during attention computation. Sparse attention is particularly attractive for this workload because many visual generation applications tolerate moderate quality degradation in exchange for improved performance and efficiency. While sparse attention has been extensively explored for text-based LLM inference, it remains unclear whether its sparsity assumptions generalize effectively to autoregressive image generation. We present the first systematic characterization of attention sparsity in autoregressive image generation across diverse workloads and representative open-source models. Our analysis reveals several distinguishing properties, including a pronounced prefill-decode asymmetry, strong attention concentration on prompt and local tokens, and a unique diagonal attention sparsity pattern arising from the spatial locality of visual tokens. Motivated by these observations, we propose a diagonal-aware sparse attention mechanism that selectively skips KV entries along the diagonal attention direction within a recent window. Implemented on top of a GPU-based serving system using FlexGen, FlashAttention-2, and custom kernels, our approach achieves up to 3.1x throughput and 1.19x latency improvements with less than 2% quality degradation compared to dense inference.

</details>


### [29] [GAPrompt++: Multi-Granular Geometry-Aware Point Cloud Prompt for 3D Vision Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19716)
*Zixiang Ai,Zhenyu Cui,Yufei Guo,Wenwen Qiang,Lei Chen,Jiwen Lu,Jiahuan Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GAPrompt++ introduces a multi-granular geometry-aware prompting method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained 3D vision models on point cloud analysis tasks. It addresses the limitation of existing prompting methods that ignore geometric structures by proposing three key components: Point Shift Prompter, Keypoint Prompter, and Prompt Propagation mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained 3D vision models are effective for point cloud analysis but full fine-tuning is computationally expensive and storage-intensive. While Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) offers a solution, existing prompting-based approaches ignore the intrinsic geometric structures of point clouds, limiting their adaptation capability. These methods fail to encode both fine-grained geometric cues and coarse-grained structural semantics, and cannot propagate such information effectively through the model hierarchy.

Method: The proposed GAPrompt++ includes three components: (1) Point Shift Prompter that extracts multi-granular geometric features across different scales for instance-specific geometric adjustments; (2) Keypoint Prompter that adaptively generates point-level prompts to highlight local geometric saliency and fine-grained structural details; (3) Prompt Propagation mechanism that injects multi-granular geometric cues throughout the feature extraction hierarchy. Additionally, two new challenging benchmarks were constructed from 3D Gaussian Splatting and Multi-View Stereo reconstruction.

Result: GAPrompt++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among prompting-based PEFT methods and even surpasses full fine-tuning across diverse benchmarks, while requiring less than 2% trainable parameters.

Conclusion: The multi-granular geometry-aware prompting approach effectively addresses the limitation of existing PEFT methods by incorporating geometric structure awareness. The success demonstrates that encoding geometric information at multiple granularities is crucial for efficient 3D task adaptation. The introduced benchmarks provide diverse and realistic point cloud scenarios for future research.

Abstract: Pre-trained 3D vision models have substantially advanced point cloud analysis, yet adapting them to downstream tasks via full fine-tuning is computationally expensive and storage-intensive. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) offers a promising alternative by reducing both adaptation cost and storage burden. However, existing prompting-based approaches ignore the intrinsic geometric structures of point clouds, thereby limiting their adaptation capability. This limitation stems from their inability to encode both fine-grained geometric cues and coarse-grained structural semantics, as well as failing to propagate such information effectively through the model hierarchy. To address these challenges, we propose GAPrompt++, a multi-granular geometry-aware prompting method that provides richer geometric guidance for efficient 3D task adaptation. Specifically, we introduce a Point Shift Prompter that extracts multi-granular geometric features across different scales, enabling instance-specific geometric adjustments during adaptation. Next, a Keypoint Prompter adaptively generates point-level prompts to highlight local geometric saliency and fine-grained structural details. Furthermore, a Prompt Propagation mechanism injects these multi-granular geometric cues throughout the feature extraction hierarchy, strengthening the ability to capture essential geometric characteristics. Extensive experiments show that GAPrompt++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among prompting-based PEFT methods and even surpasses full fine-tuning across diverse benchmarks, while requiring less than 2\% trainable parameters. In addition, to address the saturation of existing evaluation datasets, we construct two more challenging benchmarks derived from 3D Gaussian Splatting and Multi-View Stereo reconstruction, offering diverse and realistic point cloud scenarios to promote future research.

</details>


### [30] [SeetaPsych v1.0: An Open-source Computer Vision Toolkit for Behavior-based Psychological Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19719)
*Jiabei Zeng,Chiqin Li,Kaizhou Li,Fei Chang,Yong Li,Yuanhao Zhao,Dan Han,Wenqiang Yang,Xilin Chen,Shiguang Shan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SeetaPsych v1.0 is an open-source, unified computer vision toolkit for behavior-based psychological measurement from facial images and videos. It provides four core modules (emotion analysis, heart rate estimation, gaze estimation, scene gaze following) and auxiliary preprocessing tools, with a modular Pipeline/Runner architecture and Python APIs plus WebUI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing technological modules for visual behavior analysis are scattered across task-specific systems with heterogeneous interfaces and disparate deployment requirements, creating a need for a unified, extensible toolkit.

Method: The paper presents SeetaPsych v1.0, featuring: (1) Four core modules for face-based emotion analysis (simultaneous expression recognition, action unit detection, valence-arousal estimation), camera-based heart rate estimation, screen point-of-gaze estimation, and scene gaze following; (2) Auxiliary preprocessing modules for face detection, facial landmark detection, and head detection; (3) A modular Pipeline/Runner architecture with automatic attribute dependency resolution, computation graph construction, and intermediate result sharing; (4) Standardized Python APIs and an interactive WebUI.

Result: SeetaPsych provides an integrated platform with standardized Python APIs for reproducible, large-scale analyses and an interactive WebUI for code-free method evaluation.

Conclusion: SeetaPsych offers an integrated and accessible visual measurement platform for research in psychology, behavioral science, human-computer interaction, and related fields.

Abstract: Automated visual analysis opens new avenues for behavior--based psychological measurement. Nevertheless, existing technological modules are typically scattered across task specific systems with heterogeneous interfaces and disparate deployment requirements. In this work, we present SeetaPsych v1.0, an open source, unified and extensible computer vision toolkit designed to extract psychologically relevant signals from facial images and/or face based videos. The current release encompasses four major core modules aiming at behavior--based physiological perception: unified face based emotion analysis (simultaneous facial expression recognition, facial action unit detection, and valence--arousal estimation), camera based heart rate estimation, screen point--of--gaze estimation, and scene gaze following. A suite of auxiliary preprocessing modules for human centric visual analysis is also included, comprising face detection, facial landmark detection, and head detection. These functionalities are encapsulated within a modular Pipeline/Runner architecture that automatically resolves attribute dependencies, constructs computation graphs, and support intermediate result sharing among modules. SeetaPsych provides standardized Python APIs to facilitate reproducible, large scale analyses, alongside an interactive WebUI for rapid, code--free method evaluation. Overall, SeetaPsych offers an integrated and accessible visual measurement platform for research in psychology, behavioral science, human computer interaction, and related fields.

</details>


### [31] [Recency Forcing: Bridging the Long-Horizon Gap in Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19729)
*Tri Cao,Hung Nguyen,Phong Nguyen,Khoi Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses a train-inference discrepancy in autoregressive video generation called "KV eviction mismatch" - where models train on short clips with all context in KV cache, but at inference, memory constraints force distant frames to be evicted. The authors propose Recency Forcing, which progressively reduces the influence of distant frames rather than discarding them, using a Temporal Response Bias (TRB) derived from a positional sensitivity measure R(Δ, t_denoise). They also introduce Biased Attention Reparameterization (BAR) for zero-overhead implementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive video generation degrades over long horizons due to KV eviction mismatch - a train-inference discrepancy where models train on short clips with all context in KV cache, but at inference, memory constraints force distant frames to be evicted, removing context the model was conditioned on. Existing solutions like context truncation discard temporal information needed for motion coherence.

Method: The authors introduce the positional response R(Δ, t_denoise), a perturbation-based sensitivity measure that reveals context influence decays with temporal distance and varies across denoising steps. Based on this analysis, they propose Recency Forcing with two components: (1) Temporal Response Bias (TRB) - a non-positive, timestep-dependent bias on pre-softmax attention logits derived from R; (2) Biased Attention Reparameterization (BAR) - an exact reformulation that moves the bias outside softmax, enabling standard FlashAttention implementation at zero overhead. The method works in both training-free and training-based modes.

Result: Experiments on VBench and VBench-Long demonstrate state-of-the-art long-horizon generation quality at no additional inference cost.

Conclusion: Recency Forcing effectively closes the train-inference gap in autoregressive video generation without modifying context length or training objectives. The method achieves superior long-horizon generation quality while maintaining computational efficiency through BAR's efficient implementation.

Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation degrades over long horizons due to an overlooked train-inference discrepancy we term KV eviction mismatch: models train on short clips where all context frames reside in the KV cache, but at inference, memory constraints force distant frames to be evicted from the KV cache - removing context the model was conditioned on. Rather than simulating eviction via context truncation - which discards temporal information the model still needs and degrades motion coherence - we keep the context but while progressively reducing the influence of distant frames, making their eventual eviction negligible. To guide this design, we introduce the positional response $R( Δ, \, t_{\text{denoise}})$, a perturbation-based sensitivity measure revealing that context influence decays steeply with temporal distance and varies systematically across denoising steps. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Recency Forcing, which applies a non-positive, timestep-dependent bias, termed Temporal Response Bias (TRB), on pre-softmax attention logits derived directly from $R$, closing the train-inference gap without modifying context length or training objectives. We further introduce Biased Attention Reparameterization (BAR), an exact reformulation that moves the bias outside the softmax, making TRB a standard FlashAttention call at zero overhead. Recency Forcing operates in both training-free mode and training-based mode. Experiments on VBench and VBench-Long demonstrate state-of-the-art long-horizon generation quality at no additional inference cost.

</details>


### [32] [Federated Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Kidney Stone Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19740)
*Najiyya Younas,Omar Abdulkader,Yaser Ali Shah,Muhammad Jawad Ikram,Jebran Khan,Amaad Khalil*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This research proposes a Federated Learning (FL) framework combined with an optimized YOLOv8 network for privacy-preserving kidney stone detection in CT images. The model achieves mAP@50 of 0.733 while maintaining data confidentiality and enabling real-time edge deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional deep learning for medical image diagnosis relies on centralized data storage, which poses severe threats to patient privacy and medical data security. This approach risks violating data protection regulations like GDPR and HIPAA.

Method: The proposed system integrates Federated Learning with an optimized YOLOv8 network. Architectural improvements include residual feature fusion and DropBlock regularization to enhance detection robustness and minimize overfitting. The federated approach allows multiple medical organizations to jointly train a model without sharing patient data.

Result: Experimental analysis on a distributed CT dataset demonstrated that the federated YOLOv8 model achieves a mAP@50 of 0.733 while preserving data confidentiality. The lean design facilitates fast edge deployment and real-time inference across clinical settings.

Conclusion: Federated Learning combined with sophisticated object detection models like YOLOv8 provides a safe and efficient solution for AI-assisted diagnosis in contemporary healthcare, enabling collaborative model training while maintaining patient privacy and complying with GDPR and HIPAA regulations.

Abstract: Recent innovations in deep learning have significantly enhanced the diagnosis of medical images, although they are based on the use of centralized data storage that pose severe threats to patient privacy and medical data security. To address this issue, this research proposes a Federated Learning (FL) model that is coupled with an optimized YOLOv8 network to detect the kidney stones on a computed tomography (CT) image and at the same time, protect privacy of the patients. The suggested system can help various medical organizations to jointly train a common model without exchanging the information about the patients. This is to ensure that data protection laws like GDPR and HIPAA are adhered to. The residual feature fusion and DropBlock regularization among other architectural improvements are also included in YOLOv8 to enhance detection robustness and minimize overfitting. Experimental analysis carried out on a distributed CT dataset demonstrated that the federated YOLOv8 model has a mAP at 50 of 0.733 and is able to keep the data confidential. Moreover, its lean design facilitates fast edge deployment and real-time inference across a clinical setting. Altogether, these findings indicate that Federated Learning is a safe and efficient solution to AI-assisted diagnosis in contemporary healthcare when combined with the use of sophisticated object detection models.

</details>


### [33] [Region-Level Policy Optimization for Fine-grained MLLM Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19745)
*Yuheng Shi,Xiaohuan Pei,Minjing Dong,Chang Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Vision-RL2, a method to improve fine-grained visual perception in Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by decoupling localization from recognition using different resolution levels. It uses region-level reinforcement learning to optimize a lightweight proposal network, enabling sparse encoding that focuses on visual evidence while reducing token costs by approximately 4x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs is improved by raising resolution, but this inflates vision-encoding and language-model prefilling costs. The authors observe that localization and recognition have different resolution requirements - localization tolerates 3-4x stronger token compression than recognition.

Method: The method localizes from a coarse view and concentrates resolution on selected evidence. A lightweight proposal network distilled from the model's attention is optimized using region-level reinforcement learning (Vision-RL2). It treats coherent regions as actions, and a frozen MLLM reader scores each region by how its removal changes answer likelihood. Complementary subtractive and additive objectives suppress distracting proposals and recover missing evidence. The refined proposal enables sparse encoding that magnifies evidence and excludes background tokens.

Result: Across six fine-grained benchmarks and four MLLM backbones, Vision-RL2 improves accuracy over the base model at every token budget and surpasses its largest-budget accuracy with about 4 times fewer visual tokens.

Conclusion: Vision-RL2 successfully decouples localization and recognition with different resolution requirements, using reinforcement learning to train a proposal network without region annotations, response sampling, or reasoning trajectories. This achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced computational costs.

Abstract: Fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs is commonly improved by raising the resolution, but the added visual tokens inflate vision-encoding and language-model prefilling costs. We show that the two operations underlying fine-grained perception, localizing the region of interest (RoI) and recognizing its content, have different resolution requirements. In a controlled diagnostic, localization tolerates roughly 3 to 4 times stronger token compression than recognition, which motivates localizing from a coarse view and concentrating resolution on the selected evidence. Decoding coordinates with the MLLM can be trained end-to-end from answers, but costs a full model pass per query and depends on grounding ability. A lightweight proposal network distilled from the model's attention is fast, but inherits the noise of its attention targets. The RoI from the proposal network reaches the answer through a discrete region choice, so its faithfulness to the answer cannot supervise the network. We therefore optimize the proposal network with region-level reinforcement learning, which we call Vision-RL2. It treats coherent regions as actions, and a frozen MLLM reader scores each one by how its removal changes the answer likelihood. Complementary subtractive and additive objectives suppress distracting proposals and recover missing evidence, updating only the predictor without region annotations, response sampling, or reasoning trajectories. The refined proposal further enables a sparse encoding that magnifies evidence and excludes background tokens. Across six fine-grained benchmarks and four MLLM backbones, Vision-RL2 improves accuracy over the base model at every token budget and surpasses its largest-budget accuracy with about 4 times fewer visual tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/YuHengsss/VisionRL2 .

</details>


### [34] [STAR: Structure-aware Test-time Adaptation for diffusion-based light field Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19747)
*Wontae Choi,Ki Ryum Moon,Jae Young Lee,Hyung Sup Yun,Il Yong Chun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STAR is the first test-time adaptation framework for reconstructing light fields from focal stack measurements. It uses three lightweight adapters to adapt a pre-trained diffusion prior to the spatial-angular structure of each test light field, without modifying the core model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is highly ill-posed due to limited and noisy focal stack measurements. Additionally, light field spatial-angular structure varies across scenes, so a fixed pre-trained prior cannot optimally capture the structure of each test light field.

Method: The method freezes a pre-trained diffusion prior and fits three lightweight adapters to the observed focal stack. These adapters jointly adapt three components of the light field's spatial-angular structure: within-view spatial details, cross-view angular dependencies, and disparity across views.

Result: STAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both two- and three-focal-sheet settings.

Conclusion: STAR achieves superior performance while maintaining shorter inference times compared to methods that involve test-time parameter updates.

Abstract: Light field (LF) reconstruction from limited and noisy focal stack (FS) measurements is a highly ill-posed inverse problem. Although the LF-to-FS imaging geometry is fixed for a given optical setup, LF spatial-angular structure---including within-view spatial details, cross-view angular dependencies, and disparity across views---varies across scenes. Consequently, a fixed pre-trained prior may not optimally capture the spatial-angular structure of each test LF. We propose Structure-aware Test-time Adaptation for diffusion-based light field Reconstruction (STAR), the first test-time adaptation framework for reconstructing an LF from FS. For each test LF, STAR freezes a pre-trained diffusion prior and fits three lightweight adapters to the observed FS to jointly adapt the three components of the LF's spatial-angular structure. STAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both two- and three-focal-sheet settings, with shorter inference times than those with test-time parameter updates.

</details>


### [35] [Benchmarking MLLMs via Cognitive Expected Scene Graph for Safety-Critical Visual Negation Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19767)
*Zhiyun Jiang,Hanyong Wang,Binbin Liang,Yu Xie,Menglong Yang,Wei Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of visual negation understanding in Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Current models suffer from affirmation bias and fail to comprehend negative semantics. The authors propose SNUS (Scene Negation Understanding under Safety Cognition), a task focused on safety as a cognitive dimension, along with a negative caption dataset and CESG Score evaluation metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: True machine intelligence requires understanding visual negation (top-down functional reasoning over absent information), but existing MLLMs and evaluation metrics fail under negative semantics due to pervasive affirmation bias. Visual negation paradigms remain overly open-ended, necessitating a systematic approach.

Method: 1) Define SNUS task by anchoring negation reasoning within safety cognition (a pragmatic critical cognitive dimension)
2) Construct a high-fidelity negative caption dataset mapping dense assertions of localized hazards
3) Propose CESG Score (Cognitive Expected Scene Graph), a structure-grounded, polarity-aware evaluation metric

Result: Current models struggle significantly on SNUS task, while traditional metrics completely collapse under semantic reversals. The proposed framework provides a solid benchmark for SNUS, offering a rigorous foundation for advancing risk-aware situational comprehension and counterfactual cognition.

Conclusion: The paper introduces a systematic framework (SNUS + dataset + CESG metric) that establishes a rigorous benchmark for visual negation understanding in safety cognition. This work addresses the critical gap in MLLM capability for understanding negative semantics and provides a foundation for advancing risk-aware situational comprehension and counterfactual reasoning in machine intelligence.

Abstract: True machine intelligence requires transcending passive pixel registration to master top-down functional reasoning over absent information via visual negation understanding. However, unconstrained visual negation paradigms remain overly open-ended, and pervasive affirmation bias causes both existing Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and evaluation metrics to fail under negative semantics. To solve these intertwined challenges systematically, we first anchor the boundaries of negation reasoning within specific cognitive goals. Specifically, by focusing on safety as a highly pragmatic and critical cognitive dimension, we define the task of \textbf{S}cene \textbf{N}egation \textbf{U}nderstanding under \textbf{S}afety Cognition (\textbf{SNUS}). Under this framework, we construct a high-fidelity negative caption dataset mapping dense assertions of localized hazards. Concurrently, we propose the Cognitive Expected Scene Graph (CESG) Score, a structure-grounded, polarity-aware evaluation metric. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current models struggle on the task, traditional metrics completely collapse under semantic reversals. Conversely, our framework delivers a solid benchmark for SNUS, providing a rigorous foundation to advance risk-aware situational comprehension and counterfactual cognition.

</details>


### [36] [AI Smart Glasses for Wearable Intelligence: From Egocentric Sensing to Agentic Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19793)
*Xu Yuan,Yi Wang,Zhuohang Jiang,Haohao Qu,Yujuan Ding,Shanru Lin,Guoliang Xing,Hongxia Yang,Jiannong Cao,Qing Li,Wenqi Fan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This survey examines AI smart glasses as wearable intelligence platforms that transform egocentric capture devices into personalized assistance systems. The paper organizes research around four dimensions: hardware foundations, wearable intelligence, interaction design, and application scenarios. Five future research challenges are identified: next-generation hardware, trustworthy egocentric intelligence, lifelong personalized memory, proactive intelligence, and embodied foundation models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the transition of smart glasses from simple egocentric capture and display devices to comprehensive wearable AI systems. The authors aim to provide a unified framework for organizing the diverse technologies, applications, and challenges in this emerging field, recognizing that smart glasses increasingly serve as platforms connecting first-person observation with real-time assistance under strict form-factor constraints.

Method: This is a survey paper that organizes the analysis around four connected dimensions: (1) hardware foundation - examining sensing, computation, feedback delivery, and sustained deployment; (2) wearable intelligence - studying how egocentric signals are transformed into perceptual, contextual, and agentic capabilities; (3) interaction design - discussing how users request, receive, correct, and regulate assistance; (4) application scenarios - analyzing healthcare, accessibility, situated learning, daily life assistance, cultural tourism, and industrial support domains.

Result: The paper presents a comprehensive survey organizing the landscape of AI smart glasses research into a unified framework. It identifies five cross-cutting research challenges for future work: next-generation hardware, trustworthy egocentric intelligence, lifelong personalized memory, proactive intelligence, and embodied foundation models.

Conclusion: The conclusion positions AI smart glasses as wearable-intelligence platforms and provides a unified framework for organizing technologies, applications, and open challenges in this emerging area. The survey aims to guide future research by systematically addressing the identified challenges across the four dimensions and five cross-cutting research areas.

Abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping smart glasses from egocentric capture and display devices into platforms for wearable intelligence. Smart glasses increasingly serve as wearable AI systems that connect first-person observation with real-time assistance under strict form-factor constraints. We frame this transition through the lens of \emph{AI smart glasses} and define them as a system-level concept in which egocentric sensing, resource-aware computing, intelligent reasoning, multimodal interaction, and real-world application constraints are co-designed for personalized assistance in the physical world. To systematically study this perspective, we organize the survey around four connected dimensions. First, we examine the hardware foundation that bounds sensing, computation, feedback delivery, and sustained deployment. Second, we study wearable intelligence, where egocentric signals are transformed into perceptual, contextual, and agentic capabilities. Third, we discuss interaction design, through which users request, receive, correct, and regulate assistance during ongoing activity. Fourth, we analyze application scenarios across healthcare, accessibility, situated learning, daily life assistance, cultural tourism, and industrial support, showing how domain requirements reshape system design and evaluation. We further identify five cross-cutting research challenges for future AI smart glasses: next-generation hardware, trustworthy egocentric intelligence, lifelong personalized memory, proactive intelligence, and embodied foundation models. By centering smart glasses as wearable-intelligence platforms, this survey provides a unified framework for organizing technologies, applications, and open challenges in this emerging area.

</details>


### [37] [Absence is Presence: Understanding Visual Scene Negative Events Under Safety Cognitive Constraint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19812)
*Zhiyun Jiang,Hanyong Wang,Binbin Liang,Yu Xie,Menglong Yang,Wei Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces visual scene negative captioning for safety-critical domains, where the goal is to identify semantic omissions (safety-relevant objects that should exist but are absent). The proposed CRCD framework uses counterfactual reconstruction and contrastive decoding to overcome affirmation bias, limited mental filling, and representation bias challenges in existing vision-language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional scene understanding only captures affirmative information present in images. However, in safety-critical domains (e.g., autonomous driving, industrial safety), understanding what should exist but is actually absent is crucial for risk mitigation. Existing VLMs struggle with this because they are biased toward affirmative reasoning and lack the ability to infer absent information.

Method: The proposed CRCD framework has three main components: (1) Counterfactual latent change captioning - reformulates the task by contrasting synthesized safe expectations with reality to identify semantic omissions; (2) Dual-branch counterfactual reconstruction architecture - amodal completion branch restores defective objects while functional association branch infers completely absent safety objects; (3) Multi-condition representation learning - projects universal features onto predefined safety criteria subspaces to mitigate representation bias. Decoding uses feature-level semantic residuals between reconstructed scene prototype and raw input to activate negative logic.

Result: The method establishes a high-performance baseline for this pioneering task of visual scene negative captioning with safety constraints.

Conclusion: This work addresses a critical gap in scene understanding by enabling VLMs to reason about absence rather than just presence. The CRCD framework demonstrates the feasibility of negative captioning through counterfactual reconstruction and contrastive decoding, providing a foundation for safety-aware visual reasoning in critical applications.

Abstract: Traditional scene understanding focuses on affirmative information objectively present in images. However, in safety-critical domains, comprehending key information that should exist but is actually absent is vital for risk mitigation. To bridge this gap, we focus on visual scene negative captioning with safety as the cognitive constraint. The core challenge is to convert physical absence into semantic negative events. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with this process because affirmation bias suppresses negative reasoning, while limited mental filling capability and representation bias further hinder the inference of absent information. To address these challenges, we propose a negative captioning framework based on counterfactual reconstruction and contrastive decoding (CRCD). Inspired by human cognition, CRCD reformulates the task as counterfactual latent change captioning to bypass affirmation bias. It contrasts a synthesized safe expectation with reality to identify semantic omissions. To address limited mental filling, we design a dual-branch counterfactual reconstruction architecture. The amodal completion branch restores defective objects, while the functional association branch infers completely absent safety objects. Concurrently, a multi-condition representation learning mechanism is integrated to mitigate representation bias by projecting universal features onto predefined safety criteria subspaces, thereby capturing information across more dimensions. By decoding feature-level semantic residuals between the reconstructed scene prototype and raw input, CRCD bounds the non-existence search space and activates the decoder's negative logic. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of CRCD, establishing a high-performance baseline for this pioneering task.

</details>


### [38] [SnapPhysics: A Physics-Aware Scene Graph from a Single View for Interactive Mixed Reality Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19815)
*Suji Kang,Seok-Young Kim,Young Bin Kim,Taewook Ha,Dieter Schmalstieg,Shohei Mori,Woontack Woo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SnapPhysics is a training-free framework that reconstructs 3D objects and estimates physical properties (mass, friction, center of gravity) from a single image for mixed reality applications. It combines instance-level 3D reconstruction with a physics-aware scene graph that provides structured context for VLM-based property reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical properties (mass, friction, center of gravity) are as important as geometry for physically coherent interactions in mixed reality (MR). Prior approaches either require analyzing object dynamics in video (computationally costly) or querying vision-language models on single images (lacks geometric grounding and inter-object relationships).

Method: SnapPhysics combines instance-level 3D reconstruction and spatial alignment with a physics-aware scene graph that encodes inter-object relationships and per-object metric geometry as structured context for VLM-based property reasoning. The framework is training-free.

Result: On 3D-FRONT dataset, SnapPhysics improves scene-level F-Score by 18.6% over the best learning-based method. On real captured scenes with ground-truth mass, it reduces mean absolute log difference error (mALDE) by up to 20.5% and improves log-scale correlation (r²_ls) by up to 19.6% compared to VLM-only estimation.

Conclusion: SnapPhysics enables physically interactive MR experiences without manual parameter tuning by accurately reconstructing 3D objects and estimating physical properties from a single image, outperforming both learning-based methods and VLM-only approaches.

Abstract: We propose SnapPhysics, a training-free framework that reconstructs 3D objects and estimates their physical properties such as mass, friction, and center of gravity from a single image. For physically coherent interactions in mixed reality (MR), such properties are as important as geometry. Prior approaches infer them by analyzing object dynamics in video, which is computationally costly, or by querying vision-language models (VLMs) on single images, which lacks geometric grounding and inter-object relationships. We address these limitations by combining instance-level 3D reconstruction and spatial alignment with a physics-aware scene graph that encodes these relationships and per-object metric geometry as structured context for VLM-based property reasoning. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that SnapPhysics improves scene-level F-Score by 18.6% over the best learning-based method, and on real captured scenes with ground-truth mass, it reduces the mean absolute log difference error (mALDE) by up to 20.5% and improves log-scale correlation ($r^2_{\mathrm{ls}}$) by up to 19.6% over VLM-only estimation. SnapPhysics enables physically interactive MR experiences without manual parameter tuning. Project page: https://snapphysics-ismar2026.github.io/.

</details>


### [39] [KoUniTalk: A Lightweight Articulation-Centered Korean-English 3D Talking Face Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19840)
*Hyunjung Chung,Unsang Park*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: KoUniTalk is a Korean-English 3D talking face benchmark that unifies VOCASET and Korean 3D facial motion data into a shared mesh topology using deformation transfer. It provides an identity-neutral canonical output space with 1,176 vertices focusing on the mouth and adjacent facial regions, reducing dimensionality by 4.27-fold (vs VOCASET/FLAME) and 20.45-fold (vs original Korean mesh).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-quality 3D talking face datasets are predominantly English-centric, and Korean 3D facial motion data cannot be directly combined with English benchmarks due to differences in mesh topology, spatial scale, coordinate system, and temporal sampling, preventing cross-dataset evaluation.

Method: Deformation transfer is used to retarget VOCASET and Korean speech-based 3D talking face data to a unified mesh topology. The method does not propose new deformation-transfer algorithms but creates an identity-neutral canonical output space for controlled speech-driven facial articulation training and evaluation.

Result: The unified template contains 1,176 vertices (reduced from 15,069 and 72,147 dimensions to 3,528 dimensions). The processed benchmark contains 22 speakers, 4,978 sequences, and 642,781 frames. Semantic mouth-landmark trajectories (mouth opening, mouth width, aperture ratio, mouth-opening dynamics) are evaluated to verify speech-relevant motion preservation.

Conclusion: KoUniTalk enables Korean-English cross-dataset evaluation of speech-driven 3D facial animation models in a single compact articulation-template space. A subject-disjoint Korean benchmark split is also defined since the official test set is not publicly released.

Abstract: High-quality 3D talking face datasets remain largely English- centric, and Korean 3D facial motion data are difficult to combine with standard English benchmarks because of differences in mesh topology, spatial scale, coordinate system, and temporal sampling. We present KoUniTalk, a lightweight articulation-centered Korean-English 3D talk- ing face benchmark that retargets VOCASET and the released Korean speech-based 3D talking face data to a shared mesh topology using de- formation transfer. Rather than proposing a new deformation-transfer algorithm or a full-head identity-preserving avatar dataset, KoUniTalk provides an identity-neutral canonical output space for controlled speech- driven facial articulation training and evaluation across English and Ko- rean. The unified template contains 1,176 vertices and focuses on the mouth and adjacent lower- and mid-face regions, reducing the output dimensionality from 15,069 and 72,147 dimensions to 3,528 dimensions, corresponding to 4.27-fold and 20.45-fold reductions compared with VO- CASET/FLAME and the original Korean mesh, respectively. To exam- ine whether retargeting preserves speech-relevant motion, we evaluate semantic mouth-landmark trajectories, including mouth opening, mouth width, aperture ratio, and mouth-opening dynamics. Since the official test set of the Korean dataset is not publicly released, we additionally define a subject-disjoint Korean benchmark split. The processed matched benchmark contains 22 speakers, 4,978 sequences, and 642,781 frames, enabling Korean-English cross-dataset evaluation of speech-driven 3D fa- cial animation models in a single compact articulation-template space. Source-reported inventory counts are listed separately from these pro- cessed counts

</details>


### [40] [PACE: Precise AI Cinematic Expression: A Typed Specification for Script-Grounded Previsualization and Geometric Conformance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19853)
*Bing Duan,Qiang Guo,Linpu Li,Zhijian Mao,Min Zhu,Zhirui Ren,Yiwei Yan,Xi Chu,Xiaoding Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PACE (Precise AI Cinematic Expression) is a typed representation system that bridges the gap between screenplay and film by explicitly specifying spatial planning (character positions, camera placement, framing) and compiling this into both diffusion model prompts and 3D scenes, with measurable accuracy metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current image diffusion models settle spatial planning (who stands where, what camera sees) through their own defaults, creating a gap between screenplay intent and generated output. The paper addresses the need for precise, declarative control over cinematic composition in AI-generated imagery.

Method: PACE uses a hierarchical typed representation where values (script, scene, shot, or panel level) are written once and inherited downward. A compiler converts PACE specifications into both text prompts for diffusion models and 3D scene geometry in metres. A camera solver places cameras to achieve declared framing. The system measures field-by-field discrepancies between declared values and compiled camera/staged render outputs.

Result: Single-subject panels achieve 1.2% frame width accuracy. Multi-subject shots (2-3 subjects) cannot be satisfied by one camera pose—residuals are reported. On 204 external director-storyboard shots: delivered head height is 1.906x from director words, 1.733x from compiled prompt, 0.955x with greybox control. Declaring pose on 30 shots improved action drawing from 58.9% to 74.4% without affecting framing.

Conclusion: PACE enables precise declarative control over cinematic composition in AI generation. The approach demonstrates that explicit pose declaration significantly improves action depiction (58.9%→74.4%) while maintaining framing. However, a fundamental trade-off exists: conditions that best hold framing draw the described action least. Open problems include transitions, fitted motion, and human review of generated panels.

Abstract: Between a screenplay and a film sits a planning problem that is spatial first: who stands where, and what a camera sees from where it stands. An image diffusion model asked for a shot in free text settles that plan by its own defaults. We present PACE (Precise AI Cinematic Expression), a typed representation for the plan: the screenplay evidence, the characters, props and locations it needs, where each subject stands, and what the camera does. A value is written once at the level it belongs to (script, scene, shot or panel) and inherited below it. A compiler turns the result into both the prompt sent to the diffusion model and a 3D scene built in metres, and a camera solver places the camera so that the declared framing is the framing built. Where a declared value becomes geometry, PACE measures, field by field, how far the compiled camera and the staged render sit from the declaration, rather than asking a model to judge.
  On the 11-scene Automatic Drive screenplay, every staged single-subject panel places its subject within 1.2% of frame width of its declared position; with two or three subjects one camera pose cannot satisfy every position, and the residual is reported rather than absorbed. On 204 external director-storyboard shots, delivered head height is 1.906 times the staged target from the director's words, 1.733 from the compiled prompt, and 0.955 with the greybox control; the condition that holds framing best draws the described action least. Declaring the pose on 30 shots raises the action drawn from 58.9% to 74.4% without moving the framing. Transitions, fitted motion and human review of the generated panels remain open. Code: https://github.com/StudioPiLabs/pace-core

</details>


### [41] [Socialized UAV Cross-Task Learning: Towards Cross-Granularity Collaboration through Hierarchical Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19867)
*Xinjie Yao,Ruipu Zhao,Yunqi Zhu,Zhihe Fan,Zhoupeng Guo,Weihao Li,Zhen Wang,Qilong Wang,Pengfei Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses cross-granularity learning in UAV perception, where joint object detection and instance segmentation suffer from interference due to mismatched representational and supervisory granularities. The authors propose CrossUAV benchmark and CGSC framework that progressively and adaptively regulates cross-task interactions across network hierarchies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current cross-task learning methods treat task coupling through feature sharing, distillation, or auxiliary supervision, which leads to interference, teacher bias, or unidirectional collapse. This is particularly problematic in UAV perception where visual shifts and detection-segmentation objectives form coarse- and fine-grained knowledge sources with different granularities.

Method: The authors propose two contributions: (1) CrossUAV, a unified benchmark for joint object detection and instance segmentation in UAV perception; (2) Cross-Granularity Socialized Collaboration (CGSC), a progressive and adaptive framework that regulates when, where, and how tasks exchange information across network hierarchies. It progressively activates cross-task interactions and adaptively adjusts strength according to task contribution, suppressing harmful interference while exploiting complementary coarse- and fine-grained structures.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements on both detection and segmentation tasks, validating hierarchical dynamic interaction as an effective mechanism for cross-granularity collaboration.

Conclusion: Cross-granularity learning should be viewed as hierarchical interaction regulation rather than simple task coupling. The proposed CGSC framework with progressive activation and adaptive strength adjustment effectively addresses the interference problem in joint detection-segmentation tasks for UAV perception.

Abstract: Joint learning across heterogeneous tasks is often treated as task coupling through feature sharing, distillation, or auxiliary supervision. However, in cross-task learning, mismatched representational and supervisory granularities make such coupling prone to interference, teacher bias, or unidirectional collapse. We argue that cross-granularity learning is fundamentally a problem of hierarchical interaction regulation rather than simple task coupling. This issue is particularly evident in UAV perception, where visual shifts and detection--segmentation objectives naturally form coarse- and fine-grained knowledge sources. To systematically study this problem, we introduce CrossUAV, a UAV benchmark for joint object detection and instance segmentation that provides a unified evaluation platform for cross-granularity task collaboration. To address these challenges, we propose Cross-Granularity Socialized Collaboration (CGSC), a progressive and adaptive framework that regulates when, where, and how tasks exchange information across network hierarchies. CGSC progressively activates cross-task interactions and adaptively adjusts the strength according to task contribution, suppressing harmful interference while exploiting complementary coarse- and fine-grained structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements on both tasks, validating hierarchical dynamic interaction as an effective mechanism for cross-granularity collaboration.

</details>


### [42] [BINDER: A Latent Variable Model for Probabilistic Medical Image Registration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19875)
*Stefano Cerri,Amirhossein Hassankhani,Yaël Balbastre,Koen Van Leemput*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BINDER (Bayesian INference for DEformable Registration) is a new probabilistic model for general-purpose medical image registration that uses mutual information and latent voxel-wise correspondences with closed-form iterative updates, providing both optimization-based demons-like registration and uncertainty quantification for multimodal 3D deformations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical image registration typically relies on mutual information criteria but lacks robust uncertainty quantification, especially for multimodal registration with high-dimensional 3D deformations. Existing methods often require complex approximations or lack principled ways to assess registration uncertainty.

Method: The method introduces a spatial interpolation technique with latent voxel-wise correspondences between images. Dedicated optimization and MCMC sampling techniques are derived that involve only closed-form iterative updates. This yields a demons-like optimization algorithm and a corresponding Bayesian sampler for uncertainty quantification.

Result: The approach demonstrates robust out-of-the-box performance across various monomodal and multimodal registration tasks. For the first time, it enables uncertainty quantification in multimodal registration scenarios with very high-dimensional 3D deformations.

Conclusion: BINDER provides a unified probabilistic framework that combines efficient registration (competitive with demons methods) with rigorous uncertainty quantification. The code is freely available, facilitating reproducibility and further development in medical image registration research.

Abstract: We propose a new probabilistic model for general-purpose medical image registration that builds upon the mutual information registration criterion. It centers around a spatial interpolation technique that assumes latent voxel-wise correspondences between the images being registered. By exploiting these latent variables, we derive dedicated optimization and MCMC sampling techniques that only involve closed-form iterative updates. When applied to nonlinear registration, an efficient demons-like optimization algorithm is obtained that shows robust out-of-the-box performance across a variety of monomodal and multimodal registration tasks. We also demonstrate a corresponding sampler that can quantify, for the first time, uncertainty in multimodal registration scenarios with very high-dimensional 3D deformations. Our code, which we call BINDER (Bayesian INference for DEformable Registration), is freely available at https://github.com/ste93ste/BINDER.

</details>


### [43] [SlugTrails: An Egocentric Benchmark for Floor Plan Localization in Large Buildings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19876)
*Yunqian Cheng,Roberto Manduchi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SlugTrails is a new floor plan localization benchmark for large indoor spaces using 30Hz Aria glasses recordings across three campus buildings and six floors (22089 m²), with CAD-derived floor plans and three practical data collection protocols. Stock checkpoint models perform poorly (max 0.004 R@1m30°), but fine-tuning on this benchmark significantly improves performance and enables cross-dataset generalization on LaMAR, suggesting indoor data availability is the limiting factor rather than architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Floor-plan-based indoor visual localization enables infrastructure-free positioning, but existing methods are developed and evaluated in small residential environments unlike real-world large public buildings. There is a need for a benchmark covering large indoor spaces under realistic egocentric sensing.

Method: Created a comprehensive benchmark with: (1) 30 Hz Aria glasses recordings across three campus buildings and six floors (22089 m²); (2) CAD-derived floor plans with semantic classes and circulation space masks; (3) Trajectories aligned using laser-surveyed anchors; (4) Three data collection protocols: single walking frame, stationary multi-view sweep, and walking stream with odometry. Evaluated five representative geometric and learned systems under native sensing configurations.

Result: Stock checkpoints (official released weights) perform near zero on SlugTrails (max 0.004 R@1m30°). Fine-tuning on SlugTrails improves every trainable family on all three tasks (e.g., F³Loc: 0.0 → 0.141 single-frame, 0.03 → 0.66 sequential). Gains compound as observations accumulate. Cross-dataset generalization improves on LaMAR without LaMAR training (F³Loc sequential R@1m: 0.048 → 0.143; UnLoc: 0.063 → 0.127). Train-from-scratch on SlugTrails alone stays far below fine-tuning from stock weights.

Conclusion: Floor plan localization is currently limited by indoor data availability rather than by architecture. Fine-tuning from stock weights on the new benchmark enables significant performance gains and cross-dataset generalization, demonstrating the value of large-scale indoor localization data.

Abstract: Floor-plan-based indoor visual localization enables infrastructure-free positioning, but most methods are developed and evaluated in small residential environments unlike the large public buildings of real deployment. We introduce SlugTrails, a floor plan localization benchmark for large indoor spaces under realistic egocentric sensing: $30$ Hz Aria glasses recordings across three campus buildings and six floors ($22089$ m$^2$ of floor plan outline), CAD-derived floor plans with semantic classes and circulation space masks, and trajectories aligned into the floor plan frame using laser-surveyed anchors. One protocol covers three practical ways of gathering geometry under a limited field of view -- a single walking frame, a stationary multi-view sweep, and a walking stream with odometry -- so methods designed for different regimes are compared on the same buildings and ground truth. Evaluating five representative geometric and learned systems under their native sensing configurations, we find that stock checkpoints (official released weights) are near zero on SlugTrails (at most $0.004$ R@1m30$^{\circ}$ on walking single frames), while fine-tuning on SlugTrails improves every trainable family on all three tasks (e.g., F$^3$Loc $0.0 \rightarrow 0.141$ single-frame and $0.03 \rightarrow 0.66$ sequential), with gains compounding as observations accumulate. The same fine-tuned weights also improve cross-dataset generalization on LaMAR with no LaMAR training (sequential R@1m $0.048 \rightarrow 0.143$ for F$^3$Loc and $0.063 \rightarrow 0.127$ for UnLoc), whereas train-from-scratch on SlugTrails alone stays far below fine-tuning from stock weights -- evidence that floor plan localization is currently limited by indoor data rather than by architecture. We release the dataset, protocols, and tools at https://github.com/Head-inthe-Cloud/SlugTrails.

</details>


### [44] [CitySTAR: Structured and Topology-Aware Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Urban 3D Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19911)
*Shuai Zhang,Hongye Hou,Qinghe Liu,Zhuoxiao Li,Dongli Wu,Jing Ou,Yuan Liu,Wufan Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CitySTAR is a training-free framework for reasoning-driven urban 3D grounding that lifts billion-scale point clouds into query-ready scene graphs and uses CodeLLM-driven tools, paired hypergraphs, and bidirectional topology verification to connect natural language with implicit semantic and geometric structures in urban scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D grounding approaches rely on feature similarity or direct matching, making it difficult to connect natural-language intent with implicit semantic and geometric structures hidden in billion-scale urban point clouds. There is a need for structured constraint reasoning to handle open-vocabulary 3D entities, attributes, and spatial relations in city-scale environments.

Method: 1) Lift raw point clouds into query-ready scene graph of open-vocabulary 3D instances using CodeLLM-driven tools for multimodal evidence on node attributes and 3D spatial relations. 2) Model target-context topology with paired hypergraphs and perform bidirectional topology verification for structural disambiguation. 3) Integrate topology consistency and candidate-centered 2D visual evidence via Reflective Cross-modal Grounding module over metric-aware 3D context graph.

Result: CitySTAR consistently improves open-world urban 3D grounding while maintaining strong interpretability and generalization. The method is training-free and works at city scale.

Conclusion: CitySTAR demonstrates that structured constraint reasoning is more effective than feature similarity approaches for city-scale 3D grounding. The proposed CitySTAR-3D benchmark provides enhanced semantic coverage, instance completeness, bounding-box fidelity, and spatial-relation complexity for evaluation.

Abstract: 3D grounding aims to localize target entities in complex scenes from natural language and plays a fundamental role in embodied perception and spatial reasoning. However, existing approaches mostly rely on feature similarity or direct matching, making it difficult to connect natural-language intent with the implicit semantic and geometric structures hidden in billion-scale urban point clouds. We reformulate city-scale 3D grounding as structured constraint reasoning, where description semantics are organized into computable cross-modal constraints over open-vocabulary 3D entities, attributes, and spatial relations. We present CitySTAR, a training-free framework for reasoning-driven urban 3D grounding. CitySTAR lifts raw billion-scale urban point clouds into a query-ready scene graph of open-vocabulary 3D instances, with CodeLLM-driven tools supplying multimodal evidence for node attributes and 3D spatial relations. It then models target-context topology with paired hypergraphs and performs bidirectional topology verification for structural disambiguation. Finally, a Reflective Cross-modal Grounding module integrates topology consistency and candidate-centered 2D visual evidence to make decisions over a metric-aware 3D context graph. To further support this setting, we introduce CitySTAR-3D, an enhanced benchmark that improves semantic coverage, instance completeness, bounding-box fidelity, and spatial-relation complexity in city-scale 3D grounding. Extensive experiments show that CitySTAR consistently improves open-world urban 3D grounding while maintaining strong interpretability and generalization.

</details>


### [45] [DirtyMoCap: Robust Motion Capture from Unconstrained Markers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19927)
*Long Wang,Shuting Zhao,Shen Yan,Siyuan Yu,Xiaoben Li,Zeyu Cai,Yumeng Hou,Yuliang Xiu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DirtyMoCap is a robust, marker-layout-free framework that reconstructs full-body human motion from sparse, noisy, and unordered marker observations by mapping them to proxy anchors and fitting a SMPL-H model using a differentiable Gauss-Newton solver.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optical motion capture requires strict marker layouts and clean trajectories, but real-world data is often sparse, noisy, and unordered with unknown configurations, severely limiting practical applicability.

Method: 1) Map unordered marker observations to fixed "proxy anchors" (skeletal joints and body surface points) as stable intermediate representation. 2) Initialize and track anchors over long sequences using recurrent sliding-window architecture. 3) Fit SMPL-H model to tracked anchors using custom differentiable Gauss-Newton solver that derives geometric residuals and learns adaptive observation confidence, smoothness, and prior weights end-to-end.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art configuration-specific baselines in both joint and vertex reconstruction accuracy. Custom CUDA solver achieves up to 100x speedup over standard PyTorch implementations. Successfully applied to heterogeneous raw optical MoCap recordings of traditional Chinese martial arts, yielding a Kung Fu motion dataset.

Conclusion: DirtyMoCap can generalize across arbitrary marker layouts using only a single trained model, demonstrating practical applicability for real-world motion capture scenarios.

Abstract: Optical motion capture delivers high-fidelity human motion, but its reliance on strict marker layouts and clean trajectories severely limits its real-world applicability. In practice, tracking systems frequently output unconstrained markers: sparse, noisy, and unordered point clouds with unknown or varying configurations. To bridge the gap between corrupted raw markers and parametric human models, we introduce DirtyMoCap, a robust, marker-layout-free framework. Our core insight is to map unordered marker observations to a fixed set of "proxy anchors" comprising skeletal joints and body surface points, which serve as a stable intermediate representation. We first initialize and track these anchors over long sequences using a recurrent sliding-window architecture. Then, a custom differentiable Gauss-Newton solver fits the SMPL-H model to the tracked anchors to recover full-body pose, translation, and shape.
