By explicitly deriving geometric residuals, our solver learns adaptive observation confidence, smoothness, and prior weights end-to-end, adapting dynamically to the reliability of the input data. Extensive experiments on diverse, noisy marker configurations demonstrate that DirtyMoCap successfully generalizes across arbitrary layouts using only a single trained model. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art configuration-specific baselines in both joint and vertex reconstruction accuracy, while our custom CUDA solver achieves up to a 100x speedup over standard PyTorch implementations. We further apply DirtyMoCap to heterogeneous raw optical MoCap recordings of traditional Chinese martial arts, yielding a Kung Fu motion dataset of temporally coherent SMPL-H reconstructions. Code and data are available at https://wanglongzju.github.io/DirtyMoCap-Project-Page.

</details>


### [46] [Enhanced Knowledge Distillation for Detection Transformer via Teacher Prediction Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19964)
*Yitong Xing,Yuhao Cheng,Yanping Li,Yichao Yan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TPRD is a plug-and-play distillation method for Detection Transformers (DETRs) that improves teacher supervision quality by refining predictions before distillation. It addresses the issue of stage-wise non-monotonic prediction behavior where predictions can degrade or become overconfident in later stages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DETRs achieve strong object detection performance but are computationally expensive for edge deployment. Existing distillation methods focus on aligning distillation points but overlook the quality of teacher's supervision. The key insight is that due to stage-wise non-monotonic prediction behavior in DETRs, well-localized or correctly classified predictions from earlier stages may degrade in later ones, and some negative predictions become increasingly overconfident, leading to inaccurate and inconsistent supervision.

Method: The proposed TPRD includes three components: (1) Positive Prediction Correction (PPC) - corrects degraded positive predictions by restoring more accurate ones from earlier stages, ensuring reliable localization and classification signals; (2) Negative Prediction Suppression (NPS) - suppresses the influence of overconfident negatives to prevent misleading supervision; (3) Maximum Dark Knowledge Preservation (MDKP) - selectively refines target-class logits while retaining non-target relations to preserve informative dark knowledge.

Result: Extensive experiments on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.

Conclusion: TPRD provides a plug-and-play solution that significantly improves distillation quality for DETRs by addressing the quality of teacher supervision through prediction refinement, enabling better student model training for edge deployment.

Abstract: Detection Transformers (DETRs) achieve strong performance in object detection but remain challenging to deploy on edge devices due to their high computational cost. Existing DETR distillation methods mainly focus on aligning distillation points, while largely overlooking the quality of the teacher's supervision itself. We observe that due to stage-wise non-monotonic prediction behavior in DETRs, well-localized or correctly classified predictions from earlier stages may degrade in later ones, and some negative predictions become increasingly overconfident. As a result, relying solely on the current stage's predictions yields inaccurate and inconsistent supervision. To address this issue, we propose Teacher Prediction Refinement Distillation (TPRD), a plug-and-play module that refines teacher predictions before distillation by exploiting stage-wise prediction information. TPRD improves supervision quality through Positive Prediction Correction (PPC), which corrects degraded positive predictions by restoring more accurate ones from earlier stages, ensuring reliable localization and classification signals, and Negative Prediction Suppression (NPS) suppresses the influence of overconfident negatives, preventing them from providing misleading supervision to the student. To preserve informative dark knowledge, we further introduce Maximum Dark Knowledge Preservation (MDKP), which selectively refines target-class logits while retaining non-target relations. Extensive experiments on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method. Our code is available at https://github.com/xingyitong1/TPRD.

</details>


### [47] [Beyond the Foreground: FOV-Aware Polyp Image Synthesis via Lesion-Guided Adaptive Mucosal Context Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19966)
*Tong Wang,Yuting He,Bin Ren,Yutong Xie,Guanyu Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LAMP is the first foreground-guided framework for polyp image synthesis that addresses non-mucosal contamination and inconsistent texture issues by using lesion-guided adaptive mucosal context propagation with FOV masks, cross-attention, and multidirectional propagation mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing foreground-guided image synthesis methods treat all non-foreground pixels as background, causing two problems when applied to colonoscopy: (1) non-mucosal black regions contaminate generated tissue, and (2) local reasoning produces inconsistent mucosal texture and illumination.

Method: LAMP uses three key components: (1) FOV mask to explicitly separate lesion, valid mucosa, and camera exterior; (2) Lesion-to-Mucosa cross-attention to extract lesion appearance conditions for valid-mucosa locations; (3) FOV-constrained multidirectional Vision Receptance Weighted Key Value to propagate conditions over legal tissue support, with an adaptive gate controlling residual fusion into the diffusion U-Net.

Result: Extensive experiments on five polyp datasets demonstrate that LAMP substantially outperforms existing methods in overall generation quality and consistently improves five downstream segmentation models.

Conclusion: LAMP successfully addresses the limitations of existing foreground-guided methods for colonoscopy image synthesis, providing high-quality synthetic polyp images that benefit downstream segmentation tasks.

Abstract: Synthetic image and mask pairs can alleviate scarce colonoscopy annotations, but realistic synthesis requires preserving the supplied lesion while generating compatible mucosa. Existing foreground-guided methods treat all non-foreground pixels as background and rely mainly on local integration. Directly applying them to colonoscopy causes two problems: non-mucosal black regions contaminate generated tissue, and local reasoning produces inconsistent mucosal texture and illumination. We propose LAMP, the first foreground-guided framework for polyp image synthesis based on lesion-guided adaptive mucosal context propagation. LAMP explicitly separates the lesion, valid mucosa, and camera exterior using a field-of-view (FOV) mask. Lesion-to-Mucosa cross-attention extracts lesion appearance conditions for valid-mucosa locations, while FOV-constrained multidirectional Vision Receptance Weighted Key Value propagates them over legal tissue support. An adaptive gate then controls their residual fusion into the diffusion U-Net. Extensive experiments on five polyp datasets demonstrate that LAMP substantially outperforms existing methods in overall generation quality and consistently improves five downstream segmentation models. Our code will be released at https://github.com/wangtong627/LAMP.

</details>


### [48] [An Event Preserving Velocity Invariant Representation for Event Cameras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19973)
*Mikihiro Ikura,Luna Gava,Jiahang Wu,Chiara Bartolozzi,Arren Glover*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SCARF is a novel real-time velocity-invariant representation for event cameras that preserves raw events while handling fast motion, stationary scenes, and independently moving objects, achieving state-of-the-art performance in computational efficiency and representation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Event cameras offer low-latency, high temporal resolution perception but face algorithmic challenges due to their novel asynchronous, independent pixel circuitry. Existing velocity-invariant representations alleviate motion issues but discard temporal information by converting events into image-like representations.

Method: The paper proposes Set of Centre Active Receptive Fields (SCARF), a real-time velocity-invariant representation that preserves raw events while consistently handling fast motion, stationary scenes, and independently moving objects.

Result: SCARF achieves state-of-the-art performance in both computational efficiency and representation quality for event camera vision tasks such as robotics.

Conclusion: SCARF successfully addresses the limitations of prior velocity-invariant representations by maintaining temporal information while handling various motion scenarios, making it suitable for real-time robotics applications.

Abstract: Event cameras provide low-latency, high temporal resolution perception for real-time vision tasks such as robotics.The novel circuitry (i.e. asynchronous, independent pixels) that enables these advantages also introduces new algorithmic challenges. Velocity-invariant representations alleviate missing observations under slow motion and motion blur under fast motion, but most discard temporal information by converting events into image-like representations. We propose Set of Centre Active Receptive Fields (SCARF), a real-time velocity-invariant representation that preserves raw events while consistently handling fast motion, stationary scenes, and independently moving objects. SCARF achieves state-of-the-art performance in both computational efficiency and representation quality.

</details>


### [49] [QCPruner: Query-Conditioned Population Coverage for Visual Token Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19990)
*Shengli He,Yongchao Liang,Roumeng He,Junjie Zeng,Jiyuan He,Can Wu,Li Zheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: QCPruner is a training-free pruning method for multimodal LLMs that uses query-conditioned bilateral utility weighting to reduce visual tokens while preserving query-relevant evidence. It achieves up to 96.1% performance retention at aggressive pruning ratios (32/576 tokens) across multiple MLLM architectures, outperforming existing baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) suffer from high visual-token load, motivating training-free pruning to reduce later-layer computation. However, existing pruning methods fail to use a shared per-visual query utility to jointly weight both visual targets and candidate representatives, leading to suboptimal preservation of query-relevant evidence.

Method: QCPruner introduces bilateral utility weighting where both visual targets and candidate representatives are query-conditioned. Using keyword-matched query anchors, it fuses two cross-modal cues into a unified utility metric applied within visual-affinity-based coverage. This forms a nonnegative facility-location objective that is monotone and submodular, retaining the standard (1-1/e) greedy approximation guarantee without requiring any model training or parameter updates.

Result: Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-Video, and Qwen2.5-VL, QCPruner achieves the highest average relative performance among evaluated complete-system pruning methods at every reported token budget. At 32 of 576 tokens on LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 96.1% of unpruned performance versus 93.9% for the strongest baseline. At 256 of 1296 tokens on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it achieves 96.7% versus 92.5% for the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: QCPruner demonstrates that query-conditioned bilateral utility weighting effectively addresses the visual token pruning challenge in MLLMs. By jointly optimizing visual target and representative selection through a submodular objective, it achieves superior performance-efficiency tradeoffs across diverse MLLM architectures without any training, making it a practical solution for reducing inference computation.

Abstract: The high visual-token load in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) motivates training-free pruning to reduce later-layer computation, but under a fixed budget, pruning must preserve query-relevant evidence while avoiding redundancy. Existing methods rank tokens, diversify selected subsets, or optimize coverage without using a shared per-visual query utility to weight both visual targets and candidate representatives. We introduce QCPruner, which makes both roles query-conditioned through bilateral utility weighting. Using keyword-matched query anchors, QCPruner fuses two cross-modal cues into utility and applies it to both visual targets and candidate representatives within visual-affinity-based coverage. The resulting nonnegative facility-location objective is monotone and submodular, retains the standard (1-1/e) greedy guarantee, and requires no model training or parameter updates. Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-Video, and Qwen2.5-VL, QCPruner achieves the highest average relative performance among evaluated complete-system pruning methods at every reported token budget. At 32 of 576 tokens on LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 96.1% of unpruned performance, versus 93.9% for the strongest evaluated baseline. At 256 of 1296 tokens on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the corresponding values are 96.7% and 92.5%.

</details>


### [50] [AVTrace: Diagnosing Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning in Omni Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19991)
*Longyin Zhang,Parth Sakhare Mahendra,Chengwei Wei,Ning Zhang,Lim Ming Chong,Sirui He,Ai Ti Aw*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AVTrace is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating omni models on audio-visual temporal reasoning tasks, including onset/span grounding, synchronization verification, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension. It contains 34,114 training examples and balanced dev/test splits. Evaluation of five open omni models reveals all score below the majority-label baseline (0.556) on synchronization, with low performance on chain parsing and event-conditioned tasks. Parameter-efficient temporal post-training improves some metrics, but task metrics change modestly on external image benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current omni models can describe video content but struggle with temporal reasoning: locating events in time, preserving event order, and judging audio-visual synchronization. No comprehensive diagnostic suite exists to assess these capabilities across different temporal reasoning tasks.

Method: AVTrace is introduced as a silver-standard diagnostic suite spanning six task types: onset and span grounding, synchronization verification, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension. The benchmark contains 34,114 training examples with category-balanced development (3,500) and test (7,000) splits. Five open omni models are evaluated under their respective input configurations using reference-blind response normalization followed by deterministic scoring. Experiments include development-set perturbations to test modality removal and visual input processing sensitivity, and parameter-efficient temporal post-training.

Result: All five off-the-shelf omni models score below the test split's majority-label baseline of 0.556 on synchronization verification. Low scores are observed on chain parsing and event-conditioned grounding and comprehension. Development-set perturbations reveal task-dependent sensitivity in Qwen3-Omni-30B to modality removal and visual input processing changes, without isolating underlying causes. Parameter-efficient temporal post-training improves Gemma4-E4B-it on several benchmark metrics. On three external image benchmarks, task metrics change modestly (including some degradations), while teacher-forcing perplexity decreases.

Conclusion: Semantic reference-text overlap should not be treated as a proxy for temporal localization. AVTrace can identify task-specific weaknesses in omni models while providing a testbed for temporal post-training. The benchmark reveals that current omni models lack sufficient temporal reasoning capabilities across multiple dimensions, and parameter-efficient training can yield improvements but does not fully resolve the limitations.

Abstract: Omni models can describe video content, but can they locate events in time, preserve event order, and judge audio-visual synchronization? We introduce AVTrace (Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning Assessment and Capability Evaluation), a silver-standard diagnostic suite spanning onset and span grounding, synchronization, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension. It contains 34,114 training examples and category-balanced development and test splits of 3,500 and 7,000 examples. We evaluate five open omni models under their respective input configurations using reference-blind response normalization followed by deterministic scoring. All five off-the-shelf systems score below the test split's majority-label baseline of 0.556 on synchronization verification, and obtain low scores on chain parsing and event-conditioned grounding and comprehension. Development-set perturbations reveal task-dependent sensitivity in Qwen3-Omni-30B to modality removal and changes in visual input processing, without isolating their underlying causes. Parameter-efficient temporal post-training improves Gemma4-E4B-it on several benchmark metrics. On three external image benchmarks, task metrics change modestly, including some degradations, while teacher-forcing perplexity decreases. Together, these findings show that semantic reference-text overlap should not be treated as a proxy for temporal localization, and that AVTrace can identify task-specific weaknesses while providing a testbed for temporal post-training.

</details>


### [51] [GRF-Recon: Global Ray-Field Optimization for Long-Sequence Feed-forward Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20012)
*Enpeng Li,Yunzhou Zhang,Zhiyao Zhang,Dexuan Lyu,Chenyu Wang,Chiyuan Cui,Cheng Cheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified framework for stable and scalable feed-forward 3D reconstruction from long monocular sequences, addressing GPU memory constraints, local geometry degradation, and trajectory drift through trajectory alignment, LoRA-based geometric prior injection, hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization, and trajectory stitching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction is efficient for scene modeling but scaling to large monocular scenarios faces three key challenges: excessive GPU memory footprint, degraded local geometry, and long-term trajectory drift. Existing chunk-based optimization strategies provide limited geometric constraints and fail to maintain global consistency over extended trajectories.

Method: The approach uses three main techniques: (1) Coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment with lightweight geometric prior injection via LoRA adaptation to improve depth accuracy on fine structures while preserving inference efficiency; (2) Hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization that leverages high-frequency geometric features to guide local point-cloud refinement and enforce consistent inter-frame ray constraints, establishing strong cross-frame geometric coupling while maintaining scalability; (3) Efficient trajectory stitching strategy with joint ray-error optimization to reduce accumulated drift.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that the approach achieves competitive trajectory accuracy compared with representative SLAM systems while maintaining globally consistent 3D reconstruction in large-scale scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed unified framework successfully addresses the challenges of scaling feed-forward 3D reconstruction to large monocular scenarios, achieving both stability and scalability with global consistency in 3D reconstruction.

Abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction provides an efficient paradigm for scene modeling from image sequences. Scaling these models to large monocular scenarios are constrained by excessive GPU memory footprint, degraded local geometry, and long-term trajectory drift. Existing chunk-based optimization strategies provide limited geometric constraints and fail to maintain global consistency over extended trajectories. We present a unified framework for stable and scalable feed-forward 3D reconstruction from long monocular sequences. Our approach builds on coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment augmented by lightweight geometric prior injection. Distilling monocular geometric cues into the feed-forward backbone via LoRA adaptation improves depth accuracy on fine structures while preserving inference efficiency. We introduce a hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization that leverages high-frequency geometric features to guide local point-cloud refinement and enforce consistent inter-frame ray constraints. Unlike prior chunk-based methods, this establishes strong cross-frame geometric coupling while maintaining scalability. Finally, an efficient trajectory stitching strategy with joint ray-error optimization explicitly reduces accumulated drift. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves competitive trajectory accuracy compared with representative SLAM systems, while maintaining globally consistent 3D reconstruction in large-scale scenarios.

</details>


### [52] [Astronex-World 1.0: Real-Time Interactive World Model Foundation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20034)
*Xin Zhou,Cong Miao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Astronex-World 1.0 is an open controllable video world-model foundation that generates future visual states from text prompts or initial images, with control over camera trajectories, continuous actions, and embodiment. It achieves 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full, competitive with larger models while running in real-time on a single NVIDIA L20 GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to create an open, controllable video world model that supports both text-to-video and image-to-video generation with precise control over camera parameters, actions, and embodiment. The goal is to enable applications in embodied intelligence and autonomous driving through reserved action interfaces.

Method: The method uses two model variants: (1) a bidirectional model for full-context generation, and (2) a causal model with block-causal attention and cross-block KV caching for persistent generation. Both are built on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B prior. PRoPE injects camera intrinsics and extrinsics, while a 64-dimensional action stream modulates every Transformer layer. Training involves a five-stage path: developing bidirectional camera/action control, converting to block-causal generation, distilling a few-step student, restoring mixed-domain dynamics, and applying asymmetric DMD/DMD2 distribution matching.

Result: The causal model generates 832x480 video at 24 fps and streams in real-time on one NVIDIA L20 GPU. It scores 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full. On Full, this 5B model outperforms the 13.6B LongCat-Video and 14B Helios, is within one point of the 22B LTX-2.3, and exceeds YUME 1.5 (post-trained from the same 5B prior on A100 GPUs).

Conclusion: Astronex-World 1.0 demonstrates that a 5B parameter model can achieve competitive performance with larger models (up to 22B parameters) while enabling real-time generation on consumer-grade GPUs. The reserved action interfaces make it suitable for post-training in embodied intelligence and autonomous driving applications.

Abstract: We present Astronex-World 1.0, an open controllable video world-model foundation. Given a text prompt (text-to-video) or an initial observation (image-to-video), the model predicts future visual states under frame-aligned camera trajectories, continuous actions, and an embodiment identifier, and accepts text events inserted at a specified position of a rollout. The family provides a bidirectional model for full-context generation and a causal model with block-causal attention and cross-block KV caching for persistent generation, both built on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B prior. PRoPE injects camera intrinsics and extrinsics, while a 64-dimensional action stream modulates every Transformer layer. A five-stage training path develops bidirectional camera and action control, converts the backbone to block-causal generation, distills a few-step student, restores mixed-domain dynamics, and applies asymmetric DMD/DMD2 distribution matching. The causal model generates 832x480 video at 24 fps. All five training stages run on two NVIDIA L20 48 GB GPUs, and the causal model streams in real time on one. It scores 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full. On Full, this 5B model is above the 13.6B LongCat-Video and the 14B Helios, within one point of the 22B LTX-2.3, and above YUME 1.5, which is post-trained from the same 5B prior on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The reserved action input and output interfaces allow post-training for embodied intelligence and autonomous driving.

</details>


### [53] [A Free Lunch? Adapting PP-OCRv6 for Historical Text Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20064)
*Benjamin Kiessling*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates PP-OCRv6, a lightweight recurrence-free text recognizer, against traditional CRNN models for historical automatic text recognition (ATR), finding that heterogeneous pretraining significantly improves generalization and that fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform large vision-language models like Qwen3.5-based Medusa on historical Latin-script materials.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite large vision-language models showing impressive scores, they have limited practical use in historical ATR due to computational cost, dependence on large-scale pretraining, and hallucination issues. The field continues to rely on compact CRNN line recognizers. This paper investigates whether lightweight recurrence-free recognizers can offer the accuracy of larger models while maintaining the practical advantages of CRNNs.

Method: The researchers adapted PP-OCRv6 (a compact text recognizer without strong language modeling) for historical line recognition and compared it with a conventional CRNN across four training scenarios: generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation. The evaluation used multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script historical material. They also compared with a Qwen3.5-based Medusa recognizer.

Result: PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform the baseline CRNN when trained from scratch. However, heterogeneous pretraining produces markedly better generalization. Importantly, fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM (Qwen3.5-based Medusa) that was specifically tailored for historical Latin-script HTR.

Conclusion: Lightweight recurrence-free recognizers like PP-OCRv6, when properly pretrained, can achieve competitive or superior performance compared to both traditional CRNNs and large vision-language models for historical text recognition, offering a promising balance between accuracy and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Despite impressive reported scores, large vision-language models have seen limited practical uptake in historical automatic text recognition because of their computational cost, dependence on large-scale pretraining, and hallucination. Historical ATR therefore continues to rely largely on compact CRNN line recognizers, which are visually grounded and trainable on modest data. Lightweight recurrence-free recognizers promise the accuracy of larger models with the practical advantages of CRNNs, yet have not been comprehensively evaluated on historical writing. We adapt PP-OCRv6, a recent compact text recognizer without strong language modeling, for historical line recognition and compare it with a conventional CRNN across generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation on multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script material. While PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform the baseline when trained from scratch, heterogeneous pretraining produces markedly better generalization. Comparisons with the Qwen3.5-based Medusa recognizer further show that fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM tailored towards historical Latin-script HTR.

</details>


### [54] [PointEvent: Rethinking Event-based Tiny Object Detection via Serialized Motion Evidence Accumulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20066)
*Zongze Wu,Baofeng Jia,Weiqi Yan,Jingyuan Zhang,Yu Zang,Xiaoyu Chen,Jing Han*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PointEvent is a lightweight event-wise state-space framework for tiny UAV detection using event cameras. It introduces serialized motion evidence accumulation that treats motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process, organizing event streams into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through latent complementary serializations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, but distant targets generate sparse and fragmented events that are easily overwhelmed by clutter and ego-motion. Existing methods rely on dense event representations or local sparse spatiotemporal modeling, resulting in redundant computation or fragmented modeling of motion continuity across distant asynchronous events.

Method: The proposed method introduces serialized motion evidence accumulation, organizing the same event stream into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through latent complementary serializations. Based on this principle, PointEvent alternates serialized scans across complementary orders, progressively consolidating fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods. A high-resolution event branch preserves fine-grained target responses while compact context modulation suppresses interference.

Result: PointEvent achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among compared methods.

Conclusion: The serialized motion evidence accumulation approach effectively addresses the challenge of sparse and fragmented event representation for distant tiny UAV detection. By modeling motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process and leveraging complementary spatiotemporal serializations, PointEvent achieves superior performance with minimal computational resources, making it highly suitable for real-time UAV detection applications.

Abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, yet distant targets generate sparse and fragmented events that are easily overwhelmed by clutter and ego-motion. Existing methods mainly rely on dense event representations or local sparse spatiotemporal modeling, resulting in redundant computation or fragmented modeling of motion continuity across distant asynchronous events. To address this limitation, we introduce serialized motion evidence accumulation, which treats motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process. Specifically, the same event stream is organized into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through the latent complementary serializations. Based on this principle, we propose PointEvent, a lightweight event-wise state-space framework that alternates serialized scans across the complementary orders, progressively consolidating fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods. A high-resolution event branch preserves fine-grained target responses, while compact context modulation suppresses interference. Experiments demonstrate that PointEvent achieves SOTA with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among the compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent

</details>

### [56] [A Smaller Transformer in Your Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20100)
*Dhananjay Tomar,Marius Aasan,Andreas Kleppe,Adín Ramírez Rivera*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TWT (Transformer-Within-Transformer) is a post-hoc method that reduces Vision Transformer depth by fusing redundant contiguous layers into single learned surrogate layers, achieving comparable performance with half the depth on natural images and improved results in histopathology tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision Transformers exhibit depthwise computational redundancy with locally similar computational phases across layers. Existing methods to exploit this redundancy either fail to reduce inference compute or significantly degrade model expressivity. The authors seek a unified framework for block redundancy that decouples geometry from specific interventions.

Method: The paper formalizes a unified view of block redundancy that decouples layer geometry from surrogate interventions. TWT then fuses contiguous groups of redundant layers into a single learned surrogate layer, reducing both parameter count and inference compute.

Result: TWT achieves competitive performance with original models using half the depth on natural images. In downstream histopathology settings, TWT matches or even improves upon the original baseline, demonstrating the method's effectiveness across different domains.

Conclusion: TWT provides an effective post-hoc solution for reducing Vision Transformer depth and computational cost while maintaining or improving performance. The approach successfully balances efficiency gains with model expressivity, making it particularly valuable for resource-constrained deployment scenarios.

Abstract: Recent findings indicate that Vision Transformers settle into locally similar computational phases, implying a level of depthwise computational redundancy. However, existing methods to exploit this redundancy either fail to reduce inference compute or severely degrade model expressivity. In this work, we formalise a unified view of block redundancy that decouples the geometry from specific surrogate interventions. We then introduce Transformer-Within-Transformer (TWT), a post-hoc method that fuses contiguous groups of redundant layers into a single learned surrogate layer. TWT reduces parameter count and inference compute while remaining competitive with original models using half the depth on natural images, and in several downstream histopathology settings, TWT matches or even improves on the original baseline.

</details>


### [57] [AnyviewMeter: Adapting Robotic Reward Models with Camera Geometry and Multi-View Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20106)
*Yuang Tu,Runjia Tan,Yujie Yan,Jinghan Hu,Chen Lv*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AnyviewMeter is a geometry-conditioned adaptation framework for robotic reward models that addresses viewpoint and occlusion sensitivity by combining low-rank fine-tuning with token-aligned Plucker rays and synchronous block attention. It enables both single-view and joint multi-view reward prediction through parameter-efficient adaptation of a pretrained Robometer model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robotic reward models evaluate task execution from visual observations, but their predictions can change with camera viewpoint and occlusion even when the underlying task state remains unchanged. Adapting a pretrained reward model to a local task requires accounting for how that task is observed across different camera configurations.

Method: The framework combines three key components: (1) Low-rank fine-tuning for parameter-efficient adaptation, (2) Token-aligned Plucker rays for incorporating camera geometry into visual features and attention queries/keys, and (3) Synchronous block attention for fusing synchronized views inside the pretrained decoder. It supports both single-view reward prediction and joint multi-view evaluation.

Result: On PickCube, single-view adaptation improves progress prediction in every camera group and reduces mean absolute error under changed field of view by ~21% relative to RGB fine-tuning. Across simulated manipulation tasks, joint multi-view prediction reduces progress error by 41-69% compared with averaging single-view RGB predictions and improves temporal ordering in ~88% of task-camera groups. On real tasks, mean absolute error decreases by ~21% relative to averaged RGB fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Camera geometry and joint visual evidence are useful components of task-specific robotic reward adaptation. The approach effectively addresses viewpoint and occlusion sensitivity in robotic reward models through parameter-efficient adaptation.

Abstract: Robotic reward models evaluate task execution from visual observations, but their predictions can change with camera viewpoint and occlusion even when the underlying task state is unchanged. Adapting a pretrained reward model to a local task therefore requires accounting for how that task is observed. We introduce AnyviewMeter, a geometry-conditioned adaptation framework for robotic reward models that represent task progress as a scalar reward signal. It combines low-rank fine-tuning with token-aligned Plucker rays and synchronous block attention: ray conditioning incorporates camera geometry into visual features and attention queries and keys, while block attention fuses synchronized views inside the pretrained decoder. The framework supports both single-view reward prediction and joint multi-view evaluation through parameter-efficient adaptation of a pretrained Robometer model. On PickCube, single-view adaptation improves progress prediction in every camera group and reduces mean absolute error under a changed field of view by approximately 21% relative to RGB fine-tuning. Across simulated manipulation tasks, joint multi-view prediction reduces progress error by 41-69% compared with averaging single-view RGB predictions and improves temporal ordering in approximately 88% of task-camera groups. On real tasks with fixed and wrist-mounted cameras, mean absolute error decreases by approximately 21% relative to averaged RGB fine-tuning. These results support camera geometry and joint visual evidence as useful components of task-specific robotic reward adaptation.

</details>


### [58] [Cross-Modal Attention Acts as a Frequency Filter: Why Verbose Prompts Improve Robustness in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20139)
*Farooq Ahmad Wani,Maria Sofia Bucarelli,Mujtaba Hussain Mirza,Oleksandr Pryymak,Aryo Pradipta Gema,Iacopo Masi,Pasquale Minervini,Fabrizio Silvestri*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper reveals that question wording significantly affects Vision-Language Models' robustness under image corruption. Verbose questions (e.g., "Please look carefully and answer: is there a cat?") enhance robustness, while fine-grained questions (e.g., "what colour is the cup left of the chair?") increase fragility. This occurs because question-conditioned cross-modal attention acts as a spectral filter over image patches, with verbose questions broadening frequency support and fine-grained questions concentrating it onto fewer visual scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models are known to be fragile under image corruption, but the underlying reasons for this vulnerability are not well understood. The researchers observed that the same model can exhibit dramatically different robustness levels depending on how questions are phrased, suggesting that question wording itself plays a critical role in model performance under corrupted inputs.

Method: The researchers analyzed the cross-modal attention mechanism in VLMs and discovered it acts as a spectral filter over image patches. They investigated how different question types (verbose vs. fine-grained) affect this filter's frequency response. They conducted experiments on Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-OneVision models using GQA and CLEVR datasets, testing various question phrasings under different image corruptions.

Result: Verbose paraphrasing reduces answer drift variance by 70-81% on 8B models. The spectral filter and corruption alignment on the same spatial frequencies causes maximum answer drift. The practical recommendation (padding the prompt) yields measurable accuracy gains even under image corruption.

Conclusion: Question wording is a crucial factor in VLM robustness under image corruption. The cross-modal attention acts as a question-conditioned spectral filter, explaining why verbose questions improve robustness (broader frequency support) while fine-grained questions reduce it (narrower frequency support). A simple practical intervention—padding prompts—can significantly improve model reliability in real-world applications where image corruption may occur.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are fragile under image corruption. We find that the wording of the question affects VLMs in two opposite ways. Verbose questions make VLMs substantially more robust---e.g., rephrasing "Is there a cat?" into "Please look carefully and answer: is there a cat?". Conversely, VLMs become more fragile under corruption when the question is semantically complex or finer-grained, e.g., "what colour is the cup left of the chair?" instead of "is there a cup?". Both effects stem from question-conditioned cross-modal attention, which induces a spectral filter over image patches: verbose questions broaden its frequency support, while fine-grained questions concentrate it onto fewer visual scales. The model's answer drifts most when this filter and the corruption sit on the same spatial frequencies. We test the filter view on Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-OneVision across GQA and CLEVR; verbose paraphrasing reduces drift variance by 70--81% on the 8B models. The practical recipe---pad the prompt---further yields measurable gains in accuracy, even under image corruption.

</details>


### [59] [Bridging Modalities on the Cortex: Surface-based MRI to PET Translation with a Diffusion Bridge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20147)
*Yitong Li,Alexandra Samoylova,Fabian Bongratz,Timo Grimmer,Dennis M. Hedderich,Igor Yakushev,Christian Wachinger*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces DB-SUiT, a surface-based diffusion bridge framework for MRI-to-PET translation that operates on the cortical manifold to synthesize FDG-PET scans from MRI, addressing the limitations of FDG-PET (cost, radiation, accessibility) while preserving disease-related cortical patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FDG-PET is highly sensitive for dementia diagnosis but has constraints (high costs, radiation exposure, limited accessibility). While MRI-to-PET cross-modal synthesis offers an alternative, existing volumetric methods fail to account for the highly folded cortical geometry where disease-related patterns primarily reside.

Method: A conditional Spherical U-shaped vision Transformer (SUiT) designed for surface-based MRI-to-PET translation. It uses spherical convolutional encoders for multi-scale surface feature extraction, bottleneck Transformers for long-range spatial dependencies, and incorporates demographic and subcortical conditions. The framework operates natively on the cortical manifold using a diffusion bridge approach.

Result: DB-SUiT demonstrates high-fidelity synthesis outperforming baselines. In automated dementia classification, synthesized PET surfaces improve performance over MRI by 14.2% and PET volumes by 11.3%, approaching real PET performance. In a blinded reader study, synthetic PET achieved 85.5% accuracy vs 75.8% for MRI and 95.2% for real PET. The model shows strong cross-cohort and cross-pathology generalization, including on an external cohort with unseen dementia subtypes.

Conclusion: Surface-based diffusion bridge frameworks operating on cortical geometry can effectively synthesize FDG-PET from MRI, offering a promising alternative to FDG-PET for dementia diagnosis with improved accessibility and reduced constraints. The approach generalizes well across different dementia types and cohorts.

Abstract: Cortical hypometabolism measured by Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography (FDG-PET) is a highly sensitive biomarker for dementia diagnosis. However, high costs, radiation exposure, and limited accessibility constrain its clinical utility. While cross-modal synthesis from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers a promising alternative, existing volumetric generation methods do not explicitly account for the highly folded cortical geometry, where disease-related patterns predominantly reside. To address this, we introduce a novel surface-based diffusion bridge framework DB-SUiT for MRI-to-PET translation that operates natively on the cortical manifold. A conditional Spherical U-shaped vision Transformer (SUiT) is specifically designed to model the intricate cross-modal relationships while preserving surface topology. It combines spherical convolutional encoders for multi-scale surface feature extraction with bottleneck Transformers to capture long-range spatial dependencies, while incorporating demographic and subcortical conditions to refine the synthesis. Evaluated on two datasets, including subjects with different dementia types, DB-SUiT demonstrates high-fidelity synthesis that substantially outperforms other baselines. In automated dementia classification, synthesized PET surfaces improve performance over MRI by 14.2% and PET volumes by 11.3%, approaching the performance of real PET surfaces. In a blinded reader study, synthetic PET achieved 85.5% diagnostic accuracy, compared with 75.8% for MRI and 95.2% for real PET. This further demonstrates cross-cohort and cross-pathology generalization, as the model was evaluated without retraining on an external cohort that included a dementia subtype not represented during training. Our code is available at https://github.com/ai-med/DB-SUiT.

</details>


### [60] [Task-Oriented Semantic Feature Transmission for Multi-Task Satellite Remote Sensing over Low-SNR Channels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20150)
*Shuoyuan Sun,Hongyu Wang,Mugen Peng,Wenjia Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a task-oriented semantic communication framework for satellite remote sensing that bypasses traditional image reconstruction and directly transmits semantic features for downstream tasks like classification and detection, achieving superior performance over reconstruction-based methods especially at low SNR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional satellite remote sensing transmission follows a reconstruct-then-infer paradigm that optimizes pixel-level fidelity, creating an objective mismatch with downstream tasks such as classification and detection, particularly at low SNR conditions.

Method: The proposed framework uses a multitask-pretrained backbone to extract semantic features, a lightweight Channel Adaptation Module (CAM) for feature compression and bandwidth reduction, and a feature restorer to recover task-relevant structure after channel corruption. With the backbone frozen, the CAM and task-specific downstream heads are jointly optimized with task and feature-level supervision under random-SNR training.

Result: Experiments on scene classification and object detection under AWGN setting show consistent gains over reconstruction-oriented JSCC baselines across different SNR conditions, with the largest improvements in the low-SNR regime.

Conclusion: The task-oriented semantic communication framework outperforms reconstruction-based approaches, particularly in low-SNR scenarios, demonstrating the effectiveness of directly transmitting semantic features for downstream tasks in satellite remote sensing.

Abstract: Conventional satellite remote sensing transmission follows a reconstruct-then-infer paradigm that optimizes pixel-level fidelity, creating an objective mismatch with downstream tasks such as classification and detection, especially at low SNR. This paper investigates a task-oriented framework that bypasses image reconstruction and directly transmits semantic features extracted by a multitask-pretrained backbone. A lightweight channel adaptation module (CAM) compresses feature dimensionality for bandwidth reduction, and a feature restorer recovers task-relevant structure after channel corruption. With the backbone frozen, the CAM and task-specific downstream heads are jointly optimized with task and feature-level supervision under random-SNR training. Under the adopted AWGN setting, experiments on scene classification and object detection show consistent gains over reconstruction-oriented JSCC baselines across different SNR conditions, with the largest improvements in the low-SNR regime.

</details>


### [61] [Ischemic Stroke Segmentation and Net Water Uptake Quantification on Multicenter Non-Contrast CT Using Supervised Target-Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20151)
*Linus Britt,Maximilian Nielsen,Susan Klapproth,Andre Kemmling,Michael H. Lev,Gabriel Broocks,Rene Werner,Thilo Sentker*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This study developed an nnU-Net-based deep learning framework for automated ischemic stroke segmentation on non-contrast CT (NCCT) and evaluated its suitability for net water uptake (NWU) quantification across heterogeneous multicenter data. The model achieved median Dice scores of 0.68 (Boston) and 0.56 (ISLES) for lesions ≥30 mL, with NWU mean absolute error of 1.37 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current quantitative assessment of infarct hypodensity on NCCT, including NWU measurement, requires manual or semi-manual lesion delineation often guided by CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI, limiting clinical applicability. An automated segmentation solution could enable efficient biomarker extraction but faces challenges across heterogeneous multicenter data.

Method: Retrospective multicenter study with 801 patients from four datasets. An nnU-Net-based model was trained on NCCT scans from University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf and Acute Ischemic Stroke Dataset, then fine-tuned on target-domain subsets from Boston (n=11) and ISLES (n=75), with evaluation on held-out cases. Automated segmentations and NWU values were compared with expert references.

Result: For lesions ≥30 mL, median Dice was 0.68 (Boston) and 0.56 (ISLES). Including smaller lesions, median Dice was 0.54 (IQR 0.30-0.70) for Boston and 0.20 (IQR 0.03-0.41) for ISLES when compared to post-treatment infarct. Automated NWU mean absolute error was 1.37 percentage points (SD 1.61, Boston).

Conclusion: Target-domain adaptation supported NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous external cohorts, though performance varied across domains. The approach enabled low-error NWU quantification from baseline NCCT without advanced imaging, supporting further prospective clinical evaluation.

Abstract: Objectives: Quantitative assessment of infarct hypodensity on non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), including net water uptake (NWU), requires manual or semi-manual lesion delineation, often guided by CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI, limiting clinical applicability. Automated segmentation on NCCT could enable efficient biomarker extraction such as NWU but remains challenging across heterogeneous multicenter data. This study aimed to develop and externally test a domain-aware deep learning framework for ischemic stroke segmentation on NCCT and assess its suitability for NWU quantification.
  Materials & Methods: In this retrospective multicenter study of 801 patients from four datasets, an nnU-Net-based model was trained on NCCT scans from the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf and the Acute Ischemic Stroke Dataset. To adapt to new domains, the model was fine-tuned on target-domain subsets from Boston (n=11) and ISLES (n=75), with evaluation on held-out cases not used for fine-tuning. Automated segmentations and NWU values were compared with expert references.
  Results: For lesions $\geq$ 30 mL, median Dice was 0.68 (Boston) and 0.56 (ISLES). Including smaller lesions, which predominated in ISLES, median Dice was 0.54 (interquartile range [IQR] 0.30-0.70) for acute lesion segmentation (Boston dataset) and 0.20 (IQR 0.03-0.41) for NCCT lesion segmentations when compared to post-treatment infarct (primary target of the ISLES challenge). Automated NWU mean absolute error was 1.37 percentage points (SD 1.61, Boston).
  Conclusion: Target-domain adaptation supported NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous external cohorts, although performance varied across domains. The approach enabled low-error NWU quantification from baseline NCCT without advanced imaging, supporting further prospective clinical evaluation.

</details>


### [62] [Needles in a Raystack: Ultra-Sparse LiDAR Occupancy Detection for Bat Tracks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20160)
*Nico Klar,Pankaj Rana,Nizam Gifary,Jakob Traub,Aamir Ahmad*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of monitoring nocturnal bats using LiDAR, which produces ultra-sparse 3D data where standard reconstruction losses fail to detect real flight paths. The authors propose a lightweight 3D U-Net for voxel-wise occupancy detection that handles class imbalance through combined weighted BCE and Dice loss. The method successfully recovers bat flight trajectories in real LiDAR recordings, enabling applications in biodiversity monitoring and turbine curtailment strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monitoring flying animals, particularly nocturnal species like bats, is crucial for biodiversity understanding and protection. However, bats are difficult to observe in the field at night. LiDAR technology can capture bat movements, but produces ultra-sparse 3D spatio-temporal data where standard reconstruction losses tend to predict only background and miss real flight paths.

Method: The problem is framed as voxel-wise occupancy detection in sensor-centric LiDAR raystacks. A lightweight 3D U-Net is proposed with three key design elements: (1) preservation of temporal resolution, (2) skip connections for spatial detail, and (3) combination of weighted binary cross-entropy with Dice loss to handle the strong class imbalance between background and foreground (bats).

Result: In real LiDAR recordings of bats over open fields (cross-validated with acoustic monitoring), a reconstruction-based 3D convolutional autoencoder baseline fails to recover foreground trajectories. In contrast, the proposed U-Net successfully recovers sparse foreground occupancy in diagnostic experiments and produces coherent occupancy patterns along bat flight trajectories.

Conclusion: The proposed U-Net provides a practical basis for validation-scale experiments, flight track clustering, and future integration of bat activity information into biodiversity-aware turbine curtailment strategies. This enables better monitoring and protection of bat populations.

Abstract: Monitoring flying animals is important for understanding and protecting biodiversity, but nocturnal species such as bats are difficult to observe in the field. Using LiDAR, bat movements at night result in ultra-sparse 3D spatio-temporal data in which standard reconstruction losses tend to predict only background and miss real flight paths. We study this problem as voxel-wise occupancy detection in sensor-centric LiDAR raystacks. A lightweight 3D U-Net is proposed that preserves temporal resolution, uses skip connections for spatial detail, and combines weighted binary cross-entropy with Dice loss to handle the strong class imbalance.
  In real LiDAR recordings of bats over open fields, cross-checked with acoustic monitoring, a reconstruction-based 3D convolutional autoencoder baseline fails to recover foreground trajectories. In contrast, the proposed U-Net recovers sparse foreground occupancy in diagnostic experiments and produces coherent occupancy patterns along bat flight trajectories, providing a practical basis for validation-scale experiments, later clustering of flight tracks, and future integration of bat activity information into biodiversity-aware turbine curtailment strategies.

</details>


### [63] [MTF-Net: Multi-Modal Temporal Feature Fusion Network for Pedestrian Intention Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20178)
*Md Mahfuzur Rahman,Pengzhan Zhou,A. F. M. Abdun Noor,Md Imam Ahasan,Md Mustafizur Rahman,Fang Qu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MTF-Net proposes a multi-modal temporal feature fusion approach for pedestrian intention prediction in autonomous vehicles. It jointly models kinematic, appearance, and contextual cues using four complementary modalities (bounding-box dynamics, human pose keypoints, local context, scene-level semantics) within a recurrent fusion framework enhanced by gated linear units (GLUs). The model achieves 0.95 AUC on PIE and 0.94 AUC on JAAD benchmarks while maintaining real-time performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for pedestrian intention prediction have two key limitations: (1) they only model temporal dependencies within individual modalities, and (2) they fuse modalities only at coarse semantic levels. This restricts the ability to accurately predict pedestrian crossing intentions in advance.

Method: MTF-Net integrates four complementary modalities within a recurrent fusion framework enhanced by gated linear units (GLUs). The architecture includes: (1) Three dedicated temporal encoding branches for different modalities, (2) GLU-based modules that adaptively regulate cross-modal information flow across temporal scales, and (3) An attention-guided fusion head for robust prediction. The GLUs enable interpretable and efficient feature interaction.

Result: MTF-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance on both PIE and JAAD benchmarks, reaching 0.95 AUC on PIE and 0.94 AUC on JAAD. It surpasses recent transformer- and graph-based models while maintaining real-time performance.

Conclusion: Reliable pedestrian intention prediction arises from principled multi-modal fusion rather than excessive architectural complexity. The success of MTF-Net demonstrates that effectively combining multiple modalities (kinematic, appearance, and contextual cues) with adaptive gating mechanisms can achieve superior performance without requiring overly complex architectures.

Abstract: Accurately predicting pedestrian intentions is crucial for ensuring safe and proactive interaction between autonomous vehicles and pedestrians. However, existing approaches often depend on architectures that either model temporal dependencies within individual modalities or fuse modalities only at coarse semantic levels. To address these limitations, we propose MTF-Net, a novel Multi-Modal Temporal Feature Fusion Network that jointly models kinematic, appearance, and contextual cues for pedestrian intention prediction. MTF-Net integrates four complementary modalities-bounding-box dynamics, human pose keypoints, local context, and scene-level semantics within a recurrent fusion framework enhanced by gated linear units (GLUs). These GLU-based modules adaptively regulate cross-modal information flow, enabling interpretable and efficient feature interaction across temporal scales. Through three dedicated temporal encoding branches and an attention-guided fusion head, the proposed model robustly anticipates pedestrian crossing intentions several frames before they occur. Extensive evaluations on the PIE and JAAD benchmarks demonstrate that MTF-Net surpasses recent transformer- and graph-based models, achieving up to 0.95 AUC on PIE and 0.94 AUC on JAAD, while maintaining real-time performance. The results highlight that reliable pedestrian intention prediction arises from principled multi-modal fusion rather than excessive architectural complexity.

</details>


### [64] [MoSSGate: Memory-Modulated State-Space Gating for Skin Lesion Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20181)
*Anum Awan,Mahnoor Buriro,Muhammad Younas Khan,Md Imam Ahasan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MoSSGate is a plug-and-play module for U-Net that enhances skin lesion segmentation by combining boundary-aware spatial gating, external memory modulation, and parallel 2D state-space modeling to capture global context while preserving fine boundary details, achieving 86.3%/85.9% mIoU and 92.6%/90.6% Dice on ISIC 2017/2018 with improved efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CNN and transformer-based models struggle to jointly capture long-range spatial dependencies and fine boundary details under limited computational budgets, leading to over-segmentation, fragmented predictions, or missing thin peripheral structures. This trade-off between global context and boundary-aware localization is the core problem.

Method: MoSSGate integrates three components: (i) boundary-aware spatial gating to restrict long-range propagation to informative regions, (ii) an external memory modulator for sample-adaptive dynamic control, and (iii) parallel 2D state-space modeling for efficient global context aggregation with linear complexity. This module is designed as plug-and-play for U-Net architectures.

Result: On ISIC 2017 and ISIC 2018 benchmarks, MoSSGate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 86.3% and 85.9% mIoU, 92.6% and 90.6% Dice respectively, while requiring substantially fewer FLOPs than competing CNN-based methods.

Conclusion: MoSSGate demonstrates a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for high-resolution medical image segmentation, successfully balancing global context modeling with boundary-aware localization through its innovative gating and state-space mechanisms.

Abstract: Accurate skin lesion segmentation is crucial for reliable computer-aided dermatological diagnosis, yet existing convolutional and transformer-based models often struggle to jointly capture long-range spatial dependencies and fine boundary details under limited computational budgets. This trade-off between global context modeling and boundary-aware localization frequently leads to over-segmentation, fragmented predictions, or missing thin peripheral structures. To address this challenge, we propose MoSSGate, a plug-and-play module for U-Net that integrates (i) boundary-aware spatial gating to restrict long-range propagation to informative regions, (ii) an external memory modulator that provides sample-adaptive dynamic control, and (iii) parallel 2D state-space modeling for efficient global context aggregation with linear complexity. The proposed design enables adaptive, context-aware information propagation while preserving sharp and accurate lesion boundaries. Extensive experiments on the ISIC 2017 and ISIC 2018 benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with strong efficiency, achieving 86.3% and 85.9% mIoU and 92.6% and 90.6% Dice, respectively, while requiring substantially fewer FLOPs than most competing CNN-based methods. These results highlight a favorable accuracy efficiency trade-off for high-resolution medical image segmentation.

</details>


### [65] [A Two-Stage Multi-Scale Attention-Based Network for Weakly Supervised Cataract Fundus Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20222)
*Xiaoyong Fang,Yue Wang,Xiangyu Li,Wanshu Fan,Dongsheng Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes TSMSA-Net, a two-stage multi-scale attention-based network for weakly supervised cataract fundus image enhancement. It addresses the challenge of limited paired training images by using domain transformation to synthesize paired real-like cataract images, and employs a multi-scale attention mechanism to extract fine details while reducing artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cataract is a major cause of vision loss that hinders further diagnosis. Existing cataract fundus image enhancement methods struggle with two key challenges: 1) difficulty in acquiring paired cataract retinal images, and 2) insufficient recovery of fine details in enhanced retinal images.

Method: The proposed TSMSA-Net consists of two stages: (1) Domain transformation module that synthesizes paired real-like cataract images from unpaired data to solve the paired image acquisition problem; (2) Multi-scale attention-based stage that extracts detailed information from fundus images while reducing artifacts during enhancement.

Result: Experimental results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K datasets show that TSMSA-Net outperforms current state-of-the-art cataract fundus image enhancement methods, even without paired images. The method also demonstrates certain generalization ability and can improve vessel segmentation and classification performance in cataract images.

Conclusion: The two-stage multi-scale attention-based network successfully addresses the challenges of limited paired training data and insufficient detail recovery in cataract fundus image enhancement. It achieves superior performance compared to existing methods while maintaining generalization capability and downstream task improvement (vessel segmentation and classification).

Abstract: Cataract is a major cause of vision loss and hinders further diagnosis. However, cataract fundus image enhancement often grapples with challenges such as limited paired cataract retinal images and insufficient recovery of fine details in the retinal images. To mitigate these challenges, we in this paper propose a two-stage multi-scale attention-based network (TSMSA-Net) for weakly supervised cataract fundus image enhancement. Our TSMSA-Net leverages the domain transformation to synthesis paired real-like cataract images, solving the problem of difficult acquisition of paired images. To further extract detailed information from fundus images and reduce the generation of artifacts during the enhancement process, we propose a multi-scale attention-based stage to learn more useful features for cataract image enhancement. Experimental results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K demonstrate that our TSMSA-Net outperforms current state-of-the-art cataract fundus images enhancement even without paired images and exhibits certain generalization ability. Experimental results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K datasets indicate that our TSMSA-Net outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods for cataract fundus image enhancement, even in the absence of paired images. Additionally, it demonstrates a certain level of generalization capability. The enhancement also can improve the performance of vessel segmentation and classification in cataract images.

</details>


### [66] [Scene-Q: Confidence-Aware Coarse-to-Fine Querying of 3D Scenes with Selective VLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20235)
*Juno Kim,Yesol Park,Hye-Jung Yoon,Byoung-Tak Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Scene-Q is a confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying framework for indoor mobile robots that combines fast contrastive retrieval with selective VLM reasoning for ambiguous queries, improving open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation and natural-language 3D instance retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current systems rely on cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image-text encoders, which is efficient but brittle when labels are near-synonymous or multiple similar instances appear in indoor scenes.

Method: Scene-Q normalizes encoder scores with temperature scaling and selectively invokes a reasoning VLM only for low-confidence cases. High-confidence queries use fast retrieval, while ambiguous queries are reranked over a small top-K candidate set using multi-view images and instance bounding boxes for context-aware disambiguation.

Result: Scene-Q improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet200 and natural-language 3D instance retrieval on real-world reconstructions, with largest gains on spatial and relational queries while maintaining a substantial fraction of queries on the fast path.

Conclusion: The framework successfully balances efficiency and accuracy by using a hybrid approach: fast retrieval for high-confidence queries and VLM-based reasoning for ambiguous cases, achieving improved performance on spatial and relational queries at low computational cost.

Abstract: Indoor mobile robots require open-vocabulary scene understanding that grounds natural-language queries in a consistent 3D map. Many existing systems ultimately rely on cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image--text encoders, which is efficient but brittle when labels are near-synonymous or multiple similar instances appear. We present Scene-Q, a confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying framework that normalizes encoder scores with temperature scaling and selectively invokes a reasoning VLM only for low-confidence cases. High-confidence queries are answered by fast retrieval, while ambiguous ones are reranked over a small top-K candidate set using the original multi-view images and instance bounding boxes, enabling context-aware disambiguation at low cost. Scene-Q improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet200 and natural-language 3D instance retrieval on real-world reconstructions, with the largest gains on spatial and relational queries while keeping a substantial fraction of queries on the fast path.

</details>


### [67] [SAGE-Yoga: Multi-Cue Learning for Yoga Pose Classification and Joint-Level Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20245)
*Hung Le Chi,Khanh Minh Huynh,Long Nghia Tran Pham,Tan Phuc Huynh,Trong-Thuan Nguyen,Minh-Triet Tran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SAGE-Yoga is a unified coarse-to-fine framework for yoga pose classification and joint-level correction from single RGB images. It combines a bagging-based ensemble of visual backbones with margin-based gating for geometric verification, achieving 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1 on Yoga-82 dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing yoga analysis methods have three key limitations: (1) rely on single visual predictions, (2) struggle to distinguish visually similar poses, and (3) treat pose classification and correction as separate tasks rather than unified framework.

Method: The framework employs: (1) Bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones for generating ranked candidate pose classes; (2) Margin-based gating mechanism that preserves confident predictions while invoking geometric verification only for ambiguous cases; (3) Medoid reference pose retrieval for final pose class; (4) Joint angle comparison with class-specific distributions to identify misaligned joints; (5) Translation of deviations into actionable corrective feedback.

Result: Visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy. Complete framework improves to 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1 on Yoga-82 dataset.

Conclusion: Combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification improves fine-grained pose classification while enabling interpretable, joint-level correction. The coarse-to-fine approach effectively addresses visually similar pose distinctions and provides actionable feedback.

Abstract: Automated yoga analysis requires both accurate pose classification and interpretable feedback on pose execution. However, existing methods often rely on a single visual prediction, struggle to distinguish visually similar poses, and treat pose classification and correction as separate tasks. To address these limitations, we propose SAGE-Yoga, a unified coarse-to-fine framework for yoga pose classification and joint-level correction from a single RGB image. Inspired by how yoga instructors assess posture using multiple complementary cues, SAGE-Yoga first employs a bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones to generate a ranked set of candidate pose classes. Additionally, a margin-based gating mechanism preserves confident visual predictions while invoking geometric verification only for ambiguous cases. Moreover, once the final pose class is determined, SAGE-Yoga retrieves a medoid reference pose and compares the observed joint angles with class-specific distributions to identify misaligned joints. Finally, these deviations are translated into actionable corrective feedback. Empirically, experiments on the Yoga-82 dataset show that the visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy, while the complete framework improves performance to 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1. These results demonstrate that combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification improves fine-grained pose classification while enabling interpretable, joint-level correction.

</details>


### [68] [Distance to Class Prototypes: Active Learning for Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20248)
*Licheng Zhang,Zheng Gong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel active learning criterion for object detection that uses supervised contrastive learning to create an embedding space where distance encodes class membership. The method scores unlabeled images based on how far detections lie from their predicted category region, achieving better performance than class posterior while requiring only a single forward pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key bottleneck in deploying deep object detectors is the cost of annotating data for new settings. Existing active learning signals either use class posterior (cheap but poorly calibrated) or model disagreement (better but requires multiple inferences). The authors sought a richer signal that comes from a single forward pass of one network.

Method: The method adds a supervised contrastive term to the training objective, shaping a per-object embedding space where distance encodes class membership. Unlabeled detections are scored by measuring how far they lie from the region occupied by their predicted category, weighted by confidence. This requires only 2.89M additional parameters (8.3% increase over baseline detector).

Result: On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO, the proposed criterion outperforms the posterior of the same detector in every selection round, with improvements up to 1.08% mAP50. The method remains competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria that cost 3-50x more forward passes per image.

Conclusion: The supervised contrastive embedding approach provides a cost-effective active learning criterion for object detection, achieving better performance than posterior-based methods while requiring only a single forward pass, making it practical for real-world deployment where annotation costs are prohibitive.

Abstract: Deploying a deep object detector in a new setting is limited less by architecture than by the cost of annotating data from that setting. Active learning lowers the cost by choosing which images to label, and the choice is only as good as the signal used to score an unlabeled image. That signal is usually the class posterior, which is cheap but poorly calibrated, or the disagreement across several models or several stochastic passes, which is better but multiplies inference over a pool far larger than the labeled set. We propose a signal richer than the posterior yet still read from one forward pass of one network. A supervised contrastive term added to the training objective shapes a per-object embedding space in which distance encodes class membership, and an unlabeled detection is scored by how far it lies from the region occupied by its predicted category, weighted by its confidence. The criterion needs no ensemble, no auxiliary predictor and no repeated inference, and its entire cost is 2.89M parameters, an increase of 8.3% over a bare detector. On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO it beats the posterior of the same detector in every round in which a selection is made, by up to 1.08% mAP50 against run to run deviations of 0.02% to 0.18%, and it stays competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria costing three to fifty forward passes per unlabeled image. Experiments use the single-stage detector under which the compared criteria report their results, so that the selection decision is isolated from the strength of the detector.

</details>


### [69] [Generative Verification: Rethinking the Uncertainty Signal for Active Learning of Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20262)
*Licheng Zhang,Zheng Gong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes "generative verification" for active object detection, where an independent conditional diffusion model re-derives labels from detection box crops. The disagreement between the detector and verifier becomes the acquisition signal, eliminating the need for hand-weighted classification and localization terms. The method outperforms existing criteria on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current active object detection methods use the same model for both detection and interrogation. This creates a fundamental limitation: the model being improved is also the model being interrogated. Additionally, confidently wrong detections are problematic because they score low on uncertainty-based methods but are costly to leave unlabeled.

Method: The approach uses a conditional diffusion model as an independent verifier. The diffusion target is a label representation (not an image). The reverse process is stochastic, so repeated generations return a distribution whose concentration reports how firmly the evidence determines the label. The disagreement between the detector's prediction and the verifier's re-derived label becomes the acquisition signal.

Result: On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO datasets, the signal outperforms output-uncertainty, feature-geometry, perturbation, and ensemble criteria. It gains about one mAP50 point per round on MS-COCO, with largest margins in early rounds where confident detector errors are most common.

Conclusion: Generative verification is a promising approach that addresses the limitations of traditional active object detection by using an independent verifier. The key advantages are: (1) failure modes are already combined in one scalar, eliminating hand-weighted classification and localization terms; (2) confidently wrong detections naturally score highest, making them more likely to be labeled. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Nearly every acquisition function for active object detection shares one arrangement, in that the model being improved is also the model being interrogated. We depart from it. In generative verification an independent generative model re-derives the label of a detection from the pixels inside its predicted box, and the disagreement between the two becomes the acquisition signal. Two properties follow from the arrangement itself rather than from any tuning. A displaced box, a box on background and a correct box carrying the wrong label all yield a crop that fails verification, so the failure modes arrive already combined in one scalar and the hand-weighted classification and localization terms of existing criteria are no longer needed.
