And because the verifier never observes the detector confidence, confidently wrong detections score highest, although a self-derived signal reads them as uninteresting and they are the costliest to leave unlabeled. We build the verifier as a conditional diffusion model whose diffusion target is a label representation rather than an image. Its reverse process is stochastic, so repeated generations return a distribution whose concentration reports how firmly the evidence determines the label, where a classifier returns a single point estimate. On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO the signal outperforms output-uncertainty, feature-geometry, perturbation and ensemble criteria, gaining about one mAP50 point per round on MS-COCO, with its largest margins in the early rounds where confident detector errors are most common.

</details>


### [70] [AI or Real: Detecting Partially Altered Videos Under Resource-Constrained Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20263)
*Tamoghna Chakraborty,Md Nurul Absur,Sourya Saha,Saptarshi Debroy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A lightweight full-frame detector for partially manipulated AI-generated video that can run on edge hardware. It distills a DINOv2-Base teacher into a MobileNetV3-Small student, achieving 0.766 AUC while running at 3.65ms per 16-frame clip with only 150.4MB model size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of generative video models has shifted the threat from fully fabricated clips to partially manipulated footage. While modern detectors achieve strong accuracy using large foundation backbones (400M+ parameters), their resource footprint prevents edge deployment. There is a need for lightweight detectors that can run on edge hardware without face-detection preprocessing.

Method: The system uses knowledge distillation with four key components: (1) temperature-annealed soft-label transfer, (2) attention-diversity regularization, (3) frame-level supervision, and (4) a residual feature adapter that conditions ImageNet features for artifact detection. It also addresses two specific failure modes: false positives on legitimate scene cuts (using within-video temporal hard negatives) and threshold-level miscalibration on the pure-real class (through calibration-aware sampling).

Result: The student model achieves AUC of 0.766, closing 58% of the gap to the DINOv2-Base teacher. It runs at 3.65 ms per 16-frame clip on RTX A4000 with a 150.4 MB checkpoint, suitable for edge-device memory and latency budgets.

Conclusion: The proposed distilled MobileNetV3-Small model successfully balances detection accuracy and computational efficiency, making it viable for edge deployment in detecting partially manipulated AI-generated video without requiring face-detection preprocessing.

Abstract: The proliferation of generative video models has shifted the practical detection threat from fully fabricated clips to partially manipulated footages. Although modern detectors achieve strong accuracy using foundation backbones of 400M+ parameters, their resource footprint precludes edge deployment. In this paper, we present a lightweight full-frame detector for partially manipulated AI-generated video, designed for deployment on edge hardware without face-detection preprocessing. The system distills a DINOv2-Base teacher into a frozen MobileNetV3-Small student through a pipeline that combines temperature-annealed soft-label transfer, attention-diversity regularization, frame-level supervision, and a residual feature adapter that conditions ImageNet features for artifact detection. We additionally target two failure modes specific to the partial-manipulation regime: false positives on legitimate scene cuts, addressed through within-video temporal hard negatives; and threshold-level miscalibration on the dominant pure-real class, addressed through calibration-aware sampling. Evaluation on a 55,393-sample spliced test set across fake-frame ratios from 6.2% to 31.2% demonstrates the student model closing 58% of the gap to the DINOv2-Base teacher (AUC 0.766) while running at 3.65 ms per 16-frame clip on RTX A4000 with a 150.4 MB checkpoint compatible with edge-device memory and latency budgets.

</details>


### [71] [CleanVideo: Adaptive Concept Erasure for Text-to-Video Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20267)
*Junchi Liao,Hongji Li,Wenrui Zhou,Lijie Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CleanVideo is a framework for erasing undesired concepts from video diffusion models using a tri-modal gating mechanism that controls low-dimensional subspace intervention. It processes spatiotemporal visual features, timestep signals, and textual semantics to determine where, when, and whether to intervene.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extending concept erasure from images to video is challenging because target concepts emerge gradually and vary across frames and denoising steps, causing fixed interventions to miss targets or introduce visual artifacts like blurring and jitter.

Method: CleanVideo uses a tri-modal gating mechanism that jointly processes spatiotemporal visual features, timestep signals, and textual semantics to determine intervention locations. It performs low-dimensional subspace intervention to steer erased content toward natural surrogate concepts while preserving non-target content.

Result: Experiments on three video diffusion models show CleanVideo effectively erases target concepts while maintaining visual fidelity and temporal coherence, outperforming existing baselines under frame-level and video-level evaluations and under concept-recovery attacks.

Conclusion: CleanVideo successfully bridges concept erasure from images to video by using adaptive, tri-modal controlled intervention that addresses the temporal dynamics of concept emergence, achieving superior erasure performance without compromising visual quality.

Abstract: Concept erasure aims to selectively eliminate undesired visual semantics from pre-trained generative models without compromising their general utility. Extending concept erasure from images to video is nontrivial. Target concepts emerge gradually and vary across frames and denoising steps. As a result, fixed interventions may miss the target or introduce blurring, jitter, and content distortion. We propose CleanVideo, a selective erasure framework that performs low-dimensional subspace intervention controlled by a tri-modal gating mechanism. By jointly processing spatiotemporal visual features, timestep signals, and textual semantics, CleanVideo determines where, when, and whether to intervene, steering erased content toward natural surrogate concepts when such surrogates can be clearly defined while preserving non-target content. Experiments on three video diffusion models show that CleanVideo effectively erases target concepts while maintaining visual fidelity and temporal coherence, outperforming existing baselines under frame-level and video-level evaluations and under concept-recovery attacks when the protected pipeline remains intact.

</details>


### [72] [Queries Knew More Than We Thought: Uncovering Latent Knowledge in Segmentation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20283)
*Ignacio M. De la Jara,Cristian Rodriguez-Opazo,Damith Ranasinghe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses an "output-selection bottleneck" in frozen DETR-family segmenters where useful masks exist among computed candidates but are not exposed by the selection rule. The proposed method HYDRA is a small selector trained on cached frozen outputs that recovers this hidden headroom without adding queries, generating new masks, rerunning the backbone, or updating weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observe that ground-truth-only oracle shows substantial hidden headroom in already-computed mask proposals, meaning useful masks exist but are suppressed by the deployed selection rule. This raises the question of how to better use masks the segmenter has already computed but does not expose.

Method: HYDRA is a small selector trained only on cached frozen outputs. At inference time, it scores cached candidates against an explicit keep-baseline option and acts only when a held-out calibrated margin indicates the selected candidate is sufficiently better. The method uses calibration on held-out data to decide when to override the baseline selection.

Result: HYDRA improves Mask2Former, MaskDINO, and OneFormer by up to +7.41 dataset mIoU points on ADE20k and COCO, and improves SAM 3 by +9.4 class-macro prompt-IoU points on average across eight domains. Paired LoRA controls show that lightweight weight adaptation does not remove the bottleneck - exposed predictions remain flat or worse while routing over adapted candidates still recovers accuracy.

Conclusion: Frozen segmenters should be evaluated not only by the masks they expose, but also by the useful candidates they suppress. The output-selection bottleneck is a significant issue that can be addressed without expensive computation by properly selecting from already-computed candidates.

Abstract: Modern segmenters often fail after the expensive computation has already been done: a useful mask is present among the model's query-conditioned candidates, but the deployed selection rule does not expose it. We study this output-selection bottleneck in frozen DETR-family models. A ground-truth-only oracle first shows substantial hidden headroom in already-computed mask proposals. This raises a simple question: How can we better use the masks a segmenter has already computed but does not expose? We then ask whether that headroom can be recovered without adding queries, generating new masks, rerunning the backbone, or updating weights. HYDRA is a small selector trained only on cached frozen outputs. At inference time, it scores the cached candidates against an explicit keep-baseline option and acts only when a held-out calibrated margin indicates the selected candidate is sufficiently better. Trained on training-split caches and calibrated on held-out data, HYDRA improves Mask2Former, MaskDINO, and OneFormer by up to +7.41 dataset mIoU points on ADE20k and COCO, and improves SAM 3 by +9.4 class-macro prompt-IoU points on average across eight domains while preserving useful predictions through calibration. Paired LoRA controls show that lightweight weight adaptation does not remove the bottleneck: exposed predictions are often flat or worse, while routing over the adapted candidates still recovers accuracy. Finally, we connect the effect to query specialization under bipartite matching and verify it in a controlled TinyDETR study. These results show that frozen segmenters should be evaluated not only by the masks they expose, but also by the useful candidates they suppress.

</details>


### [73] [TinyCNN: A 193K-Parameter Network for On-Device Plant Disease Detection, with a Cross-Dataset Robustness Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20290)
*Ngoc-Bao Ho-Lam,Thai-Anh Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TinyCNN is a lightweight convolutional neural network (193,190 parameters, 110.05M MACs) for on-device plant disease classification, achieving 98.88% accuracy on PlantVillage while being 58x smaller than ResNet18. Knowledge distillation achieves 98.81% accuracy, but cross-dataset evaluation reveals a significant robustness gap attributed to shortcut learning via background-driven attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early crop disease detection is critical for sustainable agriculture and food security (UN SDG 2 - Zero Hunger), particularly in resource-constrained regions where expert diagnosis is scarce but low-cost mobile devices are widespread. The need for energy-efficient, deployable models that can run on edge devices aligns with Green AI principles.

Method: TinyCNN uses depthwise separable convolution blocks for lightweight design. The paper evaluates vanilla knowledge distillation with varying alpha {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} and temperature T {2, 4}. Grad-CAM analysis is used to interpret model attention and explain robustness gaps in cross-dataset evaluation (PlantVillage to PlantDoc).

Result: On the 38-class PlantVillage benchmark, TinyCNN achieves 98.88% test accuracy and 98.03% macro-F1. It is 58x smaller than ResNet18 and 11.8x smaller than MobileNetV2 teacher. The best distilled model uses alpha=0.3, T=4, achieving 98.81% test accuracy. Cross-dataset evaluation from PlantVillage to PlantDoc reveals a substantial robustness gap due to off-leaf, background-driven attention consistent with shortcut learning.

Conclusion: TinyCNN serves as an energy-efficient, deployable building block for sustainable agricultural intelligence, directly reducing energy, memory, and cost footprint in line with Green AI principles. However, field robustness remains the key barrier to durable real-world impact, as the model relies on shortcut features (background) rather than disease-specific features when transferred to real-world conditions.

Abstract: Detecting crop disease early is central to sustainable agriculture and food security under United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger), and is especially urgent in resource-constrained regions where expert diagnosis is scarce but low-cost mobile devices are widespread. This paper presents TinyCNN, a lightweight convolutional neural network for on-device plant disease classification. TinyCNN uses depthwise separable convolution blocks and contains only 193,190 trainable parameters with 110.05M MACs for a 224x224 input image. On the 38-class PlantVillage benchmark, TinyCNN achieves 98.88% test accuracy and 98.03% macro-F1 while being approximately 58x smaller than ResNet18 and 11.8x smaller than a MobileNetV2 teacher, directly reducing the energy, memory, and cost footprint of inference in line with Green AI principles. The paper further analyzes vanilla knowledge distillation as a sustainable model-compression strategy; an ablation over alpha in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} and T in {2, 4} selects alpha=0.3, T=4, producing a distilled TinyCNN with 98.81% test accuracy. Finally, cross-dataset evaluation from PlantVillage to PlantDoc reveals a substantial robustness gap under real-world conditions, which a Grad-CAM analysis attributes to off-leaf, background-driven attention consistent with shortcut learning. TinyCNN is thus an energy-efficient, deployable building block for sustainable agricultural intelligence, while field robustness remains the key barrier to durable real-world impact.

</details>


### [74] [Not All Layers Are Equal: Dynamic Layer Routing for Reliable CLIP OOD Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20299)
*Ignacio M. De la Jara,Cristian Rodriguez-Opazo,Damith Ranasinghe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Voyager is a learnable routing method that selects optimal CLIP layers for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection through a lightweight router, achieving state-of-the-art performance with 8.8 point improvement over prompt-learning methods on ImageNet-1K (FPR@95 of 18.86) while being 20x more efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates whether layer selection in CLIP can be learned rather than manually crafted. While prior work focuses on how to fuse layers, this work asks "which layers to trust" for a given input. The motivation is to move from fixed aggregation methods to a learnable, input-dependent layer selection approach.

Method: The method uses a weak, generalizable OOD context crafting approach for supervision to train a lightweight router. This router selects a sparse, final-layer-anchored expert over CLIP's layer depth. The key innovation is the learnable routing mechanism rather than the supervision source itself.

Result: On ImageNet-1K, Voyager achieves an average FPR@95 of 18.86, outperforming the strongest comparable prompt-learning method by 8.8 points. The gains persist across multiple supervision sources. The router learning takes approximately 2 minutes using less than 1 GB of memory, making it approximately 20x more efficient than current prompt-learning approaches.

Conclusion: The key advantage comes from the learnable router component rather than the supervision source. Voyager demonstrates that learnable routing is a superior approach for OOD detection, achieving better performance while being significantly more efficient than existing prompt-learning methods. The method is highly practical and generalizable across diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: Information aggregation across model layers are revealed to improve OOD detection. In contrast to crafting a method for layer-wise information aggregation in recent work, we investigate if layer selection is a learnable problem. In other words, we transpose the question from how to fuse layers to one asking which layers to trust for an input. Using a generalizable, weak, out of distribution context crafting approach for supervision, shown to be more effective than state of the art methods' mechanisms, we formulate learning a lightweight router to select a sparse, final-layer-anchored expert over CLIP's layer depth for OOD detection.
  Across three diverse benchmarks we demonstrate our learnable routing method dubbed Voyager improves OOD detection. On ImageNet-1K, Voyager achieves an average FPR@95 of 18.86, outperforming the strongest, comparable, prompt-learning method by 8.8 points. These gains persist across multiple supervision sources, including those used by existing state-of-the-art prompt-learning methods, demonstrating that, whilst our weak OOD supervision context is highly effective, the key advantage is realized from the learnable router component rather than the supervision source. Significantly, Voyager is highly practical; router learning takes approximately two minutes using less than 1 GB of memory, making it approximately 20x more efficient than current prompt-learning approaches.
  Anonymized Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Voyager/

</details>


### [75] [AgriScope: Pixel-Grounded Multimodal Understanding for Agricultural Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20325)
*Abderrahmene Boudiaf,Mohamad Alanssari,Irfan Hussain,Sajid Javed*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Agricultural image understanding requires fine-grained recognition of plant diseases, pests, crop structures, and botanical species under complex real-world conditions. Despite recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), existing models remain limited to text-only outputs and lack pixel-level visual grounding capabilities. In this work, we introduce AgriScope, a unified pixel-grounded multimodal framework for agricultural image understanding. AgriScope jointly supports image-level, region-level, and pixel-level understanding within a unified framework, enabling tasks such as grounded caption generation, referring expression segmentation, and multi-turn multimodal interaction for agricultural imagery. AgriScope integrates biologically specialized semantic representations with dense spatial grounding through biological-semantic encoding, dense spatial representations, and pixel decoding. To support large-scale grounded learning, we introduce AgriGround, a large-scale pixel-grounded agricultural multimodal instruction-tuning dataset containing over 500K images and 11M instruction-following samples spanning plant disease analysis, crop and weed identification, insect pest recognition, and fine-grained botanical understanding. AgriGround is constructed through a multi-stage automatic annotation pipeline that integrates multimodal caption generation, phrase-level grounding, segmentation mask generation, and task-oriented instruction synthesis to produce densely grounded supervision. Extensive experiments across multiple agricultural vision-language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of AgriScope in pixel-grounded multimodal understanding, establishing a strong benchmark for agricultural vision-language learning and visual grounding. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at (https://github.com/boudiafA/AgriScope)

</details>


### [76] [FreqDINO++: A Frequency-Guided Multi-Task Routing Vision Foundation Model for Universal Ultrasound Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20340)
*Qing Xu,Yixuan Zhang,Yue Li,Xiangjian He,Qian Zhang,Mainul Haque,Rong Qu,Wenting Duan,Jieyun Bai,Zhen Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FreqDINO++ is a frequency-guided multi-task vision foundation model for universal ultrasound image analysis, addressing lesion segmentation and benign-malignant classification tasks through parameter-efficient fine-tuning of vision encoders, with a Multi-task Routing Adapter, Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer, and Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ultrasound image analysis is crucial for cancer screening and prenatal diagnosis, but existing methods face three key challenges: 1) the domain gap between natural images and ultrasound is large, 2) heavy vision encoders require substantial computational overhead for fine-tuning, and 3) heterogeneous tasks (segmentation, classification) are addressed in isolation, overlooking their commonalities.

Method: The proposed FreqDINO++ consists of three key components: 1) Multi-task Routing Adapter (MR-Adapter) for parameter-efficient integration of task-common and task-specific knowledge; 2) Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer (F²-Enhancer) to capture multi-scale frequency characteristics of ultrasound images; 3) Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder (TC-Decoder) to promote collaboration between dense (segmentation) and global (classification) prediction tasks through global-local token interaction.

Result: FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 diverse clinical task scenarios on large-scale multi-task and external single-task ultrasound benchmarks, while showing promising generalization to unseen data.

Conclusion: The frequency-guided multi-task routing approach effectively bridges the domain gap between natural images and ultrasound, achieving superior performance across multiple clinical tasks with parameter-efficient fine-tuning, demonstrating both effectiveness and generalization capability.

Abstract: Ultrasound image analysis plays a crucial role in cancer screening and prenatal diagnosis, yet comprehensive assessment requires jointly addressing tasks such as lesion segmentation and benign-malignant classification. While recent vision foundation models have shown remarkable universal representations, unlocking their potential for ultrasound is bottlenecked by the considerable domain gap from natural images. Existing methods typically fine-tune heavy vision encoders for isolated tasks, incurring substantial computational overhead while overlooking the underlying commonalities across heterogeneous tasks. In this work, we propose FreqDINO++, a frequency-guided multi-task routing vision foundation model for universal ultrasound analysis. We first introduce a Multi-task Routing Adapter (MR-Adapter) to support parameter-efficient integration of task-common and task-specific knowledge, a Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer (F$^2$-Enhancer) is then designed to capture the rich multi-scale frequency characteristics of ultrasound images, and a Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder (TC-Decoder) is devised to promote collaboration between dense and global prediction tasks through global-local token interaction. Extensive experiments on large-scale multi-task and external single-task ultrasound benchmarks demonstrate that FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 diverse clinical task scenarios, while also showing promising generalization to unseen data. The code is at https://github.com/MingLang-FD/FreqDINO-Plus.

</details>


### [77] [Fast Cross-Strength Multi-Contrast Brain MRI Translation using Latent Bridge Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20341)
*Siddharth Srivastava,Till Bretschneider*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified conditional model for controllable MRI field-to-field synthesis using conditional latent bridge matching, achieving competitive results across all three MRIxFields2026 challenge tasks without task-specific architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MRI images acquired at different field strengths exhibit significant variations in noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast, limiting comparability across acquisition settings and complicating downstream analysis. There was a need for a unified approach to synthesize MRI across different field strengths.

Method: The proposed method uses a conditional latent bridge matching framework to build a unified conditional model for controllable field-to-field synthesis. The model requires no task-specific architectures or training, achieving generation through a single inference step.

Result: The model achieves highly competitive results across all three validation tasks of the MRIxFields2026 challenge. Fast generation is demonstrated: producing all modality and field-strength combinations for 30 axial slices in under 90 seconds, and cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume in under 70 seconds, on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU.

Conclusion: The conditional latent bridge matching framework provides an effective unified solution for MRI field-to-field synthesis, delivering strong performance across multiple tasks with efficient inference times using a single model architecture.

Abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) acquired at different field strengths exhibits pronounced variation in noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast, which limits comparability across acquisition settings and complicates downstream analysis. We address this with a unified conditional model for controllable field-to-field synthesis, built on the framework of conditional latent bridge matching. Our single model achieves highly competitive results across the validation phase for all three tasks of the MRIxFields2026 challenge without task-specific architectures or training. We achieve fast generation with only a single inference step, producing all modality and field-strength combinations for $30$ axial slices in under $90$ seconds, as well as cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume in under $70$ seconds, on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU. We further provide extensive ablations regarding different components of our solution. Code: https://gitlab.com/siddharthsrivastava/mrixfields-2026

</details>


### [78] [EliGSiR: Continual RGB-D Mapping with Gaussian Splatting under Bounded Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20348)
*Björn Ellensohn,Elmar Rueckert,Christian Rauch*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EliGSiR is a continual Gaussian mapper for RGB-D mapping that adapts optimization budget usage through three mechanisms: Map-Guided View Scheduling (filters redundant views), Load-Adaptive Fidelity (adjusts supervision resolution), and Targeted Geometry Growth (adds geometry capacity where needed). It addresses the challenge of online new observations while preserving previously reconstructed regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting assumes closed set of observations and long optimization schedules, while continual RGB-D mapping requires handling online arriving observations while preserving previously reconstructed regions. The goal is to efficiently use available optimization budget as reconstruction evolves.

Method: EliGSiR combines three key mechanisms: 1) Map-Guided View Scheduling filters redundant incoming views and reconsiders retained views according to current map state; 2) Load-Adaptive Fidelity adjusts supervision resolution to current mapping load instead of fixed resolution schedule; 3) Targeted Geometry Growth separates depth supervision from Gaussian creation and adds geometric capacity only where repeated RGB-D observations indicate missing or misplaced structure.

Result: On TUM RGB-D fr3/long_office_household, EliGSiR achieves 21.52 dB (vs 19.42 dB for SplaTAM) with ground-truth poses. With live ORB-SLAM3 poses, EliGSiR reaches 23.02 dB in 155.5s (vs 20.10 dB in 230.9s for CaRtGS). The method improves use of available mapping budget through adaptive view scheduling, supervision fidelity, and geometry growth.

Conclusion: EliGSiR successfully addresses continual RGB-D mapping by adaptively controlling which views are optimized, how much image detail is used, and where the representation grows. The three mechanisms work together to maintain reconstruction quality while preserving previously mapped regions as new observations arrive.

Abstract: Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting assumes a closed set of observations and long optimization schedules. Continual RGB-D mapping in contrast poses the problem that new observations arrive online, while previously reconstructed regions must be preserved. We present EliGSiR (Evidence-guided Load-adaptive Incremental Gaussian Splatting with Image Replay), a continual Gaussian mapper that controls how the available optimization budget is used as the reconstruction evolves. Map-Guided View Scheduling filters redundant incoming views and reconsiders retained views according to the current state of the map. Load-Adaptive Fidelity adjusts supervision resolution to the current mapping load instead of following a fixed resolution schedule. Targeted Geometry Growth separates depth supervision from Gaussian creation and adds geometric capacity only where repeated RGB-D observations indicate missing or misplaced structure. Together, these mechanisms adapt which views are optimized, how much image detail is used, and where the representation grows while mapping remains active. We evaluate EliGSiR on Replica, TUM RGB-D, ScanNet++, and real RGB-D sensor sequences, considering both the final reconstruction and the map available throughout acquisition. On TUM RGB-D fr3/long_office_household, EliGSiR reaches 21.52 dB with the same ground-truth mapping poses used by the controlled baselines, compared with 19.42 dB for SplaTAM. In the tracked-pose comparison, EliGSiR with live ORB-SLAM3 poses reaches 23.02 dB in 155.5 s, compared with 20.10 dB in 230.9 s for CaRtGS using its native tracker. We further evaluate reconstruction throughout acquisition and show how EliGSiR adaptive view scheduling, supervision fidelity, and geometry growth improve the use of the available mapping budget.

</details>


### [79] [MM-Future: Multi-Mode Joint World-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20377)
*Shuai Liu,Hechangle Gong,Hao Jiang,Runlin He,Junxiang Zhan,Kai Huang,Sheng Yang,Shaoqing Ren*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MM-Future is a world-action model for autonomous driving that generates multiple paired scene-action hypotheses and models bidirectional interaction within each pair, using modality-aware diffusion Transformer and MM-Tokens representation compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous driving involves coupled decision-making and scene evolution under multi-mode uncertainty, requiring methods that can capture this coupling and uncertainty effectively.

Method: MM-Future initializes hypotheses from structured action prior and independent future scene source, co-evolves them through modality-aware diffusion Transformer, compresses multi-view video into planning-oriented MM-Tokens, and ranks trajectory candidates using future-conditioned proposal scorer.

Result: On NAVSIM navtest: 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS. On HUGSIM zero-shot closed-loop evaluation: 32.3 HD-Score. Ablations validate multi-mode joint world-action modeling benefits over single-mode and action-only variants.

Conclusion: Multi-mode joint world-action modeling with bidirectional interaction significantly improves autonomous driving performance, achieving state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM and HUGSIM benchmarks.

Abstract: Autonomous driving involves coupled decision-making and scene evolution under multi-mode uncertainty. To capture this coupling and uncertainty, we introduce MM-Future, a world-action model that generates multiple paired scene-action hypotheses and models bidirectional interaction within each pair. Each hypothesis is initialized from a structured action prior and an independent future scene source, which are then co-evolved through a modality-aware diffusion Transformer. To support efficient multi-mode rollout, MM-Future compresses multi-view video into planning-oriented representations, dubbed MM-Tokens. Finally, a future-conditioned proposal scorer ranks trajectory candidates by shared history context and their paired predicted future. On NAVSIM navtest, MM-Future achieves 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS, while attaining a 32.3 HD-Score in zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show consistent improvements over both single-mode and action-only variants, validating the benefit of multi-mode joint world-action modeling.

</details>


### [80] [Compact Vision Models for Iris Presentation Attack Detection under Presentation Attack Instrument Shift and Environmental Degradation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20386)
*Athanasios Angelakis,Marta Gomez-Barrero*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks three compact scratch-trained computer vision models (≤0.26M parameters) for iris presentation attack detection (PAD) on LivDet-Iris 2017, evaluating their robustness under unknown attacks and environmental degradation. The study reveals significant performance degradation when transitioning from known to unknown attack presentations, with APCER increases of 17-30 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Iris PAD systems that appear reliable during development may fail when encountering presentation attack instruments (PAIs) or conditions absent from validation data. This work addresses the critical security concern of domain shift and environmental degradation in real-world deployment scenarios.

Method: Three compact scratch-trained computer vision models (with at most ~0.26M trainable parameters) were benchmarked on the Notre Dame subset of LivDet-Iris 2017. Models were trained without external pretraining or data augmentation and evaluated over five seeds. A validation-selected threshold was transferred unchanged to known-attack, unknown-attack, corrupted, and pooled test partitions.

Result: From known to unknown attack presentations, Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate (APCER) increases by 17.11-30.47 percentage points and Detection Equal Error Rate (D-EER) increases by 7.38-12.73 percentage points. ZACH-ViT achieves the lowest unknown-attack APCER (47.69 ± 4.84%) and D-EER (38.87 ± 0.93%). Compact-TransMIL achieves the lowest Bona Fide Presentation Classification Error Rate (BPCER). ZACH-ViT also gives the lowest unknown-attack BPCER at an APCER limit of 10% (81.29 ± 1.95%).

Conclusion: The high absolute errors demonstrate that the comparative advantage of the best compact model (ZACH-ViT) does not constitute deployment readiness under unknown PAIs. Significant performance gaps remain when systems face novel attack types or degraded acquisition conditions not present in validation data.

Abstract: Iris presentation attack detection (PAD) is security-critical when a subsystem that appears reliable during development encounters presentation attack instruments (PAIs) or acquisition conditions absent from validation data. We benchmark three compact scratch-trained computer-vision models, each with at most approximately 0.26 million trainable parameters, on the Notre Dame subset of LivDet-Iris 2017 under PAI-driven domain shift and environmental degradation. All models are trained without external pretraining or data augmentation and evaluated over five seeds. A validation-selected threshold is transferred unchanged to the known-attack, unknown-attack, corrupted, and pooled test partitions. From known to unknown attack presentations, Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate (APCER) increases by 17.11-30.47 percentage points and Detection Equal Error Rate (D-EER) increases by 7.38-12.73 percentage points. At the validation-selected threshold, ZACH-ViT obtains the lowest unknown-attack APCER (47.69 +/- 4.84%) and D-EER (38.87 +/- 0.93%), while Compact-TransMIL obtains the lowest Bona Fide Presentation Classification Error Rate (BPCER). ZACH-ViT also gives the lowest unknown-attack BPCER at an APCER limit of 10% (81.29 +/- 1.95%). The high absolute errors show that the comparative advantage of the best compact model does not constitute deployment readiness under unknown PAIs.

</details>


### [81] [TouchSight: Bare-Handed Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Video via Generative Visual Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20414)
*Danyan Zhou,Jinxuan Lu,Jiawei Lin,Tianxing Chen,Chuqiao Lyu,Wenbo Ding*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TouchSight is a monocular egocentric vision framework that predicts dense full-hand contact forces from video, using 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and a synthetic data generation approach (TwinTouch-20H) that converts gloved hand data into bare-hand observations to bridge the domain gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection intrusive, costly, and restrictive. This work aims to recover dense tactile signals from egocentric vision alone, eliminating the need for tactile instrumentation at capture time.

Method: The framework uses 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings with hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand scenarios, they construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data where generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations while preserving original tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos.

Result: TouchSight outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and shows consistent improvement as glove supervision scales.

Conclusion: Dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time, enabling large-scale data collection for robotic manipulation and physical interaction understanding.

Abstract: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.

</details>


### [82] [WeVisDoc: From Coverage to Capability for Robust End-to-End Document Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20423)
*Hao Yu,Kang Liu,Linnan Zhao,Jiabo Zhan,Chong Sun,Chen Li,Jing Lyu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WeVisDoc is a two-stage data-centric framework for robust end-to-end document parsing that addresses training data bias toward common document types and clean digital pages. Stage I expands data coverage through heterogeneous data and degradation synthesis, while Stage II uses diagnostic probing to identify residual errors and guide targeted data construction. The 4B model achieves state-of-the-art performance, ranking first on both OmniDocBench and PureDocBench benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training corpora for document parsing are biased toward common document types and clean digital pages. Expanding coverage alone does not specify how to address a parser's remaining weaknesses, necessitating a systematic approach to identify and fix specific failure modes.

Method: Two-stage framework: Stage I broadens semantic, structural, and appearance coverage through heterogeneous data and structure-preserving degradation synthesis. Stage II uses a held-out probe to measure residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters, guiding targeted data construction and reallocation of target-token budget.

Result: WeVisDoc-4B achieves Overall score of 95.38 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and mean Overall score of 75.54 across three PureDocBench tracks, ranking first among compared end-to-end parsers in all four settings. Stage II improves Overall scores for both 2B and 4B models, with larger gains on degraded PureDocBench tracks (4.03-point gain for 4B model on Real Degraded track).

Conclusion: The two-stage data-centric approach effectively addresses document parsing robustness across diverse layouts and acquisition conditions. The diagnostic-guided data construction in Stage II significantly improves performance, particularly on degraded documents, demonstrating the value of identifying and targeting specific model weaknesses.

Abstract: Document parsing converts document images into structured content and requires reliable performance across diverse layouts and acquisition conditions. Yet training corpora are biased toward common document types and clean digital pages, while expanding coverage alone does not specify how to address a parser's remaining weaknesses. We present WeVisDoc, a two-stage data-centric framework for robust end-to-end document parsing. Stage I broadens semantic, structural, and appearance coverage through heterogeneous data and structure-preserving degradation synthesis. Stage II uses a held-out probe to measure the Stage I parser's residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters. These diagnostics guide targeted data construction and reallocation of the target-token budget. WeVisDoc-4B achieves an Overall score of 95.38 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and a mean Overall score of 75.54 across the three PureDocBench tracks, ranking first among the compared end-to-end parsers in all four settings. Compared with Stage I, Stage II improves Overall scores for the 2B and 4B models on both benchmarks, with larger gains on the degraded PureDocBench tracks, including a 4.03-point gain for the 4B model on the Real Degraded track.

</details>


### [83] [When Do Language-Grounded Explanations Help? A Graph-Bottleneck for Farm Monitoring Interpretable Sheep Facial Pain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20427)
*Alam Noor,Miguel Guti'errez Gait'an*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses trust issues in automated sheep pain recognition by comparing two approaches: (1) attention-based model using text embeddings of clinical descriptors, which failed to produce meaningful explanations, and (2) a concept bottleneck model using SPFES concept scores, which demonstrated learned concepts but with slight accuracy trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated pain recognition from facial expressions in sheep could enable continuous welfare assessment, but adoption requires trust—stockpersons need justification for pain scores. The researchers investigated whether neural network explanations actually correspond to meaningful clinical cues.

Method: Two approaches were compared: (1) attention mechanism over text embeddings of SPFES clinical descriptors, tested via ablation studies and attention map analysis; (2) concept bottleneck model using per-region state annotations (discarded by image-level pipelines) to predict SPFES concept scores. The study also provided a cross-validated, protocol-matched benchmark of seven methods.

Result: The attention-based approach failed: ablating descriptors changed predicted logit by only ~10^{-4}, and most-attended cues agreed with predicted pain level in only 32.6% of regions. The concept bottleneck approach recovered minority pain-indicating states at 3.5-8.3× base rates and produced ear and eye severity orderings without severity supervision, but cost 0.05-0.10 in Cohen's κ. Without supervision, concept accuracy dropped to 0.109. Pooled concept accuracy was found misleading under clinical imbalance.

Conclusion: Architectural necessity (concept bottleneck improving performance) does not imply semantic validity—explicit supervision is required for meaningful concept learning. The study demonstrates the importance of grounded, interpretable models in clinical applications and provides a benchmark for future work on sheep pain recognition.

Abstract: Automated pain recognition from facial expression could make continuous welfare assessment practical in sheep, but adoption depends on trust: a stockperson cannot act on a score that arrives without justification. We ground a model in the Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale (SPFES) by letting each detected facial region attend over text embeddings of the clinical descriptors and then test whether the resulting explanations mean anything. They do not. Ablating an entire descriptor changes the predicted logit by about $10^{-4}$, and the most-attended cue agrees with the predicted pain level in only $32.6\%$ of regions, although the attention maps, the learned gate, and the generated text all proposed otherwise. We therefore remove the appearance bypass with a concept bottleneck whose classifier reads only SPFES concept scores, supervised by per-region state annotations that image-level pipelines discard. This costs $0.05$--$0.10$ in Cohen's $κ$ but yields concepts that are demonstrably learned: minority pain-indicating states are recovered at $3.5$--$8.3\times$ their base rates, and the ear and eye severity orderings emerge without severity supervision. Removing the supervision alone leaves $κ$ unchanged while concept accuracy falls to $0.109$, showing that architectural necessity does not imply semantic validity. We also show that pooled concept accuracy is misleading under clinical imbalance and provide a cross-validated, protocol-matched benchmark of seven methods on this dataset.

</details>


### [84] [Cross-Architecture Foundation-Model Distillation for Edge Flood Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20441)
*Fabian Schmalstieg,Karsten Mueller,Wojciech Samek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses the challenge of deploying large geospatial foundation models for flood segmentation on memory-constrained edge devices. The solution uses knowledge distillation to compress a 300M parameter teacher model into a 0.7M parameter student, while leveraging unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery to expand the training set beyond manual annotations. The resulting compact model achieves competitive performance (0.787 IoU vs teacher's 0.822) while running at 5.57ms on edge hardware with only 14MB memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geospatial foundation models offer strong flood segmentation but are too large for deployment on memory-constrained edge hardware (e.g., Jetson devices). This limits practical applications in disaster response scenarios where edge deployment is critical.

Method: 1) Fine-tune Prithvi-EO-2.0 (300M params) teacher on 252 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 scenes. 2) Use teacher to supervise training on additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery (self-training/distillation). 3) Distill knowledge from teacher into EfficientViT-B0 student (0.7M params). 4) Apply activation replacement and quantization-aware training for edge deployment. 5) Compare with geometry-matched control and fixed MNDWI threshold baseline.

Result: At matched 252 scenes: teacher-supervised training improves STURM-Flood performance. At 2,500 scenes: student reaches 0.787 water IoU on Sen1Floods11 test (teacher: 0.822), matches teacher on STURM-Flood, remains below on WorldFloods-v2. Deployed model: 1.5MB INT8 TensorRT engine, 5.57ms inference on Jetson Xavier NX, ~14MB memory. Fixed MNDWI threshold is competitive on clean external benchmarks, suggesting those benchmarks test generalization rather than learned-model superiority.

Conclusion: Foundation-model supervision can amplify a fixed manual annotation budget into a substantially larger training set and yield a compact, deployable edge model. The fixed MNDWI baseline performs competitively on clean benchmarks, indicating these benchmarks measure generalization capability rather than absolute model superiority over spectral rules.

Abstract: Geospatial foundation models can provide strong flood-segmentation performance, but their size limits deployment on memory-constrained edge hardware. We distill a 300-million-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher, fine-tuned on the 252 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 training scenes, into a 0.7-million-parameter EfficientViT-B0 student. The teacher supervises additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery, allowing the student training set to grow without new manual annotations. At the matched budget of 252 scenes, teacher-supervised training is competitive with direct training and improves STURM-Flood performance across tested configurations; a geometry-matched control shows that label source alone does not explain the difference. Scaling the teacher-supervised pool to 2,500 scenes narrows the remaining student--teacher gap: the float student reaches 0.787 water intersection over union on the Sen1Floods11 test split against 0.822 for the teacher, matches the teacher on STURM-Flood under our evaluation protocol, and remains below it on WorldFloods-v2. After activation replacement and quantization-aware training, the student runs as a 1.5-megabyte 8-bit integer (INT8) TensorRT engine on a Jetson Xavier NX at 5.57 milliseconds of graphics processing unit (GPU) compute per 512-by-512 image, with approximately 14 megabytes of runtime device memory. A fixed modified normalized difference water index (MNDWI) threshold is competitive with both models on the two clean external benchmarks, so we interpret those benchmarks as generalization tests rather than as evidence of learned-model superiority over a spectral rule. The results support the conclusion: foundation-model supervision can amplify a fixed manual annotation budget into a substantially larger training set and yield a compact, deployable edge model.

</details>


### [85] [SenseFuse: Label-Free Fusion of Image and Shape Encoders for Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20475)
*Euiseok Han,Tri Ton,Hwanhee Kim,Seungyeon Ryu,Chang D. Yoo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SenseFuse is a label-free fusion method for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation that combines 2D image and 3D shape encoders to improve mask labeling accuracy. It uses an adaptive mechanism to select fusion weights based on a sensitivity measure estimated from unlabeled proposals, without requiring ground truth labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-vocabulary scene understanding is crucial for robotics, but existing methods rely mainly on 2D image features or image-distilled representations for mask labeling. The key insight is that 2D and 3D encoders have largely disjoint failure patterns, making them inherently complementary, while two 2D encoders tend to repeat the same errors.

Method: The paper proposes SenseFuse, which balances 2D image and 3D shape encoders for robust open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation. It introduces an adaptive mechanism that selects a scene-level fusion weight to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure. This measure is estimated directly from a single scene's unlabeled proposals in milliseconds, requiring no ground truth labels.

Result: SenseFuse improves labeling accuracy in every evaluated setting across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++ benchmarks. It recovers 67-100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle weight, and raises instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings.

Conclusion: The fusion of 2D image and 3D shape encoders through SenseFuse's adaptive mechanism effectively improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation. The method achieves substantial improvements without requiring additional labels, demonstrating the complementary nature of 2D and 3D representations.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary scene understanding is fundamental for robotics, laying the groundwork for spatial reasoning and object manipulation. While closed-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation heavily leverages 3D shape information, state-of-the-art open-vocabulary methods remain predominantly restricted to 2D image features or image-distilled representations during mask labeling. In this paper, we propose SenseFuse, a label-free fusion method that balances 2D image and 3D shape encoders for robust open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, refining only the mask-labeling stage of existing pipelines. We reveal that 2D image and 3D shape encoders exhibit largely disjoint failure patterns and rarely share identical wrong labels, whereas two 2D image encoders frequently repeat the same errors. This distinct behavior makes the 2D and 3D pair inherently complementary. We introduce an adaptive mechanism that selects a scene-level fusion weight to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure, estimated directly from a single scene's unlabeled proposals in milliseconds. SenseFuse improves labeling accuracy in every evaluated setting across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++, recovering 67-100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle weight, and it raises instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings. Code is available at https://github.com/hanes1207/SenseFuse.

</details>


### [86] [Grounded Product Understanding in Livestream Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20508)
*Xinyu Zhang,Junjie Chen,Jiawei Ge,Qianlong Li,Libin Ma,Baokun Pan,Yahui Luo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GPUB is a large-scale benchmark for e-commerce livestream product understanding, containing 3,000 livestream instances with 31K fashion products. It introduces Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU) task that requires jointly identifying target products and localizing their supporting moments. The developed UniPro model achieves 21.53% Pair mAP@.3, significantly outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for product understanding evaluate product retrieval and temporal localization in isolation, failing to assess the correspondence between product identity and temporal evidence. E-commerce livestreams contain multiple products scattered across different moments, posing challenges for downstream applications like product-centric livestream clipping.

Method: The authors created GPUB with 3,000 livestream instances and over 31K fashion products with quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations. They developed UniPro, a unified product understanding model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from shared multimodal encoding.

Result: GPrU remains highly challenging - best baseline achieves only 10.13% Pair mAP@.3. UniPro improves performance to 21.53% Pair mAP@.3 and achieves 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.

Conclusion: The benchmark and model address a critical gap in product understanding for e-commerce livestreams. UniPro demonstrates that unified modeling of product identification and temporal localization significantly improves performance, though substantial room for improvement remains.

Abstract: E-commerce livestreams have emerged as an important channel for presenting products to online consumers, containing multiple products whose information is scattered in different moments. This poses significant challenges for downstream product understanding applications, such as product-centric livestream clipping, where models need to identify the product and its relevant segments for information gathering. However, existing benchmarks for general product understanding typically evaluate product retrieval and temporal localization in isolation, leaving the critical correspondence between product identity and temporal evidence largely unassessed. To address this limitation, we introduce GPUB, a large-scale benchmark comprising 3,000 livestream instances with quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations and a catalog of over 31K fashion products. GPUB supports three evaluation tasks: the main task Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU) requires jointly identifying the target product and localizing its supporting moments from a livestream video and a candidate product set; Product Retrieval and Product Moment Localization serve as two complementary subtasks. Evaluation of existing multimodal models shows that GPrU remains highly challenging, with the best-performing baseline achieving only 10.13% Pair mAP@.3. To narrow the performance gap, we further develop UniPro, a unified product understanding model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from shared multimodal encoding, improving Pair mAP@.3 to 21.53% while achieving 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.

</details>


### [87] [Automated Goldsmith's Mark Retrieval in Silverware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20509)
*Atmik Tiwari,Vincent Christlein,Mark Fichtner,Freya Gohlke,Birgit Schübel,Theresa Witting,Heike Zech,Mathias Zinnen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed

  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: For art historians, goldsmith marks play a critical role in the identification and dating of artifacts. In practice, experts must manually compare a query mark against hundreds of documented examples, a process that is both tedious and highly dependent on specialist knowledge. To address this, we present an AI-assisted retrieval pipeline that combines mark localization with metric-learning fine-tuning across three backbone architectures: an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, a supervised ViT-S/16, and a self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14. We conduct a systematic evaluation of cropping strategies, where we measure the impact of no cropping, manual ground-truth cropping, and learned detection-based cropping, and assess their interaction with each backbone. Our strongest configuration, DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with manual crop and metric-learning fine-tuning, achieves an mAP of 62.63% and a Top-1 accuracy of 73.74%. Our experiments show that self-supervised pretraining and mark localization are the two most impactful factors, with learned cropping recovering the majority of the gain from manual cropping without requiring ground-truth annotations at inference time. To enable reproducibility and adoption in the digital humanities, we release our manually annotated dataset and codebase, and deploy the system via a public web interface.
