### [88] [A Dual-Stream Regulated Reconstruction and Segmentation Network with Hierarchical Artifact-Prior Modeling for Ultra-Low-Field Pediatric Neuroimaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20562)
*Bahram Jafrasteh,Leo Milecki,Qingyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified framework for the LISA 2026 Challenge that performs quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation of 0.064T ultra-low-field pediatric MRI in a single inference pipeline, addressing challenges of low SNR, weak boundaries, and artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated analysis of 0.064T ultra-low-field pediatric MRI is challenging due to low signal-to-noise ratio, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts, limiting quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation tasks.

Method: A 3D U-Net with two coupled streams reconstructs enhanced uLF volumes and combines original/enhanced images for subcortical segmentation. An auxiliary class covers brain tissue outside target structures for boundary stability. A head conditioned on an artifact graph predicts seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features. Diffeomorphic registration from atlas to target addresses annotation scarcity for label propagation and anatomical reconstruction regularization.

Result: Validation results reported across all three tasks (quality assessment, enhancement, segmentation).

Conclusion: The unified framework successfully performs all three tasks within one inference pipeline, effectively addressing the challenges of ultra-low-field pediatric MRI processing.

Abstract: Automated quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation of multiple structures in $0.064\,\mathrm{T}$ ultra-low-field pediatric MRI are limited by a low signal-to-noise ratio, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts. We present a unified framework for the LISA 2026 Challenge that performs all three tasks together within one inference pipeline. A network with two coupled streams, built on a 3D U-Net, first reconstructs an enhanced uLF volume and then combines the original and enhanced images for subcortical segmentation. To improve boundary stability, we add an auxiliary class covering brain tissue outside the target structures, derived from whole brain masks. A head conditioned on an artifact graph predicts the seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features. We address the scarcity of dense annotations using diffeomorphic registration from atlas to target for label propagation and to regularize anatomical reconstruction. We report validation results across all three tasks.

</details>


### [89] [DocAttriBench: Benchmarking Answer Grounding in Document Visual Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20574)
*Luca De Grandis,Silvia Cappelletti,William Raccagni,Marcella Cornia,Lorenzo Baraldi,Rita Cucchiara*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DocAttriBench (DAB) is a large-scale benchmark for element-level source attribution in Document VQA, built using a novel Mask-based Perplexity-Derived Attribution method (MAPPET). The benchmark contains 237k documents and 296k question-answer pairs with grounding annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Answer grounding in document visual question answering lacks quality annotations or requires costly manual effort. Existing benchmarks either lack grounding annotations or provide limited-quality labels, making it difficult to develop and evaluate grounded, verifiable Document VQA models.

Method: MAPPET combines document layout and language modeling to identify the most informative element for each answer. It measures the increase in perplexity after masking candidate elements and attributes the answer to the element contributing most to model confidence. This method was applied to multiple existing Document VQA datasets to create DAB.

Result: DAB contains 237k documents and 296k question-answer pairs with element-level grounding. Benchmarking grounding-capable multimodal LLMs shows that while larger models achieve higher answer accuracy, even the strongest models often fail to localize the supporting elements.

Conclusion: DAB provides a scalable benchmark for developing grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA models. The work enables future research on element-level attribution in document understanding.

Abstract: Answer grounding in document visual question answering remains an open challenge: most benchmarks lack grounding annotations or provide limited-quality labels, while constructing grounded datasets still requires costly manual effort. We introduce DocAttriBench (DAB), a large-scale benchmark for fine-grained, element-level source attribution in Document VQA, grounding answers to specific layout elements such as text blocks, tables, and images. To build DAB, we propose a Mask-based Perplexity-Derived Attribution method (MAPPET) that combines document layout and language modeling to identify the most informative element for each answer. MAPPET measures the increase in perplexity after masking candidate elements and attributes the answer to the element contributing most to model confidence. Applying MAPPET to multiple existing Document VQA datasets yields DAB, with 237k documents and 296k question-answer pairs with element-level grounding. We benchmark grounding-capable multimodal LLMs on DAB, evaluating answer accuracy, attribution accuracy, and overall answer quality. Results show that while larger models generally achieve higher answer accuracy, even the strongest models often fail to localize the supporting elements. DAB provides a scalable benchmark for developing grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA models. Dataset and code are available at https://aimagelab.github.io/DocAttriBench/.

</details>


### [90] [RawSLAM: Online HDR Gaussian SLAM from Linear Radiance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20589)
*Marina Orozco González,Luis Merino*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: First online Gaussian SLAM framework that processes 16-bit linear HDR imagery directly, featuring an MLP-free logarithmic parameterization, Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective, and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. Outperforms MonoGS and transfers to other SLAM systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current dense visual SLAM systems rely on 8-bit LDR inputs, causing tracking drift and mapping collapse in extreme lighting. Existing HDR reconstruction pipelines are offline-only and require Structure-from-Motion preprocessing, making them unsuitable for large inter-frame motion.

Method: Three core components: (1) Architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module with MLP-free logarithmic parameterization of Gaussian color features; (2) Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; (3) Structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. Also introduces RawSLAM dataset with 10 real-world indoor sequences featuring 16-bit RAW imagery, aligned depth, IMU measurements, and OptiTrack poses.

Result: Outperforms direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in trajectory and reconstruction accuracy while rendering in linear scene radiance. On standard 8-bit inputs, roughly halves MonoGS baseline error. Transfers seamlessly to SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, and DROID-S, eliminating tracking failures on challenging illumination sequences.

Conclusion: The proposed HDR Gaussian SLAM framework achieves state-of-the-art performance by processing HDR imagery directly, with the logarithmic parameterization and photometric objectives enabling robust tracking and mapping under extreme lighting conditions. The method generalizes to multiple existing SLAM systems and works on both HDR and standard LDR inputs.

Abstract: Current dense visual SLAM systems rely almost exclusively on 8-bit tonemapped Low Dynamic Range (LDR) inputs, limiting their robustness in extreme lighting where shadows and highlights trigger tracking drift and mapping collapse. Conversely, existing raw and High Dynamic Range (HDR) reconstruction pipelines operate strictly offline. They depend on Structure-from-Motion preprocessing and are not suited for large inter-frame motion. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first online Gaussian SLAM framework that tracks and maps directly on single-exposure 16-bit linear HDR imagery. Our method rests on three core components: an architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module featuring an MLP-free logarithmic parameterization of Gaussian color features; a Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. Combined, these components allow our approach to outperform a direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in both trajectory and reconstruction accuracy, while rendering natively in linear scene radiance for post-rendering processing. The same formulation runs unchanged on standard 8-bit inputs, roughly halving the MonoGS baseline error. Furthermore, our HDR Gaussian module transfers seamlessly to SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, and DROID-W, eliminating all tracking failures these systems suffer on challenging illumination sequences. To enable this research, we introduce RawSLAM: a dataset of 10 real-world indoor sequences featuring 16-bit RAW imagery, aligned depth, IMU measurements, and external OptiTrack poses. Code and dataset will be made publicly available soon.

</details>


### [91] [PhGS: Post-Hoc Pruning and Refinement of Single-View Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Reconstructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20623)
*Rinto Yagawa,Han Cheng,Dieter Schmalstieg,Hideo Saito,Shohei Mori*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a backbone-agnostic compaction pipeline for single-view feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses importance-score-based pruning combined with a trainable recurrent refinement module to reduce spatial redundancy while preserving rendering quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-view feed-forward 3DGS models predict a fixed number of Gaussians per camera ray, causing severe spatial redundancy. Existing compaction strategies are designed for multi-view setups and are incompatible with single-image models. Retraining the base network is not desirable.

Method: The method keeps the base feed-forward network frozen and applies: (1) an importance-score-based pruning mechanism to remove redundant Gaussians, and (2) a lightweight trainable recurrent refinement module that iteratively updates surviving primitives to restore image quality. The approach supports flexible inference-time keep ratios.

Result: The method achieves seamless integration with existing baselines, preserves novel-view rendering fidelity, and delivers high memory reduction with flexible keep ratios for different application needs.

Conclusion: This post-hoc compaction approach provides an effective solution for reducing spatial redundancy in single-view 3DGS without requiring base model retraining, offering a versatile and memory-efficient pipeline compatible with various backbone architectures.

Abstract: Recent single-view feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) generation predicts a fixed number of Gaussians per camera ray, introducing severe spatial redundancy. Most existing compaction strategies target multi-view setups to exploit cross-view consistency and are incompatible with single-image models. Instead of retraining the base feed-forward network to directly output compact representations, our insight is to keep the base models frozen and apply post-hoc pruning and recurrent refinement to the generated Gaussians. Consequently, we propose a backbone-agnostic compaction pipeline for single-view feed-forward 3DGS that couples an importance-score-based pruning mechanism with a trainable, lightweight recurrent refinement module, which iteratively updates the surviving primitives to restore image quality. Our results demonstrate seamless integration with existing baselines while preserving novel-view rendering fidelity and achieving high memory reduction. Furthermore, our method supports flexible inference-time keep ratios for application needs.

</details>


### [92] [Refinement Is Inherently Editable: Training-Free Prompt-to-Prompt Image Editing with Generative Refinement Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20633)
*Yulong Chen,Ziqian Zhang,Haoyu Zhang,Ao He,Senmao Li,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RefineEdit is a training-free text-guided image editing framework that addresses limitations in diffusion-based and causal autoregressive editors. It uses a Generative Refinement Network that couples edit localization with content generation through global refinement of binary image codes, allowing editing evidence to be dynamically reassessed as the image evolves.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-guided image editing must introduce requested changes while preserving unrelated source content. Existing diffusion-based editors rely on spatial controls that can be inaccurate, leaving edits incomplete or altering unrelated regions. Causal autoregressive editors face additional constraints from their fixed decoding order that limits revision of earlier decisions.

Method: RefineEdit initializes an editing branch from an intermediate source state, reusing the emerging layout. It compares probabilities assigned by two branches to the same source-sampled bits, using signed differences to select editable positions and bits. Selected bits follow editing refinement while remaining bits copy the evolving source state. Adaptive spatial freezing stabilizes editing by limiting unnecessary mask expansion, while finite bit locking keeps recently selected bits editable. The framework requires no additional training, external masks, or attention control.

Result: Across nine editing categories of PIE-Bench, RefineEdit achieves the best background-preservation scores in PSNR, LPIPS, MSE and SSIM, together with the highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among evaluated methods.

Conclusion: RefineEdit successfully addresses text-guided image editing challenges by introducing a training-free framework that dynamically reassesses editing evidence throughout the generation process. It outperforms existing methods in both background preservation and edit quality metrics without requiring additional training, external masks, or attention control mechanisms.

Abstract: Text-guided image editing must introduce the requested changes while preserving unrelated source content. Diffusion-based editors rely on spatial controls whose inaccuracies can leave edits incomplete or alter unrelated regions. Causal autoregressive editors face a further constraint: their fixed decoding order limits revision of earlier decisions. We introduce RefineEdit, a training-free prompt-to-prompt image editing framework built on a Generative Refinement Network. Our key idea is to couple edit localization with content generation through the global refinement of binary image codes, allowing editing evidence to be reassessed as the image evolves. RefineEdit initializes an editing branch from an intermediate source state, reusing the emerging layout. We compare the probabilities assigned by the two branches to the same source-sampled bits, using their signed differences to select editable positions and bits. Selected bits follow editing refinement, while the remaining bits copy the evolving source state. To stabilize editing across refinement steps, adaptive spatial freezing limits unnecessary mask expansion, while finite bit locking keeps recently selected bits editable. The framework requires no additional training, external masks, or attention control. Across nine editing categories of PIE-Bench, RefineEdit achieves the best background-preservation scores in PSNR, LPIPS, MSE and SSIM, together with the highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among the evaluated methods.

</details>


### [93] [PROVIA: Procedure State Tracking for Online Mistake Detection in Egocentric Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20638)
*Di Wen,Kailun Yang,Jimmy Weissert,Luc Maria Scherrer,Cedric Zöllner,Ruiping Liu,Yufan Chen,Jiale Wei,Junwei Zheng,Kunyu Peng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PROVIA is a computer vision system for egocentric video that detects mistakes made by humans in real-time, distinguishing between factual state (what was actually done) and accepted progress (what should have been done according to correct demonstrations). It uses Bayesian state merging and sequential testing to achieve better mistake detection than baseline methods at a false alarm budget of 0.1 per minute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods use a "first-mistake protocol" that cuts recordings at the first mistake, which is unrealistic because it doesn't handle natural mistakes and recoveries. The problem is that an assistant must notice mistakes from past frames before the next step begins, and continue working after recovery. A mistake changes the work state, requiring all later steps to be evaluated against what was actually done rather than the original plan.

Method: PROVIA maintains two separate records: (1) a factual state - a learned summary of steps each actor performed including mistakes, and (2) accepted progress - an exact posterior over the state of an automaton induced from correct demonstrations using Bayesian state merging, and over execution status of each actor. Procedure-state transitions occur only in the correct-status branch; mistake and correction branches retain the source state. A sequential test converts per-frame mistake probability into alarms.

Result: PROVIA outperforms all controlled baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, HoloAssist, and IMPACT-ego datasets. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute, it achieves recall of 0.154 vs 0.128 on CaptainCook4D, and 0.034 vs 0.015 on HoloAssist, leading at every budget level. The pipeline runs at 58-70 frames per second.

Conclusion: PROVIA successfully addresses the problem of mistake detection in egocentric video by separating factual state from accepted progress, using Bayesian state merging and sequential testing. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks while maintaining real-time processing speed. The code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/PROVIA.

Abstract: An assistant watching egocentric video should notice a mistake from past frames alone, before the next step begins, and keep working once the person recovers. A mistake changes the state of the work, so every later step has to be read against what was done rather than against the plan. The first-mistake protocol that current online methods report on cuts each recording at its first mistake, so a fixed-time rule that never looks at the video is right on every case. We evaluate on complete trials, where mistakes and recoveries arise naturally, under a validation false-alarm budget and against controls that use timing alone. PROVIA keeps two records apart: a factual state, a learned summary of the steps each actor performed, mistakes included, and the accepted progress, an exact posterior over the state of an automaton induced from correct demonstrations by Bayesian state merging and over the execution status of each actor. Procedure-state transitions occur only in the correct-status branch; the mistake and correction branches retain the source state. A sequential test turns the per-frame mistake probability into alarms. With one filter and one optimization rule, PROVIA ranks mistakes best among the evaluated controlled baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, HoloAssist and IMPACT-ego. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute it recalls .154 against .128 on CaptainCook4D and .034 against .015 on HoloAssist, where it leads at every budget. The pipeline runs at 58-70 frames per second. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/PROVIA.

</details>


### [94] [Earth Surface Immune System for Rapid Monitoring of Unknown Anomalies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20662)
*Jingtao Li,Qian Zhu,Xinyu Wang,Deren Li,Liangpei Zhang,Yanfei Zhong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ESIA (Earth Surface Immune System) is a bio-inspired framework for detecting and recognizing earth surface anomalies from satellite imagery, using three immune system principles: innate detection, adaptive recognition, and test-time mutation. It achieves 37% F1 improvement over baselines in localization (14.51 km²/s) and >80% recognition F1, validated on 19,801.60 km² across 6 anomaly categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Earth surface anomalies (e.g., disasters, environmental damage) are increasing due to climate change and human activities, but differ fundamentally from conventional remote sensing targets due to limited historical data and unpredictability. Existing methods either address specific anomaly categories or stop at localization, leaving a gap between detection and actionable information.

Method: The architecture follows three immune system principles: (1) Non-specific innate immune stage treats anomalies as unobserved changes in time-series satellite imagery, generating binary localization maps without assuming any anomaly category; (2) Specific adaptive immune stage applies negative selection to filter text prompts and matches surviving prompts with localized patches through a multi-modal foundation model for open-vocabulary recognition; (3) Mutation mechanism tunes minimal embeddings at test time using a single reference image pair for scene adaptation.

Result: Localization achieves 14.51 km²/s processing speed, surpassing the strongest general baseline by 37% in F1. Recognition F1 exceeds 80% for unknown anomaly attributes (category, affected area, damage severity). Test-time adaptation completes in 3.26s using a single reference image pair. Validated on global-scale dataset covering 19,801.60 km² across six anomaly categories against 22 models. Successfully applied to quantify degraded farmland in Dnipro Delta (Kakhovka Dam collapse) and assess burn severity from 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles.

Conclusion: The bio-inspired architecture enables unprecedented flexibility in handling unknown anomalies, bridging the gap between detection and actionable information. This opens new avenues for real-time disaster response and environmental surveillance by providing both localization and open-vocabulary recognition of diverse anomaly types without prior category specification.

Abstract: Earth surface anomalies, driven by escalating climate change, and expanding human activities, are increasing in both frequency and diversity, yet their limited historical data and unpredictability make them fundamentally different from conventional remote sensing targets. Existing methods address specific anomaly categories or stop at localization, leaving a gap between detection and actionable information. Here we present ESIA, an Earth Surface Immune System whose architecture is constrained by three principles from the biological immune system, refined over millions of years against equally diverse and uncertain threats. A non-specific innate immune stage treats anomalies as unobserved changes in time-series satellite imagery, generating binary localization maps at 14.51 km2/s without assuming any anomaly category, surpassing the strongest general baseline by 37% in F1. A specific adaptive immune stage applies negative selection to filter text prompts and matches surviving prompts with localized image patches through a multi-modal foundation model, enabling open-vocabulary recognition of unknown anomaly attributes including category, affected area, and damage severity, with recognition F1 exceeding 80%. A mutation mechanism tunes minimal embeddings at test time, adapting to each scene in 3.26s using a single reference image pair. We validate ESIA on a global-scale dataset covering 19,801.60 km2 across six anomaly categories, comparing against 22 models, and further apply it to quantify degraded farmland in the Dnipro Delta following the Kakhovka Dam collapse and assess burn severity from 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. This unprecedented flexibility in handling unknown anomalies opens new avenues for real-time disaster response and environmental surveillance.

</details>


### [95] [FunArt: Decoding Functional Structure and Articulation from Generative 3D Latents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20673)
*Dennis Rotondi,Abdelrhman Werby,Kai O. Arras*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FunArt is a framework that constructs articulation-aware functional 3D scene graphs from single static RGB-D observations, enabling robots to identify articulated objects, segment movable parts and functional elements, and estimate kinematic models without physical interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robots need to understand articulated objects (objects with moving parts like doors, drawers, lids) in human environments to operate effectively. Existing methods either require physical interaction to recover kinematics or decouple articulation from functional elements in static scans. This work aims to infer articulated structure and functional components from a single static observation.

Method: FunArt reconstructs object instances from posed RGB-D observations, converts geometry into O-Voxel representation (from TRELLIS.2), and uses its frozen VAE as a structural prior. A lightweight query-based decoder combines object-level latents with surface-aligned features to jointly segment movable parts, functional elements, and estimate motion parameters (type, axis, origin, range).

Result: On Articulate3D dataset, FunArt achieves state-of-the-art results. In end-to-end setting: +1.5 AP50 for movable parts, +2.8 AP50 under joint origin-and-axis constraints, and +6.7 AP50 for functional elements compared to strongest baselines.

Conclusion: Generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction, enabling robots to understand articulated objects from single static observations without requiring physical manipulation.

Abstract: To operate effectively in human environments, robots must identify articulated objects, segment their movable and interactive parts, and estimate their kinematic models. Existing articulated scene representations typically recover kinematics from observed interactions, while methods operating on static scans often decouple articulation from functional interactive elements. We present FunArt, a framework that constructs articulation-aware functional 3D scene graphs from posed RGB-D observations captured in a single static configuration. FunArt reconstructs object instances, converts their fused geometry directly into the O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2, and exploits its frozen, sparse-compression VAE as a structural prior. A lightweight query-based decoder combines compact object-level latents with dense, surface-aligned features to jointly segment movable parts and functional interactive elements while estimating motion type, axis, origin, and range. On the Articulate3D dataset, FunArt achieves state-of-the-art performance across movable-part segmentation, articulation estimation, and functional-element segmentation, both with and without ground-truth object input. In the end-to-end setting, it outperforms the strongest baselines by 1.5 AP_{50} points for movable parts, 2.8 AP_{50} points under joint origin-and-axis constraints, and 6.7 AP_{50} points for functional elements. These results demonstrate that generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction.

</details>


### [96] [Should This Case Be Adapted? Prediction Fragmentation Controls Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20700)
*Lili Wang,Jing Li,Xiaowen Sun,Xiangyu Hu,Zhuangzhuang Gu,Jian Liu,Srihari Nelakuditi,Yan Tong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical flaw in episodic test-time adaptation for medical image segmentation: while adaptation appears beneficial on average, it actually harms a majority of individual cases. The authors propose using "prediction fragmentation" (disagreement between source and adapted masks) as a no-label, low-latency signal to route cases—deciding whether to apply adaptation on a per-case basis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key insight is that cohort-level metrics (mean Dice) hide the fact that most individual cases are actually harmed by adaptation. On cross-vendor cardiac MRI, 58.7% of cases are made worse by adaptation, even though the mean ΔDice appears statistically indistinguishable from zero. This reveals that fixed-horizon adaptation conflates two distinct decisions: how far to adapt and whether to adapt at all.

Method: The authors propose: (1) quantifying harm as "harmful accepted area" (HA) - the fraction of edited area that is harmful; (2) using prediction fragmentation (disagreement geometry between source weights M0 and adapted mask Mk) as a predictor of HA, requiring no labels or extra backward passes at decision time; (3) building a case-level router on this fragmentation score to decide whether to adapt each case.

Result: Prediction fragmentation predicts HA with Spearman ρ of 0.50-0.60 across three benchmarks. The router cuts HA from 0.228 to 0.139 on a held-out benchmark, and from 0.129 to 0.013 on the cardiac benchmark (reducing cases made worse from 58.7% to 20.0%). The method transfers across architectures (nnU-Net→SegFormer) and domains (Cityscapes→ACDC) with only threshold recalibration.

Conclusion: Per-case routing based on prediction fragmentation successfully reduces harm from test-time adaptation without requiring labels or gradients at decision time. This addresses the fundamental limitation that no single global budget can condition on individual cases. The approach represents a practical solution for deploying adaptive segmentation in real clinical settings where per-case decisions are critical.

Abstract: Episodic test-time adaptation resets a frozen segmenter to source weights $M_0$ on each case and adapts for a fixed step count. A fixed horizon conflates a cohort-level question, how far to adapt, with an irreducibly per-case one, whether this case should be adapted at all. Cohort means hide that decision: on cross-vendor cardiac MRI the mean $Δ$Dice from adaptation is statistically indistinguishable from zero while 58.7% of cases are individually made worse. We quantify this harm as harmful accepted area (HA), the harmful fraction of the edited area a controller deploys. Held-out tuning gives a stronger baseline than a fixed horizon, but the budget it selects transfers on neither of the two main medical benchmarks, and no global budget can condition on the case. We show that prediction fragmentation---the disagreement geometry between $M_0$ and the adapted mask $M_k$---predicts HA with no labels or extra backward passes at decision time, comparably on three benchmarks (Spearman $ρ$ 0.50--0.60), at a quarter of gradient-norm's latency. A case-level router built on it cuts HA from 0.228 to 0.139 on a benchmark that took no part in its design, with the design frozen and only cut-points recalibrated there. On the cardiac benchmark the design was selected on, the router cuts HA from 0.129 to 0.013 at matched Dice and 1.10 deployed updates, against the retrospective-best budget found post hoc on evaluation labels, and reduces that 58.7% to 20.0%, an upper bound we quantify. Where the retained cases are not net-helped (as on prostate), the router still cuts HA but concedes accuracy, a boundary we report. Thresholds are fit once on a labeled split disjoint from evaluation; decisions use no labels or gradients. The template ports across architecture and domain (nnU-Net$\to$SegFormer, Cityscapes$\to$ACDC) with coordinate, thresholds and per-bucket actions instantiated per domain.

</details>


### [97] [FlowSGS: Improving Flow Matching Priors for Inverse Imaging with Stochastic Interpolants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20769)
*Tianao Li,Xinhui Qian,Emma Alexander*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FlowSGS is a flow-based posterior sampling method for solving inverse problems in computational imaging. It uses Split Gibbs Sampling to decompose the posterior into likelihood and prior steps, combining Langevin dynamics with Stochastic Interpolants framework. It achieves state-of-the-art performance and is the first flow-based solver to handle nonlinear inverse problems like Fourier phase retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow-based inverse solvers assume linear forward models and/or make simplifying approximations in posterior sampling. There is a need for a method that can handle general (nonlinear) inverse problems while maintaining computational efficiency.

Method: FlowSGS uses Split Gibbs Sampling (SGS) to decompose the posterior into two steps: (1) likelihood step sampled using Langevin dynamics, and (2) prior step leveraging Stochastic Interpolants (SI) framework with a pretrained flow model. The method uses SI's reverse-time SDE for the prior step with a novel timestep correction technique.

Result: FlowSGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on a range of inverse problems. Notably, it is the first flow-based inverse solver to handle nonlinear inverse problems, specifically demonstrating experiments on Fourier phase retrieval.

Conclusion: FlowSGS successfully extends flow-based inverse solvers to handle nonlinear forward models through Split Gibbs Sampling and Stochastic Interpolants integration. The novel timestep correction technique and straight probability paths reduce network evaluations compared to existing PnP diffusion samplers.

Abstract: Flow matching has emerged as the state-of-the-art generative model and has been used for plug-and-play (PnP) priors to solve inverse problems in computational imaging. However, existing flow-based inverse solvers assume linear forward models and/or make simplifying approximations in posterior sampling. To circumvent these problems, we introduce FlowSGS, a flow-based posterior sampling method using Split Gibbs Sampling (SGS) to decompose the posterior into a likelihood step and a prior step. Specifically, we sample from the likelihood step using Langevin dynamics and leverage the Stochastic Interpolants (SI) framework to integrate a pretrained flow model into the prior step. We provide a form for the prior step that uses SI's reverse-time SDE, and show connections to previous PnP methods. Moreover, with the aid of the flow prior's straight probability paths and a novel timestep correction technique for the reverse-time SDE, FlowSGS requires fewer network evaluations in its prior step than plug-and-play diffusion samplers. Our experiments show state-of-the-art performance on a range of inverse problems. For the first time, we provide an experiment on a nonlinear inverse problem (Fourier phase retrieval) for flow-based inverse solvers.

</details>


### [98] [ERCPMP-Gx: Endoscopic Image and Video Dataset for Morphological, Histopathological, and Genomic Characterization of Colorectal Polyposis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20815)
*Zahra Ghaffari,Massih Bahar,Mojgan Forootan,Ali Darvishi,Hamidreza Bolhasani*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ERCPMP-Gx is a novel patient-level dataset combining endoscopic images, histopathology, and germline findings to support AI development for recognition and classification of hereditary colorectal polyposis syndromes (FAP, PJS, JPS, GNS).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hereditary polyposis syndromes are precursors to colorectal cancer with extracolonic tumor associations. Early identification is crucial, but existing public endoscopic datasets focus on individual sporadic polyps and lack linkage to polyposis phenotype, histopathology, and germline findings at the patient level.

Method: Endoscopic procedures performed using Olympus EVIS X1 system with multiple imaging modes (WLE, NBI, M-NBI, NBI with near focus). Dataset includes 160 images and video clips, with ~80% hereditary polyposis cases (FAP, PJS, JPS, GNS) and ~20% non-hereditary mimics. Each record linked to standardized endoscopic annotations, histopathology, and clinically reported germline findings.

Result: Created an AI-ready, patient-level annotation framework for hereditary polyposis classification, publicly accessible at Mendeley (DOI: 10.17632/nzyfc544bx.2).

Conclusion: ERCPMP-Gx fills a critical gap in medical imaging datasets by providing linked endoscopic, histopathological, and genomic data specifically for hereditary polyposis syndromes, enabling AI-driven recognition and differential classification of these conditions.

Abstract: Hereditary polyposis syndromes can be precursor lesions to colorectal cancer and are associated with a broad spectrum of extracolonic tumors. Early identification and accurate classification of these syndromes are essential for timely diagnosis, individualized patient management, and targeted surveillance strategies for affected families. However, public endoscopic datasets are largely organized around the individual sporadic polyp, and none links the polyposis phenotype to histopathology and germline findings at the patient level. Here, we present ERCPMP-Gx, an endoscopic, histopathological, and genomic dataset developed to support the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the recognition, characterization, and classification of colorectal polyposis. Most procedures were performed using the Olympus EVIS X1 system with white-light endoscopy (WLE), narrow-band imaging (NBI), magnifying NBI (M-NBI), and NBI with near focus modes, yielding 160 images and accompanying video clips. Approximately eighty percent of cases represent clinically and/or genetically confirmed hereditary polyposis syndromes (PG), including familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS), and ganglioneuroma syndrome (GNS), while the remaining twenty percent comprise non-hereditary polyps and polyp-mimicking lesions with overlapping morphological features (Non-PG), included to support differential classification. Each released record is linked, where available, to standardized endoscopic annotations, representative histopathology, and clinically reported germline findings, forming an AI-ready, patient-level annotation framework. The dataset is publicly accessible at Mendeley (https://doi.org/10.17632/nzyfc544bx.2). For the latest updates and further information, readers are referred to the DataBioX website: https://databiox.com.

</details>


### [99] [Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20816)
*Ji Xie,Dewei Zhou,Xinyu Huang,Zhennan Chen,Xun Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Paint-Anything enables professional design by allowing any 24-bit hex color specification for both image generation and editing. It uses a shared hex-prompt interface learned through object-level color supervision, trained on Paint-500K dataset with pure-color anchors at high-noise timesteps. The method achieves 85.3% and 28.3% improvements on ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit respectively, over FLUX.2-4B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Professional design requires precise color control - the ability to specify any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior approaches rely on dedicated color representations or specialized inference, making them complex. Large language models offer a simpler alternative since even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics.

Method: 1) Data pipeline constructing Paint-500K from real images through object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis; 2) Pure-color anchors (pixels exactly matching hex values) used only at high-noise timesteps, while low-noise training uses natural images; 3) Shared hex-prompt interface for both generation and editing tasks; 4) Any Color Benchmark (ACBench) with ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit for evaluation.

Result: On FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I scores by 85.3% and ACBench-Edit scores by 28.3% relative to the base model. It also achieves the highest average CompColor score among compared methods.

Conclusion: The proposed Paint-Anything successfully enables any-color control through a hex-prompt interface, significantly outperforming prior methods on object-level hex color fidelity across both text-to-image generation and editing tasks.

Abstract: Professional design requires any-color control: the ability to specify an object's target color with any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior work has explored color generation, editing, and colorization, but often relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures. Advances in large language models offer a simpler starting point: even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics. We present Paint-Anything, which learns a shared hex-prompt interface for generation and editing through object-level color supervision. We develop a data pipeline that constructs Paint-500K from real images through object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. Since shadows make real-image labels only approximate colors, we complement this supervision with pure-color anchors whose pixels exactly match their paired hex values. These anchors are used only at high-noise timesteps, leaving low-noise training to natural images. We further introduce Any Color Benchmark (ACBench), comprising ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit, to measure object-level hex color fidelity across both tasks. On FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit scores by 85.3% and 28.3%, respectively, relative to the base model, with ablations supporting the training recipe. It also achieves the highest average CompColor score among the compared methods.

</details>


### [100] [FAMOS: Feed-Forward 3D Articulation Modeling from Sparse Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20817)
*Kevin Qu,Tao Sun,Massimiliano Viola,Liyuan Zhu,Zhizhuo Zhou,Sayan Deb Sarkar,Konrad Schindler,Iro Armeni*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FAMOS is a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from sparse, unordered partial point clouds of articulated objects. It uses a Multi-state Articulation Transformer to aggregate articulation cues across multiple observations and includes an observed articulation span objective to supervise motion range.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging because each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion evidence. Existing feed-forward methods infer articulation from a single observation and rely heavily on learned category-level shape priors. Additionally, the limited scale and diversity of existing datasets hinders progress.

Method: 1) Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention to jointly reason over multiple observations (supporting variable number of inputs including single view). 2) Observed articulation span objective to supervise motion range each part exhibits across input observations. 3) Procedural data generator to synthesize self-annotated assets during training to overcome limited dataset scale and diversity.

Result: Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines.

Conclusion: FAMOS successfully predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from sparse observations by jointly reasoning over multiple views and leveraging a procedural data generator for training, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging because each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion evidence. Most feed-forward methods infer articulation from a single observation and therefore rely heavily on learned category-level shape priors. We present FAMOS, a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds. Our model jointly reasons over multiple observations and naturally supports a variable number of inputs, including a single view. To aggregate articulation cues across observations, we introduce a Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention. We further propose an observed articulation span objective that supervises the motion range each part exhibits across the input observations, encouraging the model to leverage the full observation set. To overcome the limited scale and diversity of existing datasets, we introduce a procedural data generator that synthesizes self-annotated assets during training. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines. Project page: https://kevinqu7.github.io/famos

</details>


### [101] [Can 4D Foundation Models Remember?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20819)
*Guangzhao He,Hadar Averbuch-Elor,Wei-Chiu Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PersistBench introduces a benchmark for evaluating visual memory in 4D foundation models using 360° videos as omniscient ground truth, revealing that current models struggle to maintain object consistency once objects leave the field of view.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 4D foundation models can perceive and reconstruct dynamic environments, but existing benchmarks lack ground truth for objects once they leave the field of view, making it impossible to evaluate visual memory in an object-centric manner. This gap motivated the creation of a proper evaluation framework for visual memory.

Method: The researchers created PersistBench, a dataset and metric suite leveraging 360° videos as omniscient ground truth. They evaluated various models across three aspects: object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation.

Result: Current models can only maintain short-term consistency that degrades significantly once objects leave the field of view. The evaluation reveals a substantial gap in visual memory capabilities.

Conclusion: There is a significant gap between current model capabilities and robust visual memory. The phrase "seeing is not remembering" captures the core finding, indicating that perception alone does not equal memory retention. This provides guidance for future development of 4D foundation models.

Abstract: Perceiving and remembering the visual world is fundamental to navigating and interacting with our environment. Current 4D foundation models, such as camera-controllable video models or 4D reconstruction models, can perceive and reconstruct dynamic environments, but how well they remember what they have perceived remains an open question. Existing benchmarks largely rely on pixel-level metrics and lack ground truth for objects once they leave the field of view, making them unable to evaluate visual memory in an object-centric manner against references. To fill this gap, we introduce PersistBench, a dataset and metric suite that leverages 360° videos as omniscient ground truth and proposes three evaluation aspects: object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation. Evaluating various models across diverse categories reveals that current models can only maintain short-term consistency that degrades significantly once objects leave the field of view. Our findings highlight the gap between current model capabilities and robust visual memory ("seeing is not remembering"), providing guidance for future development of 4D foundation models. Dataset and code are available on the project page: https://guangzhaohe.com/persistbench.

</details>

# cs.GR [[Back]](#toc)

### [102] [FootprintRAG: Visual Analytics for Evidence Context Refinement in RAG-based Scientific Literature Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19601)
*Xingyu Liu,Yu Dong,Qizhen Yu,Shiyu Cheng,Zhe Wang,Guan Li,Guihua Shan,Dong Tian,Christy Jie Liang,Quang Vinh Nguyen*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: FootprintRAG is a visual analytics system that makes the RAG evidence context explicit, inspectable, and revisable before generation. It addresses the "black box" problem in RAG-based literature exploration by allowing users to see, understand, and refine how evidence is retrieved, ranked, and filtered.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In open-ended scientific literature exploration using RAG, the evidence context used for generation is produced through hidden retrieval, reranking, assessment, and filtering steps. Users receive retrieval summaries without knowing how the system constructed the evidence context, which evidence was retained/discarded, or whether potentially useful evidence was excluded.

Method: FootprintRAG parses scientific literature into text and figure evidence units, expands initial queries into parallel query variants, retrieves and assesses evidence across iterative rounds, and surfaces ERS-ranked supplementary candidates from corpus-level evidence space. It provides coordinated views connecting retrieval trajectories, evidence-state revision, and provenance-aware summary generation into a user-steerable workflow.

Result: The system helps users compare retrieval directions, revise candidate evidence, recover potentially overlooked evidence, and trace generated summaries back to supporting evidence units. Evaluated through two case studies, a user study, and workflow-level comparison with representative RAG systems.

Conclusion: FootprintRAG provides transparency and user control in RAG-based literature exploration by making the evidence context an explicit analytical object, enabling users to inspect, revise, and understand the retrieval process before generation.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly used to ground large language model (LLM) outputs in scientific literature. However, in open-ended literature exploration, the evidence context used for generation is often produced through hidden retrieval, reranking, assessment, and filtering steps. Users may receive retrieval summaries without knowing how the system constructed the evidence context, which evidence units were retained or discarded, or whether potentially useful evidence was excluded before synthesis. We present FootprintRAG, an LLM-agent-powered visual analytics system for evidence context refinement in RAG-based scientific literature exploration. The core idea is to treat the RAG evidence context as an explicit, inspectable, and revisable analytical object before generation. FootprintRAG parses scientific literature into text and figure evidence units, expands an initial query into parallel query variants, retrieves and assesses evidence across iterative rounds, and surfaces ERS-ranked supplementary candidates from the corpus-level evidence space. Through coordinated views, the system connects retrieval trajectories, evidence-state revision, and provenance-aware summary generation into a user-steerable workflow. We evaluate FootprintRAG through two case studies, a user study, and a workflow-level comparison with representative RAG systems. The results show that FootprintRAG helps users compare retrieval directions, revise candidate evidence, recover potentially overlooked evidence, and trace generated summaries back to supporting evidence units. FootprintRAG is available at https://github.com/meteorshowering/FootprintRAGVA.git.

</details>


### [103] [DELUGE: Decomposed Entropy-coded Live Unstructured Geometry Exchange for Real-time Particle Streaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19750)
*Hikari Yanagawa,Yuichi Hiroi,Takefumi Hiraki*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: DELUGE is a streaming compression architecture for dynamic particle physics simulations in VR/AR that exploits temporal coherence and velocity predictability to achieve sub-frame-latency encoding/decoding, enabling real-time collaborative experiences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Particle-based physics simulations (fluids, smoke, granular media) are fundamental for visual realism in VR/AR. With growing adoption of social VR and digital twins, there is increasing demand for shared experiences where multiple users interact with the same simulation in real time. However, existing point cloud compression methods (G-PCC/TMC13 and Draco) assume static geometric structures and have encoding latency exceeding the frame period, failing to meet real-time delivery requirements.

Method: DELUGE uses three complementary techniques exploiting temporal coherence and velocity predictability inherent in physics simulation particles. The system was evaluated on dynamic point cloud datasets, with end-to-end client implementations built for web browsers and Apple Vision Pro. A within-participants perceptual quality evaluation and a two-person collaborative task study on Vision Pro were conducted.

Result: DELUGE achieves approximately 20x faster decoding than G-PCC (TMC13) and 6x faster encoding than Draco. The perceptual quality evaluation and collaborative task study confirmed the method supports real-time collaborative experiences with hand-tracked fluid interaction.

Conclusion: DELUGE enables real-time collaborative VR/AR experiences with hand-tracked fluid interaction by providing sub-frame-latency compression for dynamic particle streaming, successfully supporting two-person collaborative tasks on Apple Vision Pro.

Abstract: Particle-based physics simulations, including fluids, smoke, and granular media, are fundamental to visual realism in immersive VR and AR. With the growing adoption of social VR and digital twins, demand is increasing for shared experiences in which multiple users interact with the same simulation in real time. Realizing such experiences requires low-latency streaming of large-scale particle data from a server to each client, yet existing point cloud compression methods such as G-PCC (TMC13) and Draco assume static geometric structures; when applied to dynamic particle streaming, their encoding latency exceeds the frame period, failing to meet real-time delivery requirements. We propose DELUGE, a streaming compression architecture that exploits the temporal coherence and velocity predictability inherent in physics simulation particles, achieving sub-frame-latency encoding and decoding through three complementary techniques. Evaluation on dynamic point cloud datasets demonstrates that DELUGE achieves approximately $20\times$ faster decoding than G-PCC (TMC13) and $6\times$ faster encoding than Draco. We further build end-to-end client implementations for both web browsers and Apple Vision Pro, and confirm through a within-participants perceptual quality evaluation and a two-person collaborative task study on Vision Pro that the proposed method supports real-time collaborative experiences with hand-tracked fluid interaction.

</details>


### [104] [Printing the Underdetermined: Materializing Multi-solutionness in Figurative Paintings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19782)
*Yutao Ming,Teng Xu,Youjia Wang,Yunyang Liu,Fengmin Yang,Fuqiang Zhao,Jingyi Yu,Hua Yang,Yanjun Zhou*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a computational framework for exploring the non-uniqueness of 3D reconstructions from figurative paintings. Instead of treating paintings as depicting a single recoverable 3D scene, the authors embrace "multi-solutionness" - the idea that multiple valid 3D interpretations can be compatible with a single painted image. Their pipeline generates multiple camera-orbit video sequences from a painting, reconstructs each using 3D Gaussian Splatting, and fabricates physical artifacts via DreamPrinting, making multiple interpretations visible and tangible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional approaches to figurative painting treat them as depicting a single recoverable 3D scene, with viewers and reconstruction pipelines converging to one stable model. However, this approach ignores the fundamental ambiguity in interpreting 2D paintings into 3D spaces. The authors want to foreground this non-uniqueness and provide a framework for exploring multiple valid interpretations rather than treating alternatives as errors.

Method: The pipeline has three main stages: 1) Sample multiple camera-orbit multi-view video sequences from one painting using a video generative model (without explicit 3D constraints, allowing small frame-level drifts); 2) Reconstruct each sequence with 3D Gaussian Splatting into point-based Gaussian scene representations where density halos and ghosting expose unresolved degrees of freedom; 3) Fabricate these representations as physical artifacts using DreamPrinting.

Result: The method produces multiple 3D reconstructions from a single painting, with the Gaussian representation's visual artifacts (density halos, ghosting) serving as visual indicators of unresolved degrees of freedom. The reconstructions can be inspected in both digital and physical form, allowing for comparison and discussion of different spatial interpretations.

Conclusion: By treating multiple compatible interpretations as explicit outputs rather than residual error, this work provides a computational framework for spatial readings of figurative painting that makes ambiguity visible and material. It shifts the paradigm from seeking a single "correct" 3D reconstruction to embracing and exploring the space of valid interpretations.

Abstract: Figurative paintings are often approached as if they depict a single recoverable 3D scene: viewers infer depth and occlusion, and reconstruction pipelines attempt to converge to one stable model. We instead foreground multi-solutionness, the non-uniqueness of 3D configurations compatible with a single painted image, and propose a workflow that keeps this non-uniqueness visible and material. Multi-solutionness arises from two sources: unobserved content, where backsides and occluded volumes admit multiple plausible completions, and observed cues, where perspective, shading, and occlusion still underconstrain geometry. When additional views are synthesized by a video generative model without explicit 3D constraints, small frame-level drifts become inevitable rather than exceptional. Our pipeline samples multiple camera-orbit multi-view video sequences from one painting, reconstructs each sequence with 3D Gaussian Splatting into a point-based Gaussian scene representation where density halos and ghosting expose unresolved degrees of freedom, and fabricates these representations as physical artifacts using DreamPrinting. By treating multiple compatible interpretations as explicit outputs rather than residual error, we provide a computational framework for spatial readings of figurative painting that can be inspected, compared, and discussed in both digital and physical form.

</details>


### [105] [An Elementary Expression for Multiple Scattering in Homogeneous Microflake Media](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20394)
*Jonathan Dupuy*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: A novel diffuse-like BRDF based on microfacet theory is proposed, which has an elementary expression for both evaluation and importance sampling while exactly accounting for all scattering orders under the Smith shadowing assumption. It produces Lambertian reflectance at normal incidence and concentrates reflected light around the mirror direction as incidence approaches grazing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research aims to address whether a BRDF construction that admits an elementary expression for both evaluation and importance sampling while accounting exactly for all scattering orders under the Smith shadowing assumption is possible. This fills a gap in existing BRDF models by providing the first such construction.

Method: The method derives a novel diffuse-like BRDF based on microfacet theory, ensuring it has an elementary expression for both evaluation and importance sampling and accounts for all scattering orders under the Smith shadowing assumption.

Result: The BRDF produces Lambertian reflectance at normal incidence and progressively concentrates reflected light around the mirror direction as incidence approaches grazing. Rendering results demonstrate this effect compared to Lambertian and state-of-the-art stochastic microfacet BRDFs.

Conclusion: This work establishes that such a construction is possible, representing the first BRDF to achieve this combination of properties. It provides a practical BRDF model with both computational tractability and physical accuracy under the Smith shadowing assumption.

Abstract: We derive a novel diffuse-like BRDF based on microfacet theory. Its main novelty lies in the fact that it admits an elementary expression for both evaluation and importance sampling, while accounting exactly for all scattering orders under the Smith shadowing assumption. As such, it is the first to settle the question of whether such a construction was possible. In practice, the BRDF produces Lambertian reflectance at normal incidence and progressively concentrates reflected light around the mirror direction as incidence approaches grazing. We showcase this effect by comparing rendering results against Lambertian and state-of-the-art stochastic microfacet BRDFs.

</details>


### [106] [S4R: Scaling for Rigid-Body Interpenetration Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20524)
*Zhiyang Dou,Ang Zhao,Chen Peng,Minghao Guo,Haixu Wu,Cheng Lin,Yuan Liu,Junfeng Yao,Xiaohu Guo,Wenping Wang,Wojciech Matusik*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: S4R is a scale-continuation method for resolving rigid-body interpenetration in procedurally assembled scenes. It shrinks bodies to a penetration-free state, then restores full scale through sequential convex contact quadratic programs, achieving zero penetration with minimal displacement and fastest runtime on benchmarks up to 5000 bodies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigid-body interpenetration frequently occurs in procedurally assembled and generated scenes and must be removed before downstream applications such as physical simulation. Existing methods struggle with deep penetrations and large-scale scenes.

Method: S4R uses a scale-continuation approach: (1) uniformly shrink each body about a fixed reference center to a small initial scale where the layout is penetration-free, (2) restore full scale through a sequence of minimum-norm convex contact quadratic programs (QPs) targeting linearized separation margin during continuation, (3) use conservative scale-event bound and frozen-witness gap predictions to reduce exact mesh queries, (4) end with full-scale evaluator check and bounded tail refinement.

Result: On Kubric, HY3D-Bench, and Thingi10K benchmarks with up to N=5000 bodies, S4R achieves zero reported penetration with displacement that stays small and nearly independent of scene size, and at the lowest wall time within each hardware tier among compared methods. A GPU implementation extends results to large-scale scenes.

Conclusion: S4R presents an effective scale-continuation approach for static interpenetration repair that replaces one deep correction with a sequence of shallow-contact subproblems, achieving superior performance in terms of penetration resolution, displacement bounds, and computational efficiency across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Rigid-body interpenetration frequently occurs in procedurally assembled and generated scenes and must be removed before downstream applications such as physical simulation. We present S4R (Scaling for Rigid-Body Interpenetration Resolution), a scale-continuation method for static interpenetration repair. S4R first uniformly shrinks each body about a fixed reference center to a small initial scale, at which the layout is penetration-free, and then restores full scale through a sequence of minimum-norm convex contact quadratic programs (QPs) that target the linearized separation margin during continuation. Resolution thereby replaces one deep correction with a sequence of shallow-contact subproblems. A conservative scale-event bound and frozen-witness gap predictions cut the number of exact mesh queries; the continuation then ends with a full-scale evaluator check and bounded tail refinement. We evaluate S4R on Kubric, HY3D-Bench, and Thingi10K using a shared mesh-level evaluator and a unified per-scene timing protocol. In the main comparisons on all three benchmarks, up to N=5000 bodies, S4R reaches zero reported penetration with displacement that stays small and nearly independent of scene size, and at the lowest wall time within each hardware tier among the compared methods. A GPU implementation extends these results to large-scale scenes. Our code and data can be found on our project page: https://frank-zy-dou.github.io/projects/S4R/index.html.

</details>


### [107] [Programming-by-Example for Batch-Editing Collision Meshes in 3D Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08804)
*Gengyang Xu,Dongwei Xiao,Hengcheng Zhu,Yiteng Peng,Wei Meng,Shuai Wang,Shing-Chi Cheung*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: MeshForge is a neuro-symbolic program synthesis tool that enables batch-editing of collision meshes in 3D software through programming-by-example, requiring only 2.2 demonstrations on average to synthesize reusable editing programs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As 3D software proliferates, collision meshes (critical for physics engines) require manual editing which is time-consuming and challenging to scale, despite existing tools that can auto-generate collision meshes from visual meshes.

Method: Formulated the task as a programming-by-example problem: given a family of collision meshes with the same editing intent and a small number of user demonstrations, the approach synthesizes a reusable program that captures the editing intent and applies it to non-demonstration meshes.

Result: MeshForge successfully synthesizes 23/24 tasks, requiring 2.2 demonstrations and 3.5 seconds of synthesis time on average across 24 tasks on 600 collision meshes.

Conclusion: The neuro-symbolic program synthesis approach effectively addresses the problem of batch-editing collision meshes, enabling developers to capture editing intent with minimal demonstrations and apply it at scale.

Abstract: As 3D software proliferates, software artifacts now extend beyond code and 2D user interfaces to include 3D assets. Among these assets, collision meshes are critical as they define the geometry used by physics engines for collision detection and physical interaction. Although existing tools can automatically generate collision meshes from visual meshes, they often fail to capture the intended interaction behavior. As a result, developers need to manually edit many heterogeneous collision meshes, a process that is time-consuming and challenging to scale.
  To address this problem, we present a neuro-symbolic program synthesis approach for batch-editing collision meshes. We formulate the task as a programming-by-example problem: given a family of collision meshes with the same editing intent and a small number of user demonstrations, our approach synthesizes a reusable program that captures the editing intent and applies it to non-demonstration meshes. We implement this in a tool named MeshForge, and evaluate it across 24 tasks on 600 collision meshes. MeshForge successfully synthesizes 23/24 tasks, requiring 2.2 demonstrations and 3.5 seconds of synthesis time on average.

</details>


<div id='cs.MM'></div>

# cs.MM [[Back]](#toc)

### [108] [From Models to Systems: A Comprehensive Survey of Efficient Multimodal Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19445)
*Pan Wang,Siwei Song,Hui Ji,Siqi Cao,Heng Yu,Zhijian Liu,Huanrui Yang,Yingyan Celine Lin,Beidi Chen,Mohit Bansal,Xiaoming Liu,Pengfei Zhou,Ming-Hsuan Yang,Tianlong Chen,Jingtong Hu*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: This survey systematizes Efficient Multimodal Learning (EML) research by introducing a model-to-system taxonomy covering three hierarchical levels (model, algorithm, system). Through analysis of 300+ works and a case study on Multimodal Large Language Models, it provides optimization blueprints and posits a paradigm shift toward self-regulating intelligence with natively embedded efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid expansion of multimodal models has created significant bottlenecks in computation, memory, and deployment, necessitating a cohesive understanding of how efficiency is manifested across the learning stack. Existing research remains fragmented, lacking a unified framework to address the Efficiency-Utility-Privacy trade-off.

Method: The authors distill insights from over 300 seminal works into a structured taxonomy across three hierarchical levels: (1) Model level - architectural parsimony, (2) Algorithm level - execution refinement, and (3) System level - hardware-aware orchestration. They provide methodological synthesis of vertical synergies between layers and present an integrative case study of MLLMs.

Result: The survey establishes a structured framework for understanding EML across layers, traces the evolutionary trajectory of MLLMs from structural adjustments to full-stack resource orchestration, and provides application-specific optimization blueprints for diverse domains.

Conclusion: The authors propose a paradigm shift toward self-regulating intelligence where efficiency becomes an intrinsic, emergent property of the model's fundamental design rather than a post-hoc constraint. They present open challenges and future directions that will define EML research trajectory, aiming for multimodal systems that are high-performing, generalizable, and natively efficient for ubiquitous deployment.

Abstract: The rapid expansion of multimodal models has surfaced formidable bottlenecks in computation, memory, and deployment, catalyzing the rise of Efficient Multimodal Learning (EML) as a pivotal research frontier. Despite intensive progress, a cohesive understanding of what, how, and where efficiency is manifested across the learning stack remains fragmented. This survey systematizes the EML landscape by introducing the first structured, model-to-system taxonomy. We distill insights from over 300 seminal works into three hierarchical levels--model, algorithm, and system--addressing architectural parsimony, execution refinement, and hardware-aware orchestration, respectively. Moving beyond a purely categorical review, we offer a methodological synthesis of the vertical synergies between these layers, elucidating how cross-layer co-design contributes to the fundamental "Efficiency-Utility-Privacy" trade-off. Through an integrative case study of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), we trace the field's evolutionary trajectory from initial structural adjustments to modern full-stack resource orchestration. Furthermore, we provide a holistic discussion and application-specific optimization blueprints for diverse domains and posit a paradigm shift toward self-regulating intelligence, where efficiency is an intrinsic, emergent property of the model's fundamental design rather than a post-hoc constraint. Finally, we present open challenges and future directions that will define the trajectory of EML research. This survey establishes a structured framework for multimodal systems that are not only high-performing and generalizable but natively efficient and ready for ubiquitous deployment. A continuously updated version is available at https://github.com/pwang322/Efficient-Multimodal-Learning-Survey.

</details>


### [109] [Trigger Timing, Deadline Readiness, and Event-Aligned Accounting for Dynamic Ad Insertion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19899)
*Prashant Chaudhary,Kapil Khandelwal*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: This paper addresses methodological issues in dynamic ad insertion (DAI) comparisons, where common metrics conflate distinct events like trigger, reach, readiness, and playback. The authors propose an observed-event ledger with a candidate-invariant reference deadline and pod-level contribution accounting to separate these events. Through offline synthetic studies across 45,000 scripts, they demonstrate that playhead summaries substantially misclassify reach events in nonmonotone mixtures, and that subtle definition changes (validity vs. completion at deadline, or readiness scoring timing) can reverse or alter comparison outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic ad insertion comparisons often produce misleading results not because of arithmetic errors, but because they conflate distinct measurement events (trigger, reach, readiness, playback, billability). This conflation can lead to incorrect conclusions about ad performance even when the accounting is technically correct.

Method: The paper introduces: (1) an observed-event ledger framework to separate events, (2) a candidate-invariant reference deadline with fixed rules tested before candidate assignment, (3) a restricted monotone-playback representation, and (4) an offline synthetic study testing 9 short-lifetime conditions and 9 long-lifetime conditions across 45,000 shared scripts with two trigger policies.

Result: Key findings: (1) Playhead summaries substantially misclassify reach events in nonmonotone mixtures, though errors sometimes cancel under shared design. (2) Replacing "validity at deadline" with "completion by deadline" reverses the contribution comparison in 3 of 9 informative conditions. (3) Scoring readiness at actual viewer arrival vs. reference deadline shifts pause-path readiness but doesn't change contribution sign. Conservative bounds can retain uncertainty when records are missing.

Conclusion: The outcomes are consequences of the event definitions applied to established misclassification mechanisms. The paper provides artifact records including code, seeds, event histories, and checking procedures. The evidence is synthetic, uses no commercial telemetry, and does not rank server-side vs. server-guided insertion approaches.

Abstract: Dynamic ad insertion comparisons can conflate trigger, reach, readiness, playback, billability and measurement even when the accounting is arithmetically correct. We separate these events with an observed-event ledger, a candidate-invariant reference deadline and pod-level contribution accounting. The deadline rule is fixed before candidate assignment and tests whether an admissible transition state remains valid, not whether preparation merely finished earlier. A restricted monotone-playback representation states when media-position summaries suffice; a counterexample shows why they fail over a wider path class. An offline synthetic study exercises the definitions over nine short-lifetime conditions informative for the readiness comparison and nine long-lifetime conditions serving as analytic controls. Across 45,000 shared scripts, two trigger policies share imposed playback paths, latency draws and hypothetical value and cost coefficients. Playhead summaries substantially misclassify reach events in the nonmonotone mixtures, yet neither shortcut reverses the contribution contrast in this grid, because some errors cancel under the shared design. Replacing validity at the deadline with completion by the deadline reverses the comparison in three of the nine informative conditions, all at one of the three latency settings. Scoring readiness at actual viewer arrival rather than at the reference deadline shifts pause-path readiness but changes no contribution sign. These outcomes are consequences of the event definitions applied to established misclassification mechanisms. Conservative bounds retain uncertainty when records are missing, and the artifact records code, seeds, event histories and checking procedures. The evidence is synthetic, uses no commercial telemetry, and ranks neither server-side nor server-guided insertion.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [110] [Generative Query Suggestion via Intent Coverage and Query-Level Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19209)
*Xinpeng Liu,Lu Ma,Jiayi Qiao,Mengyu Zhou,Linglong Li,Xiaofeng Bian,Haonan Chen,Xiaoxi Jiang,Guanjun Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization to generate query slates that are both useful individually and diverse in intent coverage. The framework combines intent-aware diversity modeling for supervised fine-tuning with query-level credit assignment for signal routing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The central challenge in generative query suggestion is creating slates where individual queries are useful while ensuring the slate covers distinct user intents. This addresses the trade-off between query-level quality and slate-level diversity.

Method: The proposed framework has two stages: (1) Intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. (2) Query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate.

Result: Experiments on a large-scale production dataset show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage, validated through both offline evaluation and online A/B testing.

Conclusion: The dual-stage optimization approach effectively balances individual query usefulness with slate-level intent diversity, demonstrating practical value in production environments.

Abstract: Generative query suggestion aims to enhance user engagement by anticipating user intents and recommending relevant follow-up queries. A central challenge is to generate slates whose individual queries are useful while the slate covers distinct intents. We propose an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization. First, intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. Second, query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to the corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate. Experiments on a large-scale production dataset, including online A/B testing and offline evaluation, show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.

</details>


### [111] [Layer-wise Curriculum Learning for Efficient LLM Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19213)
*Donggeon Lee,Dooyeon Na,Seungmin Oh,Jongbin Ryu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes layer-wise curriculum learning for efficient LLM compression, which partitions models into segments of layers and uses curriculum learning (easy to hard) to transfer knowledge from teacher to student models. The method includes a feature caching mechanism with multi-threading to address cross-layer feature misalignment. Experiments show >50% reduction in GPU memory and training hours on BERT/GPT-2, with state-of-the-art performance on LLaMA and Qwen models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
