Motivation: The motivation stems from the challenge of compressing large language models (LLMs) efficiently. The authors address the cumulative error phenomenon in layer-wise knowledge transfer, where errors accumulate across layers during knowledge distillation. They aim to accelerate convergence and stabilize the knowledge transfer process while improving computational efficiency in terms of memory usage and training time.

Method: The proposed method consists of three key components: (1) Layer-wise curriculum learning - partitioning the model into segments of layers and applying curriculum learning that starts with easier optimization tasks and progressively tackles harder ones; (2) Theoretical analysis of cumulative error phenomenon to guide the curriculum design; (3) Feature caching with multi-threading strategy to handle feature misalignment across layers and maximize GPU utilization.

Result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets. It reduces GPU memory usage and training hours by more than 50% on BERT and GPT-2 models. Additionally, it outperforms other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models under the same training hours, with lower GPU memory footprint.

Conclusion: Layer-wise curriculum learning is an effective approach for LLM compression, providing both superior model compression performance and high computational efficiency. The curriculum learning approach successfully accelerates convergence and stabilizes knowledge transfer, while the feature caching mechanism efficiently addresses feature misalignment issues. The method demonstrates versatility across different LLM architectures (BERT, GPT-2, LLaMA, Qwen).

Abstract: In this paper, we introduce layer-wise curriculum learning for efficient LLM compression. The proposed method facilitates the knowledge transfer from the teacher model to the student model, utilizing a curriculum learning approach that begins with easier optimization tasks and progressively tackles harder ones. In order to adopt the layer-wise learning in LLM compression, we partition the whole model into multiple segments consisting of layers, thereby enabling more computationally efficient knowledge transfer for LLMs. Based on our theoretical analysis of cumulative error phenomenon, layer-wise curriculum learning accelerates convergence while stabilizing the knowledge transfer process. In addition, we present a feature caching method with a multi-threading strategy to efficiently address feature misalignment across layers, maximizing GPU utilization. Consequently, our method exhibits advanced model compression performance, as well as high computational efficiency in terms of minimized memory usage and short training hours. Experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing GPU memory usage and training hours by more than 50\% on BERT and GPT-2. Moreover, it outperforms the other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models under the same training hours, with a lower GPU memory footprint.

</details>


### [112] [Block Parallelism For Efficient Distributed Long-Context Diffusion Language Model Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19242)
*Tarun Suresh,Pranshu Chaturvedi,Hangoo Kang,Parth Shroff,Ishan S. Khare,Hermann Kumbong,Azalia Mirhoseini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Context-Sharded Block Parallelism (CSBP), a new distributed training method for Block Diffusion Language Models (BDLMs) that enables efficient long-context training by sharding both corrupted blocks and the shared clean sequence across GPU ranks. CSBP achieves 1.18-1.45x throughput improvement for SFT and 1.27-1.33x for model conversion at 256K context, with full-model speedup reaching 1.61x at 512K, while matching or reducing peak HBM memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Block diffusion language models (BDLMs) combine autoregressive dependencies across blocks with parallel denoising within blocks, but long-context training is constrained by two major limitations: (1) distributed attention communication overhead and (2) activation memory constraints. Conventional context parallelism (CP) shards the combined clean-plus-corrupted sequence by position, requiring communication of shared clean K/V together with block-specific corrupted K/V and their gradients.

Method: The authors observe that the BDLM objective separates over target blocks, enabling a new parallelism dimension. They introduce block parallelism (BP), which assigns each corrupted-block computation to one GPU rank. To scale BP to long contexts, they propose context-sharded block parallelism (CSBP), which shards the shared clean sequence across ranks while keeping corrupted K/V and gradients local. This approach avoids replicated clean prefixes and preserves BDLM training semantics.

Result: On 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context, CSBP improves throughput over the best baseline by 1.18-1.45x for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and 1.27-1.33x for conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, while matching or reducing peak HBM memory. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K context. On eight H100 GPUs, CSBP accelerates DFlash2 speculative-decoder training by 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M context. In matched 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite.

Conclusion: CSBP enables efficient scaling of block diffusion language models to extremely long contexts (up to 1M tokens) with significant throughput improvements and reduced memory footprint. The method maintains training quality while substantially accelerating both fine-tuning and model conversion workflows, demonstrating particular effectiveness for speculative decoder training and practical downstream evaluation benchmarks.

Abstract: Block diffusion language models (BDLMs) combine autoregressive dependencies across blocks with parallel denoising within blocks, but long-context training is constrained by distributed attention communication and activation memory. Conventional context parallelism (CP) shards the combined clean-plus-corrupted sequence by position, communicating shared clean K/V together with block-specific corrupted K/V and their gradients. We observe that the BDLM objective separates over target blocks. We introduce block parallelism (BP), a new distributed parallelism dimension that assigns each corrupted-block computation to one rank. To scale BP to long contexts, we introduce context-sharded block parallelism (CSBP), which also shards the shared clean sequence across those ranks. CSBP keeps corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoids replicated clean prefixes, and preserves BDLM training semantics. On 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context, CSBP improves throughput over the best baseline by 1.18-1.45x for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27-1.33x for conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, while matching or reducing peak HBM. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On eight H100 GPUs, CSBP accelerates DFlash2 speculative-decoder training by 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In matched 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite. Code: https://github.com/ScalingIntelligence/Turbo-dLLM

</details>


### [113] [Randomized SVD Approximations for Spectral Co-Clustering of Word-Document Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19243)
*Fateme Mazdarani,Carlos Toxtli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents two randomized approximation methods for normalized spectral co-clustering on bipartite text data, addressing the computational expense of SVD on high-dimensional data. The methods are randomized SVD via random projection and partial SVD combined with random sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spectral co-clustering is useful for discovering latent structure in word-document matrices, but its reliance on singular value decomposition (SVD) makes it computationally expensive on high-dimensional data.

Method: The paper proposes two randomized approximation methods: (1) randomized SVD through random projection, and (2) partial SVD combined with element-wise random sampling. Both handle cases where the numbers of document and word clusters may differ.

Result: Both methods reduce runtime compared to the full-SVD baseline, but their effectiveness depends on matrix sparsity. The random projection method is more reliable across tested settings, while the sampling-based method is most useful on denser matrices and provides limited benefit on already sparse text data.

Conclusion: Randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering should be selected based on the underlying data structure (sparsity), rather than applied uniformly.

Abstract: Spectral co-clustering is a useful tool for discovering latent structure in word-document matrices, but its reliance on singular value decomposition (SVD) can make standard formulations expensive on high-dimensional data. This paper presents two randomized approximations for normalized spectral co-clustering of bipartite text data when the numbers of document and word clusters may differ. The first method uses randomized SVD through random projection, while the second combines partial SVD with element-wise random sampling. Across real-world and synthetic datasets, both methods reduce runtime relative to the full-SVD baseline, but their behavior depends on matrix sparsity. The random projection method is the more reliable approximation across the tested settings, whereas the sampling-based method is most useful on denser matrices and provides limited benefit on already sparse text data. These results show that randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering should be selected according to the underlying structure of the data.

</details>


### [114] [SAGG: Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating for Robust Multimodal Learning under Heterogeneous Corruption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20302)
*Wentao Zhang,Yifan Zhu,Yutong Zhang,Wentao Mo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses multimodal learning under heterogeneous modality corruption, where different samples in a batch have different modalities corrupted. Existing gradient balancing methods assume uniform corruption, leading to irreducible bias. The authors prove that sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the only unbiased strategy, and propose SAGG (Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating) which uses feature-norm quality testing to make per-sample retain-or-discard decisions. SAGG achieves O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence to clean loss stationary points without corruption-dependent error floor, and provides certified robustness bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal gradient balancing methods assume uniform corruption across the training batch, but in practice corruption is sample-heterogeneous - different samples may have different modalities corrupted within a single mini-batch. This mismatch causes irreducible bias in gradient estimation.

Method: The authors first prove theoretically that under heterogeneous corruption, any batch-level sample-agnostic linear estimator with shared modulation parameter incurs irreducible bias. They then propose Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating (SAGG), which makes binary retain-or-discard decisions per sample via an online feature-norm quality test, with a truncation mechanism for variance control. The method uses independent-encoder architecture.

Result: SAGG consistently outperforms ten existing methods on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under Gaussian noise injection, partial modality missing, and natural contribution imbalance, with largest gains in high-corruption regimes where batch-level bias is most severe.

Conclusion: Sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the unique unbiased strategy for heterogeneous modality corruption. SAGG achieves standard O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate to stationary points of clean loss without corruption-dependent error floor, and provides certified robustness radius connecting per-modality Lipschitz constants to classification margin.

Abstract: Multimodal gradient balancing methods modulate encoder gradients with a shared scalar per modality, implicitly assuming that corruption is uniform across the training batch. In practice, corruption is sample-heterogeneous: within a single mini-batch, different samples may have different modalities corrupted. We prove that under this heterogeneous corruption model, any batch-level sample-agnostic linear estimator with a shared modulation parameter incurs an irreducible bias with respect to the clean-data gradient, and that sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the unique unbiased strategy within a natural distribution-free estimator class. Motivated by this result, we propose Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating (SAGG), which makes a binary retain-or-discard decision per sample via an online feature-norm quality test and incorporates a truncation mechanism for variance control. We prove that SAGG-based SGD converges at the standard O(1/sqrt(T)) rate to stationary points of the clean loss without a corruption-dependent error floor, and derive a certified robustness radius for the independent-encoder architecture that connects per-modality Lipschitz constants to the classification margin. Experiments on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under Gaussian noise injection, partial modality missing, and natural contribution imbalance show that SAGG consistently outperforms ten existing methods, with the largest gains in high-corruption regimes where batch-level bias is most severe.

</details>


### [115] [Radio-Frequency Convolutional Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19279)
*Zhihui Gao,Shi-Yuan Ma,Yiran Chen,Dirk Englund,Tingjun Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces radio-frequency convolutional neural networks (RF-CNNs), which repurpose existing wireless radio hardware (frequency mixers) for CNN inference, enabling energy-efficient deep learning on edge devices without additional hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge devices lack sufficient computing capability for modern neural networks, while adding dedicated accelerators increases size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). The authors propose exploiting the frequency mixers already present in wireless radios, which natively perform convolution in the frequency domain.

Method: The researchers mapped multi-channel convolutions onto frequency tones, allowing passive mixers to execute convolutions in a single pass. Weights arrive over the air, and analog hardware is shared with communication functions.

Result: RF-CNN successfully ran deep CNNs with up to 26.4 million parameters and nine layers, achieving close to full-precision performance on wireless signal classification, image classification, and controllable image generation. Energy consumption was reduced to 0.72 femtojoules per multiply-accumulate—two orders of magnitude lower than digital processors.

Conclusion: Deployed wireless infrastructure can deliver efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference to billions of edge devices by repurposing existing communication hardware, eliminating the need for additional computing hardware while maintaining extremely low power consumption.

Abstract: Running artificial intelligence (AI) models directly on edge devices such as smartphones, wearables, and drones offers low latency, pervasive scalability, and data privacy, but these devices rarely carry the computing capability that modern neural networks demand. Edge accelerators have been developed in response, yet each adds computing hardware to devices already constrained in size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). An alternative lies in what these devices already carry: the frequency mixer in every wireless radio multiplies signals in time, natively performing convolution in the frequency domain. Here we introduce radio-frequency convolutional neural networks (RF-CNNs), which repurpose existing communication hardware for CNN inference. Multi-channel convolutions are mapped onto frequency tones for a passive mixer to execute in a single pass. We experimentally demonstrate that RF-CNN runs deep CNNs up to 26.4 million parameters and nine layers from classification of wireless signals and images to controllable image generation, close to full-precision performance. Because the weights arrive over the air and the analog hardware is shared with communication, the edge device spends energy only on data preparation and readout-down to 0.72 femtojoules per multiply-accumulate, two orders of magnitude less than it would cost on an added digital processor. These results suggest that deployed wireless infrastructure can bring efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference to the billions of devices it already connects.

</details>


### [116] [Learning-Induced Dynamical Transition in Recurrent Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19288)
*Varun Vaidya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper develops a non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to describe how learning in recurrent neural networks transforms initially chaotic activity into stable task-dependent behavior through a bifurcation transition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand the fundamental mechanism by which training transforms chaotic neural dynamics into stable, task-relevant behavior in recurrent networks.

Method: Non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) combined with derivation of two-time correlation functions throughout learning.

Result: The study identifies a critical feedback strength and learning rate-dependent critical time that separates chaotic and stable regimes. The transition results from progressive deformation of an effective dynamical landscape by the growing learned feedback structure.

Conclusion: The theory successfully predicts the time evolution of network output during training and shows quantitative agreement with numerical simulations, providing a theoretical framework for understanding learning-induced dynamical transitions in RNNs.

Abstract: Learning in recurrent neural networks can fundamentally reshape their underlying dynamics, transforming initially chaotic activity into stable task-dependent behavior. We develop a non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory(DMFT) to describe this transition during learning. We show that a slow feedback-driven learning process generates an evolving effective feedback strength that drives the network through a transition from chaotic to stable dynamics defined by a bifurcation of the DMFT solution. By deriving the two-time correlation function throughout learning, we identify a critical feedback strength and a corresponding learning rate dependent critical time separating these regimes. The transition arises from the progressive deformation of an effective dynamical landscape by the growing learned feedback structure. Starting from the untrained state, the theory predicts the time evolution of the network output during training and shows quantitative agreement with numerical simulations.

</details>


### [117] [Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Privacy-Preserving Modeling of Heterogeneous Distributed Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19337)
*Xianjian Xie,Hao Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: pFedHGP is a federated learning framework for probabilistic regression and classification that decomposes each client's latent function into shared global, client-specific deviation, and local residual components, using sparse approximations and federated variational inference to keep data local while synchronizing only low-dimensional statistics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable probabilistic machine learning across heterogeneous distributed clients while preserving data privacy, allowing uncertainty-aware decisions in settings where data cannot be centralized (e.g., industrial monitoring, environmental sensing).

Method: Hierarchical Gaussian Process decomposition with (i) shared global component, (ii) client-specific deviation sharing global kernel structure, and (iii) flexible local residual. Uses sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference, with server synchronizing only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component.

Result: Achieved perfect fault classification in press tonnage monitoring using only 13.77% of labeled cycles, and successfully recovered geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series.

Conclusion: pFedHGP effectively handles federated learning with heterogeneous clients while maintaining full predictive distributions for uncertainty quantification, with the hierarchical structure linked to multi-output Gaussian processes for correlated sensors.

Abstract: We present Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes (pFedHGP) for probabilistic regression and classification when data are distributed across heterogeneous clients. Each client's latent function decomposes into (i) a shared global component, (ii) a client-specific deviation that shares the global kernel structure, and (iii) a flexible local residual. Sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference keep raw data local while the server synchronizes only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component. Full predictive distributions support uncertainty-aware decisions. In application studies, pFedHGP attains perfect fault classification in press tonnage monitoring using 13.77% of labeled cycles and recovers geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series. An Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model viewpoint links the hierarchy to multi-output Gaussian processes for correlated sensors.

</details>


### [118] [How to Guide Your Language Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19356)
*Rohit Dilip,Tianrong Chen,Yuyang Wang,David Van Valen,Joshua Susskind,Miguel Angel Bautista*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Probe guidance is a new method to improve flow matching models by using frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal, eliminating the need for additional forward pass at inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve flow matching models and address limitations of autoguidance, which requires additional forward passes and lacks clear understanding of its mechanism.

Method: Probe guidance uses frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal. It applies the method to continuous diffusion language models, where a strong model provides guidance to a weak model. The approach studies how weak models from low-entropy training regions interact with autoguidance.

Result: Sets new state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation for continuous diffusion language models. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, it consistently improves performance on multiple choice question answering benchmarks.

Conclusion: Probe guidance provides a practical method to improve diffusion language models and offers insights into the mechanism behind autoguidance, revealing that weak models must come from low-entropy regions of training for effective guidance.

Abstract: We introduce a new method to guide flow matching models. Our approach, which we call probe guidance, uses the frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal. This works using a similar principle as autoguidance, but eliminates the need for an additional forward pass at inference time and provides a reliable path to ensure that the weak and strong model share similar dynamics. We apply and benchmark this method on continuous diffusion language models, where probe guidance sets a new state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, probe guidance consistently improves on multiple choice question answering benchmarks. Using our probes, we study the traditional autoguidance setting where the strong model is a weak checkpoint, and find that the weak model must come from a low-entropy region of training. These findings both provide a practical way to improve diffusion language models and shed light on the actual mechanism behind autoguidance, which is currently poorly understood.

</details>


### [119] [Smart Insole Human Activity Recognition for Continuous Monitoring in Elderly Care](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19359)
*Edwin Rios,Antony Garcia,Fengpei Yuan,Xinming Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A wireless smart insole platform with 16 pressure sensors and a 6D IMU per foot, combined with machine learning (HGB and 1D-CNN models), can accurately recognize sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking from plantar-pressure and inertial signals for fall prevention in older adults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Falls in older adults are often preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions. Early detection of these changes could enable fall prevention, requiring a wearable system that can continuously monitor activity states through plantar-pressure and inertial measurements.

Method: Data were collected from 15 healthy adults at 80Hz using smart insoles with 16 pressure sensors and a 6D IMU (tri-axial acceleration and angular velocity). Data were segmented into overlapping windows. Window length and model families were screened with stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Primary performance was evaluated with participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation, ensuring all windows from a participant remained in a single fold. Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) and a compact 1D-CNN were compared.

Result: HGB achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 and 0.959 for left and right feet, respectively, and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. The 1D-CNN did not significantly outperform HGB (p=0.0625) using the same participant-independent folds.

Conclusion: Low-profile footwear sensing with pressure and IMU measurements can accurately infer activity states for participants unseen during training. This establishes a basis for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care, with bilateral sensing providing the best performance.

Abstract: Falls in older adults are often preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions. This paper presents a wireless smart insole platform and machine-learning workflow for recognizing sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking from plantar-pressure and inertial signals. Each insole integrates 16 active pressure-sensing locations and a six-dimensional IMU stream consisting of tri-axial acceleration and angular velocity. Data were collected from 15 healthy adults at 80~Hz and segmented into overlapping windows. Window length and candidate model families were first screened with stratified 10-fold cross-validation; the primary performance estimate was then obtained with participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation, ensuring that all windows from a participant remained in a single fold. Under this protocol, Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 and 0.959 for the left and right feet, respectively, and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. A compact 1D-CNN evaluated with the same participant-independent folds did not significantly outperform HGB ($p=0.0625$). The results show that low-profile footwear sensing can infer activity state from pressure and IMU measurements for participants unseen during training, establishing a basis for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care.

</details>


### [120] [Stiefel Attention: When the Geometry of Transformer Projection Matrices Dominates Optimizer Choice---and When It Does Not](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19363)
*Rubén Darío Guerrero*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes constraining the query and key projection matrices in attention mechanisms to the Stiefel manifold, using a specialized Riemannian Adam optimizer. The key mechanism is that weight decay has zero Riemannian gradient on this manifold, which prevents the learned attention geometry from being destroyed by weight decay cycles that affect other model parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The query and key projections (WQ, WK) in attention mechanisms are typically trained with Euclidean optimizers without geometric constraints. The authors propose constraining these matrices to the Stiefel manifold to preserve learned attention geometry during training, particularly against the destructive effects of weight decay.

Method: The method involves: (1) Constraining WQ and WK to the Stiefel manifold St(d,r), (2) Using a Riemannian Adam optimizer with: one scalar second moment per frame, trust region step capping, and polar retraction, (3) Four propositions proving the update properties: steepest descent in embedded metric, gradient scale independence, well-conditioning, and O(d)-equivariance.

Result: The method achieves 97.0% validation accuracy on modular arithmetic grokking at epoch 20,000 compared to baseline's 61.1%. On CIFAR-10 patches, it gains +8.98pp over 12 paired runs (t=60.6, 12/12). The Riemannian update moves 24-40x less per step than standard AdamW, and freezing the projections costs only 0.28pp. Ablation shows the gain comes from step scale freedom, not from the projector or equivariance.

Conclusion: The key mechanism is that weight decay has identically zero Riemannian gradient on the Stiefel manifold, which preserves the learned attention geometry through decay cycles. The method provides significant improvements on grokking and image classification tasks, with the improvement widening with more data rather than eroding. Gauge removal cannot motivate the method since invariant directions carry no gradient.

Abstract: The query and key projections $\WQ,\WK$ in attention are almost always trained by Euclidean optimizers with no constraint on their geometry. We constrain them to the Stiefel manifold and optimize them there with a Riemannian Adam that carries one scalar second moment per frame, caps its step by a trust region, and retracts polarly. Four propositions prove this update is steepest descent in the embedded metric, independent of gradient scale, well conditioned, and exactly $\mathrm{O}(d)$-equivariant, each certified numerically in \texttt{float64}. A fifth supplies the mechanism: weight decay has \emph{identically zero} Riemannian gradient on $\St(d,r)$, since $W = W I_r$ lies in the normal space, so the learned attention geometry survives the collapse cycles that decay drives through the rest of the model. On modular arithmetic grokking, a single run holds $97.0\%$ validation accuracy at epoch 20\,000 against the baseline's $61.1\%$---an unstable endpoint we report as evidence for the mechanism rather than as an effect size. On CIFAR-10 patches the same rule gains $\mathbf{+8.98}$\,pp over 12 paired starts ($t{=}60.6$, $12/12$), and the gap widens with data rather than eroding. The step rule earns this: a fixed-step Riemannian update is degree one in the gradient, so it moves $24$--$40\times$ less per step than an identically shaped AdamW matrix---its frames barely leave their initialization, and freezing them outright costs only $0.28$\,pp. An ablation credits the whole gain to making the step scale free, and nothing measurable to the projector or to equivariance. A negative result sharpens the account: gauge removal cannot motivate the method, because a direction along which the loss is invariant carries no gradient at all.

</details>


### [121] [Machine-Learning Assessment of the Predictive Value of Inflammatory Biomarkers for Cognitive Impairment in an Older Hispanic Adult Cohort](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19374)
*Antony Garcia,Gabrielle Britton,Alcibiades Villarreal,Diana Oviedo,Giselle Rangel,Xinming Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study implements a leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Naive Bayes classifier for predicting cognitive impairment in small clinical tabular datasets (n=165), identifying I-309/CCL1 as a significant predictive biomarker with AUC improvement of 0.110 and strong statistical robustness across repeated cross-validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small clinical tabular datasets require interpretable machine learning because deep learning is often impractical and ensemble models are difficult to inspect. A key pitfall is that statistical significance does not necessarily imply predictive utility.

Method: Leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) classifier. Within every training fold, each continuous predictor was reduced to a supervised chi-square-derived state, while income entered the model through a categorical likelihood. All data-dependent steps were performed within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats.

Result: The demographic baseline achieved ROC-AUC of 0.630 ± 0.017. I-309 (CCL1) was the dominant incremental feature, increasing AUC by 0.110. Paired DeLong tests yielded p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. In the primary analysis, I-309 produced fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018, with median p-value of 0.0011 across 200 random partitions. Among 18 candidate markers, I-309 achieved Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q=0.032 on the frozen partition and satisfied q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions, while no other marker demonstrated reliable incremental predictive value.

Conclusion: I-309/CCL1 is identified as an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment, pending external validation. The fitted model is an inspectable table of thresholds and class-conditional probabilities.

Abstract: Small clinical tabular datasets require interpretable machine learning because deep learning is often impractical and ensemble models can be difficult to inspect. A key pitfall is that statistical significance does not necessarily imply predictive utility. Using data from the Panama Aging Research Initiative--Health Disparities (PARI-HD) cohort (n=165), we implemented a leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) classifier. Within every training fold, each continuous predictor was reduced to a supervised chi-square-derived state, while income entered the model through a categorical likelihood. All data-dependent steps were performed within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats. The demographic baseline achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.630 +/- 0.017. I-309 (CCL1) was the dominant incremental feature, increasing AUC by 0.110, with paired DeLong tests yielding p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. In the pre-specified primary analysis, I-309 produced a fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018, with robustness assessed across 200 random partitions, where the median p-value was 0.0011. Within the exploratory family of 18 candidate markers, I-309 achieved a Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q=0.032 on the frozen partition and satisfied q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions, whereas no other marker demonstrated reliable incremental predictive value. Because the fitted model is an inspectable table of thresholds and class-conditional probabilities, these results identify I-309/CCL1 as an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment, pending external validation.

</details>


### [122] [FCx: An algorithm for finding Feasible Counterfactual Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19383)
*Kleopatra Markou,Vana Kalogeraki,Dimitrios Gunopulos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx), a method that refines counterfactual explanations to ensure feasibility by using a modified VAE with multi-factor loss. It handles both hard constraints (domain knowledge) and soft constraints (causal inference), balancing realism, low-cost, and feasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods fail to ensure feasibility—they may suggest non-constructive modifications or changes incompatible with future events (e.g., changing race). There was a need for CFs that are realistic, low-cost, and feasible simultaneously.

Method: Modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. Uses LOF (Local Outlier Factor) for density estimation to ensure realism. Incorporates hard feasible constraints (domain knowledge) and soft feasible constraints (automatically inferred via causal inference). Cost measured by proximity (absolute change) and sparsity (number of features changed).

Result: Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that FCx matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.

Conclusion: FCx is the first method to efficiently generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost, and feasible simultaneously, addressing limitations of prior approaches.

Abstract: Counterfactual (CF) explanations identify changes that alter an input's classification. While existing methods produce realistic and low-cost CFs, they often fail to ensure feasibility, by suggesting non-constructive modifications or incompatible with future changes (e.g., changing an individual's race to secure a job offer). We introduce a refinement of CF explanations that explicitly enforces feasibility. Our approach is the first to efficiently generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost and feasible. We accommodate both hard feasible constraints, specified by domain knowledge users, and soft feasible constraints, inferred automatically via causal inference from the dataset. Our method, Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx), is based on a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. We measure the cost of a change based on the absolute change in values (proximity) as well as the number of features changed (sparsity) while realism is measured based on the LOF for density estimation, guaranteeing that CFs reside in densely populated regions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that our approach matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.

</details>


### [123] [Improving Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning via Selective Reward Stimulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19414)
*Jing Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RSIQL addresses the credit assignment problem in offline goal-conditioned RL by introducing reward signals at intermediate progress-making states, achieving performance competitive with hierarchical methods while maintaining a simple flat policy structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In offline goal-conditioned RL with sparse rewards and long-horizon dependencies, goal-completion information is temporally distant from early decisions that enable success. This creates a value estimation problem where goal-directed value separation becomes small relative to local estimation error, making learning difficult.

Method: RSIQL uses an auxiliary goal-conditioned value function to identify intermediate states estimated to make progress toward the goal, then applies reward stimulation to provide less-delayed training supervision. Unlike hierarchical methods, it retains a simple non-hierarchical flat policy structure without learning a separate high-level subgoal policy.

Result: Experiments on D4RL goal-reaching benchmarks and OGBench show that RSIQL improves over goal-conditioned IQL on average and achieves performance competitive with hierarchical offline goal-conditioned methods.

Conclusion: Reward stimulation at intermediate states is an effective approach to address the credit assignment problem in offline goal-conditioned RL, offering a simpler alternative to hierarchical methods while achieving comparable performance.

Abstract: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning aims to learn policies that reach specified goals, but remains challenging in offline settings with sparse rewards and long-horizon dependencies. In such settings, goal-completion information can be temporally distant from the early decisions that enable success, while offline value estimation introduces additional error. We study this issue from a reward-propagation perspective and show, in a stylized delayed-goal setting, how goal-directed value separation can become small relative to local estimation error. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Reward Stimulation Implicit Q-Learning (RSIQL), a simple non-hierarchical method that introduces additional reward signals at progress-making intermediate states in offline trajectories. RSIQL uses an auxiliary goal-conditioned value function to identify intermediate states estimated to make progress toward the goal and applies reward stimulation to provide less-delayed training supervision. Unlike hierarchical methods, RSIQL does not learn a separate high-level subgoal policy. Experiments on D4RL goal-reaching benchmarks and OGBench show that RSIQL improves over goal-conditioned IQL on average and achieves performance competitive with hierarchical offline goal-conditioned methods, while retaining a simple flat policy structure.

</details>


### [124] [Bayesian Optimization with Rich Auxiliary Information via LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19437)
*Tejus Gupta,Efe Mert Karagözlü,Rohit Sonker,Barnabás Póczos,Jeff Schnieder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to incorporate rich auxiliary information (e.g., training curves, expert notes, images, prior knowledge) into Bayesian Optimization (BO). Three methods are developed for this integration, and they are evaluated on hyperparameter optimization benchmarks and a nuclear fusion optimization task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Bayesian Optimization only uses function evaluations, but many real-world problems contain substantially richer information (training curves, expert notes, images, prior knowledge about optima) that is not being utilized.

Method: Three methods for incorporating auxiliary information into BO using LLMs. The specific methods are not detailed in the abstract, but they involve leveraging LLMs to process and guide optimization using the rich auxiliary information.

Result: The proposed methods consistently outperform both standard BO and existing LLM-based optimization approaches across hyperparameter optimization benchmarks and a real-world nuclear fusion optimization task.

Conclusion: LLMs are effective for leveraging rich auxiliary information in Bayesian Optimization, demonstrating the potential to significantly improve optimization performance in real-world scenarios.

Abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely used for optimizing expensive black-box functions, yet many real-world optimization problems contain substantially richer information than function evaluations alone. Examples include training curves in hyperparameter optimization, expert notes and images in scientific experimentation, and prior knowledge about where optima may lie. We show that large language models (LLMs) can effectively leverage such rich auxiliary information to guide optimization. Motivated by these findings, we develop three methods for incorporating auxiliary information into BO using LLMs. Across hyperparameter optimization benchmarks and a real-world nuclear fusion optimization task, our methods consistently outperform both standard BO and existing LLM-based optimization approaches. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of LLMs for leveraging rich auxiliary information in BO.

</details>


### [125] [Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) Improves Classification Accuracy of Bacterial Raman Spectral Data Enabling Portable Diagnostics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19453)
*Kaitlin Zareno,Jarett Dewbury,Siamak K. Sorooshyari,Hossein Mobahi,Loza F. Tadesse*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses antimicrobial resistance diagnostics using Raman spectroscopy enhanced by Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to improve model generalization on limited clinical bacterial datasets, achieving up to 10.5% accuracy improvement over traditional Adam optimizer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Antimicrobial resistance is projected to cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050, with resource-limited regions most affected. Current Raman spectroscopy-based pathogen diagnostics require complex pre-processing and fail to generalize well across diverse patient populations with limited datasets.

Method: The authors applied Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) optimizer to enhance model generalization in clinical bacterial isolate classification tasks using Raman spectroscopy. They compared SAM's performance against the traditional Adam optimizer across multiple data splits.

Result: SAM achieved accuracy improvements of up to 10.5% on a single split and an average accuracy increase of 2.7% across all splits in spectral classification tasks compared to Adam optimizer.

Conclusion: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) demonstrates capability to advance clinical application of AI-powered Raman spectroscopy tools by improving generalization on limited clinical datasets, potentially enabling rapid antibiotic resistance testing within hours rather than days.

Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is expected to claim 10 million lives per year by 2050, and resource-limited regions are most affected. Raman spectroscopy is a novel pathogen diagnostic approach promising rapid and portable antibiotic resistance testing within a few hours, compared to days when using gold standard methods. However, current algorithms for Raman spectra analysis 1) are unable to generalize well on limited datasets across diverse patient populations and 2) require increased complexity due to the necessity of non-trivial pre-processing steps, such as feature extraction, which are essential to mitigate the low-quality nature of Raman spectral data. In this work, we address these limitations using Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to enhance model generalization across a diverse array of hyperparameters in clinical bacterial isolate classification tasks. We demonstrate that SAM achieves accuracy improvements of up to 10.5% on a single split, and an increase in average accuracy of 2.7% across all splits in spectral classification tasks over the traditional optimizer, Adam. These results display the capability of SAM to advance the clinical application of AI-powered Raman spectroscopy tools.

</details>


### [126] [Enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network by Domain Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19466)
*Ci Lin,Futong Li,Rose Chong-Wu,Tet Yeap,Iluju Kiringa*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid neural-mechanistic framework (KAINN) that incorporates domain knowledge about fertilizer diffusion, soil respiration, and water-filled porosity into deep learning models (CNN, LSTM, Transformer) to improve prediction accuracy, interpretability, and generalization of agricultural N2O emissions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate prediction of N2O emissions from agriculture is important for environmental impact assessment and sustainable farming, but remains challenging due to complex interactions among soil, climate, biochemical processes, and management practices, combined with limited high-quality observations. Existing deep learning models lack physical interpretability and may generalize poorly.

Method: Proposed KAINN (Knowledge-enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network), a hybrid neural-mechanistic framework that extends the Agriculture-informed Neural Network (AINN) by incorporating domain knowledge about fertilizer diffusion, soil respiration, and water-filled porosity. Evaluated using CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures across multiple growing seasons and input-feature configurations.

Result: KAINN generally provides lower RMSE and MAE, higher R-squared values compared to purely data-driven models and the original AINN. The learned interfaces show smoother and more physically consistent parameter trajectories with reduced uncertainty.

Conclusion: Incorporating environmental knowledge into neural networks can improve the reliability, interpretability, and generalization of agricultural N2O-emission predictions.

Abstract: Accurate prediction of nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from agriculture is important for assessing environmental impacts and supporting sustainable farming. However, prediction remains difficult because N2O emissions result from complex interactions among soil properties, climate, biochemical processes, and management practices, while high-quality observations are limited. Deep learning models can capture nonlinear relationships but often lack physical interpretability and may generalize poorly across environmental conditions. We propose the Knowledge-enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network (KAINN), a hybrid neural-mechanistic framework that extends the Agriculture-informed Neural Network by incorporating domain knowledge about fertilizer diffusion, soil respiration, and water-filled porosity. We evaluate KAINN using CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures across multiple growing seasons and input-feature configurations. The results show that KAINN generally provides lower root mean square error and mean absolute error and higher R-squared values than purely data-driven models and the original AINN. Analysis of the learned interfaces also shows smoother and more physically consistent parameter trajectories with reduced uncertainty. These findings demonstrate that incorporating environmental knowledge into neural networks can improve the reliability, interpretability, and generalization of agricultural N2O-emission predictions.

</details>


### [127] [The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19616)
*Michael Hernandez,Tian Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a pre-generation prompt complexity index (six dimensions) to predict code generation failure. Analyzing 5,000 Python prompts rated by 4 LLM raters and 21 models generating code, they find a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite score 13.75, where pass rates differ significantly (79.9% vs 87.6%). However, this relationship is not universal and varies with task type, construction frame, and model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current output-based complexity measures fail because difficult prompts can yield short failing programs with low complexity scores. The authors argue for a prompt-side complexity measurement before generation to better predict failure.

Method: Six-dimension prompt-side structural-complexity index scored before generation; 5,000 Python prompts across six bands; four LLM raters providing 19,997 score rows (ICC = 0.872); 21 models evaluated per prompt (105,000 generations); regression analysis with task-type fixed effects and construction-frame controls; Lizard complexity for output complexity; 2SLS estimates.

Result: Pass rate shows nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 13.75 (79.9% below vs 87.6% above). Task-type fixed effects shift breakpoint to 10.75 and reduce regime gap from 7.6 to 2.1 points. Construction-frame control shifts breakpoint to 8.50 with raw gap of -3.5 points. 28.5% of zero-pass generations have prompt composite >8 but output complexity ≤10. Human agreement is moderate and rater-dependent.

Conclusion: The six-dimension composite serves as a pre-generation measurement framework, but the relationship between prompt complexity and failure is not universal—it depends on task type, construction frame, and model. The study provides bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes without causal claims.

Abstract: Complexity measured from generated code is failure-dependent: a difficult prompt can yield a short failing program and be assigned low output complexity. We introduce a six-dimension prompt-side structural-complexity index scored before generation and kept separate from correctness. We select 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater rubric. Four out-of-panel LLM raters rescore the locked prompts, giving 19,997 score rows; composite inter-rater reliability is ICC = 0.872 on the 4,998 prompts with all four ratings. We evaluate 21 models per prompt, yielding 105,000 generations. In the unadjusted mean-pooled analysis, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 13.75, with 79.9% at or below and 87.6% above. This is not a universal failure cutoff. Task-type fixed effects shift the breakpoint to 10.75 and cut the regime gap from 7.6 to 2.1 points. A construction-frame control shifts it to 8.50 with a raw gap of -3.5 points, and neither frame alone reproduces the pooled +7.6-point change. Model-specific fits include 16 upward and five downward changes. A 365-prompt audit-clean extension matches the original five-model estimates at bins 15 and 16 but adds only 14 prompts above bin 16. Among zero-pass generations with computable Lizard complexity, 28.5% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity at most 10. Human agreement is moderate and rater-dependent on a disagreement-enriched calibration set; paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve score ordering. Overidentification tests reject the joint restrictions on the six dimensions, so we treat the composite as an index and make no causal interpretation of the 2SLS estimates. The contribution is a pre-generation measurement framework and a bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes.

</details>


### [128] [Search at the Cost of Sampling: Nearly-Instant Latent Space Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19476)
*Donney Fan,Colin Doumont,Aleksandra Kalisz,Paul Duckworth,Jacob R. Gardner,Henry Moss,Geoff Pleiss*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a fast Bayesian optimization (BO) method for de novo discovery pipelines where virtual screens are cheap. By exploiting spherical symmetry in a linear model constrained to a spherical domain with high-dimensional latents, the authors derive nearly closed-form solutions, achieving 100x speedup over baselines while maintaining or improving performance on molecular and image generation benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bayesian optimization (BO) is naturally suited for de novo discovery pipelines that generate designs at scale and filter through virtual screens. However, BO's computational overhead becomes a bottleneck when virtual screens are relatively cheap, making it impractical for this setting.

Method: The authors exploit the unique combination of a linear model constrained to a spherical domain where high-dimensional latents concentrate. They build on recent work justifying linear surrogates while deriving nearly closed-form solutions to surrogate modeling and acquisition problems that exploit spherical symmetry.

Result: The method achieves at least a 100x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines, with matching or improved performance across molecular and image generation benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed method makes BO a practical drop-in for de novo pipelines where it was previously too slow to consider, enabling its use in settings where computational efficiency is critical.

Abstract: Generative models are increasingly central to many de novo discovery pipelines, in which designs are generated at scale and filtered through virtual screens to determine a set of candidates to experimentally validate. While Bayesian optimization (BO) is a natural fit for this setting, as it uses past evaluations to guide future proposals, the computational overhead required for its sequential decision-making becomes a bottleneck when virtual screens are relatively cheap. We make BO practical in this regime by exploiting the unique combination of a linear model constrained to a spherical domain where high-dimensional latents concentrate. We build off recent work justifying the use of linear surrogates, while deriving nearly closed-form solutions to the surrogate modelling and acquisition problems that exploit spherical symmetry. The result is at least a 100x speedup over state-of-the art baselines, with matching or improved performance across molecular and image generation benchmarks. Altogether, our method makes BO a practical drop-in for de novo pipelines where it was previously too slow to consider.

</details>


### [129] [Sample Count Is Not Enough: Candidate-Generation Strategy Shapes the Energy and Performance of LLM Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19499)
*Mobina Kashaniyan,Ali Jannesari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by generating multiple candidates, but candidate count (N) alone does not capture systems cost. Using fewer generation calls with larger batch sizes is more energy-efficient and has lower latency than many sequential calls with smaller batches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While test-time scaling methods often describe inference budget by candidate count N, this metric ignores how candidates are executed. The same N can be achieved via one batched call or multiple sequential calls, with potentially vast differences in systems cost (latency, throughput, energy).

Method: Experiments on Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B using 500 GSM8K prompts. First studied effect of increasing N (1→8) on accuracy. Then fixed N=8 and compared four generation schedules: 1x8, 2x4, 4x2, 8x1 (axb = a calls with b candidates per call). Measured latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy on A100 GPUs.

Result: Increasing N from 1 to 8 improved accuracy by 8.4 percentage points (Phi-3-mini) and 18.4 points (Qwen2.5-1.5B). With N=8 fixed, eight serial calls (8x1) used 4.64-4.86x more gross GPU-device energy and had 5.77-6.12x higher P95 latency than one batched call (1x8). Same pattern appeared across three independent A100 nodes and in SciQ/V100 experiments.

Conclusion: Candidate count alone is insufficient to describe the systems cost of multi-candidate test-time scaling. When candidates are independent and memory allows, fewer generation calls with larger batch sizes are more efficient. Evaluations should report not only candidate count and accuracy, but also generation schedule and GPU-level systems metrics.

Abstract: Test-time scaling can improve large language model reasoning by generating and combining multiple candidate responses. In sampling-based methods, the inference budget is often described by the number of generated candidates, N. However, N tells us how many candidates are generated, not how they are executed. The same candidate budget can be produced in one batched generation call or split across several sequential calls with smaller batch sizes. We first study the effect of increasing N on reasoning accuracy using Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on 500 GSM8K prompts. As expected, increasing N from 1 to 8 improves accuracy by 8.4 percentage points for Phi-3-mini and 18.4 points for Qwen2.5-1.5B. However, accuracy alone does not show the systems cost of using a larger candidate budget. We therefore fix N = 8 and compare four generation schedules: 1x8, 2x4, 4x2, and 8x1, where axb denotes a generation calls with b candidates per call. We measure latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy while keeping the total candidate count fixed. On A100 GPUs, eight serial calls use 4.64-4.86x as much gross GPU-device energy and have 5.77-6.12x the P95 latency of one batched call with eight candidates. The same pattern appears across three independently scheduled A100 nodes per model and in short-output SciQ/V100 experiments. These results show that candidate count alone is not enough to describe the systems cost of multi-candidate test-time scaling. When candidates are independent and memory allows it, fewer generation calls with larger batch sizes are more efficient. Evaluations should therefore report not only candidate count and accuracy, but also generation schedule and GPU-level systems metrics.

</details>


### [130] [LSTM-UT and Recurrent-Depth Transformers on Cellular Automata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19521)
*Aras Kavuncu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares three recurrent-depth Transformer variants (BUT, CoTFormer, and LSTM-UT) on Rule 30 cellular automata and delayed-recall tasks, finding that LSTM-UT with bounded gated memory outperforms both BUT and CoTFormer in depth extrapolation and delayed recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how different mechanisms for retaining information across recurrent steps affect a Transformer's ability to extrapolate to unseen recurrent depths and perform delayed recall tasks.

Method: The researchers compared Block Universal Transformer (BUT, carries only current hidden state), CoTFormer (retains expanding attention cache), and a new LSTM Universal Transformer (LSTM-UT, with bounded gated memory). They conducted experiments on Rule 30 cellular automata (testing depth extrapolation) and a delayed-recall task, with state and cache interventions to analyze failure modes.

Result: BUT extrapolates to unseen recurrent depths more reliably than CoTFormer, though its accuracy eventually degrades. CoTFormer's failure involves interaction between current state and retained history—correcting the state can temporarily help but retained history undermines corrections. In delayed recall, BUT also outperforms CoTFormer, which fails to reliably select requested cached representations. LSTM-UT improves both depth extrapolation and delayed recall over both baselines.

Conclusion: Bounded gated memory (as in LSTM-UT) is an effective inductive bias for repeated computation and later retrieval in these tasks, outperforming approaches that rely solely on hidden state or expanding attention caches.

Abstract: Recurrent-depth Transformers apply shared computation repeatedly, but differ in how they retain information across steps. We compare a Block Universal Transformer (BUT), which carries only its current hidden state; CoTFormer, which also retains an expanding attention cache; and a new LSTM Universal Transformer (LSTM-UT) with bounded gated memory. On Rule 30 cellular automata, BUT extrapolates to unseen recurrent depths more reliably than CoTFormer, although its accuracy eventually degrades. State and cache interventions show that CoTFormer's failure depends on their interaction: correcting the current state can temporarily restore accuracy, while retained history can undermine that correction. In a delayed-recall task, BUT also outperforms CoTFormer despite lacking direct access to past states; CoTFormer does not reliably select the requested cached representation. LSTM-UT improves both depth extrapolation and delayed recall over these baselines. The results support bounded gated memory as an effective inductive bias for repeated computation and later retrieval in these tasks.

</details>


### [131] [Compressed Active Subspaces for Scalable Bayesian Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19539)
*Thomas Flynn,Sanket Jantre,Byung-Jun Yoon,Kibaek Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Compressed Active Subzones (CAS), a scalable method that uses structured isometric embedding to compress high-dimensional model parameters before constructing active subspaces, enabling efficient uncertainty quantification for large neural networks that would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Active subspace methods face a critical scalability limitation: they require storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive as model size increases. This prevents their application to large neural networks and other high-dimensional models where uncertainty quantification is needed.

Method: The proposed CAS approach first maps model parameters to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding, then constructs the active subspace within this reduced parameterization. This two-step process allows gradient storage to occur in the compressed domain rather than the original high-dimensional space.

Result: CAS substantially reduces memory requirements for active subspace construction while maintaining predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates. The method is demonstrated on neural networks of increasing size.

Conclusion: Compressed Active Subspaces enables Bayesian inference for large models where standard active subspace methods become impractical, representing a significant advancement in scalable uncertainty quantification for high-dimensional models.

Abstract: Active subspace methods provide a framework for quantifying predictive uncertainty in high-dimensional models by identifying and performing inference along parameter directions that have the greatest influence on the model output. However, the construction of active subspaces requires storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive as model size increases. We address this limitation by proposing Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS), a scalable approach that first maps the model parameters to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding and then constructs the active subspace within this reduced parameterization. Our approach substantially reduces the memory required for active subspace construction and enables Bayesian inference for large models where standard active subspace methods become impractical. We demonstrate the scalability of CAS on neural networks of increasing size while maintaining predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates.

</details>


### [132] [FedFIbOS: Fisher Importance based Optimal Submodelling for Heterogeneous Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19559)
*Yasmeen Afzal,Jeremiah D. Deng,Haibo Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses heterogeneous federated learning where clients with diverse computational capacities train capacity-constrained submodels. The authors propose FedFIbOS, which uses Fisher Information as a principled criterion for submodel parameter selection, derived from minimizing submodel masking error. The method theoretically formulates submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate and shows that Fisher top-k selection solves this under Fisher-dominant ranking conditions. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under non-IID settings demonstrate ~10% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing heterogeneous federated learning methods select submodel parameters using heuristic importance measures (parameter magnitude) without theoretical justification. There's a fundamental gap: existing parameter selection criteria lack theoretical grounding in convergence frameworks, and partial client participation introduces additional estimation effects in Fisher scores. The authors identify that magnitude-based selection lacks theoretical grounding for why these measures support convergence.

Method: The paper proposes FedFIbOS (Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling) which uses Fisher Information in a principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. The method: (1) theoretically formulates submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate; (2) shows that raw Fisher top-k rule implemented by FedFIbOS solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition; (3) retains convergence structure of underlying masked federated optimization bound; (4) efficiently estimates Fisher scores from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients, enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead.

Result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves approximately 10% higher accuracy than the state of the art. The improvements become more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.

Conclusion: The proposed FedFIbOS provides a theoretically grounded approach to submodel parameter selection in heterogeneous federated learning using Fisher Information. The method successfully addresses the gap between heuristic selection criteria and convergence theory, demonstrating significant accuracy improvements especially under strong non-IID heterogeneity conditions.

Abstract: Heterogeneous federated learning requires clients with diverse computational capacities to collaboratively train a global model, where each client trains a capacity-constrained submodel. Existing methods select submodel parameters using heuristic importance measures---most prominently parameter magnitude---without theoretical justification for why these measures support convergence. We identify a fundamental gap: existing parameter selection criteria lack theoretical grounding in the convergence framework, partial client participation introduces additional estimation effects in the Fisher scores. We propose \textbf{FedFIbOS}: Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling for heterogeneous federated learning, using Fisher Information in a principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. %We formally establish when magnitude selection is equivalent to Fisher selection fail under non-IID heterogeneous federated learning. We theoretically formulate submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate and show that the raw Fisher top-$k$ rule implemented by FedFIbOS solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition. The resulting method retains the convergence structure of the underlying masked federated optimization bound. Fisher scores are efficiently estimated from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients, enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves ${\approx}10\%$ higher accuracy than the state of the art, with improvements becoming more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.

</details>
