Abstract: Croissant is the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets: JSON-LD over schema.org. Since version 1.1 it also carries data use conditions, recommending DUO and ODRL for them. What no version specifies is how any of them is evaluated: no decision procedure, no bound on evaluation cost, no outcome for a condition an implementation cannot evaluate, no record of what was checked, and nothing on composition with caller-side authority. We supply that half. An additive profile lets a dataset declare the operations it admits and the conditions under which it admits them, over a closed set of five operators whose decision procedure is given in full, so a gate decides from the descriptor alone and records what it checked. Two corpora evaluate it and their evidence is kept apart. Three descriptors that gated a real nf-core pipeline give the deployment result: decisions from a profile document match the gate's native descriptor record for record, stripping the layer leaves a valid Croissant document, and the added cost is 11.7 $μ$s against a 119 $μ$s decision. A corpus generated from the profile's grammar gives the breadth, covering every operator, refusal class and conformance clause. Across its valid cases, 552 complete decision records agree three ways -- native descriptor, profile terms, and the same policy as ODRL in usageInfo. The carrier is therefore not the contribution; the evaluation semantics is. Finally, caller-bound and data-bound policies range over non-overlapping state spaces, so neither permit set contains the other.

</details>


### [134] [CoRe: Coherence and Relational Alignment for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19670)
*Xiaoyu Lin,Huiran Duan,Yining Liu,Zhixiang Wu,Chu Lin,Lin Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoRe is a model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate time-series forecasting that replaces pointwise supervision (like MSE) with two output-space constraints: frequency coherence loss and low-rank relational graph loss, to preserve temporal coherence and relational consistency across variables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current direct multivariate forecasting models predict the full future horizon in a single pass but use training objectives decomposed into pointwise errors (e.g., MSE). While providing stable supervision, these objectives fail to explicitly preserve the structure of future trajectories - specifically temporal coherence within each variable and relational consistency across variables.

Method: CoRe introduces two output-space constraints: (1) Frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra in the frequency domain; (2) Low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The objective is model-agnostic, introduces no trainable parameters, and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss function.

Result: Experiments on standard benchmarks show that CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings consistently.

Conclusion: CoRe provides a simple yet effective approach to improve multivariate forecasting by enforcing structural constraints in the output space. Its model-agnostic nature and parameter-free design make it a versatile addition to existing forecasting architectures.

Abstract: Direct forecasting has become a standard paradigm for multivariate time-series forecasting because it predicts the full future horizon in a single pass. However, its training objective is often still decomposed into pointwise errors such as MSE. Such objectives provide stable supervision, but they do not explicitly preserve the structure of the future trajectory: temporal coherence within each variable and relational consistency across variables can both be weakened. We propose CoRe, a model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate forecasting. CoRe replaces pointwise supervision with two output-space constraints: a frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra, and a low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The resulting objective introduces no trainable parameters and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings overall consistently.

</details>


### [135] [Conservation Buys Stability and Factoring Buys Counterfactuals in Physical World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19674)
*Yufeng Wang,Parivesh Priye,Lu Wei,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: A learned simulator can reproduce its training conditions accurately yet fail in two distinct ways once those conditions change. Over long rollouts, small errors accumulate until the trajectory drifts away from physically plausible behavior; under an intervention on a physical parameter, the model may continue to follow the law seen during training rather than the intervened one. We show that these two failures require different structural remedies. Evolving a learned energy with a symplectic integrator preserves the geometry of the conservative dynamics and keeps rollouts bounded and physically meaningful for up to $100\times$ the training horizon, while equal-capacity predictors, an energy-regularized predictor, and a tuned neural ODE diverge. By contrast, encoding the physical coupling through an explicit linear factorization enables the model to follow a never-seen sign of that coupling, whereas an unrestricted parameterization remains locked to the training law. Crucially, the two mechanisms are separable: removing the structure responsible for long-horizon stability leaves counterfactual transfer intact, while removing the factorized coupling destroys counterfactual transfer without eliminating stability. This double dissociation, established with matched controls that remove or replace one structural component at a time, persists beyond the headline three-body system and remains visible when the physical state must be inferred from pixels rather than provided directly. The result is a concrete design principle for physical world models: long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization arise from distinct structural commitments, and each can be imposed deliberately without requiring the other.

</details>


### [136] [Opinion Dynamics-based Coalition Formation for Federated Learning in Heterogeneous IoT Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19695)
*Mohammed El Hanjri,Anas Abouaomar,Hamidou Tembine,Abdellatif Kobbane*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of statistical heterogeneity in Federated Learning for IoT water-metering networks by proposing a coalition formation approach using Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion dynamics. The method forms client coalitions in local-weight space and aggregates at the coalition level, eliminating the need for additional computation or communication compared to FedAvg.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) aggregation averages dissimilar local models into a single global model that fails to capture client-specific patterns in heterogeneous IoT deployments like smart-city water-metering networks where each smart meter observes household-specific consumption time series.

Method: The proposed method models coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process acting on local weights. Two variants are developed based on Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. The framework is applied to short-term water-consumption forecasting using local Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models.

Result: The proposed HK-based coalition formation produces stable, endogenous coalition structures within at most ten inner iterations, incurs no additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg, and reduces the average MAE by up to 54% relative to FedAvg, 39% relative to FedProx, and 24% relative to Per-FedAvg, while achieving the highest global accuracy (83-85%).

Conclusion: The HK-based coalition formation approach effectively addresses statistical heterogeneity in federated learning for IoT applications, significantly outperforming baseline methods like FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, and FedProx in both prediction accuracy and coalition stability without adding computational or communication overhead.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving, on-device training across heterogeneous Internet-of-Things (IoT) deployments such as smart-city water-metering networks, where each smart meter observes a household-specific consumption time series. Under such statistical heterogeneity, the standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) aggregation averages dissimilar local models into a single global model that may fail to capture client-specific patterns. We address this by forming client coalitions directly in the local-weight space and aggregating at the coalition level. Extending a prior weight-driven coalition-formation scheme, we model coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process acting on the local weights, and develop variants of the HK interaction based on Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. The framework is applied to short-term water-consumption forecasting with local Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models and evaluated against FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAvg with Euclidean-distance or cosine-similarity coalition formation. Experiments on a real smart-metering dataset of water consumption show that the proposed HK-based coalition formation produces stable, endogenous coalition structures within at most ten inner iterations, incurs no additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg, and reduces the average MAE by up to 54% relative to FedAvg, 39% relative to FedProx, and 24% relative to Per-FedAvg, while achieving the highest global accuracy (83-85%).

</details>


### [137] [Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling: A Specification and Design Guide for Contrast-Based Multi-Armed Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19709)
*Sulgi Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS), a novel approach to batched multi-armed bandits that addresses the stale memory problem when baseline reward rates (shared levels) change between updates. Instead of carrying absolute reward rates forward, OR-TS maintains the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and re-estimates the common level fresh in each batch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard batched multi-armed bandit implementation carries each arm's absolute reward rate from one update to the next. When the shared level (baseline) moves between batches, this memory becomes stale and unreliable, even though the comparisons between arms may still be valid. This degradation affects the accuracy of arm selection in A/B testing scenarios where the baseline is not stationary.

Method: The authors specify the OR-TS update mechanism, which carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and fits the common level fresh in every batch, marginalizing it out. They incorporate two control parameters: (1) decay - controlling how much past evidence survives an update, and (2) aggressiveness - controlling how sharply belief becomes allocation. The method was evaluated against absolute-rate memory across 86 public A/B series and in synthetic environments, plus a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments.

Result: Across 86 public A/B series, the level varies about twenty-five times more than the contrast. In prespecified synthetic environments with a moving level, absolute-rate memory incurs five times the regret compared to OR-TS, and the best arm falls below majority traffic in 7 of 20 runs (vs. none for OR-TS). In the policy simulation from 71 real experiments (where contrasts are too small to resolve), expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 experiments, yet contrast memory still ends on the better arm more than twice as often as absolute-rate memory.

Conclusion: OR-TS significantly outperforms absolute-rate memory when the baseline level moves between batches, reducing regret by approximately 5x and maintaining the best arm in the majority of traffic. However, when the contrasts themselves move, the method fails - this is a key limitation that requires careful monitoring of assumption validity in practical deployment.

Abstract: Batched multi-armed bandits update on a service's own schedule, and the usual implementation carries each arm's absolute reward rate from one update to the next. When the shared level moves between batches, that memory goes stale even though the comparisons between arms may not have. Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS) instead carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and fits the common level afresh in every batch, marginalizing it out. This paper specifies that update, places it inside a Bayesian bandit agent with two controls, decay for how much past evidence survives an update and aggressiveness for how sharply belief becomes allocation, and evaluates it against absolute-rate memory. Across 86 public A/B series the level varies about twenty-five times more than the contrast. In prespecified synthetic environments a moving level costs absolute-rate memory five times the regret and leaves the best arm below a majority of traffic in 7 of 20 runs, against none for OR-TS. In a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments, where the contrasts are too small to resolve, expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 of them, yet contrast memory still ends on the better arm more than twice as often. Where the contrasts themselves move, the bet fails, and that case is reported too.

</details>


### [138] [Learn Your Own Thoughts: Abstract Token Curriculum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19717)
*Khashayar Gatmiry,Avrajit Ghosh,Parsa Mirtaheri,Jason D. Lee,Nika Haghtalab,Emmanuel Abbe,Peter Bartlett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC), a curriculum learning framework that trains Large Language Models to develop internal continuous "thoughts" without requiring explicit supervision on thinking tokens or manual scratchpad design. The method gradually increases problem complexity to elicit effective intermediate representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-thought (CoT) techniques have shown strong reasoning capabilities but require explicit supervision on thinking tokens, which demands rich task-specific data. There is a need for methods that can develop internal thoughts without direct supervision or manual scratchpad design.

Method: ATC is a curriculum learning framework that gradually increases problem complexity through a sequence of distributions, training the model to develop internal abstract "thoughts" in continuous representation space. The theoretical analysis examines learning parity functions with single-layer softmax attention.

Result: Theoretically, for learning parity functions with ATC, attention naturally focuses on CoT tokens that provide the "easiest path" to predicting the next token. Experimentally, ATC demonstrates effectiveness on graph reachability and arithmetic learning tasks.

Conclusion: ATC provides both theoretical and experimental evidence for its benefits, showing advantages over previous methods for training continuous thoughts in LLMs without requiring explicit supervision or manual design.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable reasoning capabilities by utilizing chain-of-thought (CoT) as a scratchpad for intermediate stages of thinking. However, CoT techniques require explicit supervision on thinking tokens, which requires rich, task-specific data. In this work, we propose Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC), a novel curriculum learning framework that elicits effective continuous intermediate representations without direct supervision or manual scratchpad design. ATC gradually increases problem complexity through a sequence of distributions, training the model to develop internal abstract ``thoughts'' in the continuous representation space. This paper provides both theoretical and experimental evidence for the benefits of ATC and its advantages over previous methods for training continuous thoughts. Theoretically, we show that for learning parity functions with single-layer softmax attention using ATC, attention naturally focuses on the CoT tokens in the context that provide the ``easiest path'' to predicting the next token. Experimentally, we show ATC's effectiveness on graph reachability and arithmetic learning tasks.

</details>


### [139] [Alliance Beats Isolation: Unifying Heterogeneous Allied Datasets Improves Classifier Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19748)
*Girish Keshav Palshikar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of combining "allied" heterogeneous datasets—datasets with same class labels but disjoint objects and largely distinct feature spaces—with few shared features. The authors propose merging feature-spaces and using matrix completion to create a unified dataset that enables knowledge transfer between datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many domains (student dropout, insurance fraud, loan approval, machine failures), multiple labeled datasets exist that are allied: same type of objects but disjoint, same class labels, but heterogeneous feature spaces. Current methods cannot train a single classifier on both datasets or transfer knowledge between them. This limits the potential to leverage multiple allied datasets to improve classification performance.

Method: The proposed method has two main steps: (1) Merge the feature-spaces of paired allied heterogeneous datasets into a single unified feature-space; (2) Use matrix completion to create a unified dataset based on the merged feature-space. This unified representation enables training classifiers that can leverage knowledge from both datasets.

Result: Experiments on several pairs of allied heterogeneous datasets with multiple classifiers demonstrate that classifiers trained on the unified representation consistently outperform classifiers trained separately on the constituent allied datasets.

Conclusion: This work provides a simple yet effective approach to substantially improve classifier performance by unifying and leveraging multiple allied datasets together, enabling transfer of classification knowledge across heterogeneous feature spaces.

Abstract: In many application domains, such as student dropout, insurance fraud, loan approval, and machine failures, several labelled public datasets are available where (i) data is about the same type of objects but the set of actual underlying objects are disjoint; and (ii) the class labels are same; and (iii) the feature spaces of the datasets are largely distinct (heterogeneous), with a few shared features. We call such datasets as allied. A single classifier cannot be trained on both datasets together, and one classifier trained on one dataset cannot be tested on the other. In this paper, we propose a method to merge the feature-spaces into a single feature-space for a pair of given allied heterogeneous datasets. We then use a matrix completion method to create a unified dataset based on the merged feature-space. The hypothesis is that the merged representation facilitates the transfer of classification knowledge from one dataset to another. We conduct experiments on several pairs of allied, heterogeneous datasets and several classifiers to demonstrate that any classifier trained on the unified representation always outperforms classifiers separately trained on the constituent allied datasets on several pairs of allied datasets. This work provides an easy way to substantially improve classifier performance by unifying and using multiple allied datasets together.

</details>


### [140] [OceanMoE: Structured Conditional Sparse Computation for Long-Horizon Multivariate Ocean Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19768)
*Yishun Zhu,Jian Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OceanMoE is a Mixture-of-Experts framework for multivariate ocean forecasting that balances shared ocean context with adaptive specialization by using content-conditioned sparse routing, geographic bias via spherical-harmonic bases, and shared residual/seasonal pathways. It achieves lower forecasting error on ORAS5 data compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multivariate ocean forecasting requires exploiting shared evolution in coupled ocean systems while adapting to heterogeneous statistical and dynamical characteristics of different prediction variables and locations. Existing approaches either use fully shared models (lacking flexibility for heterogeneity) or fully independent models (discarding common ocean context). The key challenge is retaining shared context in a unified model while allowing computation to specialize according to prediction target and local state.

Method: OceanMoE uses a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework with three key components: (1) Cross-variable information fusion to construct target-specific local representations; (2) Content-conditioned sparse routing at each spatial location with expert count adapted to router confidence; (3) In the decoder, routing augmented with learned geographic bias parameterized by spherical-harmonic spatial bases; (4) Shared residual and seasonal pathways for common cross-variable and month-dependent context.

Result: Experiments on long-horizon autoregressive ORAS5 forecasting show that OceanMoE lowers aggregate forecasting error in both evaluated settings and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE than baselines over most later rollout months. Routing analyses reveal that expert allocation varies with prediction targets and spatial locations.

Conclusion: Structured conditional computation is an effective modeling strategy for balancing shared ocean context with adaptive specialization in multivariate ocean forecasting. The method successfully combines sharing and specialization, with expert allocation adapting to prediction targets and spatial locations.

Abstract: Multivariate ocean forecasting must exploit shared evolution in a coupled ocean system while adapting to the heterogeneous statistical and dynamical characteristics of different prediction variables and locations. Fully shared models may lack the flexibility to handle this heterogeneity, whereas fully independent models discard the common ocean context shared across variables. The key question is how to retain shared context in a unified model while allowing computation to specialize according to the prediction target and local state. We propose OceanMoE, a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework that combines sharing and specialization for multivariate ocean forecasting. OceanMoE fuses cross-variable information to construct target-specific local representations and uses them to perform content-conditioned sparse routing at each spatial location, with the number of active experts adapted to router confidence. In the decoder, routing is augmented with a learned geographic bias parameterized by spherical-harmonic spatial bases, while shared residual and seasonal pathways provide common cross-variable and month-dependent context. Experiments on long-horizon autoregressive ORAS5 forecasting show that OceanMoE lowers aggregate forecasting error in both evaluated settings and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE than the corresponding baselines over most later rollout months. Routing analyses further show that expert allocation varies with prediction targets and spatial locations. These results support structured conditional computation as a modeling strategy for balancing shared ocean context with adaptive specialization.

</details>


### [141] [PhyRestore: Physics-Structured Latent-Factor Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19776)
*Ahmed Shafee,Chayan Lahiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PhyRestore is a physics-structured latent-factor restoration framework for estimating temporal soil-loss change under noisy/corrupted input factors in RUSLE. It restores corrupted physical factors (rainfall erosivity, cover management) through known physical relationships rather than directly predicting soil loss change.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating temporal soil-loss change is challenging when physically meaningful input factors are noisy or corrupted, especially since substantial changes are rare relative to locations with little change.

Method: PhyRestore restores corrupted physical factors and reconstructs temporal change through the known physical relationship (RUSLE), rather than directly predicting soil-loss change or correcting a degraded physical estimate. Evaluated in watershed-scale bitemporal raster setting under isolated and simultaneous corruption of rainfall erosivity and cover management.

Result: Factor restoration improves high-magnitude recovery when corrupted factors remain identifiable, but advantage weakens under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside training support.

Conclusion: PhyRestore demonstrates the value of physics-based factor restoration for soil-loss estimation, though its effectiveness is limited by joint corruption scenarios and data distribution issues.

Abstract: Estimating temporal soil-loss change is challenging when physically meaningful input factors are noisy or corrupted, particularly because substantial changes are rare relative to the large number of locations exhibiting little change. We study this problem through the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and introduce PhyRestore, a physics-structured latent-factor restoration framework. Rather than directly predicting soil-loss change or correcting a degraded physical estimate, PhyRestore restores corrupted physical factors and reconstructs temporal change through the known physical relationship. We evaluate PhyRestore in a watershed-scale bitemporal raster setting under isolated and simultaneous corruption of rainfall erosivity and cover management, comparing it with the degraded RUSLE estimate and Direct RF, XGBoost, MLP, and CNN models. Factor restoration improves high-magnitude recovery when the corrupted factors remain identifiable, but its advantage weakens under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside the training support.

</details>


### [142] [Learning-Based Reconstruction of Optical Properties in Bilayered Media from Single-distance Time-Resolved Reflectance Measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19786)
*Caterina Amendola,Giulia Maffeis,Lorenzo Buffoni,Lorenzo Chicchi,Francesco Coghi,Duccio Fanelli,Raffaele Marino,Fabrizio Martelli,Riccardo Paoli,Lorenzo Pattelli,Lorenzo Spinelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A machine learning framework is proposed to reconstruct optical properties (absorption and scattering coefficients) in bilayered biological media from time-domain reflectance measurements, outperforming traditional model-based inverse solvers in accuracy and speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional analytical models and diffusion equation-based inverse solvers struggle with structural heterogeneity in layered biological media, yielding poor accuracy for superficial absorption and deep-layer scattering.

Method: A robust synthetic dataset of forward diffuse time-of-flight (DTOF) was generated using exact Monte Carlo simulations at multiple source-detector distances. A machine learning pipeline was trained on this dataset and validated against state-of-the-art model-based reconstruction methods.

Result: The machine learning approach achieves higher accuracy than model-based inverse solvers, with significant reconstruction speed-up, and provides an estimate of parameter space dimensionality without requiring a priori information about the number of layers.

Conclusion: Machine learning is a promising alternative for optical properties reconstruction, with potential for further enhancement through joint multi-distance reconstruction approaches using multiple DTOF curves from the same medium.

Abstract: The inverse problem of reconstructing optical properties, specifically absorption and scattering coefficients, in layered biological media from time-domain reflectance measurements remains a significant challenge for traditional analytical models. Inverse solvers based on the diffusion equation often struggle with structural heterogeneity, frequently yielding poor accuracy for superficial absorption and deep-layers scattering. In this work, we propose a machine learning framework as an alternative approach to reconstruct the optical properties of a bilayered medium, benchmarking its efficiency and accuracy against model-based algorithms. To overcome the intrinsic approximations of diffusion theory and inverse reconstruction, we generated a robust synthetic dataset of forward DTOF using exact Monte Carlo simulations at multiple source-detector distances. A machine learning pipeline was then trained on this dataset and validated against state-of-the-art model-based reconstruction methods. Besides the significant reconstruction speed-up, the machine learning approach achieves higher accuracy than model-based inverse solvers, further providing an estimate of the parameter space dimensionality without requiring any a priori information about the number of layers in the investigated geometry. Further enhancements in the reconstruction accuracy can be expected in future extensions of this work, by training the pipeline over multiple DTOF curves from the same medium, in a joint multi-distance reconstruction approach.

</details>


### [143] [DeliveryGym: An RL Environment for Long-Horizon Embodied Agent Planning with Adaptive Curriculum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19801)
*Haoqiang Kang,Yiming Zhang,Yiyang Guo,Chuying Li,Jianzhi Shen,Tianruo Rose Xu,Xiaokang Ye,Lianhui Qin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>

Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Executable environments enable LLM agents to learn from the consequences of their actions. For embodied agents, those consequences extend beyond whether the current task succeeds: completing a delivery can consume the time, energy, or money needed for later work. Learning to plan therefore requires environments that preserve these dependencies and turn them into feedback across a complete trajectory. We introduce DeliveryGym, a 3D environment for evaluating and training agents on continuous courier shifts. It couples multimodal tool interaction with persistent world dynamics and computes trajectory rewards from simulator events, making the costs of an agent's decisions available for reinforcement learning (RL). The environment also adapts future training shifts to the policy's observed weaknesses while keeping evaluation fixed. Across six models and 13 city maps, evaluation exposes a gap between reliably executing assigned deliveries and choosing and sequencing work over a shift. On the fixed test suite, RL improves Qwen3-VL-4B's net income by 54.3%, showing that learning from complete shifts improves performance under these coupled constraints. Adapting the training environment improves test income by 16.5% over uniform sampling at the same rollout budget, indicating that which situations an agent practices also matters. DeliveryGym provides an executable setting for studying how agents learn to coordinate deliveries and preserve resources for later orders within an episode.

</details>


### [144] [Beyond Flattened Tokens: Structure-Preserving EEG Decoding with Reusable TriDim Blocks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19842)
*Shiyue Su,Song Wang,Zekai Zhan,Junjie Zeng,Ziling Lu,Zongsheng Li,Xinyuan Ye,Zhiyuan Ma,Xinke Shen,Quanying Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TriDim is a novel neural network block for EEG decoding that explicitly preserves three axes of information: channel (spatial), sample position within patches (short-term temporal), and patch position across recording (long-term temporal). Stacking these blocks creates TriDimEEG, which achieves state-of-the-art performance across 8 datasets and 4 different EEG tasks, while also serving as an effective replacement for Transformer blocks in existing EEG foundation models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective EEG decoding requires preserving three distinct types of information: spatial organization among channels, local waveform dynamics (short-term temporal), and long-range temporal context. Existing EEG architectures often either use separate specialized modules for each or collapse all information into a single token sequence, making it difficult to maintain their distinct roles and coordinate their interactions throughout the backbone.

Method: TriDim keeps three EEG axes explicit: (1) channel axis for spatial information, (2) sample position within each patch for short-term temporal information, and (3) patch position across the recording for long-term temporal information. Each TriDim block applies feed-forward transformations along individual axes and uses cross-axis attention to coordinate information exchange among them. The complete model TriDimEEG stacks multiple TriDim blocks with a multi-level tri-axis readout for final predictions.

Result: Under strict cross-subject evaluation on eight datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, and emotion recognition, TriDimEEG achieves the best overall performance among fifteen evaluated models, with a 4.3% relative improvement in average accuracy over the second-best model. When replacing Transformer blocks in three EEG foundation models with TriDim blocks, there is an average relative improvement of 7.4% in downstream accuracy while reducing parameter counts by 17.0% to 47.3%.

Conclusion: TriDim is established as an effective and reusable building block for EEG processing, and TriDimEEG is demonstrated as a strong standalone EEG decoder. The approach successfully maintains distinct representations for spatial, short-term temporal, and long-term temporal information while enabling effective coordination through cross-axis attention.

Abstract: Effective EEG decoding requires representations that preserve organization among channels, local waveform dynamics, and long-range temporal context. Existing EEG architectures often capture these structures using separate specialized modules or collapse them into a single token sequence, making it difficult to maintain their distinct roles and coordinate their interactions throughout the backbone. We propose TriDim, a reusable block that preserves the representation shape and keeps three EEG axes explicit: channel, sample position within each patch, and patch position across the recording. These axes correspond to spatial, short-term temporal, and long-term temporal information, respectively. Each TriDim block applies feed-forward transformations along individual axes and cross-axis attention to coordinate information exchange among them. By stacking TriDim blocks with a multi-level tri-axis readout, we construct TriDimEEG, a standalone EEG decoder. Under strict cross-subject evaluation on eight datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, and emotion recognition, TriDimEEG achieves the best overall performance among fifteen evaluated models, with a 4.3% relative improvement in average accuracy over the second-best model. Replacing Transformer blocks in three EEG foundation models with TriDim blocks yields an average relative improvement of 7.4% in downstream accuracy while reducing parameter counts by 17.0% to 47.3%. These results establish TriDim as an effective and reusable building block and TriDimEEG as a strong standalone EEG decoder. Code and parameters of TriDimEEG are available at https://github.com/ncclab-sustech/TriDim_model.

</details>


### [145] [Expected Hypervolume Maximization for Multiobjective Optimization under Uncertainties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19858)
*Victor Trappler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Bayesian decision framework for multiobjective optimization under uncertainties, using expected hypervolume maximization with Gaussian Process surrogate models and active learning strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The traditional approach to multiobjective optimization under uncertainties uses the expectation of each objective, but this work proposes a more principled Bayesian decision framework instead.

Method: The method uses expected hypervolume maximization with respect to a finite set of input points, implemented via gradient-based stochastic optimization. Gaussian Processes serve as differentiable surrogate models. Active learning strategies through acquisition functions are proposed to construct well-designed surrogate models for the multiobjective optimization problem.

Result: The proposed active learning strategies are compared on simple analytical problems to assess their performance.

Conclusion: The approach can effectively perform multiobjective optimization under uncertainties using gradient-based stochastic optimization, provided proper handling of dominated points is implemented. Gaussian Processes provide suitable differentiable surrogate models, and active learning strategies help construct efficient surrogate models for the optimization task.

Abstract: The problem of multiobjective optimization under uncertainties is often approached by taking the expectation of each objective. In this work, we propose instead to formulate this as a Bayesian decision problem and to rely on the expected value of the hypervolume, which is to be maximized with respect to a finite set of input points. We show that this can be performed using methods based on gradients in a stochastic optimization framework, provided that care is taken with respect to dominated points. Moreover, in the absence of readily available differentiable code, we propose to use Gaussian Processes as differentiable surrogate models, in order to perform the optimization. An additional contribution in this work are some active learning strategies, through acquisition functions which helps construct a surrogate model well-designed for the multiobjective optimization problem at stake. These strategies are compared on simple analytical problems to assess their performances.

</details>


### [146] [Pretrained Medical Representations for the Practical Screening of Drug Repositioning Candidates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19865)
*Yuhei Fujioka,Daitaro Misawa,Shingo Fukuma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a unified pre-training framework for medical code representation learning that integrates hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms. The model outperforms existing methods on clinical event prediction tasks and demonstrates utility in drug repositioning for Alzheimer's disease through a hypothesis generation and prioritization workflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing BERT-based models for medical code representation fail to adequately capture: 1) the hierarchical structure of medical codes, and 2) the complex interactions between diagnoses and treatments. This limits their utility in scientific hypothesis discovery, beyond simple disease prediction tasks.

Method: The proposed framework integrates three key mechanisms: (1) Hierarchical sub-token aggregation to capture medical code hierarchy, (2) Partial masking for improved representation learning, and (3) Cross-reference mechanisms to model diagnosis-treatment interactions. For hypothesis prioritization, a Task-Adaptive Representation Approach was introduced to alleviate over-encoding of historical prescription information within diagnostic vectors.

Result: The model consistently outperformed existing methods on: (1) Pre-training objectives, (2) Downstream clinical event prediction tasks (dementia onset and hospitalization prediction). In a drug repositioning case study for Alzheimer's disease, the approach successfully rediscovered known promising drugs in a data-driven manner without external literature knowledge, and enabled robust hypothesis prioritization.

Conclusion: Domain-informed representation learning combined with task-adaptive representation control can enable a practical hypothesis discovery workflow for exploratory screening. The framework identifies promising candidates for subsequent rigorous causal inference, though it is not intended to provide causal evidence itself.

Abstract: Representation learning from medical code sequences in electronic health records and medical claims data has been successful in various clinical applications, such as those regarding disease prediction. However, significant challenges remain in extending this approach to the discovery of scientific hypotheses. One reason is that many existing BERT-based models fail to adequately capture the hierarchical structure of medical codes and the complex interactions between diagnoses and treatments. To address these limitations, we propose a new unified pre-training framework that explicitly integrates hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms. The proposed model consistently outperformed existing methods on both pre-training objectives and downstream clinical event prediction tasks, including the onset of dementia and hospitalization. We also conducted an in silico drug repositioning case study targeting Alzheimer's disease. In the hypothesis generation step, our approach successfully rediscovered known promising drugs in a data-driven manner without relying on such external knowledge sources as the literature. Subsequently, in the hypothesis prioritization step, we introduced a Task-Adaptive Representation Approach to alleviate the over-encoding of historical prescription information within diagnostic vectors, enabling the robust prioritization of generated hypotheses. This study establishes an exploratory screening workflow for hypothesis generation and prioritization based on observational associations. Importantly, this framework is not intended to provide causal evidence, but rather to identify promising candidates for subsequent rigorous causal inference. Overall, this study demonstrates that domain-informed representation learning combined with task-adaptive representation control can enable a practical hypothesis discovery workflow.

</details>


### [147] [AURA: Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis for Email Threat Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19873)
*Omran Berjawi,Walid fahs,Rida Khatoun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AURA is a multimodal email threat detection system that combines URL classification with semantic analysis using fine-tuned transformer encoders to identify spam and phishing emails. It uses a two-layer architecture where ambiguous messages are escalated for deeper analysis, achieving high macro F1-scores (0.9858 in-distribution, 0.9502 on NazPhish-Eval, 0.9436 on GuenterTrap-Eval) across diverse training corpora and real-world datasets spanning a decade of attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Email spam and phishing attacks are evolving security threats. Adversaries use large language models to create convincing malicious messages, and existing detection systems struggle to generalize across diverse and evolving attack scenarios, reducing their effectiveness in real-world deployment.

Method: AURA uses a two-layer architecture: (1) a URL classifier that quantifies prediction uncertainty, and (2) only ambiguous messages are escalated to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. The system analyzes both email content and embedded URLs multimodally.

Result: AURA achieves a macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution, and maintains 0.9502 on NazPhish-Eval and 0.9436 on GuenterTrap-Eval, demonstrating robust generalization under genuine distribution shift.

Conclusion: The proposed AURA system effectively detects email threats through adaptive uncertainty-routed analysis, showing strong generalization across heterogeneous training corpora and real-world datasets spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns.

Abstract: Email spam and phishing attacks remain a critical security threat. Adversaries increasingly exploit large language models to craft contextually convincing malicious messages, and existing spam detection systems often struggle to keep pace. Generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios is limited, which reduces effectiveness once these systems are deployed in practice. This paper introduces Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis (AURA), a multimodal email threat detection system that analyzes both the content of an email and its embedded URLs. AURA is built around two layers: the first quantifies prediction uncertainty from a URL classifier, and only ambiguous messages are escalated to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. The system is evaluated on eight heterogeneous training corpora together with two held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns. AURA reaches a macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution, and on NazPhish-Eval and GuenterTrap-Eval it maintains 0.9502 and 0.9436, respectively, which is evidence of robust generalization under genuine distribution shift.

</details>


### [148] [Uni-LaDiR: Latent Diffusion Unifies Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19878)
*Haoqiang Kang,Yizhe Zhang,Nikki Lijing Kuang,Yian Ma,Lianhui Qin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Uni-LaDiR introduces a unified latent space for multimodal reasoning by using a diffusion-based approach to generate thought tokens across vision-language models and robot manipulation tasks, achieving 7.3% and 6.1% relative gains respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal reasoning methods concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, forcing the model to bridge representational differences between modalities during reasoning. This creates a gap in effectively integrating information from different modalities.

Method: A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, trained to preserve information needed for reasoning and final answers. Since multiple valid next steps can exist from the same context, diffusion is used to predict the next block of thought tokens. The encoder and diffusion reasoner are jointly trained with shared model weights to encourage thought tokens to be both useful and predictable.

Result: Across eleven vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks and two vision-language-action (VLA) suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains over the strongest evaluated baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks.

Conclusion: The shared latent space approach with diffusion-based reasoning enables more effective multimodal integration, demonstrating significant improvements in both visual reasoning and robotic manipulation domains.

Abstract: Multimodal reasoning requires models to draw on information from multiple modalities throughout the reasoning process. Yet existing methods often concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, leaving the model to bridge representational differences as it reasons across modalities. We introduce Uni-LaDiR (Unified Latent Diffusion Reasoner), a framework that brings these thoughts into a shared latent space for reasoning. A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, trained to preserve the information needed for later reasoning steps and the final answer or action. Because the same context can support multiple valid next steps, we use diffusion to predict the next block of thought tokens from the input and preceding blocks. Jointly training the encoder and diffusion reasoner with shared model weights encourages thought tokens to be both useful for the task and predictable from the available context. At inference, the model generates these tokens without teacher observations. Across eleven vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks and two vision-language-action (VLA) suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains over the strongest evaluated baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [149] [Online Adaptive Kernel Mixing for Gaussian Process Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19891)
*Kavin Aravindan,Mani Tej Sriram,Gautam Dasarathy,Tejas Bodas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HACK GPs addresses kernel misspecification in Gaussian Processes by treating kernel selection as an online learning problem. The method uses AdaHedge to combine multiple kernel experts, achieving robust performance across Bayesian optimization, level set estimation, and Bayesian active learning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard GP kernels can lead to suboptimal decisions when misspecified, yet selecting appropriate kernels for black-box functions is challenging. Existing methods lack theoretical guarantees for kernel selection in sequential decision-making contexts.

Method: The paper proposes HACK GPs, which frames kernel selection as an online learning with expert advice problem. Each candidate kernel acts as a GP expert, with a distribution over experts updated online using AdaHedge based on a task-specific loss function. Two variants are introduced: Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and categorical sampling.

Result: Theoretically, under a loss-gap condition, the method concentrates weight on the best kernel and produces acquisition functions close to the best expert. Empirically, HACK GPs demonstrates robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL compared to standard kernels (Squared Exponential, Matern-5/2) and ensemble baselines.

Conclusion: HACK GPs provides a principled approach to kernel adaptation that combines multiple kernels effectively, offering both theoretical guarantees and empirical robustness across diverse sequential decision-making tasks.

Abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used as surrogates for black-box functions in sequential decision-making problems such as Bayesian optimization (BO), level set estimation (LSE), and Bayesian active learning (BAL). GP performance critically depends on kernels, and standard kernels can lead to suboptimal decisions under misspecification. To address this, we introduce HACK GPs (Hedge Adaptive Cumulative Kernels), a method that views kernel selection as an online learning with expert advice problem. HACK treats each candidate kernel as a GP "expert" and updates a distribution over experts online using AdaHedge, based on a loss received as a proxy for their ability to fit the function and align with the task objective. We provide two variants of HACK: (i) Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and (ii) categorical sampling. We establish general guarantees showing that, under a loss-gap condition, the weight concentrates on the best kernel and the resulting acquisition function is close to that of the best expert. Empirically, we observe robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL compared to standard kernels such as Squared Exponential and Matern-5/2, as well as simple ensemble baselines.

</details>


### [150] [REARL: A Closed-loop Autonomous Driving Simulation Enhancement Framework with Real Traffic Data and Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19903)
*Xiaojun Bi,Jun Jiang,Yiwen Sun,Quanyi Ou,Ke Cheng,Mingjie Bi,Yexin Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REARL is a closed-loop simulation enhancement framework for autonomous driving that integrates real traffic data with large language models (LLMs) to address the challenge of maintaining simulation fidelity over time. It uses traffic data clustering, a sliding-window detector for monitoring discrepancies, and LLM-based adjustments to keep simulated traffic patterns aligned with real-world behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autonomous driving simulators struggle with dynamic traffic because they rely on predefined rules or static data playback, causing the simulated distribution to diverge from real traffic as the rollout evolves. While CRITICAL uses real traffic data and LLMs to adjust initial simulation configuration, it still fails to maintain fidelity over time.

Method: REARL employs three key mechanisms: (1) Clustering real traffic data and using cluster centers as representative scenarios providing typical real-world traffic patterns; (2) A timed sliding-window detector monitoring discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing between vehicle pairs; (3) LLM-based decision-making that adjusts vehicle behavior when metrics exceed thresholds, and selects matching real vehicles from traffic snapshots to modulate simulated vehicle actions.

Result: In controlled HighD highway settings, REARL reduced the Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067 and MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371, while achieving a time headway (THW) of 22.8575 and a lane change rate of 0.0708, outperforming both CRITICAL baseline and PPO-based learning baseline.

Conclusion: The closed-loop framework with LLM-based real-time adjustments effectively maintains simulation fidelity over time. By continuously monitoring traffic metrics and dynamically adjusting vehicle decision-making using real traffic data as references, REARL successfully bridges the gap between simulated and real-world traffic behavior in autonomous driving development.

Abstract: Accurate simulation is crucial for autonomous driving development, yet capturing real-world traffic complexity remains challenging. Existing simulators that rely on predefined rules or static data playback struggle with dynamic traffic. CRITICAL uses real traffic data and a large language model (LLM) to adjust the initial simulation configuration, but the simulated distribution still diverges from real traffic as the rollout evolves. We propose REARL, a closed-loop simulation enhancement framework that integrates real traffic data with LLMs. Real traffic data are clustered, and each cluster center is used as a representative scenario that provides typical real-world traffic patterns for the LLM. A timed sliding-window detector then monitors discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing between pairs of vehicles. If a metric exceeds a threshold, the LLM adjusts vehicle decision-making; otherwise the existing controller is kept. The LLM also selects a matching real vehicle from a traffic snapshot and modulates the simulated vehicle with reference to that real action. In a controlled HighD highway setting, compared with the CRITICAL baseline and a PPO-based learning baseline, REARL reduces the Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067 and the MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371, while achieving a time headway (THW) of 22.8575 and a lane change rate of 0.0708.

</details>


### [151] [Digital Twins for Opinion Dynamics: A Generative LLM Framework for Social Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19913)
*Omran Berjawi,Giuseppe Fenza,Rida Khatoun,Sherali Zeadally*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a digital twin framework using Mistral-7B to simulate opinion dynamics in social networks by cloning real Twitter networks and validating against COVID-19 and US Election 2020 datasets, achieving significant improvements over classical baselines in prediction accuracy, structural alignment, and polarization dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to studying opinion dynamics either oversimplify by ignoring linguistic/contextual factors or use unvalidated LLM-based simulations. There's a need for a framework that combines the complexity of LLM-based opinion updates with empirical validation against real-world data.

Method: The framework creates digital twins of real Twitter networks, assigns agent attributes (persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, influence), and uses Mistral-7B to perform opinion updates based on memory and social exposure. Validated on two Twitter datasets: COVID-19 discourse and US Elections 2020.

Result: Mistral-7B achieves MAE = 0.150 (COVID-19) and 0.121 (US Election 2020), representing >50% reduction vs. classical baselines. Structural alignment: Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180. Polarization dynamics: Delta_Var = 0.106 and 0.115. Ablation studies confirm all components contribute, with agent attributes being most critical.

Conclusion: Grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks produces a realistic simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics, with significant improvements in opinion trajectory prediction, structural alignment, and polarization dynamics.

Abstract: The study of opinion dynamics in social networks is one of the key challenges in computational social science with direct relevance to understanding political polarization, misinformation, and health responses. Current approaches focus on simplified mathematical models that ignore linguistic and contextual factors related to belief updates or use Large Language Model (LLM)-based simulations that have not been validated against real data. We present a framework based on the concept of a digital twin to simulate opinion dynamics in social networks. The approach fills the gap by cloning a real-world Twitter network, assigns a set of attributes for agents (such as persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, and influence), and employs Mistral-7B to perform opinion update based on memory and social exposure. To evaluate the proposed approach, we validate it against two real Twitter datasets (COVID-19 discourse and U.S elections 2020). The results show that the capability of the proposed framework reproduces opinion trajectories and reduces individual prediction error by more than 50% compared to the best-performing classical baseline (Mistral-7B achieves Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 0.150 and 0.121 on the COVID-19 and US Election 2020 datasets, respectively). We observe similar improvements in structural alignment (Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180) and polarization dynamics (Delta_Var = 0.106 and 0.115) on the two datasets, respectively. Additionally, the ablation studies confirm that agent attributes, memory, and social exposure all contribute to the framework's predictive fidelity in reproducing opinion trajectories, with agent attributes being the most critical contributor. Overall, our results demonstrate that grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks produces a realistic simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics.

</details>


### [152] [Amortizing Physics-Informed Neural Solvers via Graph Hypernetworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19915)
*Cheng Jing,Abhishek Verma,Kallol Bera,Yixuan He,Kookjin Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces an operator graph approach to amortize physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across related PDEs, explicitly modeling relationships between fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals that were previously implicit in coefficient vectors. A graph hypernetwork generates codes to initialize meta-trained factorized PINNs for each target equation without requiring solution labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current coefficient-vector approaches for amortizing PINNs across PDEs leave operator and cross-field assignments implicit, limiting the reusable solver's ability to capture equation relationships.

Method: The authors propose an operator graph with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals, with coefficients as term attributes. A graph hypernetwork generates diagonal codes initializing a meta-trained factorized PINN. Meta-training and adaptation use governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels. They compare coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning approaches.

Result: In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy with similar performance. In two-field Fisher-KPP, after 3000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph achieves 35.7% lower error than term set and 67.7% lower than coefficient vector. In a capacitively coupled plasma model, coefficient vector performs best.

Conclusion: Explicit equation relationships (via operator graphs) can significantly improve physics-based solver adaptation for related PDEs, particularly in multi-field coupling scenarios, though coefficient vectors remain superior for fixed-structure models.

Abstract: Amortizing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across related PDEs requires describing each equation to a reusable solver. Coefficient vectors encode numerical parameters in predefined slots, leaving operator and cross-field assignments implicit. We make these relationships explicit in an operator graph, with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals and coefficients retained as term attributes. A graph hypernetwork generates diagonal codes that initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target equation. Meta-training and target-specific adaptation use governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels. We compare coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning by solution accuracy within a fixed adaptation budget. In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy, with similar performance. In two-field Fisher-KPP, meta-training sees uncoupled and one-way systems; after 3,000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph's mean final error is 35.7% below the term set and 67.7% below the coefficient vector. In a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient vector performs best. These results support extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation relationships for physics-based solver adaptation.

</details>


### [153] [One Intervention per Component is Enough: Towards Identifiability in Linear Stochastic Dynamics from Steady State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19955)
*Saber Salehkaleybar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: We study the problem of recovering the parameters of a multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process from steady-state observational and interventional data. In many applications, such as large-scale gene perturbation experiments, only stationary "snapshot" measurements are available, making standard stochastic differential equation estimation methods that rely on time-series trajectories inapplicable. We first establish an identifiability result: one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC) of the drift graph suffices to recover all OU process parameters generically up to a global scaling factor. This holds provided that the SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and certain spectral nondegeneracy assumptions hold. We propose a recursive learning algorithm that orders SCCs topologically and, for each component, isolates its marginal dynamics and solves a linear system derived from the steady-state moment equations, leveraging parameters recovered for upstream components. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose a regularized least-squares estimator that jointly minimizes residuals of the steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data. Experimental results validate our theoretical findings in recovering parameters of the underlying OU process.

</details>


### [154] [Graph-Based Stochastic Power-UCT: Monte-Carlo Graph Search with Power Mean Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19956)
*Tung Tran,Viet Bao Mai,Hoang Ta,Tuan Dam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), a novel MCTS algorithm that shares states at the same planning depth to improve sample efficiency in stochastic MDPs, with theoretical convergence guarantees and experimental validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search duplicates states when reached through different trajectories, wasting simulations in stochastic MDPs. This inefficiency is particularly problematic in problems with cycles.

Method: GS-Power-UCT shares states reached at the same planning depth while maintaining separate values for states at different depths. Two variants are also explored: GS-Power-UCT-F (single node per physical state for maximum sharing) and GS-Power-UCT-F+ (adaptive horizon to control bias).

Result: For fixed planning horizon, root estimate converges to finite-horizon value at O(n^{-1/2}) rate, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples. GS-Power-UCT-F+ converges to optimal infinite-horizon discounted value V*(s₀) when cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments show improved sample efficiency over baselines.

Conclusion: The graph-based approach successfully balances sample sharing and depth-specific value estimation, achieving better sample efficiency while maintaining theoretical convergence guarantees. The adaptive horizon variant GS-Power-UCT-F+ provides a principled approach to infinite-horizon problems.

Abstract: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) duplicates the same state when it is reached through different trajectories, which can waste simulations in stochastic MDPs. We introduce Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. This design applies to general stochastic MDPs, including problems with cycles. We prove that for a fixed planning horizon, the root estimate converges to the finite-horizon value at rate $O(n^{-1/2})$, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. We also study two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F, which stores one node per physical state to increase sample sharing but may mix values from different remaining horizons, and GS-Power-UCT-F$^+$, which uses an adaptive horizon to control this bias. The latter converges to $V^{\star}(s_0)$, the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value at the root state $s_0$, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.

</details>


### [155] [CellRFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19970)
*Jie Yan,Li Liu,Hanze Guo,Jiaxin Hu,Houxin He,Xiaoning Qi,Haoran Wang,Cong Li,Zhong-Yuan Zhang,Yong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CellRFT is a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that optimizes single-cell perturbation models directly on biological evaluation criteria using policy-gradient methods, rather than relying on surrogate losses. It demonstrates improved prediction accuracy and reveals complex interactions between different biological metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current single-cell perturbation models optimize surrogate losses that do not directly reflect biological evaluation criteria, meaning better data fitting does not necessarily yield better biological predictions. This mismatch between training objectives and actual biological evaluation hinders the utility of these models for studying gene function, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies.

Method: CellRFT is introduced as a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that uses policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations. It integrates multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation, allowing direct optimization of biological criteria rather than surrogate losses.

Result: Comprehensive experiments demonstrate CellRFT's applicability across different pretrained models and effectiveness in improving perturbation prediction. The study reveals that optimizing one biological criterion can help or hinder others, and that complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized.

Conclusion: CellRFT offers a way to probe how biological metrics shape model behavior, with the potential to inform evaluation design. The framework provides a principled approach to aligning model training with biological evaluation criteria.

Abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbations supports the study of gene function, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies. Despite advances in single-cell perturbation modeling, existing models typically optimize surrogate losses that do not directly reflect the biological criteria used for evaluation, so better data fitting need not yield better biological predictions. To address this mismatch, we introduce \textbf{CellRFT}, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that uses biological evaluation as direct training feedback. CellRFT uses policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations and integrates multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate CellRFT's applicability across different pretrained models and effectiveness in improving perturbation prediction, reveal that optimizing one biological criterion can help or hinder others, and show that complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized, offering a way to probe how biological metrics shape model behavior, with the potential to inform evaluation design. Code will be made available.

</details>


### [156] [Past, Future, All at Once: Mitigating Stability-Plasticity Dilemma via Post-hoc JANUS Rectification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19985)
*Zhilong Zheng,Letian Tao,Yang Guan,Yujie Yang,Wei Xiong,Kehua Sheng,Bo Zhang,Jingliang Duan,Keqiang Li,Shengbo Eben Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces JANUS, a post-hoc weight rectification framework that mitigates catastrophic forgetting in foundation model fine-tuning by projecting parameter updates into the Jacobian Null Space, achieving Parameter Space Orthogonality - the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning foundation models on new tasks causes catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods use overly restrictive Subspace Orthogonality conditions, which are insufficient for preserving historical performance.

Method: The proposed JANUS framework projects parameter updates into the Jacobian Null Space (JANUS) to achieve Parameter Space Orthogonality. It includes: (1) Multi-step Adaptive Rectification mechanism that uses JANUS shift to verify trust regions and adjust step sizes; (2) Ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level SVD compression techniques for temporal and spatial efficiency.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that JANUS integrates seamlessly with various fine-tuning methods, significantly mitigating the stability-plasticity dilemma by recovering historical knowledge while preserving downstream task adaptation.

Conclusion: JANUS provides a tuning-agnostic, post-hoc solution that achieves the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance during fine-tuning, offering a practical approach to the stability-plasticity trade-off without interfering with the underlying fine-tuning process.

Abstract: Fine-tuning foundation models on new tasks inevitably suffer from catastrophic forgetting. While existing works attempt to mitigate this on the basis of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, they adopted an overly restrictive Subspace Orthogonality condition. In this paper, we introduce a purely post-hoc and tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that achieves Parameter Space Orthogonality, which is the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance to the first order. By projecting parameter updates into the JAcobian NUll Space (JANUS), our method significantly recovers compromised historical knowledge without interfering with the underlying fine-tuning process. To overcome the local validity of the Jacobian approximation, we further propose a Multi-step Adaptive Rectification mechanism that utilizes the JANUS shift to dynamically verify the valid trust region and adjust step sizes. Coupled with our proposed ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level singular value decomposition compression techniques, JANUS also achieves great temporal and spatial efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that JANUS seamlessly integrates with various fine-tuning methods, significantly mitigating the stability-plasticity dilemma by recovering historical knowledge while preserving downstream task adaptation.

</details>


### [157] [EPIG-Tree: Compute-Optimal Branching for Gradient-Efficient Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20004)
*Nikita Khomich,Leopold Hermansson,Ido Hakimi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses inefficiency in reward-based reinforcement learning for language models (like GRPO), where entire trajectories receive single scalar rewards. The authors propose tree-based rollout construction that allocates compute based on where additional branches most reduce gradient uncertainty per unit of compute. They derive two allocation laws from law-of-total-variance decomposition: branches reduce decision uncertainty while repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The resulting EPIG-Tree score estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty with a suffix law formula.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reward-based RL methods collapse entire stochastic trajectories into single scalar rewards, which is inefficient because trajectories contain multiple causal decisions, recovery attempts, and environment-randomness events. Every token or action inherits one trajectory-level advantage, leading to poor exploration and reward allocation. The authors argue that branches should be placed where they most reduce uncertainty about the policy gradient per unit of compute, not merely where the policy is uncertain.

Method: The authors formulate tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem for policy-gradient estimation. They derive two allocation laws from a law-of-total-variance decomposition of the local policy-gradient random variable: (1) new branches reduce decision uncertainty, and (2) repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The EPIG-Tree score allocates branches using already computed rollouts, estimating occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty along with a suffix law: n_e ∝ w_e ||∇_θ log π(a_e|h_e)|| σ_e / √c_e.

Result: In cloned-state control experiments, EPIG reduces gradient MSE and wins in all nine dense continuous-control environments of a 13-environment sweep, recovering the reference gradient direction near-perfectly. It improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration relative to entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO, while branch placement is secondary to token-level credit assignment. In online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG attains the highest final win rate (0.850), overtaking flat GRPO (0.790) and entropy branching as training proceeds.

Conclusion: The gradient-estimation advantage of EPIG transfers to stateful, large-action settings like multi-turn Wordle. The key insight is that compute should be allocated based on where branches most reduce policy gradient uncertainty, not merely policy uncertainty. The two derived allocation laws (decision uncertainty reduction and continuation uncertainty reduction) provide a principled framework for tree-based rollout construction in RL for language models.

Abstract: Reward-based reinforcement learning for language models, exemplified by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), collapses an entire stochastic trajectory into a single scalar reward. This is clean and scalable, but it explores and allocates reward inefficiently: a trajectory may contain many causal decisions, recovery attempts, and environment-randomness events, yet every token or action inherits one trajectory-level advantage. We study tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem for policy-gradient estimation. Our central claim is that branches should be placed not where the policy is merely uncertain, but where an additional branch most reduces uncertainty about the policy gradient per unit of compute. From a law-of-total-variance decomposition of the local policy-gradient random variable, we derive two allocation laws: new branches reduce decision uncertainty, while repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The resulting EPIG-Tree score allocates branches using the already computed rollouts. It estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty, along with a suffix law $n_e \propto w_e \|\nabla_θ\log π(a_e|h_e)\| σ_e / \sqrt{c_e}$. Empirically, EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control, winning in all nine dense continuous-control environments of a 13-environment sweep and recovering the reference gradient direction near-perfectly, and it improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration relative to entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO, while branch placement is secondary to token-level credit assignment. In online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG attains the highest final win rate (0.850), overtaking flat GRPO, which saturates early at 0.790, and entropy branching as training proceeds, confirming that the gradient-estimation advantage transfers to a stateful, large-action setting.

</details>


### [158] [Dynamic Generalized Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20008)
*Junda Ying,Zhiwei Zeng,Peijie Zhou,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TP-DATE is a computational framework that generalizes Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport dynamically for reconstructing continuous trajectories in spatial transcriptomics, preserving tissue structure while matching expression patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
