Motivation: Static GW-OT formulations are widely used for structure-aware alignment in spatial transcriptomics, but a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is lacking. This limits the ability to model continuous dynamical processes while preserving spatial structure.

Method: The paper introduces (1) a formulation of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions with proof of static-dynamic equivalence, and (2) travelling-pair flow matching that allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes interactions into a single vector field. The approach is simulation-free.

Result: On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: TP-DATE provides a theoretical and computational framework for dynamic GW-OT, enabling structure-aware trajectory reconstruction in spatial transcriptomics with improved spatial structure preservation and 3D dynamics modeling.

Abstract: Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) extends classical optimal transport by introducing structure-aware transport cost. This is particularly relevant for spatial transcriptomics, where dynamical reconstruction should preserve tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns. While static formulations have been widely used for such structure-aware alignment, a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is still missing. We introduce Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE), a theoretical and computational framework to generalize GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner. We formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove the static dynamic equivalence. We further develop travelling-pair flow matching, which allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes their interactions into a single vector field. On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

</details>


### [159] [Correct Now, Insufficient Later: Auditing Update Sufficiency in Context Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20045)
*Guangzhe Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: A memory can answer a current query correctly while discarding distinctions required by a later update. We investigate this failure with a paired-history audit: two histories have the same current answer, receive a shared future update, and require different subsequent answers. A pilot evaluates 24 history pairs across six synthetic mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, two repeats, and two model backends. A deterministic frontier selector obtains strict reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek and 82/96 on GLM; a structured writer obtains 62 successes with one unresolved outcome and 56/96. The configured four-outcome joint contrast has finite-sample identification intervals of [0.521, 0.542] and [0.292, 0.313], not confidence intervals. A record-level audit distinguishes retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema compliance without changing those original scores. It finds 26 and 25 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories, while all 14 GLM frontier reveal failures contain correct values in the wrong wrapper. Tombstone removal produces 16/16 exact replay failures in the targeted mechanism. Identifier renaming then exposes a separate flaw: original frontier late-reference adequacy falls from 8/8 to 94/320 transformed instances. We provide and test a label-equivariant repair, but it preserves only 2/8 original late-reference answers: eliminating a naming shortcut does not solve unknown future relevance. These results support a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis, not general superiority of the repaired algorithm. Paid pilot evidence, retrospective diagnostics, and new offline tests are reported separately; no independent held-out or natural-task validation is claimed.

</details>


### [160] [Evaluating Explanation Methods by the Predictors They Induce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20058)
*Jacob Selbæk,Hugo L. Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new test for evaluating machine learning model explanations that checks whether an explanation can rebuild the model's predictions by summing feature effects. The test applies to any explanation writable as a function of features (PDP, ALE, SHAP, LIME).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing criteria for evaluating explanations are hard to compare. The authors propose a simpler test: if an explanation truly describes how a model uses its features, it should be possible to rebuild the model's predictions from it.

Method: Turn each explanation into a predictor by reading each feature's effect and adding them up, then measure how well that predictor reproduces the model on unseen data. Nothing is fitted, so the score reflects the explanation itself. Theoretically proved that summing partial dependence curves gives the best additive summary when features are independent, but fails when dependent.

Result: Across 13 real datasets and 9 synthetic designs with four model families: where features are independent, SHAP is slightly worse than PDP (as theory predicts); on dependent real data, SHAP leads. Some widely used quality metrics even prefer damaged explanations to intact ones.

Conclusion: Which explanation method scores best depends entirely on feature dependence. The proposed reconstruction test provides a unified, comparable metric for evaluating explanation methods.

Abstract: Explanations of machine learning models are usually judged by criteria that are hard to compare. We propose a simpler test: if an explanation really describes how a model uses its features, it should be possible to rebuild the model's predictions from it. We turn each explanation into a predictor by reading each feature's effect and adding them up, and measure how well that predictor reproduces the model on unseen data. Nothing is fitted, so the score reflects the explanation itself. The test applies to any explanation that can be written as a function of the features; we demonstrate it on partial dependence plots (PDP), accumulated local effects (ALE), SHAP and LIME. We prove that summing partial dependence curves gives the best possible additive summary of a model when its features are independent, and that this fails when they are dependent. Across 13 real datasets and 9 synthetic designs and four model families, which method scores best depends entirely on feature dependence: where features are independent SHAP is slightly worse than PDP, exactly as the theory predicts; on dependent real data SHAP leads. Some widely used quality metrics even prefer a damaged explanation to an intact one.

</details>


### [161] [MATCH: Model-Aware Tool Learning with Curriculum Scheduling and Hierarchically Gated Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20082)
*Shihao Liu,Hao Yin,Lijun Liu,Zhengzong Chen,Yuanyuan Zhao,Fei Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MATCH proposes a closed-loop framework for model-aware tool learning with curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards to optimize LLM tool-call behavior. It addresses fixed-threshold curriculum misalignment and additive reward credit leakage problems through Model-Aware Curriculum Learning (MACL) and Hierarchical Tool-call Gated Reward (HTGR).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reinforcement learning methods for tool learning face two key problems: (1) fixed-threshold curricula become misaligned with the policy's evolving capability boundary, and (2) additive rewards leak argument-level credit when the predicted tool is wrong.

Method: MATCH combines two components: (1) MACL maintains reward-derived sample difficulty that co-evolves with the policy, selecting samples near the current capability boundary plus a top-k pool of harder cases each epoch; (2) HTGR scores tool name, argument key, and argument value as a gated chain, granting credit at each level only when prerequisites hold. Both components form a closed loop between policy optimization and sample scheduling, with HTGR rewards driving both GRPO updates and MACL's difficulty refresh.

Result: MATCH achieves 72.19% overall accuracy on API-Bank and 62.87% on BFCL V3, outperforming both supervised and RL-based baselines. Consistent improvements are observed across four backbones from two model families.

Conclusion: The closed-loop framework integrating model-aware curriculum scheduling with hierarchically gated rewards effectively addresses the limitations of prior RL-based tool learning methods, demonstrating robust performance across diverse model architectures.

Abstract: Tool learning enables large language models (LLMs) to use external tools for tasks beyond parametric knowledge. Reinforcement learning can optimize tool-call behavior from feedback, but current methods still face two problems: fixed-threshold curricula can become misaligned with the policy's evolving capability boundary, and additive rewards can leak argument-level credit when the predicted tool is wrong. To address these problems, we propose MATCH, a closed-loop framework for model-aware tool learning with curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards. Model-Aware Curriculum Learning (MACL) maintains reward-derived sample difficulty that co-evolves with the policy, and each epoch selects samples near the current capability boundary together with a top-k pool of harder cases. Hierarchical Tool-call Gated Reward (HTGR) scores tool name, argument key, and argument value as a gated chain, granting credit at each level only when prerequisites hold. The same HTGR rewards drive both GRPO updates and MACL's difficulty refresh, closing the loop between policy optimization and sample scheduling. On API-Bank and BFCL V3, MATCH reaches 72.19% and 62.87% overall accuracy, outperforming the main supervised and RL-based baselines. Backbone experiments further show consistent improvements across four backbones from two model families.

</details>


### [162] [SETTer: Sparse-Encoder Transformer for Long-term Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20086)
*Abraham Ezema,Chijioke Eze,Ferdinanda Ponci,Antonello Monti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SETTer is a transformer-based model for long-term multivariate time series forecasting that addresses oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity issues through decoupled self-attention, hybrid masking, and explainable structures, outperforming state-of-the-art models in 88% of scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term multivariate time series prediction is challenging due to high dimensionality and complex relationships. While transformer-based approaches are effective for long-term forecasting due to their attention mechanism, they suffer from oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity when handling complex high-dimensional inputs.

Method: SETTer incorporates novel techniques for decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking to capture dominant short- and long-term patterns across temporal and channel dimensions. The model is enriched with simple explainable structures that indicate discriminative patterns. It uses a single-layer transformer architecture to effectively model long-term dependencies under varying data complexities.

Result: Extensive experiments on real-world benchmark datasets for long-term multivariate time series forecasting demonstrate that SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of the scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed SETTer effectively addresses the limitations of existing transformer-based approaches for long-term multivariate time series forecasting, achieving superior performance through its innovative decoupled self-attention, hybrid masking, and explainable architecture.

Abstract: Long-term multivariate time series plays a significant role in many application areas such as power systems, trading, etc. However, their accurate prediction is quite difficult for conventional forecasting methods as they often exhibit high dimensionality and complex relationships. Recent works show that transformer-based approaches are quite effective for long-term forecasting thanks to their attention mechanism. However, in the presence of complex high-dimensional inputs, they show evidence of oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity. To this end, this paper introduces SETTer, a transformer-based model that addresses these challenges by incorporating novel techniques for decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking. The proposed techniques enable SETTer to effectively capture the dominant short- and long-term patterns across the temporal and channel dimensions. In addition, we enrich the model layers with simple explainable structures that indicate the discriminative pattern of SETTer. We show that with a single-layer transformer architecture, SETTer can effectively model long-term dependencies in the presence of varying data complexities. Extensive experiments on real-word benchmark datasets for long-term multivariate time series forecasting demonstrate that SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of the scenarios.

</details>


### [163] [CARE-VI: Conservative Adaptive Reliability Estimation for Value Improvement in Off-Policy Actor-Critic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20098)
*Xiang Zou,Shengzhu Shi,Junqi Gao,Zhichang Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses reliability issues in off-policy actor-critic learning's temporal-difference (TD) targets. It proposes CARE-VI, a framework combining three components: CARS (Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening) for uncertainty-aware candidate selection, SEVA (Selector-Evaluator Value Assessment) for dual-critic value review, and DARE (Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement) for risk-regulated residual correction. Experiments on MuJoCo tasks show improved performance across SAC, TD3, and TD3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Off-policy actor-critic methods suffer from unreliable TD targets due to: (1) noisy rankings causing premature candidate commitment, (2) reused selection scores biasing target valuation, and (3) fixed enhancement weights amplifying weak evidence. These issues degrade learning stability and performance.

Method: The paper proposes three complementary mechanisms: (1) CARS retains an ordered candidate prefix within a budget and narrows it only when boundary gap exceeds disagreement-scaled uncertainty radius; (2) SEVA uses selector critics for ranking and evaluator critics for value review, capping at selector reference; (3) DARE regulates residual corrections using candidate reliability, selector-evaluator gap, and finite stage factor. Together they form CARE-VI framework.

Result: CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return in all 12 experimental settings (4 tasks × 3 algorithms: SAC, TD3, TD7). The analysis provides theoretical bounds on CARS boundary error, SEVA overestimation, and DARE residual displacement, plus establishes fixed-policy recovery after finite-stage perturbation ends.

Conclusion: The CARE-VI framework successfully improves TD target reliability in off-policy actor-critic methods through adaptive uncertainty-aware ranking, dual-critic value review, and risk-regulated enhancement. The three components work synergistically: CARS handles candidate selection under uncertainty, SEVA provides value review to prevent overestimation, and DARE ensures stable residual correction. Strong empirical results across multiple algorithms and tasks validate the approach, with ablations confirming each component's contribution.

Abstract: Reliable temporal-difference targets are central to off-policy actor-critic learning. Direct value improvement refines the next-state target with alternative actions, but the reliability of this refinement depends on how candidate actions are ranked, reviewed, and weighted. Noisy rankings may force premature candidate commitment, reusing selection scores may bias target valuation, and fixed enhancement weights may amplify weak evidence. To address these risks, we develop Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening (CARS), which retains an ordered candidate prefix within a preset budget and narrows it only when the observed boundary gap exceeds a disagreement-scaled uncertainty radius. Selector-Evaluator Value Assessment (SEVA) uses selector critics to order candidates and a separately parameterized evaluator critic to review the selected value, then caps the reviewed value at the selector reference. Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement (DARE) then regulates each residual correction using candidate reliability, the gap between selector and evaluator signals, and a finite stage factor. Together, CARS, SEVA, and DARE form CARE-VI, an evidence-regulated target construction framework that preserves the backbone interfaces for critic regression and actor updates. The analysis bounds the CARS boundary error, the SEVA selected-value overestimation, and the one-sided deviation of the DARE residual displacement from its population counterpart, and establishes fixed-policy recovery after the finite-stage perturbation ends. Experiments with SAC, TD3, and TD7 on four MuJoCo tasks show that CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return in all twelve settings. Grouped ablations and scalar diagnostics support the roles of the three components in improving target reliability.

</details>


### [164] [QoS-Aware Federated Learning for Multimodal In-Cabin Interaction in Smart Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20123)
*Baran Can Gül,Mert Nakıp,Nasser Jazdi,Michael Weyrich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedQoS is an asynchronous, event-triggered Federated Learning framework designed for smart vehicles with multimodal sensors. It uses a two-phase gating mechanism (resource-aware training gate and QoS-aware transmission policy) to decouple local computation from global communication, addressing heterogeneous QoS constraints in vehicular networks while maintaining accuracy-efficiency balance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Federated Learning approaches use rigid synchronous rounds that fail to account for resource asymmetries and time-varying QoS constraints in vehicular networks, leading to safety-critical timing violations and energy exhaustion. The problem stems from integrating high-fidelity multimodal fusion with collaborative training under heterogeneous conditions.

Method: The proposed FedQoS framework employs: 1) A resource-aware training gate that initializes local learning only when sensing buffers and energy reserves meet safety thresholds; 2) A QoS-aware transmission policy that gates uplink updates based on an efficiency score balancing model novelty against latency and energy costs; 3) A staleness-aware proximal term in local optimization that dynamically adjusts global anchor strength based on update age.

Result: FedQoS achieves competitive personalized accuracy with only marginal performance loss compared to FedAvg, while reducing QoS violations, cutting communication overhead by 76.7%, and lowering latency cost by 26.0%.

Conclusion: FedQoS demonstrates a highly favorable accuracy and efficiency balance for real-world vehicular deployments, successfully addressing the challenges of asynchronous FL in resource-constrained vehicular networks while maintaining safety and efficiency constraints.

Abstract: Modern smart vehicles leverage multimodal sensors, ranging from high-bandwidth vision systems to low-rate physiological monitors, to provide personalized in-cabin services. However, integrating high-fidelity multimodal fusion with collaborative training is often hindered by the heterogeneous and time-varying Quality of Service (QoS) constraints of vehicular networks. Standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches enforce rigid synchronous rounds that fail to account for these resource asymmetries, leading to safety-critical timing violations and energy exhaustion. In this paper, we propose FedQoS, a novel asynchronous, event-triggered FL framework that decouples local computation from global communication via a two-phase gating mechanism. First, we introduce a resource-aware training gate that initializes local learning only when sensing buffers and energy reserves meet safety thresholds, preventing ML tasks from compromising core vehicle mobility. Second, a QoS-aware transmission policy gates uplink updates based on an efficiency score that balances model novelty against instantaneous latency and energy costs. Locally, clients optimize an objective featuring a staleness-aware proximal term that dynamically adjusts the global anchor strength based on update age. Extensive experiments on multimodal vehicular datasets demonstrate that FedQoS achieves competitive personalized accuracy with only marginal performance loss compared to FedAvg, while substantially reducing QoS violations, cutting communication overhead by 76.7\%, and lowering latency cost by 26.0\%, demonstrating a highly favorable accuracy and efficiency balance for real-world vehicular deployments.

</details>


### [165] [Local Sparsity Enables Unsupervised LLM Safety Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20129)
*Xin Chen,Gil Kur,Alexander Shevchenko,Andreas Krause*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a locally masked sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based anomaly detection framework for LLM safety, leveraging the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) which shows that nearby points in concept space share small common active support. The method achieves near-optimal performance using only 1-2% of SAE neurons when calibrated with 1% out-of-distribution data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional supervised safety methods for LLMs require access to unsafe training data and cannot handle new attacks/harm categories that emerge over time. While anomaly detection (modeling safe data only) offers an alternative approach, it faces statistical challenges in high-dimensional LLM activation spaces. This work investigates whether the linear representation hypothesis and local sparsity properties can make anomaly detection feasible.

Method: The authors propose a locally masked SAE-based anomaly detection framework based on the insight from LRH that nearby points in the SAE concept space share a small common active support (local sparsity). They develop theoretical justifications for this approach and validate it across various architectures and datasets, including both capability-testing and safety-specific datasets.

Result: When allowing 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal performance while using only 1-2% of SAE neurons for computation, demonstrating the method's ability to capture meaningful safety information efficiently.

Conclusion: The linear representation hypothesis provides a theoretical foundation for making anomaly detection statistically feasible in high-dimensional LLM spaces. Local sparsity in SAE concept space enables efficient and effective safety detection, achieving strong performance with minimal computational resources. This approach offers a promising direction for deployment-time LLM safety that doesn't require extensive unsafe training data.

Abstract: Deployment-time safety methods for large language models (LLMs) are predominantly supervised and assume access to unsafe training data. Nevertheless, new attacks and harm categories regularly arise, not captured by models trained in such a supervised fashion. An alternative approach is to view this problem through the lens of anomaly detection, namely, to rely solely on modeling safe data and flagging out-of-distribution inputs. However, LLM activations lie in a high-dimensional space, raising concerns about whether anomaly detection is statistically feasible. We show that, under the linear representation hypothesis (LRH), there may indeed be hope. In the LRH concept space, which is typically recovered via a sparse autoencoder (SAE), nearby points share a small common active support. Using this local sparsity insight, we propose a framework for locally masked SAE-based anomaly detection, supported by theoretical justifications. We validate it on various architectures and datasets, including both capability-testing datasets and safety-specific datasets. Finally, when we allow algorithms to use 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal performance, demonstrating their ability to capture meaningful safety information while using only 1-2% of SAE neurons for computation.

</details>


### [166] [Fast-varying Natural Frequencies and Damping Ratio Identification for Linear Time-Varying System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20138)
*Melisa Bozaci,Alice Cicirello*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a physics-enhanced machine learning approach combining Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for system identification of Linear Time-Varying (LTV) systems, specifically applied to a 2-blade offshore wind turbine to identify fast-varying natural frequencies and damping ratios under varying operating conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify fast-varying natural frequencies and damping ratios in LTV systems under time-varying operating conditions (e.g., wind and wave loading), which is challenging due to environmental disturbances. Current methods struggle with the complexity of such dynamic systems.

Method: The approach combines LSTM network with EKF, using: (1) vibration data (displacement and velocity measurements), (2) domain knowledge of modal damping ratios, and (3) a physics-based model for approximate natural frequency time-dependency. The method is validated on synthetic data from a finite element model of a 2-blade offshore wind turbine under realistic conditions. Robustness is tested under incorrect system information (damping ratio), and the approach is extended to damping ratio identification using grid search.

Result: The approach accurately identifies the 1st Fore-Aft (FA-1) mode natural frequency with a maximum RMSE of 0.0012 Hz. Models trained on EKF estimates require accurate damping values, while models trained on physics-based data show robustness to incorrect damping assumptions. The method yields good approximation of damping ratio using grid search, improving over covariance-driven stochastic subspace identification.

Conclusion: The physics-enhanced ML approach effectively identifies fast-varying natural frequencies in LTV systems. The physics-based training data provides robustness to incorrect damping assumptions, making the approach practical for real-world applications where exact system parameters may be unknown. The method can also estimate damping ratios, offering an improvement over traditional subspace identification methods.

Abstract: This work proposes a physics-enhanced machine learning approach for the system identification of Linear Time-Varying (LTV) systems under time-varying operating conditions in terms of fast-varying natural frequencies and damping ratios by combining a long short-term memory network with an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). The proposed approach uses vibration data (displacement and velocity measurements), domain knowledge of modal damping ratios, and a physics-based model that can yield an approximate natural frequencies time-dependency model. The approach is validated using synthetic data generated from a finite element model of a 2-blade offshore wind turbine under realistic environmental and operating conditions. This system displays fast time-varying frequencies due to operating conditions, whose identification is particularly challenging because of the wind and wave loading. The robustness of the proposed approach is assessed under assumed incorrect system information (e.g. damping ratio). The proposed approach is evaluated across different environmental and operating conditions to show its applicability to different operating regimes. The results show the approach can accurately identify the selected fast-varying natural frequency, 1st Fore-Aft (FA-1) mode, with a maximum root mean square error of 0.0012 Hz. The results demonstrate that the model trained on EKF estimates depends on accurate damping values, whereas the model trained on physics-based data exhibits robustness to incorrect damping assumptions. The approach is extended to damping ratio identification for the selected mode by estimating the root mean square error between models trained on EKF estimates and physics-based data. The results show that the approach can yield a good approximation of the FA-1 mode damping ratio using grid search, offering an improvement over covariance-driven stochastic subspace identification.

</details>


### [167] [QUALS: Corpus Equilibrium for Universal Forecasting via Pattern Quantization and Learnability Synchronization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20156)
*Yujie Li,Zezhi Shao,Chengqing Yu,Yisong Fu,Weijie Zhu,Yifan Du,Jilin Hu,Bin Yang,Yongjun Xu,Fei Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QUALS is a large-scale time series corpus equilibrium framework that addresses inefficient data usage in foundation model training by combining pattern quantization (vector quantization + uniform binning) with learnability synchronization (adaptive sampling weight calibration) to achieve superior zero-shot forecasting performance with only a fraction of the original training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current time series foundation models prioritize architectural innovations while neglecting data diversity. Simple sampling strategies fail to manage complex data distributions, leading to inefficient training data use and suboptimal performance.

Method: QUALS employs two core mechanisms: (1) Pattern quantization framework - decodes heterogeneous patterns from mixed corpora via vector quantization and uniform binning; (2) Learnability synchronization framework - calibrates sampling weights for heterogeneous patterns, bridging the optimization gap between simple and complex motifs to maximize training efficiency.

Result: Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that pre-training on QUALS consistently achieves superior zero-shot performance, even under substantially reduced training budgets.

Conclusion: QUALS significantly enhances data efficiency, enabling existing models to achieve superior performance using only a small fraction of the original training data, while maintaining strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities across diverse domains.

Abstract: Ubiquitous time series data across diverse domains enables critical applications in areas such as transportation systems and power grids. Recently, training foundation models on massive datasets to achieve accurate zero-shot forecasting has emerged as a major research focus. However, current studies predominantly prioritize architectural innovations while insufficiently addressing data diversity, often relying on simple data sampling strategies that fail to manage complex data distributions effectively, leading to inefficient use of training data and suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose QUALS, a large-scale time series corpus equilibrium framework. QUALS significantly enhances data efficiency, i.e., enabling existing models to achieve superior performance using only a small fraction of the original training data. Specifically, QUALS operates through two core mechanisms. First, a pattern quantization framework systematically decodes heterogeneous patterns from mixed corpora via vector quantization and uniform binning. Second, a learnability synchronization framework calibrates sampling weights for heterogeneous patterns, bridging the optimization gap between simple and complex motifs to maximize overall training efficiency. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that pre-training on QUALS consistently achieves superior zero-shot performance, even under substantially reduced training budgets.

</details>


### [168] [A Noise Optimum in Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning: Isolation, Mechanism, and Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20162)
*Gunner Levi Howe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Injecting stochastic noise into consolidation rules creates an inverted-U relationship with retention - noise helps up to an optimal level but degrades beyond. The active ingredient is coupling anchor gain to noise variance (σ²), which differs from existing methods like Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Adaptation and MESU. This effect requires shared task structure and attenuates with task count.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why adding stochastic noise to consolidation rules can improve catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, but only up to an optimal level before degrading performance. The goal is to isolate what produces this optimum and map where it holds.

Method: Entirely simulation-based study using: (1) Benchmarks: Split-MNIST, FashionMNIST, continual Yin-Yang, permuted-MNIST, rotated-vs-permuted comparisons. (2) Ladder experiments: magnitude-matched comparisons testing coherent restoring vs random-direction forces. (3) Derivation of coupled gain rule: anchor gain coupled to σ². (4) Theoretical analysis using forced Ornstein-Uhlenbeck calculation to predict optimal noise scaling with per-task interference. (5) Boundary testing via rotated-vs-permuted task structure comparison.

Result: Key findings: (1) Retention inverted-U appears on multiple related-task benchmarks. (2) The effect requires coherent restoring toward consolidated weights - random-direction forces produce no optimum. (3) Coupling anchor gain to σ² recovers most of the optimum - a one-line rule not implemented by OU adaptation or MESU. (4) Optimal noise rises with per-task interference g. (5) Barrier-conditioning provides low-sigma safety net. (6) Optimum requires shared task structure - absent on permuted-MNIST. (7) Advantage persists but attenuates with task count. (8) No rotation family can attribute the trend (compact-group identity).

Conclusion: The optimal noise effect in consolidation rules is driven by coherent restoring forces coupled to noise variance. The phenomenon requires shared task structure between tasks and attenuates with increasing task count. A simple coupling of anchor gain to σ² outperforms existing approaches (OU adaptation, MESU), with the optimal noise level scaling with per-task interference.

Abstract: Injecting stochastic noise into a consolidation rule can improve a network's retention of earlier tasks up to an optimal level, then degrade it -- an inverted-U in retention vs. noise. This paper isolates what produces that optimum and maps where it holds, entirely in simulation. (1) Phenomenon: the retention inverted-U appears on several related-task continual-learning benchmarks (Split-MNIST, FashionMNIST, continual Yin-Yang). (2) Isolation: a magnitude-matched ladder shows the effect requires coherent restoring toward the consolidated weights -- a random-direction force of identical magnitude produces no optimum, and a coherent force toward the wrong target actively hurts. (3) Active ingredient: most of the optimum is recovered by coupling the anchor gain to the injected-noise variance sigma^2 -- a one-line rule that neither Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Adaptation (fixed gain) nor MESU (posterior-variance gain) implements. A forced Ornstein-Uhlenbeck calculation derives the rising flank and predicts that the optimal noise rises with per-task interference g -- confirmed out-of-sample in direction against pre-existing measurements (the exponent is unresolved at our grid). The barrier-conditioning of the originating Doob h-transform is a low-sigma safety net that bounds forgetting where the coupled gain is too weak. (4) Scope: the optimum requires shared task structure -- it is absent on permuted-MNIST, and a controlled rotated-vs-permuted comparison localizes the boundary to task structure; the precise governing quantity is left open. (5) Length: at matched severity the advantage persists but attenuates with task count, and we show no rotation family can attribute the trend (a compact-group identity). A single-seed BrainScaleS-2 demonstration of the originating rule is reported separately (Howe, arXiv:2607.06924); this paper makes no hardware claim.

</details>


### [169] [Small Enough to Know Everything: The Fully-Enumerable Transformer as an Instrument for the Science of Delayed Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20166)
*Yoshiyuki Ootani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using tiny transformers on fully-enumerable tasks as a "model organism" for studying grokking (delayed generalization). The authors test three task-side laws across a 4,000x parameter scale span (12K to 50M) and find that two laws (ceiling and delay) are conserved while one (weight-decay) deforms systematically. This establishes the tiny transformer regime as a valid scientific instrument for studying generalization laws.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors address a key limitation in grokking research: whether findings from small models (10^4 parameters) generalize to larger models. They propose that tiny transformers on fully-enumerable tasks offer unique advantages as a "scientific instrument" with exact measurements, controllable variables, and statistical rigor across multiple seeds.

Method: The authors conducted a preregistered conservation study testing three task-side laws (recoverability-ceiling, role-conflict delay, weight-decay response) at three model scales (12K, 1M, 50M parameters) using 360 runs plus a 44-run control arm. They used exact generalization ceilings, task surgery to manipulate single variables, direct weight observation, and survival-time statistics treating non-grokking as censored observations.

Result: The ceiling law and delay law were conserved across all scales (0/144 Holm-corrected ceiling violations; Spearman rho >= 0.75 at every scale, permutation p < 1e-4). The weight-decay law deformed systematically, steepening with scale. The 50M role-conflict deficit survived learning-rate adjustment and tripled training budget. These results show that what tiny transformers measure exactly, larger models largely obey—and where they deviate, the deviation is itself lawful.

Conclusion: The fully-enumerable transformer regime serves as a valid model organism for studying task-side laws of delayed generalization. Two of three tested laws are conserved across a 4,000x scale span, while the third shows systematic, measurable deformation. This establishes a methodology for precise, falsifiable research in grokking and generalization.

Abstract: Tiny transformers trained on fully-enumerable tasks occupy an unusual position in the study of grokking: every input can be evaluated, every generalization ceiling can be computed exactly, and hundreds of seeds cost minutes. We argue this regime is a scientific instrument with four capabilities that approximate settings cannot offer: (a) exact, falsifiable generalization ceilings; (b) task surgery that manipulates one structural variable while provably fixing all others; (c) direct observation of every weight; and (d) survival-time statistics over many seeds that recast "does not grok" as a censored observation. The obvious objection is that laws characterized at 10^4 parameters may not mean anything beyond them. We answer it with a preregistered conservation study: three task-side laws established at 12K parameters -- a recoverability-ceiling law, a role-conflict delay law, and a weight-decay response law -- are re-measured under an identical from-scratch protocol at 12K, 1M, and 50M parameters (a 4,000x span; 360 runs plus a 44-run control arm). The ceiling law and the delay law are conserved (0/144 Holm-corrected ceiling violations; Spearman rho >= 0.75 at every scale, permutation p < 1e-4), while the weight-decay law deforms systematically, steepening with scale. Preregistered controls show the 50M role-conflict deficit survives learning-rate adjustment and a tripled budget. Conservation was tested against criteria frozen before data collection, and one law's deformation shows the test could have failed. These results license the fully-enumerable transformer as a model organism for the task-side laws of delayed generalization: what it measures exactly, larger models largely obey -- and where they deviate, the deviation is itself lawful and measurable.

</details>


### [170] [Support Thresholds, Not Algorithms, Limit Rare-Association Recovery in Co-Purchase Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20171)
*Xiao Han,Zhen Zhang,Xin Zhao,Jiechun Lei,Moxuan Zheng,Youting Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares five methods for co-purchase edge filtration in market basket analysis on two large grocery datasets (Instacart and Dunnhumby). The study evaluates how different filtering approaches affect the discovery of high-lift association rules, particularly rare associations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The support threshold in Apriori algorithm presents a trade-off: high thresholds capture frequent associations but miss rare ones, while low thresholds generate excessive rules. This research seeks better methods to identify meaningful co-purchase relationships without this trade-off.

Method: The study compared five methods: Apriori, Apriori + lift post-filtering, top-K ranking based on lift, noise-corrected (NC), and disparity filter (DF). These were evaluated on Instacart (3.2M baskets) and Dunnhumby (208K baskets) datasets using rolling-origin holdout evaluation.

Result: Top-K achieves maximum average lift; NC achieves similar lift with a single significance parameter (α). NC and top-K recover substantially more rare high-lift associations than Apriori (80-100% vs 22-28%). They select 18-29% non-overlapping edges. Top-K edges recur at higher rates, but NC edges are ~12 percentage points more likely to remain statistically significant in held-out networks.

Conclusion: Top-K is better for finding recurring associations, while NC is better for maintaining statistical significance. The choice between methods depends on whether the goal is capturing frequent co-purchases (top-K) or identifying statistically validated pairs (NC).

Abstract: The support threshold of the Apriori algorithm involves a trade-off in conducting market basket analysis: the associations that occur frequently are noted with high threshold; however, the low ones lead to generating the large amount of rules. The paper compares five methods for co-purchase edge filtration on two grocery datasets: i.e., Instacart (3.2 million baskets) and Dunnhumby (208 thousand baskets), including Apriori, Apriori + lift post-filtering, top-$K$ ranking based on lift, and two methods based on networks, noise-corrected (NC) and disparity filter (DF). The top-$K$ method ensures the maximum average lift, while the NC achieves similar lift level by means of a single value of the significance parameter ($α$). These two methods recover substantially more rare high-lift associations than Apriori (80-100% against 22-28%). NC and top-$K$ select meaningfully different edges (18-29% non-overlapping): NC retains statistically validated pairs, while top-$K$ retains rare pairs with high lift but low statistical significance. A rolling-origin holdout evaluation shows that top-$K$ edges recur at higher rates at every split, but NC edges are ~12 pp more likely to remain statistically significant in the held-out network.

</details>


### [171] [Robust Federated Q-Learning with Almost No Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20174)
*Sreejeet Maity,Aritra Mitra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses federated Q-learning with adversarial agents, proposing Robust Fed-Q that combines model-based and model-free RL with median-of-means for robustness. The algorithm guarantees exact convergence and near-optimal finite-time rates with only O(1) communication rounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand collaborative sample-complexity speedups in federated RL when some agents are adversarial. The key challenge is achieving reliable learning despite Byzantine/arbitrary corruption from a minority of agents.

Method: Robust Fed-Q blends model-based and model-free RL approaches, incorporating the median-of-means device from robust statistics to handle adversarial behavior. The algorithm uses a central server to aggregate information from M agents.

Result: The paper proves that with high probability: (i) exact convergence to the optimal value function in the infinite-sample limit, and (ii) near-optimal finite-time rates that benefit from collaboration. Additionally, the method requires only O(1) communication rounds.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that federated RL can be made robust to adversarial agents while maintaining near-optimal sample complexity and minimal communication overhead, enabling practical deployment in unreliable network settings.

Abstract: We consider a federated reinforcement learning setting involving $M$ agents, all of whom interact with a common Markov Decision Process (MDP). The agents exchange information via a central server to learn the optimal value function. Our goal is to understand to what extent one can hope for collaborative sample-complexity speedups in such a setting, when a small fraction of the agents are adversarial and can act arbitrarily. To that end, we propose Robust Fed-Q}, a federated Q-learning algorithm that blends ideas from both model-based and model-free RL, along with the median-of-means device from robust statistics. We prove that despite corruption, with high-probability, Robust Fed-Q (i) guarantees exact convergence to the optimal value function in the limit of infinite samples, and (ii) enjoys near-optimal finite-time rates that benefit from collaboration. In addition, our approach requires just $\tilde{O}(1)$ rounds of communication to achieve each of the above guarantees, a feature of independent interest in FL where communication is the major bottleneck.

</details>


### [172] [When Does Retrieval Help Time-Series Forecasting?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20193)
*Mert Onur Cakiroglu,Elham Buxton,Mehmet Dalkilic,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper reveals that retrieval plug-ins for deep time series forecasters benefit from the relationship between window length (S) and seasonal period (L), not the specific mechanism. A simple control repeating the last observed period beats six standard backbones on four of seven benchmarks, challenging the utility of complex retrieval methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed that many papers claim their retrieval plug-in mechanisms are responsible for performance gains in deep forecasters, but they hypothesize that the gains actually come from the relationship between lookback window length and seasonal period - a variable the standard evaluation protocol never varies.

Method: The authors: (1) Stratified evaluations by the S/L ratio (window length to seasonal period); (2) Created a simple control that repeats the last observed period; (3) Conducted controlled synthetic sweeps varying horizon, period, and window; (4) Tested a paired control with no phase to recover; (5) Evaluated zero-shot pretraining (foundation model); (6) Developed two interpretable statistics (trend test and staleness rate) to predict benefit sign.

Result: At S=12, the simple control beats six standard backbones on 4/7 benchmarks by 8-44% MSE, beats the strongest plug-in on ETTm1, and matches on ECL. It is worse by up to 25% on three datasets lacking concentrated shared period. The benefit boundary tracks the period (correlation +0.71), not horizon (-0.23). A paired control with no phase nearly erases the effect, supporting "phase starvation" hypothesis. A foundation model trails trained backbones by 22-50% on periodic benchmarks. Two statistics predict benefit sign at 0.76 accuracy vs 0.69 majority rule.

Conclusion: The benefit of retrieval plug-ins comes from the S/L relationship (phase starvation), not the mechanism itself. The contribution is the regime map, evaluation protocol revealing it, and two screening statistics (trend test and staleness rate) for deployment. The authors propose no new plug-in.

Abstract: Retrieval plug-ins supply a deep forecaster with information its lookback window cannot carry. Published evaluations report consistent gains, and each credits its own mechanism. We show that the benefit belongs instead to the operating point: the relation between window length $S$ and dominant seasonal period $L$, an axis the standard protocol never varies. Stratifying the evaluation by that relation exposes the regime. At $S{=}12$, a simple control that repeats the last observed period beats the six standard backbones, in aggregate, on four of seven benchmarks by $8\%$ to $44\%$ of MSE. It beats the strongest plug-in we run on ETTm1 and matches it on ECL. It is worse by up to $25\%$ on the three datasets whose training-split spectra lack a concentrated, shared period. A controlled synthetic sweep of horizon, period, and window shows the benefit boundary tracks the period (correlation $+0.71$), not the horizon ($-0.23$). A paired control with no phase to recover nearly erases the effect, consistent with phase starvation. Zero-shot pretraining does not escape it: a foundation model trails trained backbones by $22\%$ to $50\%$ on the periodic benchmarks. Within our instrument, exact lookup matches graph diffusion: the payoff is consulting the record, not the machinery on top. Two interpretable statistics, a trend test and a staleness rate, predict the sign of the per-cell benefit at $0.76$ accuracy under leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, a suggestive margin over the $0.69$ majority rule, where a 22-feature stack manages $0.57$. We propose no new plug-in. The contribution is the regime map, the protocol that reveals it, and two statistics that screen it before deployment. Code: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/retrieval-regime.

</details>


### [173] [SoftTri: Smooth Triangular Membership Functions for Adaptive Fuzzy Inference Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20194)
*Babak Sarani,Rahman Ardakanian,Ali Mousavi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SoftTri proposes a differentiable triangular membership function using a smooth soft-hinge mechanism, enabling gradient-based optimization in neuro-fuzzy architectures while preserving the interpretability and locality of classical triangular MFs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Triangular MFs are widely used due to interpretability and low complexity, but their nondifferentiability at knot points limits gradient-based optimization in adaptive neuro-fuzzy systems, requiring subgradient approximations or heuristic smoothing.

Method: SoftTri constructs a differentiable triangular MF using a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations. The formulation provides C^∞ smoothness with respect to input and parameters (a,b,c) for any finite sharpness parameter β>0. Closed-form analytical gradients are derived for efficient backpropagation. The method is integrated into a Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules.

Result: Experiments on 1D/2D nonlinear approximation benchmarks and Airfoil Self-Noise dataset show SoftTri improves optimization stability and approximation accuracy compared to classical triangular MFs, while achieving comparable or better performance than Gaussian MFs under identical settings.

Conclusion: SoftTri provides an effective compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in modern neuro-fuzzy learning systems.

Abstract: Triangular membership functions (MFs) are widely used in fuzzy systems because of their interpretability, low parameterization complexity, and strong locality properties. However, their inherent nondifferentiability at knot points limits the effectiveness of gradient-based optimization in adaptive neuro-fuzzy architectures, often necessitating subgradient approximations or heuristic smoothing techniques. In this paper, we propose \emph{SoftTri}, a differentiable triangular membership function constructed using a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations. The proposed formulation preserves the geometric structure and localized behavior of classical triangular MFs while providing $C^\infty$ smoothness with respect to both the input variable and the membership parameters $(a,b,c)$ for any finite sharpness parameter $β>0$. Closed-form analytical gradients are derived to enable efficient and fully differentiable backpropagation-based learning. SoftTri is integrated into a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules and evaluated on multiple one-dimensional and two-dimensional nonlinear approximation benchmarks as well as a real-world regression task using the Airfoil Self-Noise dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SoftTri consistently improves optimization stability and approximation accuracy compared with classical triangular membership functions, while achieving performance comparable to or better than Gaussian MFs under identical rule structures and training settings. The proposed approach provides an effective compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in modern neuro-fuzzy learning systems.

</details>


### [174] [Evaluating Financial Sentiment in the Age of AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20198)
*Arslan Bisharat,Oudom Hean*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether general-purpose LLMs improve on existing finance-specific sentiment analysis methods by comparing 12 sentiment models (dictionary-based, finance-specific transformers, and open-source LLMs) using linguistic and economic validity criteria. The study finds that while LLMs achieve comparable classification performance to finance-specific transformers, higher accuracy does not translate into stronger economic relationships.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the unresolved question of whether general-purpose large language models (LLMs) improve upon existing finance-specific sentiment analysis methods, which are widely used in empirical finance but have unknown relative effectiveness.

Method: The researchers evaluated twelve sentiment models across three categories: dictionary-based methods, finance-specific transformers, and open-source LLMs. They assessed these models using two criteria: linguistic validity (classification performance) and economic validity (associations with earnings surprises and stock returns).

Result: General-purpose LLMs achieve classification performance comparable to finance-specific transformer models without task-specific fine-tuning. However, higher classification accuracy does not translate into stronger economic relationships. Several models produce sentiment measures significantly associated with earnings surprises, but none is significantly associated with next-day stock returns. Performance is strongest for announcements with large earnings beats/misses and weaker for moderate earnings surprises.

Conclusion: Financial sentiment captures information about firms' economic performance but has limited ability to explain short-run market reactions. The disconnect between linguistic validity (classification accuracy) and economic validity (predictive power for returns) suggests that while sentiment models can identify tone, they may not capture price-relevant information.

Abstract: Financial sentiment measures are widely used in empirical finance, but it remains unclear whether general-purpose large language models (LLMs) improve on existing finance-specific methods. This paper evaluates twelve sentiment models, including dictionary-based methods, finance-specific transformers, and open-source LLMs, using two criteria: linguistic validity and economic validity. We find that general-purpose LLMs achieve classification performance comparable to finance-specific transformer models without task-specific fine-tuning. However, higher classification accuracy does not translate into stronger economic relationships. Several models produce sentiment measures that are significantly associated with earnings surprises, but none is significantly associated with next-day stock returns. Model performance is strongest for announcements with large earnings beats or misses and substantially weaker for announcements with more moderate earnings surprises. These findings suggest that financial sentiment captures information about firms' economic performance but has limited ability to explain short-run market reactions

</details>


### [175] [Towards a Unified Modality-Agnostic Multimodal Framework for Cognitive Workload Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20199)
*Stefanos Gkikas,Christian Arzate Cruz,Calvin Joseph,Giorgos Giannakakis,Raul Fernandez Rojas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a unified, modality-agnostic, hierarchical Transformer-based architecture to combine heterogeneous biosignal modalities (ECG, EDA, RESP, SpO2, EEG) for cognitive workload measurement. The pilot study evaluated all 31 possible modality combinations across three cognitive tasks, finding that EEG alone performs best in most scenarios, while the full five-modality combination achieves the highest average accuracy of 73.02% on IQ tasks and 68.08% overall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cognitive workload measurement is crucial for adaptive human-machine systems design. While biosignal-based measurement has been extensively researched, there is limited investigation into combining heterogeneous biosignal modalities within a single model. This study addresses this gap by developing a unified framework to process multiple biosignal modalities.

Method: The researchers developed a hierarchical Transformer-based architecture that processes heterogeneous biosignal modalities within a single model. They conducted a pilot study evaluating all 31 possible combinations of five modalities (ECG, EDA, RESP, SpO2, and EEG) using leave-one-subject-out validation across three cognitively distinct tasks: abstract reasoning (IQ), arithmetic problem solving (MATH), and a game task (GAME).

Result: Key findings include: (i) EEG is the strongest single modality, ranking highest in IQ, GAME, and pooled ALL settings; (ii) adding more modalities does not consistently improve performance; (iii) the full five-modality combination achieves the highest Average score of 73.02% on IQ and 68.08% when averaged over all four evaluation settings; (iv) the proposed method reduces model size by approximately 50% compared with late-fusion alternatives while maintaining lower inference time.

Conclusion: The proposed hierarchical Transformer architecture successfully integrates heterogeneous biosignal modalities for cognitive workload measurement. While EEG alone performs well in most cases, the full five-modality combination achieves superior average performance. The architecture offers significant advantages in model efficiency, reducing size by ~50% and inference time compared to late-fusion approaches, making it promising for practical adaptive human-machine system applications.

Abstract: Cognitive workload reflects the mental effort required during task performance and is central to the design of adaptive human-machine systems. The use of biosignals to measure cognitive workload has been extensively researched and documented; however, studies examining the effects of combining heterogeneous biosignal modalities for this purpose remain limited. To provide insight into this area, we developed a unified, modality-agnostic, hierarchical Transformer-based architecture to process heterogeneous biosignal modalities within a single model. We use this framework in a pilot study evaluating all $31$ possible combinations of five modalities: Electrocardiogram (ECG), Electrodermal Activity (EDA), Respiration (RESP), Peripheral Oxygen Saturation (SpO$_2$), and Electroencephalogram (EEG), under leave-one-subject-out validation across three cognitively distinct tasks: abstract reasoning (IQ), arithmetic problem solving (MATH), and a game task (GAME). In this pilot setting, the results suggest that: (i) EEG is the strongest single modality, ranking highest in IQ, GAME, and the pooled ALL setting, where samples from all three tasks are combined; (ii) adding more modalities does not consistently improve performance; (iii) the full five-modality combination achieves the highest \textit{Average} score of $73.02%$ on IQ and $68.08%$ when the \textit{Average} scores are averaged over the four evaluation settings: IQ, MATH, GAME, and ALL; and (iv) the proposed method reduces model size by approximately $50%$ compared with late-fusion alternatives while maintaining a lower inference time.

</details>


### [176] [Scene-Conditioned Relation Routing for urban cellular activity forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20209)
*Qingzhong Li,Jingye Lin,Hui Ma,Yajun Zhang,Xinjun Pei,Ming Yan,Fei Xing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Urban cellular activity forecasting requires jointly modeling heterogeneous spatiotemporal signals, including SMS usage, mobile network traffic, and call activity. Existing methods often separate temporal modeling, spatial relation learning, and multi-signal prediction, relying on fixed graph structures or static multi-task learning schemes, which limits their adaptability to changing urban scenes. We propose SCRR-Net, a scene-conditioned spatial relation routing framework in which urban contextual information jointly controls spatial dependency selection and cross-task knowledge transfer. SCRR-Net includes a context encoder, a spatial graph expert routing module, a temporal Transformer encoder, and a task knowledge routing module. Experiments on the Milano and Trento datasets demonstrate that SCRR-Net consistently outperforms competing methods on SMS, network traffic, and call activity forecasting, while providing interpretable routing behaviors.

</details>


### [177] [Subdomain-aware representation compression for pretrained image embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20213)
*Poowanut Niamluang,Jittat Fakcharoenphol*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper explores applying dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA and LDA) specifically for subdomain representation compression in image domains, rather than uniform application across entire datasets. The approach shows improvements in space efficiency, computational complexity, accuracy, and transfer learning capabilities compared to full-embedding procedures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional dimensionality reduction is applied uniformly across entire datasets. This paper investigates whether applying dimensionality reduction techniques to subdomain representations can achieve better compression while maintaining or improving accuracy, particularly for edge-device ML applications where space and computational efficiency are critical.

Method: The researchers applied standard dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA and LDA) to image domains for subdomain representation compression. They conducted experiments to evaluate: (1) space and computational complexity improvements, (2) accuracy compared to direct full-embedding procedures, and (3) transfer learning capabilities using the compressed representations.

Result: The experiments demonstrated: (1) expected improvements in space and computational complexity, which are crucial for edge-device ML applications, (2) unexpected improvements in accuracy over direct full-embedding procedures, and (3) successful transfer learning capabilities using the compressed representations. The researchers suggest that dimensionality reduction effectively extracts subdomain features, which may explain the accuracy improvements.

Conclusion: Dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA and LDA can be effectively used for subdomain representation compression, achieving not only space and computational benefits but also accuracy improvements. The approach also enables transfer learning with compressed representations, making it promising for edge-device ML applications.

Abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a well-known technique for improving space efficiency, typically applied uniformly across an entire dataset. This paper investigates the possibilities of using dimensionality reduction techniques for subdomain representation compression. We explore standard techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) in image domains. The results not only demonstrate the expected improvements in space and computation complexity crucial for edge-device ML applications but also show improvements in accuracy over direct full-embedding procedure. One possible explanation is that dimensionality reduction effectively extracts subdomain features. We also performed experiments to demonstrate transfer learning capabilities using the compressed representations.

</details>


### [178] [Explaining spatial information flow in short-term traffic forecasting models using a gated graph attention network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20217)
*Yue Li,Shujuan Chen,Ying Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a gap in explaining how Graph Attention Networks (GAT) capture spatial dependence in short-term traffic forecasting by introducing a gated mechanism that quantifies the share of neighbor information used at each sensor and time step. The approach is applied to ST-MetaNet using data from 498 loop detectors in England, revealing when and where spatial information flows, and demonstrating that GAT layers are largely redundant rather than indispensable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GAT layers are standard for representing spatial dependence in traffic forecasting models, but there is no way to verify what the attention weights actually represent since they cannot be compared against any measured quantity. This raises questions about how to explain the model and which components are truly necessary.

Method: The authors add a gate to the GAT layer that learns, at every sensor and every time step, what share of a sensor's updated state is drawn from its neighbors versus from itself. Regularizing the gate progressively withdraws neighbor information, providing a graded ablation method. The gated GAT is applied to ST-MetaNet (which has an encoder and decoder, each with one GAT layer between two recurrent layers), trained on one calendar year of data from 498 loop detectors on England's strategic road network.

Result: The gate assigns a larger share of neighbor information to sensors with heavier traffic and follows daily and weekly cycles, consistent with adjacent locations being more strongly coupled when busy. Mild regularisation improves accuracy slightly, while higher regularisation decreases accuracy as the model loses needed information. The encoder gate closes before the decoder gate, but direct ablation shows this ordering is not strict. Removing either GAT layer alone leaves accuracy at least as good as keeping both, while removing both substantially degrades accuracy, indicating the two layers are largely redundant rather than indispensable.

Conclusion: The gated GAT provides a modest accuracy gain, explains where and when spatial information flows in the model, and provides evidence on which layers the architecture requires. The key finding is that GAT layers in ST-MetaNet are largely redundant—both can be removed without harm if at least one remains, suggesting the spatial modeling component may be less critical than previously thought.

Abstract: Short-term traffic forecasting supports real-time monitoring and control of road networks, and graph attention networks (GAT) are the standard means of representing spatial dependence in these models. GAT layers are widely described as capturing the influence of neighbouring locations, but this is seldom verified, because the attention weights offered in support cannot be compared against any measured quantity. That leaves two questions open, how the model should be explained and which of its components are necessary. We address this by adding a gate to the GAT layer which learns, at every sensor and every time step, what share of a sensor's updated state is drawn from its neighbours rather than from itself. Regularising the gate withdraws neighbour information progressively and thereby provides a graded form of ablation. We apply the gated GAT to ST-MetaNet, whose encoder and decoder each place one GAT layer between two recurrent layers, and train it on one calendar year of records from 498 loop detectors on the strategic road network of England. The gate assigns a larger share of neighbour information to sensors carrying heavier traffic and follows the daily and weekly cycle of travel, consistent with adjacent locations being more strongly coupled when busy. Mild regularisation improves accuracy slightly, and accuracy declines at higher strengths as the penalty withdraws information the model needs. The encoder gate closes before the decoder gate, but direct ablation qualifies that ordering. Removing either GAT layer alone leaves accuracy at least as good as keeping both, whereas removing both degrades it substantially, so the two layers are largely redundant rather than either being indispensable. The gated GAT therefore yields a modest accuracy gain, an explanation of where and when spatial information flows, and evidence on which layers the architecture requires.

</details>


### [179] [Is It Still Worth Training a Classical Model in the Era of LLMs? A Crossover Benchmark on Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20218)
*Kaihua Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the practical question of whether to use frozen LLMs for labeling tabular data (no training needed) versus collecting labeled data to train classical models. The authors introduce "labeled-data crossover N*" - the training set size where a trained model outperforms a frozen LLM. Across 126 evaluations on 18 datasets with 8 prompting configurations, they find trained models beat small frozen LLMs in 86% of cases, with median crossover at ~6% of training data. The recommendation is to collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is practical: major spreadsheet tools (Microsoft Copilot in Excel, Anthropic's Claude for Excel) now offer LLM-based labeling for tabular rows from plain-English descriptions. This raises a key question for business prediction problems where labels are expensive - should users prompt a frozen LLM or collect data and train a model?

Method: The study aggregated 126 independent student evaluations of small GPT models under eight prompting configurations across 18 tabular datasets, paired with authoritative power-law learning curves for six classical model families. They also conducted a controlled probe to understand LLM dependencies on feature-name semantics.

Result: Key findings: (1) Trained classical model beats small frozen LLM in 86% of cases even with oracle choice of best prompt; (2) Wins by smallest labeled subset in 40% of cases; (3) Median crossover at ~6% of training set; (4) In-context few-shot examples don't follow power law (don't behave like training); (5) Protocol variation has coefficient of variation 0.148; (6) LLM depends on recognizable feature-name semantics.

Conclusion: For a typical business table, the evidence is clear: collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model. The crossover N* is likely a conservative estimate since the study doesn't claim LLM memorization.

Abstract: Large language models can label a tabular row from a plain-English description with no training - a capability now shipping in mainstream spreadsheet tools such as Microsoft Copilot in Excel and Anthropic's Claude for Excel - raising a practical question for the many business prediction problems where labels are expensive: should you prompt a frozen LLM, or collect data and train a model - and if so, how much data? We quantify the answer with the labeled-data crossover N*, the training-set size at which a trained classical model's learning curve overtakes a frozen LLM's training-free (and therefore flat) error. Aggregating 126 independent student evaluations of small GPT models under eight prompting configurations across 18 tabular datasets, paired with authoritative power-law learning curves for six classical model families, we find that training wins fast: even given an oracle choice of its best prompt configuration, a trained classical model beats the small frozen LLM using no more labeled data than is already on hand in 86% of cases, and wins by the smallest labeled subset we evaluate in 40%, with the observed crossover at a median of ~6% of the training set. In-context few-shot examples do not behave like training - error versus shot count does not follow a power law - and the same protocol re-run by independent implementers varies with a coefficient of variation of 0.148. A controlled probe indicates the LLM depends on recognizable feature-name semantics, which plausibly makes our crossover a conservative estimate (we do not claim memorization). For a typical business table, the evidence is clear: collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model.

</details>


### [180] [Accuracy Is Not Enough: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Demographic Bias in Deep Knowledge Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20249)
*Dang Quang Minh,Nguyen Dung Son,Nguyen Huu Loi,Truong Viet Vu,Nguyen Thai Anh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits demographic fairness across four deep knowledge tracing architectures (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) trained under three regimes on two datasets (Eedi, OULAD). The study finds that bias is context-dependent, the most accurate model (AKT) is also the most biased, and standard mitigation techniques (reweighting, adversarial debiasing) fail to reduce bias while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Bayesian knowledge tracing has been extensively studied for demographic fairness, the deep learning models that power modern adaptive learning systems have not received comparable cross-architecture audits. This gap needs to be closed to ensure fairness in educational AI systems.

Method: The authors trained four architectures (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) under three regimes (standard, reweighting, adversarial) on two public datasets (Eedi: 15.9M interactions; OULAD: 167k after preprocessing). They evaluated using ABROCA, student-level bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests to address recent critiques of fairness-metric instability.

Result: Three key findings: (i) Bias is real but context-dependent - significant socioeconomic ABROCA on Eedi (0.018-0.023, p<0.005) with lower AUC for disadvantaged students; gender bias significant on OULAD for 3/4 architectures but negligible on Eedi. (ii) Most accurate architecture (AKT) shows largest socioeconomic ABROCA; ablating Rasch embeddings removes both accuracy gain and excess bias. (iii) Standard mitigation (reweighting, adversarial debiasing) leaves ABROCA unchanged in every accuracy-preserving configuration.

Conclusion: Demographic bias in deep knowledge tracing is architecture-dependent and strongly linked to accuracy gains from sensitive features like item-level Rasch embeddings. Standard debiasing techniques are unreliable, suggesting a need for new fairness-aware architecture design or alternative mitigation strategies.

Abstract: Deep knowledge tracing (DKT) models implicitly decide which students an adaptive system believes have mastered a skill, yet almost all evidence on their demographic fairness comes from Bayesian knowledge tracing; the deep models that power modern systems have received no comparable cross-architecture audit. We close this gap: four architectures (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) trained under three regimes (standard, reweighting, adversarial) on two public datasets with demographic metadata, Eedi (15.9M interactions) and OULAD (167k after preprocessing), evaluated with ABROCA, student-level bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests addressing recent critiques of fairness-metric instability. Three findings emerge. (i) Bias is real but context-dependent: every architecture shows a significant socioeconomic ABROCA on Eedi (0.018-0.023, $p<0.005$), with per-group AUC lower for economically disadvantaged students, while gender bias is significant on OULAD for three of four architectures after multiplicity correction yet negligible on Eedi. (ii) The most accurate architecture is the most biased: AKT gains about 4 AUC points from item-level Rasch embeddings and shows the largest socioeconomic ABROCA, exceeding every other architecture under a paired bootstrap ($p\leq0.002$); ablating only the Rasch embeddings removes the accuracy gain and the excess bias together. (iii) Standard mitigation is unreliable: reweighting and adversarial debiasing leave ABROCA essentially unchanged in every configuration that preserves accuracy, even though the adversary is pinned at chance at full reversal strength and a weak-strength positive control rules out a dead probe.

</details>


### [181] [How Far Can Sub-3B Open Language Models Go in Zero-Shot Essay Scoring on an 8 GB Consumer GPU?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20250)
*Nguyen Dung Son,Dang Quang Minh,Nguyen Huu Loi,Truong Viet Vu,Nguyen Thai Anh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates zero-shot essay scoring using small open-source LLMs (sub-3B parameters) running locally on a single 8GB consumer GPU, addressing privacy concerns in educational settings where API use is unacceptable. The study tests four instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5 at 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 at 1.7B) on the ASAP-AES dataset, examining prompting strategies and score normalization techniques. Key findings show rubric-decomposed prompting outperforms holistic approaches, and a Multi-Trait Specialization technique (min-max normalization) significantly improves performance (QWK from 0.204 to 0.388). However, the best local configuration (0.388) remains well below the human inter-rater ceiling (0.769) and a length-only baseline (0.523).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot essay scoring with LLMs is typically demonstrated using proprietary API models, but educational settings like public schools have strict privacy rules that prohibit sending student writing to third-party APIs. This creates a need to understand how well small open-source models can perform essay scoring when running locally.
