Method: Controlled study using four instruction-tuned models from two families (Qwen2.5: 0.5B/1.5B/3B; SmolLM2: 1.7B) running in FP16 on a single 8GB consumer GPU. Tested on all eight ASAP-AES prompts. Evaluation methods included bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected paired tests, and deployment-realistic variants of key design choices. Compared rubric-decomposed prompting vs. holistic prompting, and various score aggregation methods (mean, min-max).

Result: Three key findings: (i) Rubric-decomposed prompting beats holistic prompting for every model under batch min-max aggregation; Qwen2.5-3B drops significantly on one prompt; under mean aggregation, two unrelated model families perform within 0.01 at the 1.5-1.7B scale. (ii) Mapping trait scores into prompt range is fragile to grader calibration—one model compresses traits into narrow band (2-4 on 0-10), causing naive mean aggregation to collapse; Multi-Trait Specialization with min-max normalization repairs this (macro QWK 0.204 → 0.388) and stays within 0.03 when statistics are frozen on 30 held-out essays. (iii) Signed error falls with essay length in 11/12 configurations, opposite to verbosity bias reported for large LLM judges; normalized rubric decomposition largely flattens this slope for well-calibrated models. The best local configuration achieves QWK of 0.388.

Conclusion: The best local configuration (QWK 0.388) remains far below both the human inter-rater ceiling (0.769) and a length-only baseline (0.523). Therefore, sub-3B local models should be positioned strictly for formative, human-supervised feedback rather than high-stakes automated scoring. The study provides honest anchoring of results and focuses on practical deployment considerations in privacy-sensitive educational contexts.

Abstract: Zero-shot essay scoring with large language models is usually demonstrated with proprietary API models, yet the settings where automated scoring is most needed, such as public schools grading thousands of essays under strict privacy rules, are often those where sending student writing to a third-party API is unacceptable. We ask how much capability survives when the model must be a sub-3B open model running fully locally in FP16, with a controlled study of four instruction-tuned models from two families (Qwen2.5 at 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 at 1.7B) on all eight ASAP-AES prompts on a single 8 GB consumer GPU, with bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected paired tests, and deployment-realistic variants of the key design choices. Three findings emerge. (i) Rubric-decomposed prompting beats holistic prompting for every model under batch min-max aggregation (though Qwen2.5-3B drops significantly on one prompt), and under mean aggregation two unrelated families land within 0.01 at the 1.5-1.7B scale. (ii) Mapping trait scores into the prompt range is fragile to grader calibration: one model compresses traits into a narrow low band (2-4 on 0-10) and naive mean aggregation collapses, while the min-max normalization of Multi-Trait Specialization repairs it (macro QWK 0.204 to 0.388) and stays within 0.03 when its statistics are frozen on 30 held-out essays. (iii) Signed error falls with essay length in eleven of twelve configurations, opposite to the verbosity bias reported for large LLM judges; normalized rubric decomposition largely flattens this slope for well-calibrated models. We anchor results honestly: the best local configuration (0.388) remains far below both the human inter-rater ceiling (0.769) and a length-only baseline (0.523), so we position sub-3B local models strictly for formative, human-supervised feedback.

</details>


### [182] [Improving Online Reinforcement Learning via Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20268)
*Gong Gao,Xiao Lai,Jiaji Shen,Ning Jia,Xianhui Liu,Weidong Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: B2PD (Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation) is a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that addresses poor sample efficiency and unstable learning in online RL by using action-value priors to guide a CVAE in generating high-quality behavior support sets, which are then distilled into the agent to reduce exploration inefficiency and enable stable policy optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online RL algorithms suffer from poor sample efficiency and unstable learning dynamics due to critic estimation errors exacerbated by greedy policy updates. Existing behavior-prior methods rely on offline pre-training with limited-quality datasets, and the absence of expert trajectories significantly impairs online policy learning.

Method: B2PD uses action-value priors to guide a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) in generating high-value behavior support sets. The resulting expert behavior priors are distilled into the agent, establishing a bidirectional knowledge flow mechanism that reduces inefficient exploration and enables stable policy optimization.

Result: Empirical evaluations on both state-based and pixel-based tasks demonstrate that B2PD substantially improves sample efficiency while maintaining stable policy optimization. The method effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification through high-quality behavioral support.

Conclusion: Enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online learning effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification. Structured behavior priors can guide policy updates in a principled and sample-efficient manner, enabling RL agents to learn more effectively from limited data.

Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms frequently exhibit poor sample efficiency and unstable learning dynamics, stemming from systematic critic estimation errors that are exacerbated by greedy policy updates. Existing behavior-prior reinforcement learning methods attempt to alleviate this issue by relying on offline pre-training to learn behavior models from fixed datasets and using policy priors to constrain online policy updates. However, the limited quality of offline datasets often hinders the ability to provide high-value policies that can effectively guide policy updates. The absence of expert trajectories significantly impairs online policy learning, leading to low sample efficiency and suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we depart from conventional behavior prior approaches and propose a Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation (B2PD) algorithm. B2PD leverages action-value priors to guide a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) in generating a high-value behavior support set. The resulting expert behavior priors are further distilled into the agent, effectively reducing inefficient exploration and enabling stable policy optimization, while establishing a bidirectional knowledge flow mechanism. Empirical evaluations on both state- and pixel-based tasks verify that B2PD substantially improves sample efficiency while maintaining stable policy optimization. More broadly, this work shows that enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online learning effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification, enabling structured behavior priors to guide policy updates in a principled and sample-efficient manner.

</details>


### [183] [Placement Is Free, Composition Is Not: The Latin Square as a Provably-Balanced Construction for Heterogeneous Sequence-Mixer Stacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20269)
*Taebong Kim,Youngsik Hong,Minsik Kim,Sunyoung Choi,Jaewon Jang,Minseo Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the convention of using the same attention mechanism at every Transformer layer. The authors introduce Aether-7B-5Attn, a mixture-of-experts model with 7 different sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged in a 7×7 Latin square across 49 layers. Experiments reveal that heterogeneous composition across depth matters more than specific placement—rearranging mechanisms only changes validation loss by 0.16%, while clustering into contiguous bands incurs 0.59% penalty and using homogeneous stack incurs 1.68% penalty (2.63% at larger scale).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The conventional design of repeating the same attention mechanism at every Transformer layer is largely untested convention rather than evidence-based design. The authors seek to determine whether performance depends on mechanism choice, placement, or both, and to isolate these factors through controlled experimentation.

Method: The authors introduce a Latin square experimental design where 7 sequence-mixing mechanisms are arranged in a 7×7 grid across 49 layers, ensuring each mechanism appears exactly once in each row and column. This eliminates placement confounds while guaranteeing balanced exposure. They also built a parameter-matched 4×4 Latin square proxy (700.9M parameters, 8 seeds per arm) and validated at 1.514B parameter scale.

Result: Key findings: (1) Rearranging mechanisms in a balanced periodic cycle only changes validation loss by 0.16%, indicating placement has minimal effect. (2) Clustering mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurs 0.59% penalty. (3) Replacing heterogeneous stack with homogeneous one incurs 1.68% penalty (2.63% at larger scale). (4) Removing SSM-family mechanism produces 3.20% degradation at larger scale.

Conclusion: Performance depends primarily on heterogeneous composition of sequence-mixing mechanisms distributed across depth, rather than any particular permutation. The exact placement of mechanisms within the stack is relatively unimportant, but having a diverse set of mechanisms matters substantially.

Abstract: Since GPT, most Transformers have repeated the same attention mechanism at every layer. Yet this design is largely a convention rather than a tested conclusion. When multiple sequence mixers are combined in one stack, improvements may arise from mechanism choice, placement, or both, making causal attribution difficult. We introduce Aether-7B-5Attn, a 6.59B-parameter mixture-of-experts model ($\approx$2.98B active) whose 49 layers contain seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged as a $7\times7$ Latin square. Because each mechanism appears exactly once in every row and column, the design guarantees balanced exposure across depth while eliminating placement confounds. To evaluate this principle, we build a parameter-matched proxy with four mechanisms arranged as a $4\times4$ Latin square over sixteen layers, matched to 700.9M parameters and trained with eight seeds per arm. The results reveal a clear dissociation. Rearranging a distributed heterogeneous stack into a balanced periodic cycle changes validation loss by only 0.16\%, indicating that exact placement has little effect. In contrast, clustering the same mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurs a 0.59\% penalty, while replacing the heterogeneous stack with a homogeneous one incurs a 1.68\% penalty. These results indicate that performance depends primarily on heterogeneous composition distributed across depth rather than on any particular permutation. We confirm this finding at 2.16$\times$ larger scale (1.514B parameters), where the homogeneous-stack penalty increases to 2.63\% and removing the SSM-family mechanism produces a 3.20\% degradation. We further report per-mechanism cost profiles, English and Korean evaluations, and a causal-safety audit of all 49 layers. We release model weights, training recipes, training code, logs, and architecture source code.

</details>


### [184] [Labeled Incidence Structures for Native Transformer Modeling of Text, Knowledge Graphs, and Hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20278)
*Mahesh Godavarti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Labeled Incidence Structures (LIS), a unified representation framework that encodes structured data (text, knowledge graphs, hypergraphs) as (content, role, relation instance) tuples without flattening, enabling standard transformers to process heterogeneous data types natively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches flatten structured data into token sequences, losing critical information about roles and relations. This loses the distinct roles elements play within relation instances and the structural relationships between data elements.

Method: The paper proposes encoding each endpoint as (x_d, s, e) where x_d is content, s is role/slot, and e is relation instance. Structural addresses are computed via A(s,e) = R_s R_e (composing slot and instance operators). The relative transport P_{j→i} = A_i^{-1} A_j provides role- and relation-aware attention without arbitrary sequence ordering.

Result: The paper characterizes conditions for unique, path-independent addresses. It proves in a controlled example that additive encodings (position + relation terms) cannot capture joint s-e dependencies. For persistent knowledge repositories, computing relation-instance operators from content yields storage-order-independent capacity bounds independent of repository size M.

Conclusion: LIS provides a principled framework for processing heterogeneous structured data with a single transformer architecture, where structural differences are handled by operators rather than architecture modifications. The approach addresses limitations of position encodings and storage-dependent identifiers in knowledge repositories.

Abstract: Text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs all have elements that play distinct roles within relation instances, structure that is lost when data is flattened into token sequences. We introduce labeled incidence structures (LIS), a uniform representation that encodes each endpoint as $(x_d, s, e)$: content $x_d$, a role or slot $s$, and the relation instance $e$ in which that role appears. Because every data type maps to the same $(x_d, s, e)$ representation without flattening, a single standard transformer can process them all natively, structural differences are carried entirely by the operators, not the architecture.
  LIS assigns a structural address to each endpoint by composing a slot operator and an instance operator, $A(s,e) = R_s R_e$. We characterize when this factorization gives every token a unique, path-independent address. When it does, the natural operator comparing endpoint $j$ to endpoint $i$ is the relative transport $P_{j\to i} = A_i^{-1} A_j$, which gives attention a role- and relation-aware inductive bias without imposing an arbitrary sequence order.
  Additive encodings of the form "position term plus relation term" can miss information that depends jointly on $s$ and $e$. We prove this in a controlled example family: when the journey operator is approximated by the sum of a position-only term and a relation-only term, the approximation cannot capture how position and relation combine, only their separate effects.
  We also analyze persistent knowledge repositories. Identifiers tied to storage locations make models sensitive to storage order, while freely learned identifiers can become harder to control as the repository size $M$ grows relative to the sample size $n$. Computing relation-instance operators from content avoids this storage-order issue and yields a capacity bound independent of $M$, under fixed architectural and Lipschitz assumptions.

</details>


### [185] [Personalising a Cross-User Surface Electromyography Encoder Under a Small Calibration Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20296)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how to best use limited calibration repetitions (5 for DB1, 4 for DB2 and DB5) to personalize a cross-user myoelectric interface. Four approaches were compared across 77 subjects: prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning consistently performed best, but a gradient-free prototypical rule achieved 52-78% of the benefit without requiring an optimizer or per-user weight copies, enabling personalization at device donning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Myoelectric interfaces require user calibration, but prior work focused on the quantity of calibration rather than how to use those calibration repetitions. The researchers sought to determine the optimal way to leverage limited labeled data for personalization.

Method: Four personalization approaches were tested using identical calibration budgets: prototypical adaptation (gradient-free), linear probes, scaled fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. Experiments were conducted across 77 subjects from three databases (DB1, DB2, DB5) with maximum budgets of 5, 4, and 4 repetitions respectively.

Result: Full fine-tuning achieved the highest accuracy at every budget level, with no exceptions across subject subsets. Critically, the gradient-free prototypical rule recovered 52-78% of the personalization benefit without requiring an optimizer or per-user model copies. The study also found that the common intuition that a good representation only needs a fresh classifier is incorrect for this task.

Conclusion: Personalization for myoelectric interfaces can be achieved at device donning time using a simple gradient-free prototypical approach, making it practical for wearable devices. The optimal method relative to a clinical per-user classifier depends on the specific database. Full fine-tuning remains the most accurate but requires more computational resources.

Abstract: A myoelectric interface needs calibration from the user before it will function. Earlier work has treated calibration as a quantity, but has not asked the question of what a device should do with the calibration repetitions once they have been collected. This paper views personalizing the cross-user encoder as a design decision with a cost. Four alternative approaches to using exactly the same labeled repetitions were tested from a single cross-user encoder per held-out subject. Prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning and full fine-tuning were tested at every budget up to the maximum each database allows, five repetitions on DB1 and four on DB2 and DB5. Comparing four ways to spend a small calibration budget across 77 subjects, full fine-tuning is the most accurate at every budget, consistently enough that there is no exception among subsets of subjects. The result which impacts how one might make an engineering decision however is that a gradient free prototypical rule recovers 52 to 78 per cent of its benefit with no optimiser and no per-user copy of the weights, which makes personalisation something a worn device can do at donning time. The widespread intuition that a good representation only needs a fresh classifier is incorrect here. How well each method may perform relative to a per-user classifier that would be fitted by a clinic will depend on the specific database.

</details>


### [186] [Intact-to-Amputee Transfer in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding: Training Source and Calibration Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20297)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses cross-user transfer learning in EMG-based prosthetic control. A montage-agnostic encoder was tested on 11 transradial amputees. Zero-shot transfer fails completely, but with 3 labeled repetitions, the encoder achieves 0.779 macro-F1 vs 0.589 for per-user classifiers. Training on intact subjects transfers better than on amputees, but combining both sources works best. The study identifies the boundary conditions where the encoder's performance advantage holds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current myoelectric pattern recognition systems require fresh labeled calibration data for each new user, limiting clinical practicality. Amputees are severely underrepresented in research (only ~1 in 6 studies). This work seeks to develop a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder that can generalize across individuals without requiring extensive per-user labeled data.

Method: A montage-agnostic cross-user encoder was trained on 40 intact-limb subjects and tested on 11 transradial amputees using a matched protocol. Experiments compared: (1) zero-shot transfer vs few-shot learning with varying labeled repetitions, (2) training on intact subjects vs amputees as source population, and (3) combined source pools. Performance was measured using macro F1 score.

Result: Zero-shot cross-population transfer failed entirely. With labeled data from new users, the encoder exceeded per-user classifiers by 0.190 macro F1 at three repetitions. With three labeled repetitions, the encoder achieved 0.779 macro-F1 vs 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on 40 intact subjects produced better transfer to new amputees than training on 10 amputees, and combining both sources yielded the best transfer performance. The hypothesis that amputee EMG is less separable held only after a few repetitions and with enriched source pool.

Conclusion: The proposed encoder requires some labeled data from the new user before decoding but substantially outperforms per-user classifiers when even few repetitions are available. Zero-shot transfer remains infeasible. The boundary of the proposed account is located: the advantage holds at multiple repetitions but fails at single-repetition budgets and when source population is poorly matched. This work identifies the critical conditions for successful cross-population transfer in prosthetic control.

Abstract: A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A systematic review of 1077 studies quantifies where the evidence is thin: amputees appear in about one in six. Here a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder is carried to eleven transradial amputees on a protocol matched to its intact-limb training data. Zero-shot cross-population transfer fails outright: the encoder requires labeled data from the new user before it begins decoding, and it then exceeds the per-user classifier a clinic would fit by 0.190 macro F1 at three repetitions and for every subject in the cohort. Given three labelled repetitions it reaches 0.779 macro-F1 against 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on forty intact subjects produces better transfers to a new amputee than training on ten other amputees, and combining the two produces better transfers than either individually. The prediction pre-registered for this study, which extends the encoder's baseline-strength account with the premise that amputee EMG is less separable, holds true only after a few repetitions become available and after enriching the source pool with additional amputees. At a single repetition, and at every budget under a source matched to the intact-limb comparison, it fails. Thus, it locates the boundary of the proposed account.

</details>


### [187] [A Learning Algorithm for Threshold Boolean Networks with Prescribed Fixed Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20298)
*Gonzalo A. Ruz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A learning algorithm for inferring threshold Boolean networks (TBNs) with prescribed fixed points using a custom differentiable loss function. Applied to Arabidopsis thaliana's FOS-GRN model, it achieves near-perfect reconstruction (8.53±0.90 correct fixed points, no spurious) outperforming Perceptron and Logistic Regression which introduce 8-31 spurious attractors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) with specific dynamical constraints (fixed points) is challenging. Standard methods like Perceptron and Logistic Regression can recover desired fixed points but introduce spurious attractors, limiting their utility for modeling biological systems.

Method: Custom differentiable loss function combining: (1) fixed point preservation, (2) spurious attractor penalty, (3) binary output encouragement, and (4) L1 regularization for sparsity. Applied to FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana.

Result: 5/30 runs achieved perfect reconstruction (10 fixed points, no spurious). Average: 8.53±0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. Standard methods recovered up to 10 fixed points but introduced 8-31 spurious attractors. Robust to λ up to 0.01.

Conclusion: The proposed algorithm effectively captures meaningful network dynamics under prescribed dynamical constraints, outperforming standard methods by eliminating spurious attractors while maintaining stability across regularization strengths.

Abstract: We present a learning algorithm for inferring threshold Boolean networks (TBNs) with a prescribed set of fixed points. The proposed method employs a custom differentiable loss function that jointly enforces fixed point preservation, penalizes spurious attractors, encourages binary outputs, and promotes sparsity through L1 regularization. Applied to the FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana, the approach achieved perfect reconstruction (i.e., all 10 desired fixed points and no spurious ones) in 5 out of 30 independent runs, recovering on average 8.53 $\pm$ 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. In contrast, standard methods such as the Perceptron and Logistic Regression recovered up to 10 fixed points but introduced between 8 and 31 spurious ones. An additional analysis varying the sparsity coefficient ($λ$) confirmed that the method's performance and the structural properties of the inferred networks remain robust within a practical range (up to 0.01) of regularization strengths. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of the proposed algorithm in capturing meaningful network dynamics under prescribed dynamical constraints.

</details>


### [188] [Improving Generalization and Robustness in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20300)
*Gong Gao,Weidong Zhao,Xianhui Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of overfitting and poor in-distribution generalization in offline reinforcement learning (ORL). It proposes BADA (Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation), which uses neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries for generating synthetic data that preserves the original data distribution. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ORL algorithms overfit the training dataset and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness when deployed to real environments. Existing regularization techniques from computer vision are insufficient due to the high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to distributional shifts.

Method: The paper theoretically analyzes error bounds of behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation. Based on the insight that error scales positively correlated with state distance, BADA is proposed, which leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries for generating synthetic data that preserves the original data distribution.

Result: In qualitative studies, BADA generates mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness while accurately reconstructing multimodal value distributions. In extensive experiments on limited offline datasets, BADA achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.

Conclusion: BADA effectively addresses the overfitting and generalization issues in ORL by using boundary-aware data augmentation, providing a theoretically grounded and empirically validated approach for improving offline reinforcement learning performance.

Abstract: Current offline reinforcement learning (ORL) algorithms tend to overfit the training dataset and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness performance when deployed to real environments, thus compromising their effectiveness. Existing methods typically enhance in-distribution generalization and robustness by leveraging regularization techniques widely used in computer vision. However, due to the high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to distributional shifts, these methods still suffer from notable limitations in in-distribution generalization and robustness, making it difficult to achieve stable performance in complex environments. To address this issue, we theoretically analyze the error bounds of the behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation, revealing that the error scales positively correlated with the distance between states. Based on this insight, we propose a method called $\bf{B}$oundary-$\bf{A}$ware $\bf{D}$ata $\bf{A}$ugmentation (BADA), which leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, enabling the generation of synthetic data that more faithfully preserves the original data distribution. We first conduct qualitative studies in a toy environment, showing that BADA generates mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness while accurately reconstructing multimodal value distributions. Extensive experiments on limited offline datasets further demonstrate that BADA attains state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.

</details>


### [189] [Hypernetwork-Parameterized Spatially Adaptive Neural Operators for PDE Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20309)
*Jiaquan Zhang,Chaoning Zhang,Shuxu Chen,Meng Ye,Xiaofeng Zhang,Qiang He,Weifeng Huang,Guoqing Wang,Yang Yang,Caiyan Qin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SANO (Spatially Adaptive Neural Operator) is a neural operator method that replaces spatially shared parameterization with a spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters for solving heterogeneous PDEs. It uses Fourier-encoded coordinates, a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork, and a Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism for local interpolation and coupling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural operators and hypernetwork-based methods use spatially shared update rules, which underfit boundaries and high-gradient regions in spatially heterogeneous PDEs. These localized errors accumulate during autoregressive rollout, degrading prediction accuracy.

Method: SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. The Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators while allowing spatial variation. Partition-of-unity weights assemble overlapping local predictions.

Result: SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines on one-, two-, and three-dimensional PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks.

Conclusion: SANO successfully addresses the limitation of spatially shared parameterization in neural operators by introducing spatially adaptive operator parameters, achieving superior performance across various PDE benchmarks.

Abstract: Spatially heterogeneous partial differential equations (PDEs) exhibit location-dependent dynamics arising from variations in geometry and physical coefficients. Existing neural operators improve localized modeling through multiscale features, attention mechanisms, or domain decomposition, yet their update rules often remain spatially shared. Hypernetwork-based methods adapt parameters across PDE instances but typically generate only one global parameterization per instance. Consequently, shared operators may underfit boundaries and high-gradient regions, with these localized errors accumulating during autoregressive rollout. We propose a spatially adaptive neural operator (SANO), which replaces this spatially shared parameterization with a spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters. SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. A Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators while allowing their update rules to vary across space, and partition-of-unity weights assemble the overlapping local predictions. Experiments on one-, two-, and three-dimensional PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks show that SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines.

</details>


### [190] [ZeroHAT: Behavior-Conditioned Zero-Shot Human Activity Trace Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20310)
*Rongchao Xu,Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZeroHAT is a zero-shot framework for generating synthetic human activity traces (HATs) for target regions where real data is unavailable, by transferring behavioral patterns from source regions using publicly available contextual information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key problem is that large-scale HATs are difficult to access due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. Existing synthetic HAT generation methods require real data from the same region, making them infeasible for regions without available real HATs. This creates a gap for many regions that lack such data.

Method: ZeroHAT consists of three novel components: (1) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor; (2) a cross-region behavioral cloning module; and (3) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module. The framework transfers behavioral patterns learned from source regions and adapts them using publicly available contextual information about the target region.

Result: ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions in a ten-city benchmark evaluation.

Conclusion: ZeroHAT successfully enables zero-shot synthetic HAT generation for target regions without real data, outperforming existing baselines by significant margins in both downstream utility and fidelity metrics.

Abstract: Human activity traces record individuals' timestamped visits to points of interest and are essential for applications such as mobility prediction and urban simulation. However, accessing large-scale HATs is challenging due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. Synthetic HAT generation offers a promising way to make such data available and has attracted growing interest from both industry and academia. Although many efforts have been devoted to this topic, most of them rely on real data from a region to generate synthetic data for the same region, which is infeasible for the many regions where real HATs are unavailable. To fill this gap, we propose ZeroHAT, a behavior-conditioned framework that generates synthetic HATs for a target region in a zero-shot manner by transferring behavioral patterns learned from real HATs in source regions and adapting them with publicly available contextual information about the target region. ZeroHAT has three key novel components: (i) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor; (ii) a cross-region behavioral cloning module; and (iii) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module. We evaluate ZeroHAT on a ten-city benchmark, where extensive experiments show that ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions.

</details>


### [191] [EviRec: Continual Evidence Learning for Dual Cold-Start POI Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20313)
*Rongchao Xu,Lin Jiang,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses continual dual cold-start POI recommendation, where both users and POIs are dynamically changing. The authors propose EviRec, a framework that estimates historical evidence reliability for each candidate POI using three complementary views: matching (recent mobility profile), transition-memory (repeated routines), and lifecycle (candidate maturity). A key innovation is the reliability gate that adaptively routes between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence based on observation state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing POI recommendation methods assume a fixed user population and POI catalog, which is unrealistic. Through large-scale analysis of 10 U.S. cities, the authors identify significant POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory, necessitating the study of continual dual cold-start POI recommendation.

Method: EviRec uses three complementary scoring views: (1) Matching view based on user's recent mobility profile, (2) Transition-memory view capturing repeated mobility routines, and (3) Lifecycle view reflecting candidate maturity. The system applies a reliability gate that qualifies evidence using each candidate's observation state, adaptively routing between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence. Evaluation was conducted on a full-year, five-city dataset with 30,000+ users and 684,200 trajectories.

Result: EviRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with the largest gains on cold-start queries. Specifically, EviRec improves NDCG@10 by 20.4% on Dual-New cases (new user, new POI) over the strongest baseline. In-depth analyses confirm the gains primarily come from candidate-specific reliability gating while preserving previously learned mobility routines.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that addressing dynamic user and POI populations is crucial for POI recommendation. EviRec's candidate-specific reliability gating effectively handles the dual cold-start problem by distinguishing between irrelevance and insufficient observation, achieving significant improvements especially in cold-start scenarios.

Abstract: Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation is a core task in location-based services, yet most existing methods assume a fixed user population and POI catalog. Through a large-scale data-driven analysis of 10 U.S. cities, we identify substantial POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory, motivating the study of continual dual cold-start POI recommendation. To address this setting, we propose EviRec, a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates how much historical evidence should be trusted separately for each candidate POI. EviRec scores each visible candidate from three complementary views: a matching view based on the user's recent mobility profile, a transition-memory view that captures repeated mobility routines, and a lifecycle view that reflects candidate maturity. Because a near-zero transition score may indicate either irrelevance or insufficient observation, EviRec qualifies the evidence using each candidate's observation state and applies a reliability gate to adaptively route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence. We evaluate EviRec on a full-year, five-city POI check-in dataset containing more than 30,000 users and 684,200 trajectories. Experimental results show that EviRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with the largest gains concentrated on cold-start queries. In particular, EviRec improves NDCG@10 by 20.4\% on Dual-New cases over the strongest baseline. In-depth analyses further confirm that these gains arise primarily from candidate-specific reliability gating while largely preserving previously learned mobility routines.

</details>


### [192] [Sharp Reconstruction Bounds for Autoencoders Using the Same Forward Map](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20333)
*Patricia Medina,Hy P. G. Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies reconstruction error bounds in autoencoders that apply the same forward map before and after zero-masking observed coordinates. For odd input/hidden dimensions d≥3 with Jacobian singular values in [m,M], the authors derive a sharp bound on uniform reconstruction-derivative error: max{1-M(M-m)/2, 0}. They validate this theoretically with affine maps and translated radial rotations, then test predictions on a large LiDAR forest scan dataset (798,452 points), finding the theoretical bound captures ~84% of actual training error at scale 0.05.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand the fundamental limits of reconstruction in autoencoders when coordinates are zeroed out (a form of masking/compression). The authors seek theoretical bounds on reconstruction error that apply across different network architectures and depths, and to verify these bounds empirically on real-world 3D point cloud data.

Method: The authors use mathematical analysis of diffeomorphisms (smooth, invertible mappings with smooth inverses) to derive bounds on reconstruction-derivative error. They consider orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with Jacobian singular values bounded in [m,M]. They test predictions empirically on terrestrial LiDAR forest scan data across different spatial regions, depths, and random seeds, comparing theoretical bounds to normalized training errors.

Result: The main theoretical result is that the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is max{1-M(M-m)/2, 0}, with affine maps achieving this bound at every depth. A translated radial rotation can exactly reconstruct any prescribed ball with singular values arbitrarily close to 1. Empirically, at input scale 0.05, the mean theoretical bound (0.155) is about 84% of the mean normalized training error (0.185) across four spatial regions, two depths, and three seeds. Adding one hidden coordinate reduces mean reconstruction error below 6×10^-6.

Conclusion: The conclusion suggests that the derived theoretical bound provides a useful approximation (84%) of actual reconstruction error in practice. The bound is sharp and achievable by affine maps. The finding that adding one hidden coordinate dramatically reduces error (to < 6×10^-6) suggests the importance of sufficient hidden dimension for exact reconstruction. The work motivates additional conditions for finite-data bounds, as the translated radial rotation example shows certain constructions can achieve perfect reconstruction with singular values near 1.

Abstract: We study reconstruction in autoencoders that apply the same forward map before and after setting the observed coordinates to zero. For equal odd input and hidden dimensions $d\geq 3$, among orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms whose Jacobian singular values lie in $[m,M]$, we show that the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is $\max\{1-M(M-m)/2,0\}$, with affine maps attaining this sharp bound at every prescribed depth. A translated radial rotation can nevertheless reconstruct any prescribed ball exactly with singular values arbitrarily close to one, motivating additional conditions for a finite-data bound. We test this prediction on a 798,452-point terrestrial LiDAR forest scan. At input scale $0.05$, the mean theoretical bound is $0.155$, about $84\%$ of the mean normalized training error $0.185$ across four spatial regions, two depths, and three seeds. At this scale, adding one hidden coordinate reduces the mean reconstruction error below $6\times10^{-6}$.

</details>


### [193] [COMPASS: Ordered Clustered Routing at 100K Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20352)
*Ido Greenberg,Hugo Linsenmaier,Piotr Sielski,Shie Mannor,Alex Fender,Gal Chechik,Eli Meirom*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: COMPASS is an algorithm for solving the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP) that combines search with learning-accelerated routing through parallel sub-solvers. It outperforms alternatives, scales to 100K+ nodes, and achieves the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances (28.5K e-commerce nodes, 9x beyond prior ATSP benchmarks).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale routing often requires visiting clusters of nodes in a prescribed order (OCTSP). Existing methods optimize each cluster independently, missing non-local dependencies. Common large-scale routing solvers are also limited to coordinate inputs and cannot handle general distance matrices.

Method: COMPASS orchestrates parallel sub-solvers combining search with learning-accelerated routing. It exploits the clustered structure to achieve exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size. It accepts general distance matrices (not limited to coordinates).

Result: COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. It scales to 100K synthetic nodes and 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. This represents the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.

Conclusion: COMPASS provides a powerful approach to OCTSP with no quality ceiling—solutions keep improving with compute. It bridges the gap between large-scale routing practical needs and exact optimization capabilities.

Abstract: Large-scale routing often requires visiting clusters of nodes in a prescribed order, giving rise to the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP). Optimizing each cluster independently seems natural, but misses non-local dependencies. We introduce the COMPASS algorithm for OCTSP, which combines search with learning-accelerated routing by orchestrating parallel sub-solvers. COMPASS has no quality ceiling and its solutions keep improving with compute. It exploits the clustered structure, and can reach exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size. Empirically, COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. Unlike common large-scale routing solvers, COMPASS consumes general distance matrices and is not limited to coordinate inputs. We demonstrate scaling to 100K synthetic nodes and to 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. To our knowledge, the latter is the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.

</details>


### [194] [Minimax-Optimal Online Contract Design with Unrestricted Bounded Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20353)
*Rui Ai,David Simchi-Levi,Han Zhong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies repeated contract design where a principal observes outcomes but not the underlying actions. It establishes that the minimax regret over T rounds scales as T^(m/(m+1)) (up to log factors) for m ≥ 2 outcome states. The upper bound works with arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, while the lower bound shows each additional contractible outcome increases learning costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem arises because the principal cannot observe agent actions directly, only outcomes. Standard payment schemes may lead to discontinuous expected profits, making contract design challenging. The goal is to understand the fundamental learning complexity in repeated principal-agent relationships.

Method: The key methods include: (1) effective-dimension reduction to normalize benchmarks without shift-invariant tie-breaking, (2) revealed preference analysis yielding a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates, (3) a Lipschitz parametrization learning policy using only observed outcome categories, and (4) a lower-bound construction accounting for incentive losses across outcome dimensions.

Result: The minimax regret is of order T^(m/(m+1)) for every fixed number m ≥ 2 of outcomes, up to logarithmic factors. The upper bound holds for arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity without smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions. Each additional contractible outcome creates a precise increase in worst-case learning cost.

Conclusion: The regret rate T^(m/(m+1)) is tight and unavoidable. Learning in repeated contract design is fundamentally harder with more outcome dimensions, with a precise tradeoff between the number of outcomes and the learning rate.

Abstract: We study repeated contract design when a principal observes outcomes but not the actions that generate them. The principal may use any bounded outcome-contingent payment vector, and the agent's best response can make expected profit discontinuous in those payments. For every fixed number $m\ge2$ of outcomes, the minimax regret over $T$ rounds is of order $T^{m/(m+1)}$, up to logarithmic factors. The upper bound allows arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, without smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions. Its key is an effective-dimension reduction that the benchmark can be normalized even when fixed tie-breaking is not shift invariant, after which revealed preference yields a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates. A learning policy built on a Lipschitz parametrization of this map attains the rate using only observed outcome categories. The lower-bound construction accounts for how incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions. It shows that each additional contractible outcome creates a precise and unavoidable increase in the worst-case cost of learning.

</details>


### [195] [Learning Principal-Agent Contracts for Equitable Smallholder Carbon Farming under Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20404)
*Rishi Bharadwaj,Yadati Narahari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reveals that profit-maximizing carbon aggregators actually amplify the exclusion of smallholder farmers from carbon farming programs, achieving only 8.2% adoption on smallholdings versus 87.7% on large farms. The key driver is the per-hectare Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) costs, which decrease as farm size increases, causing the aggregators' pooled contracts to compound this disparity rather than offset it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While agricultural soils represent a major untapped carbon sink and smallholder farmers dominate agriculture in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, real-world carbon programs largely fail to reach these smallholders. This study addresses this critical gap through the lens of contract design.

Method: The authors formulate the evolving contracting problem as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic profit-maximizing contract. They analyze the aggregator's performance under various conditions, including a counterfactual with area-proportional MRV costs.

Result: Profit-maximizing aggregators amplify smallholder exclusion: 87.7% achievable adoption on large farms vs only 8.2% on smallholdings. Per-hectare MRV costs fall as farm size rises, and the pooling contract compounds this gradient. A counterfactual with purely area-proportional MRV costs eliminates this disparity.

Conclusion: Policy and contract design should focus on making MRV costs area-proportional to open carbon income to smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale.

Abstract: Agricultural soils are a major untapped carbon sink. Carbon farming is emerging as a promising practice for tapping this potential. Smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture across South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, are key to scaling climate mitigation via carbon farming. It is ironic that real-world carbon programs largely fail to reach them. We study this important gap through the lens of contract design. An aggregator offers a single pooled contract to a heterogeneous population of smallholder farmers who have private adoption costs (adverse selection) and exert unobserved effort (moral hazard), with agronomic outcomes evolving over multiple seasons. We formulate this evolving contracting problem as a POMDP and use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic profit-maximising contract. We analyse the performance of the aggregator under various conditions. We find that a profit-maximising aggregator does not merely inherit the exclusion of smallholders, it amplifies it. On large farms the aggregator realises 87.7% of achievable adoption, against only 8.2% on smallholdings. Per-hectare Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) costs fall as farm size rises, and the aggregator's pooling contract compounds this gradient rather than offsetting it. A counterfactual that makes MRV costs purely area-proportional eliminates this disparity. Our results and simulation can guide contract and policy design that opens carbon income to smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale.

</details>


### [196] [The Bias of Nonlinear Two-Time-scale Stochastic Approximation under Constant Step-Sizes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20409)
*Djamel Rassem Lamouri,Dorian Baudry,Nicolas Gast*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides finite-time analysis for nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) under constant step-sizes, establishing error bounds that scale as O(α + β²/α²) and revealing qualitative differences from linear TTSA settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale schemes remain difficult to obtain, especially under constant step-sizes. The authors aim to address this gap in the literature.

Method: Under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions, the authors upper bound the mean-squared error and the bias of both iterates around their limiting equilibria. The analysis separates the contributions of initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling.

Result: The bounds scale as O(α + β²/α²), which is proven to be tight when β ≤ α^(3/2). The analysis reveals qualitative differences from the linear TTSA setting, showing that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects absent in the linear case.

Conclusion: The study clarifies the origin of the β²/α² term and demonstrates that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects that are not present in linear TTSA settings.

Abstract: Two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) is a fundamental tool for analyzing coupled iterative algorithms in reinforcement learning, optimization, and stochastic control. However, finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale schemes remain difficult to obtain, especially under constant step-sizes. In this paper, we study nonlinear TTSA with step-sizes $α\ggβ$. Under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions, we upper bound the mean-squared error and the bias of both iterates around their limiting equilibria. Our bounds scale as $O(α+β^2/α^2)$, which we prove to be tight when $β\leα^{3/2}$. The analysis separates the contributions of initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling, thereby clarifying the origin of the $β^2/α^2$ term. Our results reveal qualitative differences from the linear TTSA setting previously studied, showing that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects that are absent in the linear case.

</details>


### [197] [SCGFM-ART: Amortized Relational Transport for Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20419)
*Xiaodong He,Xincheng Wang,Zhao Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCGFM-ART is a graph foundation model that learns transferable representations across heterogeneous graph domains by aligning graphs to a shared relational atlas via Amortized Relational Transport (ART), avoiding costly Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations while achieving state-of-the-art transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph foundation models face severe challenges when transferring knowledge across heterogeneous domains due to shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics. Existing methods either require expensive runtime alignment or fail to capture both global and local structural information in a unified manner.

Method: The framework uses Amortized Relational Transport (ART) to directly predict end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans, bypassing iterative Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations. Graphs are decomposed into: (1) global relational response coordinates relative to a relational atlas (universal coordinate system with finite relational landmarks), and (2) local node-to-role structural correspondences that project node attributes into a canonical role space.

Result: Achieved state-of-the-art transferability on 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks with superior average ranks of 2.29 and 1.14 respectively. The amortized formulation yields 44.2 to 85.1 times faster frozen target-domain inference. Topological perturbation analyses show node-role transport retains fine-grained structural nuances beyond global coordinates.

Conclusion: The proposed SCGFM-ART successfully addresses cross-domain graph representation learning by establishing a unified coordinate system through relational atlases and amortized transport plans. Theoretical bounds on coordinate fidelity, stability, and amortized coverage are established. The method demonstrates both superior transferability and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations across severely heterogeneous graph domains. However, severe domain shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics impede the construction of a unified, domain-agnostic representation space. To address this, we propose SCGFM-ART, a structure-centric GFM framework that aligns arbitrary graphs onto a shared relational atlas via Amortized Relational Transport (ART). The relational atlas serves as a universal coordinate system defined by a finite set of relational landmarks (bases), while ART directly predicts reusable, end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans, bypassing costly runtime Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations. Under this formulation, SCGFM-ART decomposes a graph into a unified representation: globally via its relational response coordinates relative to the atlas, and locally via its node-to-role structural correspondences. These correspondences project disparate node attributes into a canonical role space, resolving structural and semantic heterogeneity within a singular alignment interface. Rigorously modeling graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces, we establish coordinate fidelity bounds, prove stability under predicted transport plans, and derive an amortized coverage bound that guarantees our learning objective tightly surrogates ideal relational coverage. Benchmarked across 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks, SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability, securing superior average ranks of 2.29 and 1.14, respectively. Topological perturbation analyses demonstrate that node-role transport retains fine-grained structural nuances beyond global coordinates. On real-world benchmarks, the amortized formulation yields 44.2 to 85.1 times faster frozen target-domain inference by avoiding iterative alignment at test time.

</details>


### [198] [Seismic Site Response Prediction from Sparse Observations Using Finite-Element-Pretrained Latent Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20451)
*Yi Zhu,Su Chen,Xiaojun Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLARE-T is a transfer learning framework that improves numerical site-response predictions by learning low-dimensional latent dynamics from dense finite-element simulations and calibrating them with limited field records. It was validated on a centrifuge test and Lotung vertical array, showing improved multi-depth acceleration histories and response spectra across different motion intensities and components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, but correcting these discrepancies is challenging due to limited records in both sensor coverage and number of events. There is a need to combine dense numerical simulation data with limited field observations to improve prediction accuracy.

Method: FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations. It trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into learned coordinates, then uses limited records to calibrate the dynamics. Each prediction is initialized with a short response window while the complete base motion drives the response.

Result: FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to original finite-element models. It reduced errors at every evaluated sensor for motions of different intensities and both horizontal components at Lotung. Two different Lotung source models with different constitutive parameters achieved comparable test-set accuracy, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration.

Conclusion: FLARE-T provides a data-efficient means of combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions. The framework successfully addresses the challenge of limited sensor coverage and event records in site-response modeling.

Abstract: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, yet correcting these discrepancies is difficult because records are limited in both sensor coverage and number of events. This study proposes the Transfer-Enabled Forced Latent Autoencoder for Response Equations (FLARE-T) to improve these predictions by learning and calibrating low-dimensional latent dynamics that connect the base acceleration input to acceleration outputs at multiple depths. FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations. It then trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into the learned coordinates and uses limited records to calibrate the dynamics within them. A short response window initializes each prediction, while the complete base motion drives the response. The framework was evaluated using a layered-soil centrifuge test and the Lotung field vertical array. Test-set results show that FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to the original finite-element models, reducing errors at every evaluated sensor for motions of different intensities and, at Lotung, for both horizontal components. Two Lotung source models with different constitutive parameters achieved comparable test-set accuracy, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration. FLARE-T therefore provides a data-efficient means of combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions.

</details>


### [199] [Training Neural Networks to Approach the Optimum Bayes Estimator in Dense Multi-Emitter Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20465)
*Yi Sun,Mona Sharifi,Muzna Yumman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural networks trained on synthesized frames can approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization in single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Achieve high-throughput large-field-of-view (large-FOV) super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM imaging.

Method: Train neural networks on synthesized frames to approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization.

Result: The trained neural networks can approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization.

Conclusion: This approach justifies future work on training neural networks to achieve high-throughput large-FOV super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM.

Abstract: We train neural networks on synthesized frames to approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization. The result justifies the future work on training neural networks to achieve high-throughput large-FOV super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM.

</details>


### [200] [Deep Learning-Based Classification of Cognitive and Resting States Using Electroencephalography Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20467)
*K. A. Januka S. Fernando,Harshit Srivastava*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deep learning framework combining CNN and GRU is proposed to classify resting vs cognitive states (math, memory, music tasks) from EEG signals, achieving accuracies of 76-83%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG provides non-intrusive brain monitoring for resting and cognitive states, while deep learning enables automatic pattern extraction from complex EEG data. The study aims to distinguish resting from cognitive states using deep learning methodologies.

Method: CNN-GRU architecture for EEG feature extraction, time-frequency analysis, comparison with conventional deep learning and machine learning classifiers including 2D-Net architecture.

Result: Achieved accuracies of 83.177% for resting-vs-mathematical task, 76.107% for resting-vs-memory task, and 83.432% for resting-vs-music task classification.

Conclusion: Integrating signal processing with deep learning methodologies is effective for discriminating resting from cognitive states using EEG signals.

Abstract: The categorization of cognitive and resting states derived from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is crucial for comprehending fluctuations in brain activity linked to various mental states. EEG provides a non-intrusive approach for documenting brain function in both resting and task-oriented cognitive conditions, whilst deep learning techniques enable the automatic extraction of significant patterns from intricate EEG data. This study presents a deep learning framework to distinguish between resting and cognitive states through EEG records. The proposed framework integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) stacked with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for the extraction of features from EEG signals. Time-frequency analysis is conducted to explore the salient aspects of signals, and the derived features are then assessed utilizing conventional deep learning and machine learning classifiers, including the suggested 2D-Net architecture. The proposed approach and feature extraction strategy outperform the evaluated comparative methods, achieving accuracies of 83.177% for resting-versus-mathematical task classification, 76.107% for resting-versus-memory task classification, and 83.432% for resting-versus-music task classification. The findings illustrate the efficacy of integrating signal processing with deep learning methodologies to discriminate resting from cognitive states utilizing EEG signals.

</details>


### [201] [Distributionally Robust Federated Learning with Multi-Source Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20501)
*Yingzhu Liu,Zhongkui Li,Pengcheng You,Ashish Cherukuri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses robustness in federated learning by handling two sources of uncertainty: (1) cross-client mixture uncertainty due to unknown data distributions across clients, and (2) within-client distributional ambiguity from finite sample estimates. The authors propose constructing a global ambiguity set as a union of local ambiguity sets, which allows client-specific ambiguity radii and enables separable reformulation. They provide high-probability out-of-sample guarantees and develop a convergent federated algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In federated learning, data distributions differ across clients and the true mixture is often unknown. Existing worst-case mixture approaches assume accurate client-wise distribution estimates, but these estimates are unreliable with finite samples. The paper aims to handle both cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity simultaneously.

Method: The authors construct a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets. This approach allows client-specific ambiguity radii and admits a client-wise separable reformulation. They develop a federated algorithm for a penalty-based reformulation to solve the optimization problem.

Result: The proposed method provides a high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantee. The federated algorithm converges under milder regularity conditions compared to existing methods. Simulations demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness.

Conclusion: The paper successfully addresses both sources of uncertainty in federated learning through the proposed ambiguity set construction. The theoretical guarantees and convergence properties provide strong foundations for robust federated learning in practical settings with limited data at each client.

Abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model from private client data. In practice, data-generating distributions may differ, and the true mixture across clients is often unknown, making the underlying group distribution difficult to specify. Existing approaches address cross-client mixture uncertainty by optimizing against the worst-case mixture, yet assume accurate client-wise distribution estimates. However, these estimates can be unreliable when based on finite samples. To handle both cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity, we construct a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets. The construction allows client-specific ambiguity radii and admits a client-wise separable reformulation. Leveraging this structure, we establish a high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantee. We further develop a federated algorithm for a penalty-based reformulation and prove its convergence under milder regularity conditions. Simulations validate the algorithm's effectiveness.

</details>


### [202] [Radio Frequency Detection and Classification of Microplastics in Water](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20507)
*Jaden Tolbert,Md Saiful Islam,Pingshan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A machine learning-assisted radio-frequency dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform enables rapid, label-free detection and classification of 8 types of 10 μm microplastic particles in aqueous environments, achieving macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall exceeding 0.71.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing abundance of micro- and nano-plastic particles (MPs/NPs) as environmental contaminants creates an urgent need for rapid, label-free detection methods, as conventional optical and spectroscopic techniques become challenging for small particle sizes due to limited throughput and complex sample preparation.

Method: The researchers developed an ML-assisted RF dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform that characterizes MP particles suspended in deionized water by measuring RF scattering parameters (S-parameters) at four frequencies spanning 0.2-9 GHz. Supervised ML models were trained for material classification, including identification of MPs in mixed samples and saline-water environments.

Result: For eight MP classes suspended in DI water, the method achieved macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall values exceeding 0.71. PET classification performance was largely maintained in saline carrier media containing 3.3% and 6.6% sea salt.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments. Future work will focus on improving classification performance through enhanced RF calibration, increased spectral coverage, larger training datasets, and validation using environmentally aged and biologically contaminated microplastics.

Abstract: Micro- and nano-plastic particles (MPs/NPs) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants whose increasing abundance and potential health impacts have created an urgent need for rapid, label-free detection methods. As particle size decreases to the low-micrometer range, conventional optical and spectroscopic techniques become increasingly challenging because of limited throughput and/or complex sample preparation. In this work, we present a machine learning (ML)-assisted radio-frequency (RF) dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform for the label-free detection and classification of MPs. Eight types of $ 10 $ μm nominal-diameter MP particles suspended in deionized (DI) water were characterized at four frequencies spanning $ 0.2\text{-}9\text{ GHz} $. The measured alterations in RF scattering parameters (S-parameters), referenced to the carrier medium, were used to train supervised ML models for material classification, including the identification of MPs in mixed samples and saline-water environments. For eight MP classes suspended in DI water, the proposed method achieved macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall values exceeding $ 0.71 $. Furthermore, PET classification performance was largely maintained in saline carrier media containing $3.3\% $ and $ 6.6\% $ sea salt. These results demonstrate the feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments. Future work will focus on improving classification performance through enhanced RF calibration, increased spectral coverage, larger training datasets, and validation using environmentally aged and biologically contaminated microplastics.

</details>


### [203] [When EOS Tokens Disagree: Understanding Length Inflation in On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20511)
*Yuxiao Yang,Tianrun Yu,Shangzhe Li,Kaixiang Zhao,Xuchao Zhang,Chetan Bansal,Huaxiu Yao,Taylor W. Killian,Weitong Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses length inflation in on-policy distillation (OPD), where student models generate excessively long responses. The authors identify "termination-token mismatch" between base students and post-trained teachers as a key cause, where different models place stopping probability on different EOS tokens despite having identical declared stopping sets. The solution involves treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a practical problem in on-policy distillation where student responses become excessively long and can exhaust generation budgets, which is a significant issue in practical deployment of distilled models.

Method: The authors conducted experiments across three model families (Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma), analyzing termination behavior at different K2-Horizon training stages. They tested whether aligning decoding stopping sets alone is sufficient, and proposed treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action.

Result: Aligning the decoding stopping set alone is insufficient to fix the length inflation problem. However, treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action substantially mitigates mismatch-induced length inflation across all three model families. The stage-wise analysis reveals that termination preferences shift substantially during training, and a distinct length inflation persists late in OPD runs beyond termination alignment.

Conclusion: Termination mismatch is an important but not exhaustive source of OPD length dynamics. The proposed termination-handling corrections effectively mitigate the problem, and the implementation is released.

Abstract: We study length inflation in on-policy distillation (OPD), where student responses can become excessively long and even exhaust the generation budget. We identify \emph{termination-token mismatch} between base students and post-trained teachers as an important source of this behavior. Across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma, the two models can place their stopping probability on different EOS tokens, even when their declared stopping sets are identical. This mismatch can suppress the student's preferred termination action without reliably transferring the teacher-preferred alternative. We show that aligning the decoding stopping set alone is insufficient, while treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action substantially mitigates mismatch-induced length inflation across all three model families. To further understand how termination behavior evolves over training, we study OPD across different K2-Horizon training stages. This stage-wise analysis shows that termination preferences can shift substantially during training, while also revealing a distinct length inflation late in the OPD run that persists beyond termination alignment. Together, these results identify termination mismatch as an important, but not exhaustive, source of OPD length dynamics. We release an implementation incorporating the proposed termination-handling corrections.

</details>


### [204] [Parallelism, critical windows, and separations among diffusion language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20539)
*Sitan Chen,Liye Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a theoretical comparison of parallelism capabilities across three major diffusion LLM paradigms: masked, uniform, and Gaussian diffusion. It proves that uniform and Gaussian diffusion can achieve better parallelism than masked diffusion for certain distributions, challenging the intuition that masked diffusion is easier to parallelize.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite diffusion large language models (dLLMs) being marketed on their parallelism advantage over autoregressive models, there has been limited principled understanding of how different diffusion paradigms (masked, uniform, Gaussian) compare in their ability to generate text efficiently in parallel.

Method: The authors use information-theoretic analysis, specifically examining the dual total correlation of underlying distributions as a measure of intrinsic complexity. They analyze random empirical measures and critical windows in sampling processes for all three paradigms.

Result: 1) Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample in a number of forward passes scaling with the dual total correlation of the underlying distribution, which can be much smaller than context length. 2) For random empirical measures, Θ(√d) forward passes are necessary and sufficient for uniform/Gaussian diffusion, while masked diffusion requires Ω(d) passes with approximate score oracles. 3) This establishes the first provable separation between the three paradigms, with masked diffusion actually being harder to parallelize due to narrower critical windows.

Conclusion: Contrary to popular intuition that masked diffusion is harder to parallelize because it must commit to token values, the parallelism advantage of uniform and Gaussian diffusion over masked diffusion stems from the fact that masked diffusion's critical windows are asymptotically narrower. This provides the first rigorous theoretical separation between the three leading dLLM paradigms.

Abstract: A popular selling point of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) is their capacity for parallelism: the ability to generate sequences of text far more efficiently than autoregressive models, which require one forward pass per token. Yet among the many competing paradigms for dLLMs, from masked to uniform to Gaussian diffusion, principled understanding of how these different proposals compare in parallelism remains limited. In this work, we initiate a fine-grained comparison of the capacity for parallelism among these three leading approaches and prove the following:
  - Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample in a number of forward passes which scales with the dual total correlation of the underlying distribution, a measure of intrinsic complexity which can be much smaller than the context length. Previously, it was only known how to achieve this using masked diffusion.
