Abstract: AI applications have shifted from single, monolithic foundation models (FM) to compound agentic systems. Yet today's stacks remain fragmented: even as protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) ease tool/agent connectivity, each framework embeds an implicit runtime for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails, making behavior non-portable and governance brittle. It mirrors computing before operating systems, when every program re-implemented basic services. This position paper argues that the field now needs a Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS) -- a system layer that virtualizes FM interactions analogous to how virtual machines abstract physical hardware, giving applications the illusion of dedicated, trustworthy FM instances with effectively unbounded capabilities. Internally, the FMOS orchestrates knowledge across memory tiers, model selection and resource allocation, and verification and policy enforcement. Like the human brain switching between fast intuition and slow deliberation, the FMOS learns when to intervene and when to let inference proceed directly and continuously adapting its policies based on operational experience.

</details>


### [241] [What Do Current Systematic Generalization Tasks Miss? A Reasoning-Centered Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19212)
*Chengwen Qi,Deheng Ye,Yatao Bian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TranSGrid is a new testbed that combines deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning to study systematic generalization in neural models. Experiments with seven Transformers show significant performance drops on TranSGrid compared to held-out test sets (79.6% → 55.3% for the largest model), revealing that existing simplified tasks underestimate true systematic generalization capabilities by reducing either inductive or abductive demands.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing studies on systematic generalization rely on simplifications (linear action composition, productivity-based tests, action-explicit goals) that make the task easier but omit essential aspects of human intelligence. A reasoning-centered approach is needed to capture what these simplifications miss.

Method: The authors introduce TranSGrid, a unified task integrating deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning. They test seven Transformer models on 4,800 instances and conduct ablation studies by reintroducing two simplifications: (1) near-linear action composition and (2) action-explicit goals.

Result: All models perform significantly worse on TranSGrid than on held-out test sets. The largest model achieves 79.6% on test set but only 55.3% on TranSGrid (15.8% on hardest subset). The performance gap persists within training length range, showing productivity alone is insufficient. When either simplification is reintroduced, solve rates return to test set levels, demonstrating that each simplification alone reduces TranSGrid to an ordinary held-out test.

Conclusion: Existing tasks reduce either inductive or abductive demands, underestimating systematic generalization. Comprehensively measuring systematic generalization requires tasks involving all three forms of reasoning (deductive, inductive, and abductive).

Abstract: Systematic generalization, the ability to solve novel problems by recombining known atomic elements, is central to human intelligence but difficult to study rigorously under controlled settings. Existing studies therefore rely on simplifications such as approximately linear action composition, productivity-based tests, and action-explicit goals, which make systematic generalization easier to study but omit some essential aspects of this capability. To characterize what these simplifications miss, we adopt a reasoning-centered lens and introduce TranSGrid, a testbed that brings deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning together within a unified task. Experiments with seven Transformers on 4,800 TranSGrid instances show that all models perform much worse on TranSGrid than on a held-out test set: the largest model solves 79.6% of the test set, but only 55.3% of TranSGrid and 15.8% of the hardest subset. The gap remains within the training length range, showing that productivity alone is not sufficient to evaluate systematic generalization. Additionally, we reintroduce the other two simplifications into TranSGrid: one variant makes actions compose almost linearly (reducing the inductive demand), the other makes goals action-explicit (reducing the abductive one). In both, solve rates return to roughly the test set level, showing that either simplification alone is enough to reduce TranSGrid to an ordinary held-out test set. Together, our results show that existing tasks reduce either or both of the inductive and abductive demands, and that comprehensively measuring systematic generalization requires a task that involves all three forms of reasoning.

</details>


### [242] [Characterizing Web Search by Conversational LLM Agents: From Search Decisions and Strategies to Results and Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19244)
*Mahsa Amani,Seungeon Lee,Abhisek Dash,Asmaa El Fraihi,Yunah Jang,Elisabeth Kirsten,Qinyuan Wu,Krishna P. Gummadi,Manish Gupta,Abhilasha Ravichander,Muhammad Bilal Zafar,Soumi Das*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: First comprehensive study examining Web search behavior across four major conversational AI platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek), combining real-world user data with controlled API experiments. The study reveals significant variations in search invocation, query strategies, domain preferences, and response grounding quality across platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The end-to-end lifecycle of agentic search in conversational LLM agents remains poorly understood, despite increasing reliance on Web search. This study aims to fill this gap by providing the first systematic investigation of how different conversational platforms handle Web search.

Method: Combined in vivo (real-world user interactions) and in vitro (controlled experiments via API) approaches to study four major conversational platforms: ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and DeepSeek. Investigated four key dimensions: search invocation decisions, query formulation strategies, domain preferences in search results, and response transformation from search results.

Result: Web-search decisions vary substantially across platforms and models. More frequent search invocation does not necessarily improve response quality. Conversational agents employ different complex querying strategies. Platform-specific search engines show domain preferences in results. While responses are largely grounded in search results, some claims rely on uncited search results, raising attribution and reliability concerns.

Conclusion: Findings have important implications for designing future AI agents and Web search tools optimized for conversational retrieval. The study highlights the need for improved attribution mechanisms and better alignment between search frequency and response quality.

Abstract: Conversational LLM agents increasingly rely on Web search, yet the end-to-end lifecycle of agentic search remains poorly understood. We present the first study of Web search across four major conversational platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and DeepSeek), combining real-world user interactions (invivo) with controlled experiments using the same platform's models by their APIs (invitro). We investigate the quality of agentic decisions to invoke Web search, their strategies to formulate queries, the potential domain preferences in the search results they receive, and the choices they make when transforming search results into grounded responses. We find that Web-search decisions vary substantially across platforms and models, while more frequent Web-search invocation does not necessarily yield better response quality. We further show that conversational agents employ different complex querying strategies and that platform specific search engines return search results from their preferred domains. Finally, although responses are largely grounded in search results, some claims rely on uncited search results, raising concerns about attribution and reliability. Our findings have important implications for the design of future AI agents and Web search tools optimized for conversational retrieval.

</details>


### [243] [Do AI Agents Understand Computer Architecture?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19387)
*Ambika Sharan,Grigory Chirkov,Soheil Abbasloo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents AutoTuring, a framework to measure whether understanding the meaning of hardware design parameters matters for AI agents. By giving the same agent the same accelerator design task twice—once with meaningful architectural knobs and simulator counters, once with anonymous variables—authors find that meaning improves performance by 12.3% on average while using 70.1% fewer simulator calls. However, structured critique can substitute for architectural knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations show that agents can improve hardware designs but cannot determine whether agents are reasoning about the machine or simply searching over knobs. This distinction matters because reasoning transfers to new architectures while search does not. The authors aim to isolate the value of "meaning" in agent hardware design.

Method: AutoTuring presents the same 15-dimensional accelerator design space twice to identical agents: once as named architectural knobs with semantic meaning (e.g., "L1 cache size" with simulator counters), once as anonymous variables on [0,1]. The evaluator, legal space, and reachable optima remain identical so only the meaning of the problem varies. Experiments used a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM benchmark on a modeled H200 accelerator.

Result: The architect agent (with meaning) beats the blind agent by 12.3% on average and achieves 5.4% improvement over a modeled H200 baseline. The architect required 70.1% fewer simulator calls. However, adding a critic loop to the blind agent recovers most of the performance gap, indicating architectural knowledge and structured critique act as substitutes rather than complements.

Conclusion: Meaning matters in agent hardware design but is not uniquely required—structured critique can partially substitute for architectural understanding. The contribution is the comparative methodology itself (five to six runs per condition), not the specific accelerator results. This framework provides a way to measure whether agents are reasoning about machines versus simply searching.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly asked to design hardware, and increasingly reported to succeed. Such reports establish that a design improved; they cannot establish why. An agent that improves an accelerator may be reasoning about the machine, or may be searching competently over knobs whose meaning it never recovers -- and only the first transfers to the next architecture. Existing evaluations cannot tell the two apart, because they vary the agent while holding the framing of the problem fixed. We do the opposite. AutoTuring hands the same agent the same 15-dimensional accelerator space twice: once as named architectural knobs with simulator counters, once as anonymous variables on [0,1], with the evaluator, the legal space and the reachable optima held identical, so that the only thing that varies is whether the problem means anything. The gap between the two is the measurement. On a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM basket, meaning pays: the architect beats a modeled H200 by 5.4% and its blind counterpart by 12.3% on average, with 70.1% fewer simulator calls. It does not pay uniquely: a critic loop recovers most of that gap for the blind agent and buys the architect nothing, so architectural knowledge and structured critique behave as substitutes rather than as complements. We report these as preliminary findings -- five to six runs per condition on a single modeled accelerator -- and take the comparison itself, not the accelerator, to be the contribution.

</details>


### [244] [MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19391)
*Albert Wu,Nicholas Roberts,Tzu-Heng Huang,Haoran Lin,Gil Friedman,Sungjun Cho,Gabriel Orlanski,Frederic Sala*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAGS is a multi-agent framework that uses Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation to generate executable programs with formal safety guarantees. It formalizes human-audited APIs, translates code to Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles back to executable code. Evaluated on 220 tasks (CUDA kernels, terminal scripts, robotic-arm tasks), achieving 100% success rate in producing programs with safety guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM coding agents generate complex programs at scale, making thorough human review difficult and raising safety/security risks. Existing approaches (fuzz testing, static analysis, LLM-as-a-Verifier) struggle to cover all edge cases, while traditional formal verification requires substantial manual specification and proof engineering.

Method: A unified multi-agent framework (MAGS) that: 1) Formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, 2) Translates generated code into Dafny (verification-aware IR), 3) Repairs violations using verifier feedback, 4) Compiles verified programs back into executable code.

Result: 100% success rate across 220 examples (100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, 20 robotic-arm tasks) in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Strong performance in independent safety and functional evaluations, with some failures when auto-formalized semantics don't fully capture target behavior.

Conclusion: MAGS demonstrates that formal verification can be integrated into LLM code generation workflows to provide machine-checkable safety guarantees. The approach is effective across diverse domains (GPU computing, system scripting, robotics), though limitations exist when formal specifications don't fully capture target behavior.

Abstract: LLM coding agents now generate complex programs at a scale that makes thorough human review increasingly difficult, raising the risk of safety and security failures. Common approaches, including fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-Verifier, can detect many failures but struggle to cover all possible edge cases. Formal verification addresses this by providing machine-checkable guarantees over specified properties, but traditionally demands substantial manual specification and proof engineering. We introduce a unified multi-agent framework, MAGS, that generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees, using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation where safety properties can be mechanically checked. MAGS formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles verified programs back into executable code. We evaluate MAGS on 100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, and 20 robotic-arm tasks. Across all 220 examples, it achieves a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations further show strong performance across all three domains, while revealing failures when the auto-formalized semantics do not fully capture the target behavior.

</details>


### [245] [Closed-World Resolution Against Tool Hallucination in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19425)
*Laxmipriya Ganesh Iyer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies and measures a critical blind spot in tool-augmented LLM agents: hallucinated tool calls (non-existent tools with invalid arguments). The authors develop a taxonomy (H1-H5 for single-registry, M1-M5 for MCP), prove that hallucination defense must precede gating, and benchmark 10 models across 2 surfaces, finding 322 hallucinations on traditional surfaces and 154 on MCP, with model scale providing no mitigation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-security methods (selection, gating) assume the called tool exists. Hallucinated tool calls bypass all defenses by construction since they reference non-existent tools. This is a structural blind spot that needs measurement and mitigation.

Method: 1) Developed a five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5)
2) Created "Resolution Rung" - a training-free resolver using registry membership + signature check
3) Proved hallucination defense must precede causal gates
4) Benchmarked 10 hosted models across 2 invocation surfaces (raw-JSON and structured)
5) Extended analysis to Model Context Protocol (MCP), developing second taxonomy (M1-M5)
6) Released Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) for standardized evaluation

Result: 1) Found 322 genuine hallucinations across 10 models; 34 on raw-JSON surface vs 3 on structured surface
2) Model scale does not help - 675B model performs similarly to 7-8B models
3) On live MCP surface: 154 hallucinations measured
4) Frontier models clean on single-registry surface produce hallucinations on MCP due to namespace collisions/shadowing from server merging
5) Identified one "irreducible residue" - borrowed arguments schema-indistinguishable from valid calls

Conclusion: Tool hallucination is a fundamental, structural problem distinct from existing tool-security concerns. Current defenses cannot address it because hallucinated calls bypass gates by definition. The authors provide taxonomies, measurement methodology, and a benchmark (HTB) to enable future research. The Resolution Rung serves as a reference point, though the irreducible residue indicates some hallucinations may be inherently undefendable against.

Abstract: Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents fail in a way no tool-selection or tool-security method addresses: they call tools that do not exist and pass arguments no schema declares. Existing defenses either pick the right tool (selection) or constrain what an agent may do with real tools (gating), both of which presuppose the emitted call refers to a real tool at all. We show this is a structural blind spot: a hallucinated call is by construction not a decision any gate made, so no gate can reject it. This paper is primarily a measurement and benchmark study. We give a five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5) and, as a reference point, the Resolution Rung: a training-free, closed-world resolver (registry membership plus a signature check) whose interest is where it must sit, not what it computes. We prove hallucination defense must precede any causal gate, and characterize the one irreducible residue (borrowed arguments schema-indistinguishable from a valid call). Across ten hosted models under two invocation surfaces we measure 322 genuine hallucinations; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on the unconstrained raw-JSON surface (34 vs. 3), and model scale does not help (a 675B model matches a 7-8B one). We then extend to the Model Context Protocol, where merging several servers into one namespace creates hallucination surfaces a single registry cannot express (a second taxonomy, M1-M5); on the live MCP surface we measure 154 hallucinations, including from frontier models that were clean on the single-registry surface, because collisions and shadowing are structural to the merge. We release the versioned Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) so any resolver is comparable across submissions.

</details>


### [246] [The syntax and semantics of goals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19448)
*David M. Abel,Mark K. Ho*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper argues for analyzing goals as compositional representations, drawing parallels between goal representations in cognitive/computer science and the syntax-semantics interface in linguistics and logic. The authors propose that examining the form and meaning of goals reveals a design space of different goal representations, with implications for understanding cognition-motivation interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to highlight a gap in how goals are conceptualized - specifically, the need to examine goal representations themselves (their form, meaning, and constraints) rather than just treating goals as fixed constraints on behavior. This perspective draws on parallels with linguistics and logic to frame foundational questions about goal representation expressivity and design.

Method: The paper uses a synthesis approach, reviewing and characterizing work on different goal representations to identify properties and axes of variation. The method is conceptual/theoretical rather than empirical.

Result: The paper presents a framework for understanding goals as occupying a "design space" with multiple dimensions of variation. Key axes include: (1) the expressivity of goal languages, (2) whether different representations capture the same behavior, and (3) the distinction between the form and meaning of goals.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that distinguishing the form and meaning of goals can: (1) elucidate implicit assumptions about goals, (2) inform the study of interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and (3) isolate axes of variation for different conceptions of goals. This provides a new lens for understanding goal representation in both cognitive science and AI.

Abstract: In both cognitive science and computer science, goals are conceptualized as cognitive states that flexibly combine with world knowledge to organize and specify purposeful behavior. In this way, goals are compositional representations whose content relates to rational behavior. We here draw attention to goals as representations and their content because it highlights a parallel with other areas in cognitive science - in particular, the syntax-semantics interface in linguistics and logic - while also foregrounding foundational questions about the expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations. For example, goals are typically taken as fixed and imposing constraints on desirable behaviors, but we can also identify constraints on goal representations themselves, such as whether a particular goal language is sufficiently expressive to capture behaviors of interest, or whether different goal representations capture the same behavior. Here, we synthesize work that aims to characterize the properties of different goal representations and suggest these are points of a broader design space. We close by discussing how distinguishing the form and meaning of goals can elucidate the implicit assumptions we make about goals, inform the study of interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and isolate axes of variation for different conceptions of goals.

</details>


### [247] [Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19465)
*Yu He,Yingxi Li,Yifei Wang,Ellen Vitercik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how post-training methods (like RL) affect language models' ability to perform compositional reasoning - combining learned skills in novel ways. The authors propose a dependency-graph framework with three levels of compositionality and discover a key asymmetry: training on decomposed skills doesn't transfer well to composed tasks, but the reverse transfer works better. They validate this using data-structure tasks and real-world tool-calling benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training data is limited, so models must generalize by composing learned skills. While RL has improved reasoning abilities, its effects on compositional reasoning are poorly understood. This gap motivates the formal study of compositional reasoning in post-trained LMs.

Method: 1) Proposed a dependency-graph framework formalizing three levels of compositionality
2) Used data-structure tasks as testbed (deterministic rewards, clear compositional structure)
3) Conducted experiments on length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to unseen skills
4) Performed pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks

Result: Discovered a consistent "decomposed-to-composed asymmetry": training on decomposed skills fails to transfer to composed tasks, while composed-task training transfers readily to decomposed tasks. This asymmetry extends to practical settings (tool-calling benchmarks).

Conclusion: The asymmetry suggests that learning composed tasks first may be more effective for building compositional reasoning. The framework provides a theoretical foundation for understanding compositional generalization, with implications for designing better post-training curricula for LMs.

Abstract: Compositional reasoning is critical for real-world problem solving: since training data is necessarily limited, models must generalize by composing learned skills in new ways. While post-training methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the reasoning abilities of language models (LMs), their effects on compositional reasoning remain less well understood. We propose a dependency-graph framework to formalize compositional reasoning, yielding three levels of compositionality with increasing complexity. Empirically, we instantiate this framework with data-structure tasks, which provide deterministic reward computation and clear compositional structure. We find a consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, whereas composed-task training transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks. We provide theoretical explanation for this asymmetry, and further evaluate compositional generalization under length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to tasks requiring unseen skills. Finally, we present a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks, showing preliminary evidence that the decomposed-to-composed asymmetry can extend to practical settings.

</details>


### [248] [Safety Beyond the Interface: Detecting Harm via Latent States in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19472)
*Alizishaan Khatri,Chiquita Prabhu,Omkar Neogi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes using lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) trained on LLaMA-3.1-8B internal activations to detect harmful prompts, achieving competitive performance with much larger guard models while significantly reducing latency and compute costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous systems rely on LLMs but safety guardrails introduce latency and compute overhead. Existing external guardrails cannot access the model's internal states, creating an assurance gap. The authors investigate whether the model itself knows when content is harmful.

Method: Extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. Evaluated on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0 datasets.

Result: Probes achieve F1 scores of 99% on WildJailbreak, 83% on Beavertails, and 84% on AEGIS 2.0, respectively competitive with guard models that are 1000x larger while cutting latency and compute costs.

Conclusion: Internal activation-based probes can effectively detect harmful prompts with minimal computational overhead, offering a promising solution for resource-constrained, time-critical deployments where traditional external guardrails are impractical.

Abstract: Autonomous systems increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) yet the safety infrastructure surrounding these models introduces latency and compute overhead. This limits utility in resource-constrained, time-critical deployments. Existing external guardrail models remain blind to the model's internal workings, creating a fundamental assurance gap. We ask: does the model already know when the content is harmful? We extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. Evaluated on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0, our probes achieve F1 scores of 99%, 83%, and 84%, respectively competitive with 1000x larger guard models while cutting latency and compute costs.

</details>


### [249] [QVAC Genesis III: A Large-Scale, High-Quality Open Synthetic STEM Corpus for Efficient Language Model Pre-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19513)
*Davide Vitabile,N. Ranjan,Akshay Nambiar,Kamal K. Gupta,Amril Nazir*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QVAC Genesis III is a 191.43B-token STEM-focused synthetic corpus for training small language models, addressing the lack of high-quality open-source STEM data for edge AI deployment. It uses a dual generation strategy with weak student model distillation and achieves state-of-the-art results on STEM benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-quality pre-training data is a critical bottleneck for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment with tight token budgets. The open ecosystem lacks STEM-focused synthetic datasets that deliver high per-token learning value efficiently for small models.

Method: QVAC Genesis III uses a dual generation strategy with targeted teacher distillation: (1) A weak edge-scale student model identifies failures, which are converted into corrective explanations; (2) Student successes are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices. The paper also introduces an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and tracks accuracy and answer validity.

Result: Controlled from-scratch ablations with 1.7B-parameter models show that QVAC Genesis III consistently outperforms both Cosmopedia-v2 and Cosmo-1B across ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM benchmarks. Results include up to +28.57% on ARC-E, +21.35% on ARC-C, and a Valid Answer Rate of up to 99.45%.

Conclusion: QVAC Genesis III successfully provides a large-scale, high-quality STEM-focused synthetic corpus that enables small models to achieve strong performance on educational and STEM benchmarks, addressing the gap in open-source training data for edge AI deployment.

Abstract: High-quality pre-training data is a critical bottleneck for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment where token budgets are tightly constrained. While major organizations train ever-larger models on private corpora, the open ecosystem lacks STEM-focused synthetic datasets that deliver high per-token learning value efficiently for small models. To address this gap, we introduce QVAC Genesis III, a 191.43B-token, STEM-focused multi-domain synthetic corpus covering 19 domains across several difficulty levels and different educational styles. QVAC Genesis III is built via a dual generation strategy that performs targeted teacher distillation using a weak edge-scale student model as signal: the student's failures are converted into corrective explanations, while its successes are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices. We further introduce an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and tracks both accuracy and answer validity. To validate the effectiveness of our QVAC Genesis III data, we conduct controlled from-scratch ablations with 1.7B-parameter models, showing that models trained with QVAC Genesis III consistently outperform both models trained with the open-source synthetic corpus Cosmopedia-v2 and the publicly released Cosmo-1B model across ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM benchmarks, achieving up to +28.57% on ARC-E and +21.35% on ARC-C, while reaching a Valid Answer Rate of up to 99.45%.

</details>


### [250] [LLM-as-an-Improver: Turning Verification into Better Candidates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19515)
*Akiyoshi Tomihari,Yuma Ichikawa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces VRR (Verify--Repair--Reselect), a method that uses verification feedback to improve the candidate set itself, not just rank it. By generating repaired versions of initial candidates and new approaches, VRR can recover correct solutions even when all initial candidates are incorrect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing verifier-based selection methods only use verification for ranking candidates in a fixed pool, discarding valuable feedback. The authors question whether verification can also improve the candidate set itself, not just select from it.

Method: VRR retains the initial winner while conditionally generating three complementary alternatives: (1) repaired versions of the winner and runner-up, and (2) a solution based on a new approach. It filters invalid and duplicate candidates using only inference-time information, then reselects the final answer under the original evaluation criteria.

Result: VRR improves over fixed-pool verifier-based selection across diverse models and benchmarks (code-generation and reasoning). Notably, it can recover correct solutions even when all candidates in the initial pool are incorrect.

Conclusion: Verification feedback can serve a broader role—it can construct stronger candidates beyond the initial pool, not just select among existing solutions. This establishes "LLM-as-an-Improver" as a paradigm complementing LLM-as-a-judge.

Abstract: Verifier-based selection improves LLM performance by generating multiple candidate solutions and using a verifier to select the most promising one. However, existing methods typically treat verification only as a ranking step and discard its feedback once a fixed candidate pool has been evaluated. In this paper, we ask whether verification can also improve the candidate set itself. To this end, we introduce LLM-as-an-Improver and propose Verify--Repair--Reselect (VRR), which uses verification feedback to generate and reselect improved candidates. VRR retains the initial winner while conditionally generating three complementary alternatives: repaired versions of the winner and runner-up, and a solution based on a new approach. It filters invalid and duplicate candidates using only inference-time information and then reselects the final answer under the original evaluation criteria. Across diverse models and code-generation and reasoning benchmarks, VRR improves over fixed-pool verifier-based selection in many settings and can recover correct solutions even when all candidates in the initial pool are incorrect. These results highlight a broader role for LLMs as improvers: verification feedback can not only select among existing solutions but also construct stronger candidates beyond the initial pool.

</details>


### [251] [An Architecture for Long-Horizon Agents: Levels, Ticks and Cascaded Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19519)
*Erik Nijkamp,Anurag Koul,Egor Pakhomov,Bo Pang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of running language-model agents for long-horizon tasks (days/weeks) that exceed context windows and human attention intervals. The authors propose a hierarchical architecture with time-scale levels, clocked ticks, and cascaded intelligence to enable continual operation without forgetting. They demonstrate this in a ten-day experiment where an agent reproduced a reinforcement learning result with minimal human oversight, showing that the ability to run continually without forgetting lies in the harness around the model rather than in the model itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out work spanning days or weeks (e.g., operations remediation or research programmes). Such tasks outlive any context window, any process, and any interval at which a person can attend. The paper argues that a long-horizon agent must run continually without forgetting before it can learn continually.

Method: The authors derive seven bottlenecks from the long-horizon setting and answer them with a hierarchical architecture of three parts: (i) levels indexed by time scale, each keeping a bounded file summarizing the level below; (ii) a clocked tick as the unit of autonomous action; and (iii) cascaded intelligence, where work is escalated to a more capable model only after failing review.

Result: The authors report on a ten-day campaign in which an agent built on this architecture reproduced a published reinforcement-learning result with a human attending once a day. They show: (1) the agent kept the thread across every context reset and session boundary of the campaign; (2) operating knowledge written early changed later behavior with no change to model weights; and (3) where learned components would enter such a system.

Conclusion: The authors' experience suggests continual learning for these agents needs a substrate outliving every context and process, and the checks the harness already runs are where a learner belongs. The ability to run continually without forgetting lies in the harness around the model rather than in the model itself.

Abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out work spanning days or weeks, such as an operations remediation or a research programme. Such a task outlives any context window, any process and any interval at which a person can attend. In this paper, we argue that a long-horizon agent must run continually without forgetting before it can learn continually. This ability lies in the harness around the model rather than in the model itself. We derive seven bottlenecks from the long-horizon setting and answer them with a hierarchical architecture of three parts: (i) levels indexed by time scale, each keeping a bounded file summarising the level below; (ii) a clocked tick as the unit of autonomous action; and (iii) cascaded intelligence, where work is escalated to a more capable model only after failing review. We report on a ten-day campaign in which an agent built on this architecture reproduced a published reinforcement-learning result with a human attending once a day, and show (1) the agent kept the thread across every context reset and session boundary of the campaign, (2) operating knowledge written early changed later behaviour with no change to model weights, and (3) where learned components would enter such a system. Overall, our experience suggests continual learning for these agents needs a substrate outliving every context and process, and the checks the harness already runs are where a learner belongs.

</details>


### [252] [EconSkills: Studying Skill Transfer and Retrieval for Web Agents on Live Economic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19523)
*Yinzhu Quan,Zefang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EconSkills is a skill library and evaluation framework that distills verified web trajectories into parameterized standard operating procedures for retrieving live economic data, enabling reusable procedural knowledge transfer across task instances in web agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Web agents frequently revisit the same sites, yet current evaluations discard procedures learned from earlier successful interactions, wasting valuable learned knowledge and requiring agents to relearn procedures for similar tasks.

Method: The authors extract verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized skills with placeholders replacing source-instance values. Each skill records scope, navigation procedure, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps. They evaluate controlled transfer (matched skills vs. no-skill) and library-scale retrieval performance, comparing abstraction versus raw trajectory replay.

Result: In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps on paired successes; abstraction is substantially more effective than replaying raw trajectories. At library scale, retrieval performs best on directly covered tasks, while approximate matches on uncovered tasks offset gains. Procedural guidance shortens portal-specific navigation, but semantic verification remains necessary.

Conclusion: Reusable economic web procedures can transfer across task instances. The framework provides a concrete design target for coverage-aware skill selection and context delivery in web agents.

Abstract: Web agents often revisit the same sites, yet most evaluations discard the procedures learned in earlier successful interactions. We introduce EconSkills, a skill library and evaluation framework that distills verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized standard operating procedures for retrieving live economic data. Each skill records its scope, navigation procedure, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps while replacing source-instance values with placeholders. EconSkills separates two questions: whether a known relevant procedure transfers to a held-out task, and whether an agent can retain that benefit when selecting from a library. In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps on paired successes, while abstraction is substantially more effective than replaying raw trajectories. At library scale, retrieval is competitive with the no-skill baseline overall and performs best on directly covered tasks; coverage-stratified outcomes show that approximate matches on uncovered tasks offset these gains. Browser trajectories further identify when procedural guidance shortens portal-specific navigation and when semantic verification remains necessary. These results establish that reusable economic web procedures can transfer across task instances and provide a concrete design target for coverage-aware selection and context delivery.

</details>


### [253] [A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19524)
*Shaina Raza,Ahmed Y. Radwan,Imran Liaquat,Kathryn Hume*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified framework for assessing AI trustworthiness across LLMs, agentic systems, and multimodal models, connecting output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight dimensions (capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, efficiency), with meta-evaluation, safety overrides, and regulatory mappings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmark scores provide an incomplete basis for assessing AI trustworthiness. Different system types (LLMs, agentic systems, MLLMs) require different assessment forms, yet evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight.

Method: The framework connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. It preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands with uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines validity, reliability, and reproducibility. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths/weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures.

Result: The framework provides structured assessment of both system performance and evidence credibility, with mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and EU regulatory requirements. Empirical validation across deployment contexts remains an essential next step.

Conclusion: The framework offers a structured basis for assessing AI trustworthiness beyond benchmark scores, though empirical validation across deployment contexts is still needed. The integration of technical assessment with regulatory oversight needs bridges the gap between development and governance requirements.

Abstract: Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern artificial intelligence systems. Large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs) require different forms of assessment, yet their evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight. We propose a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The framework preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands, accompanied by uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs. The framework provides a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of the evidence supporting it, with empirical validation across deployment contexts remaining an essential next step.

</details>


### [254] [FINSKILLOPS: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for SEC Filing QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19680)
*Yanzhang Ma,Zhenghan Tai,Hanwei Wu,Sizhe Guan,Jianliang Lei,Hailin He,Chaolong Jiang,Jijun Chi,Tung Sum Thomas Kwok,Bohuai Xiao,Jingrui Tian,Xinlu Wu,Xingao Zhan,Peng Lu,Muzhi Li,Yihong Wu,Liheng Ma,Sicheng Lyu,Tianshuo Yan,Junhao Zhu,Yaqian Xu,Lei Ding,Yufei Cui,Ziquan Liu,Boyu Han,Hengli Liu,Ling Zhou,Xinyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FINSKILLOPS is a multi-agent system for SEC filing QA that implements controlled behavioral maintenance through scoped skill patches. It derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded failure diagnoses and governs them through validation, regression checks, and versioned management. The system achieves highest correctness and reference consistency across six benchmarks, with correctness improving from 3.70 to 4.55, and reduces monitoring non-correct rate from 20.0% to 12.5% in operational use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial QA systems have fixed reliability behavior after deployment, but new SEC-filing questions repeatedly expose heterogeneous errors in period, entity, evidence use, and calculation. Existing self-improvement methods offer limited control over where corrections apply or which previously correct answers may break.

Method: FINSKILLOPS instantiates post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance. It derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement or retirement. A single frozen skill registry is used across six financial QA benchmarks.

Result: Across six financial QA benchmarks, FINSKILLOPS achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among evaluated systems. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on the enhanced benchmark. In a 12-round operational study, only 6 of 33 proposed skills were promoted, while the monitoring non-correct rate fell from 20.0% to 12.5%.

Conclusion: Controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management establish the foundation for reliable self-improvement in financial QA systems. The approach successfully balances fixing recurring failures while preventing regressions in previously correct answers.

Abstract: Financial QA systems are typically improved before deployment through better retrieval, prompting, or agent coordination, leaving their reliability behavior fixed thereafter. In practice, new SEC-filing questions repeatedly expose heterogeneous errors in period, entity, evidence use, and calculation. Existing self-improvement methods can turn failures into new behaviors, but offer limited control over where a correction should apply or which previously correct answers it may break. We therefore frame post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance: recurring failures should become scoped skill patches, and each patch should earn deployment with- out introducing regressions. We instantiate this view in FINSKILLOPS, a multi-agent system for SEC filing QA. FINSKILLOPS derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement or retirement. Across six financial QA benchmarks, a single frozen skill registry achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among the evaluated systems. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on our enhanced benchmark. In a separate 12-round operational study, only six of 33 proposed skills are promoted, while the monitoring non-correct rate falls from 20.0% to 12.5%. These results establish controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management as the foundation for reliable self-improvement.

</details>


### [255] [Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19526)
*Xinghong Fu,Aravinth Kulanthaivelu,Yutaro Yamada*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SIFT introduces a sample-efficient self-improvement framework for coding agents that uses LLM-as-a-judge signals and a regularized Bradley-Terry model to guide tree search, reserving expensive task evaluations only for the most promising candidates. It significantly outperforms prior approaches on the Polyglot benchmark with lower computational costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-improvement approaches for coding agents are costly and compute-intensive because they evaluate candidate self-modifications by re-running benchmark tasks, which is time-consuming. The goal is to boost coding performance under strict budget constraints.

Method: 1) Use LLM-as-a-judge for pairwise comparisons between candidate patches
2) Aggregate win-loss records with a regularized Bradley-Terry model to produce strength scores
3) Use strength scores for rank-based parent sampling in a lightweight disaggregated tree search
4) Reserve expensive downstream task evaluations only for the most promising nodes

Result: SIFT outperforms existing tree-search based self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark with significantly lower resource requirements in terms of CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost.

Conclusion: The combination of LLM-judge signals with Bradley-Terry scoring and disaggregated tree search enables efficient self-improvement of coding agents by reducing expensive task evaluations while maintaining or improving performance.

Abstract: Coding agents can recursively modify their own implementations, forming a loop of self-improvement. While prior work shows this can boost performance on coding benchmarks, existing approaches are costly and compute-intensive. We introduce a simple, sample-efficient self-improvement framework that significantly improves coding performance under strict budget constraints. We identify evaluation of candidate self-modifications as the main runtime bottleneck since prior approaches estimate their effectiveness by re-running a subset of benchmark tasks with the modified agent, which is time-consuming. We introduce Recursive Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search (SIFT), which augments these downstream task evaluations with an LLM-as-a-judge signal that performs pairwise comparisons between candidate patches, where the win-loss record is aggregated with a regularized Bradley-Terry model, and the resulting strength scores drive rank-based parent sampling inside a lightweight disaggregated tree search. Expensive downstream task evaluations are reserved only for the most promising nodes. Using a fully disaggregated tree search pipeline, the judge scores provide intermediate signal to guide exploration on promising candidate patches without being bottlenecked by slow evaluation runs. SIFT outperforms existing tree-search based self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark with significantly lower resource requirements in terms of CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost.

</details>


### [256] [Q&A on Any Spreadsheet Requires Interpreting Its Grid Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20732)
*Zofia Smoleń*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of processing spreadsheets in LLM-driven RAG systems by proposing a semantic cell annotation framework that splits spreadsheets into interpretable chunks. While this approach outperforms existing methods, it encounters a fundamental limitation: classification models cannot handle the infinite, continuous nature of cell roles in 2D spreadsheet data. The authors argue that the field should move toward dimensionality-reduction techniques to flatten 2D spreadsheets directly into 1D text.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to improve how LLM-driven RAG systems handle spreadsheet data, which is fundamentally 2D unstructured data with continuous relationships. Existing approaches using cell role annotation have limitations because classification models can only handle finite, pre-defined classes, creating a bottleneck in spreadsheet-to-LLM processing.

Method: The paper proposes a novel framework that splits any spreadsheet into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation. This approach enriches context for answer generation rather than improving retrieval accuracy. The authors identify that this method faces a hard ceiling due to the inherent limitations of discrete classification models.

Result: The framework beats the state of the art but hits a hard ceiling. The key insight is that classification models cannot perfectly capture the structural nuance of spreadsheets, even with human-level annotation, because spreadsheets have infinite potential cell roles and continuous relationships.

Conclusion: The conclusion suggests that addressing the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification. The field should develop dimensionality-reduction techniques to directly flatten 2D unstructured spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text, which would be easier for downstream RAG systems to interpret and generate from.

Abstract: Semantic cell annotation improves chunking interpretability for spreadsheets in LLM-driven RAG systems, aiding answer generation through enriched context rather than improved retrieval accuracy. We propose a novel framework of splitting any spreadsheet into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation. Our framework beats the state of the art, yet it faces a hard ceiling. Spreadsheets are fundamentally two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and infinite potential cell roles. Because classification models are restricted to finite, pre-defined classes, they cannot perfectly capture this structural nuance, even with human-level annotation. We show that addressing the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification. Instead, the field must develop dimensionality-reduction techniques to directly flatten 2D unstructured spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text. Text chunks would be easier for downstream RAG to interpret and generate from.

</details>


### [257] [When Hiring Becomes Agent-Mediated: Evaluating Access and Recurrence in Two-Agent Résumé Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19530)
*Jian Gao,Hang Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-agent hiring screening system where employer-side and candidate-side agents interact, exchange evidence, and update judgments before deciding candidate advancement, compared to traditional static one-call automated résumé screening.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional résumé screening is automated as a static, one-call judgment over a résumé-job pair. This paper challenges that approach by introducing a bilateral representation where both employer and candidate sides have agents that can exchange evidence and update their assessments.

Method: The researchers compared two-agent screening vs one-call screening on 600 constructed résumé-job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. They conducted three runs on a 191-pair borderline pool and analyzed discovery-selected cases in fresh runs with one-call follow-up.

Result: Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3% to 39.3% for GPT-5.5; 34.0% to 35.5% for Opus 4.7). On the borderline pool, pass-instance rates rise from 4.5% to 26.2% (GPT) and 6.5% to 16.1% (Opus). The two-agent screening rejects applications that one-call advances and vice versa—not a uniform relaxation. At similar pass volumes, different applications are advanced, and no one-call threshold recovers applications consistently selected by two-agent screening. Two-agent-only selections recur less often than shared selections under GPT-5.5, while one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline.

Conclusion: As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening procedure itself—not just the underlying model—shapes who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs. The screening procedure is a critical factor in candidate outcomes in agent-mediated hiring systems.

Abstract: Hiring is bilateral: employers assess fit, while candidates present and defend evidence of their qualifications. Yet résumé screening, the first gate, is commonly automated as a static, one-call judgment over a résumé-job pair. We study a two-agent alternative in which employer-side and candidate-side agents represent these roles, exchange evidence, and update their judgments before deciding who advances. We compare procedures on 600 constructed résumé-job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3% to 39.3% for GPT-5.5; 34.0% to 35.5% for Opus 4.7). Across three runs on the common 191-pair borderline pool, pass-instance rates rise from 4.5% to 26.2% and from 6.5% to 16.1%, respectively. This is not a uniform relaxation: two-agent screening rejects applications one-call advances, changing decisions in both directions. At similar pass volumes, the procedures advance different applications, and no one-call threshold recovers applications consistently selected by two-agent screening. Among discovery-selected cases re-executed in fresh runs, two-agent-only selections recur less often than shared selections, clearly under GPT-5.5 and less certainly under Opus 4.7, while a separate one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline. As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening procedure, not only the model behind it, shapes who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs.

</details>


### [258] [An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20804)
*Run-Ze Fan,Zihao Zhang,Simin Ma,Yebowen Hu,Shouju Wang,Kaiqiang Song,Fei Liu,Hamed Zamani,Xiaoyang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates individual components of coding harnesses (planning, action space, context management) across 4 models on SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench, testing 176 settings to understand how each component affects autonomous coding agent performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work evaluates coding harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. This study aims to enable component-level comparisons to understand how harness design choices impact software-engineering performance.

Method: The study uses a lightweight coding harness with fixed execution loop while varying three components: planning, action space, and context management. They evaluate 176 matched settings across five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space, testing across four models on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Result: Key findings: (1) Context management is most valuable when context-window budget is tight, primarily preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Rule-based elision before LLM summarization is most effective; making elided content recoverable adds unnecessary complexity. (3) Planning serves as accuracy scaffold for weaker models but cost saver for stronger models, with minimal accuracy impact. (4) Predefined tools help models with weak bash proficiency, while bash-capable models achieve lower cost with bash-only interface. Trajectory analysis shows context management extends execution length without changing behavior, planning changes termination points, and action space changes code-writing granularity.

Conclusion: These findings provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components and inform model- and budget-aware harness design. Context management, planning, and action space each serve distinct roles depending on model capability and budget constraints.

Abstract: Coding harnesses shape how autonomous coding agents translate model capabilities into long-horizon software-engineering performance, yet existing work typically evaluates harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. To enable component-level comparisons, we study this question with a lightweight coding harness whose execution loop is fixed while three components are varied: planning, action space, and context management. Across four models evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, we evaluate 176 matched settings spanning five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space. We find that: (1) Context management becomes increasingly valuable as the context-window budget tightens, with most of its benefit coming from preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Staging rule-based elision before LLM-based summarization provides the strongest overall efficiency among the context-management strategies, whereas making elided content recoverable adds machinery that models rarely use and yields no accuracy gain. (3) Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy. (4) Predefined tools improve performance for models with weaker bash proficiency, whereas bash-capable models can operate effectively with a bash-only interface and achieve substantially lower cost, especially on command-line-centric tasks. Trajectory-level analysis explains these effects: context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior, planning changes where trajectories stop, and the action space changes the granularity at which code is written. These findings inform model- and budget-aware harness design and provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components.

</details>


### [259] [Agentic AI Networking for Heterogeneous Unmanned Aerial Systems in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19538)
*Nguyen Duc Minh Quang,Chang Liu,Shuangyang Li,Derrick Wing Kwan Ng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a hierarchical hybrid LLM-MARL architecture for managing dynamic non-cooperative games in low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs). The framework uses a dual-loop structure: an outer loop with LLM-assisted game orchestration for objective reconfiguration, and an inner loop with decentralized parameter-conditioned MARL policies for execution. A logistics-monitoring case study demonstrates the framework's ability to facilitate coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers in LAWNs rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. The dynamic non-cooperative game environment with evolving operating conditions and coordination objectives requires a more adaptive approach.

Method: The proposed method uses a hierarchical hybrid LLM-MARL architecture with a dual-loop structure: (1) Outer adaptation loop: LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, reconfigure objectives and resource priorities; (2) Inner loop: decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies executed under the configured game.

Result: The logistics-monitoring case study demonstrates that the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies.

Conclusion: The framework successfully enables adaptive, autonomous coordination in LAWNs without retraining. Key challenges remain in scalability, trustworthiness, and developing adaptive agentic LAWNs, which require further research.

Abstract: Low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) are emerging as a key infrastructure for heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems that support concurrent services within a shared three-dimensional airspace. Their coexistence creates strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared network resources, while heterogeneous services impose distinct and time-varying requirements. These interactions naturally form a dynamic non-cooperative game in which both operating conditions and coordination objectives evolve over time. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers typically rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)- multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. Specifically, an outer adaptation loop employs LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities, while an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. A logistics-monitoring case study illustrates how the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies. Finally, we discuss key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

</details>


### [260] [Continual Enterprise World Model Discovery in Dynamic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19551)
*Shambhavi Mishra,David Vazquez,Perouz Taslakian,Marco Pedersoli,Jose Dolz,Issam H. Laradji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of an agent discovering hidden business rules in enterprise systems (like ServiceNow) through interaction, and continually revising its world model as rules change over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In enterprise systems, business rules (e.g., updating one field triggers another field change, record creation, or approval processes) are custom-written by each organization and evolve over time. An agent cannot predict action outcomes without knowing these rules, necessitating a way to discover and track them.

Method: The authors introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, a benchmark built on a live ServiceNow environment with 9 tables, 25 hidden rules, and 600 evaluation actions. It tests four scenarios: discovery, revision, extension, and retirement of rules. They propose a Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) that builds a world model through interaction and carries it across rule changes.

Result: CDA predicts the effects of hidden rules more accurately than looking them up for each question (the prior approach), achieving up to 8.98 IoU (Intersection over Union) points improvement. It answers from its own model without querying the running system.

Conclusion: The Continual Discovery Agent successfully discovers and maintains a world model of enterprise business rules through continual interaction, outperforming lookup-based approaches and demonstrating the ability to adapt when rules are modified, added, or removed.

Abstract: In an enterprise system, updating one field can set another, create a record, or start an approval. These effects are produced by business rules that are not built into the platform but written by each organization and revised over time. An agent working in such a system cannot predict the result of its own actions without knowing these rules. We study continual enterprise world model discovery, where an agent starts without knowledge of these business rules and discovers them by interacting with records and observing the outcomes. From those observations it builds a world model, which it revises as the rules change. To evaluate this, we introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, built on a live ServiceNow environment with nine tables, 25 hidden rules and 600 evaluation actions. It presents four versions of the same enterprise world, with the tables and records held fixed while a rule is modified, then added, then removed, so that discovery, revision, extension and retirement are each tested in turn. Our Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) builds such a model and carries it from one world to the next. It predicts the effects of the hidden rules more accurately than looking them up for each question, the approach taken by prior work, by up to 8.98 IoU points, and it answers from its own model without querying the running system.

</details>


### [261] [SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19610)
*Run Peng,Zinnia Nie,Jing Ding,Yinpei Dai,Yichi Zhang,Zengqing Wu,Yao Fu,Ziqiao Ma,Jiayuan Mao,Joyce Chai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SimLife is a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with visual observations, action logs, and synthetic dialogues. It includes SimLife-BP benchmark (106 episodes, 1,439 QA pairs) evaluating long-context pattern understanding - the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from weeks of observations. The benchmark tests direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under various rule hint levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer what people need in the moment, how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. Current agents lack the ability to understand long-term behavioral patterns.

Method: Built SimLife platform with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Created SimLife-BP benchmark containing 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different levels of rule hints.

Result: Current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change.

Conclusion: Long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents. SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

Abstract: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer not only what people need in the moment, but also how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. We introduce SimLife, a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Built on SimLife, SimLife-BP evaluates long-context pattern understanding: the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from weeks or months of everyday observations. The benchmark contains 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, and 1,439 question-answer pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different levels of rule hints. Evaluating frontier models and architectures, we find that current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change. These findings suggest that long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

</details>


### [262] [From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19630)
*Diba Afroze,Xingli Zhang,Yazhou Tu,Xiali Hei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants. But linking natural-language requests to vehicle functions creates a safety-critical authorization problem. Before executing a command, the system must choose whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger an emergency response, or make no tool call. To our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. We introduce a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. We evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Alignment ranges from 40.1% for Llama 3.2 3B to 89.1% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. The API-based models score between 83.2% and 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models produce two to three False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios, and persistent errors remain in confirmation and manual-control decisions. A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation increases alignment to 40.1% under the structured authorization policy, versus 28.2-29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines, but it does not eliminate False Executes. Structured LLM decisions are therefore insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism, and deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

</details>


### [263] [Reach or Solve? Attributing Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19636)
*Xuan Liu,Jingbin Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "checkpoint handoff," an evaluation protocol that separates reinforcement learning (RL) improvements in language model agents into two components: REACH (how often the agent arrives at a state near success) and SOLVE (how often it completes the task from that state). This addresses the problem that endpoint success metrics mix arrival and completion, making fair comparison between SFT and RL checkpoints difficult.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of language model agents compares RL and SFT checkpoints from different states, since each agent's actions affect the environment states it encounters. This makes it impossible to disentangle whether improvements come from better arrival (reaching good states) or better completion (acting better once there). The restriction to states both policies reach selects on an outcome and can flip the sign of effects.

Method: The authors propose checkpoint handoff: cloning a state that one checkpoint reached and handing it to another checkpoint for evaluation, with no retraining. They cross a "reacher" role (determining REACH) and a "solver" role (determining SOLVE) across SFT and RL checkpoints. REACH measures how often a policy arrives at a state confirmed to be a fixed number of actions from success. SOLVE measures how often it completes from an identical cloned state.

Result: Across two benchmarks (ALFWorld) and two independently released pipelines, the reacher×solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both REACH and SOLVE terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction.

Conclusion: Checkpoint handoff provides a principled way to evaluate long-horizon agents by separating arrival from completion. RL improves both components, and the benefit is multiplicative - RL history is more valuable to RL solvers than to SFT solvers. This method allows evaluation to report arrival and completion alongside endpoint success without requiring retraining.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning now trains language-model agents that act over dozens of steps in live environments. The gains are large, and they are read as better decision-making. An agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs. Each observation follows from its own earlier actions, so the states it meets late in an episode are partly of its own making. An SFT checkpoint and an RL checkpoint are then scored from different states, even on identical tasks. Endpoint success mixes two changes: where the agent arrives, and what it does once it is there. Restricting the comparison to states both policies reach does not separate them. That restriction selects on an outcome, and in our data it flips the sign of the effect. We introduce checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that clones a state one released checkpoint reached and hands it to another, with no retraining. Crossing a reacher role and a solver role over SFT and RL splits an endpoint gain into REACH and SOLVE. REACH is how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success. SOLVE is how often it finishes from an identical cloned state. Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher by solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction. Handoff asks only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, so long-horizon evaluation can report arrival and completion beside endpoint success.

</details>


### [264] [ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19644)
*Jaehyun Nam,Jinsung Yoon,Yanzhou Pan,Yubo Wang,Rui Meng,Parthasarathy Ranganathan,Tomas Pfister*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ScientistTwo is a fully autonomous multi-agent AI framework that performs end-to-end scientific discovery without human intervention.
