It can take an initial problem, establish baselines, formulate hypotheses, conduct experiments, refine methodologies through ablation studies, and validate findings via a simulated peer-review system. The framework achieves state-of-the-art results and produces papers that receive higher review ratings than human-authored papers at top-tier conferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to realize the ultimate vision of AI in science: problem-driven autonomous research where AI can independently navigate the scientific landscape, identify theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expand the frontier of knowledge without human intervention.

Method: ScientistTwo uses a multi-agent architecture that coordinates specialized agents to: (1) establish state-of-the-art baselines, (2) formulate novel hypotheses, (3) conduct experiments with diverse datasets and metrics, (4) perform automated ablation studies for methodology refinement, and (5) validate findings through a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine.

Result: ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. Benchmarking was performed against papers accepted at top-tier conferences (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS).

Conclusion: ScientistTwo represents not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery, demonstrating that AI can independently perform high-quality scientific research comparable to or exceeding human achievement.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/

</details>


### [265] [Replan, Repair, or Edit? A Unified Empirical Evaluation of Travel Agents for Itinerary Revision under Resource Disruptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19654)
*Xiaofei Yuan,Yan Zhang,Shaobo Qiao,Huangleshuai He,Leyan Ni,Mingchen Ju,Lujia Yang,Sijia Xu,Yifu Tang,Zhengyi Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically compares three approaches for revising travel itineraries that become infeasible due to disruptions: LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and iTIMO local-revision adapter. Using 500 single-disruption and 200 compound-disruption benchmark cases, the study evaluates effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance due to disruptions (flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, attraction closures). Existing approaches (full replanning, classical plan repair, LLM-based revision) use different task formulations and evaluation protocols, making comparison difficult. This study aims to provide a systematic empirical comparison to guide practical implementation.

Method: Empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases (including feasible and infeasible instances) and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. Three approaches were compared: LLM-Z3 full replanning (with Gemini), IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and iTIMO local-revision adapter. Metrics included effectiveness (success rate), plan stability (preservation of accepted itinerary), and computational cost.

Result: LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched LLM-Z3's single-disruption success rate while preserving substantially more of the original itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed significantly: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, LLM-Z3 used compact one-call inference, and iTIMO consumed substantially more tokens.

Conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost in travel itinerary revision. Key findings: (1) LLM-Z3 excels at compound disruptions, (2) IPyHOPPER offers best balance of success and plan stability for single disruptions, (3) choice of approach depends on priorities between feasibility, preservation, and computational resources.

Abstract: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance because of flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, or attraction closures. Revising these itineraries involves full replanning, classical plan repair, and LLM-based travel-agent revision, whose differing task formulations and evaluation protocols hinder comparison. We conduct a systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases, including feasible and infeasible instances, and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. We compare LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter across effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost. LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration's single-disruption overall success, while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, the evaluated LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and the iTIMO adapter consumed substantially more tokens. The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings.

</details>


### [266] [When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19671)
*Jaejun Shim,HyunJin Kim,Young Jin Kim,JinYeong Bak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When2Think is a post-training framework that enables Large Reasoning Models to dynamically allocate computation based on problem difficulty. It learns when to use fast "System 1" (NoThink) for easy problems versus slow "System 2" (Think) for hard problems, achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Reasoning Models exhibit systematic inefficiency: they overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches using uniform length penalties or rigid routing trade accuracy loss on hard instances for reduced computation on easy instances, creating an "efficiency tax." The goal is to achieve instance-adaptive computation allocation that preserves accuracy while reducing token usage.

Method: The paper proposes Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that uses pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. The method learns when to use direct answering (easy instances) versus extended reasoning (hard instances).

Result: On AIME24: Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model. On AIME25: When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

Conclusion: When2Think successfully enables hybrid reasoning in LRMs by dynamically allocating computation based on problem difficulty. The approach achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs compared to compression and routing-only baselines, demonstrating that instance-adaptive computation allocation is a promising direction for efficient reasoning.

Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

</details>


### [267] [LearnActCoder: Role-Aware Error Memory for Adaptive Clinical Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19721)
*Meysam Ghaffari,Bhaskar Sen,Nasim Sabetpour,Nina Fatehi,Animesh Agarwal,Carlos Morato*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Learn-Then-Act is an inference-time adaptation framework for clinical coding that converts errors from a small labeled batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database, routing false-negative lessons to a recall-oriented Coder and false-positive lessons to a precision-oriented Judge. The framework improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points on MIMIC-III while maintaining stable performance across datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical coding agents repeatedly encounter the same failure modes: unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches. The authors aim to address these recurring errors without requiring weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow.

Method: The Learn-Then-Act framework converts errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB). False-negative lessons are routed to a recall-oriented Coder, while false-positive lessons are routed to a precision-oriented Judge. The framework is instantiated in LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge clinical coding pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available.

Result: On 150 matched MIMIC-III notes, structured MistakeKDB improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points, while raw-example and reflection-style memories remain near the no-memory baseline; the ICD-9 improvement is not significant. On a matched MIMIC-IV cohort, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 statistically unchanged. Applying the same memory to 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes maintains a stable ICD operating point.

Conclusion: Structured, feedback-derived error memory is useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow. Absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low, and the system is evaluated retrospectively rather than in clinical deployment.

Abstract: Clinical coding agents repeatedly encounter the same failure modes, including unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches. We introduce Learn-Then-Act, an inference-time adaptation framework that converts errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB). False-negative lessons are routed to a recall-oriented Coder, while false-positive lessons are routed to a precision-oriented Judge. We instantiate the framework in LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge clinical coding pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available. On 150 matched MIMIC-III notes, structured MistakeKDB improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points, while raw-example and reflection-style memories remain near the no-memory baseline; the ICD-9 improvement is not significant. On a matched MIMIC-IV cohort, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 statistically unchanged. Applying the same memory to 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes maintains a stable ICD operating point, providing scale/stability evidence. Overall, the results are consistent with structured, feedback-derived error memory being useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow. Absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low, and the system is evaluated retrospectively rather than in clinical deployment.

</details>


### [268] [AutoData: Agentic Search for Pre-training Data Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19754)
*Yan Meng,Dhruv Srikanth,Bingchen Zhao,Zhengyao Jiang,Yuxiang Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoData is an LLM agent that automates pre-training data selection by searching over executable selection algorithms (scoring, stratification, stochastic selection rules) using validation feedback from a proxy model, outperforming human-designed curation pipelines and transferring to larger scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data selection for pre-training remains largely outside the agentic optimization loop that has shown promise for model and training code. Prior data mixture methods only optimize weights over fixed domains, limiting the search space for data engineering.

Method: Framing pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features (lexical statistics, categorical labels, perplexity). AutoData searches a rich program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules, discovering feature interactions automatically through iterative refinement with validation feedback from a proxy model.

Result: Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. The discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE.

Conclusion: Data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data domain.

Abstract: LLM agents have recently shown promise in automating machine learning engineering by editing model and training code under execution feedback. Data, however, remains largely outside this agentic optimisation loop. We frame pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features, i.e., lexical statistics, categorical labels, and perplexity. We introduce AutoData, an agent that searches directly over executable selection algorithms. Unlike prior data mixture methods that optimise weights over a fixed set of domains, AutoData searches a richer program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules, discovering feature interactions automatically by iteratively refining algorithms with validation feedback from a proxy model. Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Despite being searched only on this small proxy, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE. These results suggest that data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data.

</details>


### [269] [Rethinking Multi-Agent Collaboration: When More Is Less](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19759)
*Yishuo Yuan,Yibo Wu,Yihan Zhang,Minyuan Sun,Shenliang Li,Xinkai Ma,Yifan Li,Jiaheng Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates when multi-agent collaboration provides genuine value over single-agent systems as LLM capabilities scale. The authors propose SAIGE, a lightweight multi-agent mechanism using Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution, which models collaboration as dynamic graphs with content-based semantic dependencies. Experiments on long-horizon tasks show multi-agent collaboration excels in sparse-dependency scenarios but single-agent approaches remain superior for tightly coupled workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid advancement of LLMs and single-agent systems raises a critical question: when does multi-agent collaboration actually offer value? As individual agent capabilities scale, multi-agent approaches face diminishing returns while incurring growing context overhead. The research aims to delineate the capability boundaries between multi-agent collaboration and single-agent alternatives.

Method: The authors conducted systematic analysis to identify capability boundaries between multi-agent and single-agent approaches. They proposed SAIGE (Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution), a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism that models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph. Nodes represent agent instances spawned on demand, while edges encode semantic dependencies through content-based information retrieval. Experiments were conducted on long-horizon, complex task benchmarks.

Result: Multi-agent collaboration provides systematic benefits specifically in long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies, while single-agent harnesses remain superior for tightly coupled, sequential workflows. SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance. Scaling the agent pool or deepening recursion levels does not consistently improve outcomes.

Conclusion: Multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than being universal. More agents do not necessarily make a system more intelligent. The value of multi-agent collaboration depends on the specific task structure, particularly the presence of sparse dependencies in long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models and single-agent harnesses has reshaped the landscape of autonomous systems, raising a critical question of when multi-agent collaboration offers genuine value. As individual agent capabilities continue to scale, multi-agent collaboration faces diminishing returns while incurring growing context overhead. Through systematic analysis, we delineate the capability boundaries of multi-agent collaboration relative to single-agent alternatives, showing that it confers systematic benefits specifically in long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies, while single-agent harnesses remain superior in tightly coupled, sequential workflows. Building on these insights, we propose SAIGE, a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism based on Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution. SAIGE models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph, where nodes are agent instances spawned on demand and edges encode semantic dependencies established through content-based information retrieval. Experiments on long-horizon, complex task benchmarks show that SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance, and that scaling the agent pool or deepening the recursion level does not consistently improve outcomes. Our findings suggest that multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than universal, and that more agents do not necessarily make a system more intelligent.

</details>

Implemented in TorchFold, TorchCraft combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives within a shared optimization procedure for minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins. Abstract: Multi-agent trading systems built on large language models (LLMs) are beginning to appear in quantitative finance, yet their robustness to adversarial inputs is largely unknown. We study the vulnerability of LLM trading stacks to black-box, input-only attacks that enter solely via admissible social-media feeds. We introduce the Generic Multi-Agent Trading System (GMATS), a framework that captures modern multiagent trading architectures and instantiate a class of black-box poisoning attackers that treat an LLM as a post generator and inject budget-constrained, plausibly benign social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream. We define contagion metrics that trace how adversarial content propagates through the stack, including belief-shift scores at analyst and coordinator layers and attack-clean deltas on standard backtest metrics. Experiments on a safe offline benchmark with historical market and social data show that even simple input-only attackers can materially degrade risk-return profiles, sharply reducing Sharpe ratios. At the same time, we find that suitably designed multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts can dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under identical poisoning budgets.

### [273] [Steering Equilibrium Selection in Regularized Self-Play via the Reference Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19820)
*Luis Leal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether the reference policy in regularized self-play can be used to deliberately select a specific equilibrium from a polytope of value-equivalent equilibria in two-player zero-sum games. The authors find that anchoring the reference at a target equilibrium and refining steers self-play to that target with high precision (mean coordinate error 0.007, median exploitability 5×10^-5), following the reach-weighted I-projection. The method has limitations at boundaries and with off-manifold references, but provides a new interpretation of RLHF's KL anchor as a selection mechanism rather than just a stability tool.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In two-player zero-sum games with multiple value-equivalent equilibria, regularized self-play (used by DeepNash) implicitly selects the maximum-entropy equilibrium via the uniform reference. The authors question whether this selection can be controlled intentionally by manipulating the reference policy, which would have significant implications for game playing and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

Method: The authors tested their equilibrium selection method on five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope using exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds. They anchored the reference at target equilibria and refined the policy, comparing table-based and MLP steering maps with matched control arms to isolate the effects of attention mechanisms.

Result: Anchoring the reference at a target equilibrium and refining steers self-play to that member with mean coordinate error 0.007 and median exploitability 5×10^-5 (TOST-equivalent within ±0.05). Selection follows the reach-weighted I-projection (slope 0.969 [0.950, 0.987]). Fixed off-manifold references cost 0.08-0.25 exploitability; boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts boundary saturation (rank correlation 0.90, p=0.037). Attention's signature is excess seed variance, with any systematic shift bounded at 0.018 and not significant. Steering only matters against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents.

Conclusion: The reference policy in regularized self-play can be deliberately used to select specific equilibria by anchoring at the desired member and refining. This reinterprets the KL anchor in RLHF-style RL as a selection knob rather than merely a stability leash. Limitations include boundary effects, off-manifold reference costs, and the need for smaller mirror steps for stiff/flat families. The method is robust across seeds but only provides advantages against non-equilibrium opponents.

Abstract: Regularized self-play -- the family behind DeepNash's Stratego play -- drives a two-player zero-sum policy to a Nash equilibrium by best-responding to a slowly moving, entropy-regularized reference policy $ρ$. When the game has a polytope of value-equivalent equilibria, the regularizer silently breaks the tie: with a uniform reference it selects the maximum-entropy member, the I-projection of $ρ$ onto the Nash set. Can the reference be used to choose the equilibrium on purpose? On five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope, with exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds, anchoring the reference at a target member and refining steers self-play to that member with mean coordinate error 0.007 at median exploitability $5\times10^{-5}$, TOST-equivalent to the request within $\pm0.05$; the anchoring persists through refinement and follows the reference, not the initialization. Selection follows the reach-weighted I-projection (slope 0.969 [0.950, 0.987]). We report with equal emphasis where the story breaks: fixed off-manifold references cost 0.08-0.25 exploitability; stiff or flat families require a smaller mirror step, set by a pre-registered rule; boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts where boundary saturation bites (rank correlation 0.90, p=0.037) while interior precision is curvature-independent. Table and MLP steering maps are equivalent within $\pm0.03$ at every target (30 seeds); matched control arms show attention's robust signature is excess seed variance, any systematic shift bounded at 0.018 and not significant. Against a best response the selection-robustness trade-off is degenerate: steering matters only against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents. The recipe -- anchor the reference at the desired member and refine -- reinterprets the KL anchor of RLHF-style RL as a selection knob, not only a stability leash.

</details>


### [274] [Dual-Axis Policy Optimization for LLM Agents: Bayesian Feedback Attribution and Trajectory Mass Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19830)
*Yingxuan Zhuang,Binhe Yu,Jingxiao Yang,Ruopei Sun,Ziting Li,Cheng Tan,Xuhong Zhang,Jianwei Yin,Jintao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BATON is a dual-axis policy optimization framework for reinforcement learning in LLM agents that addresses two key dimensions: how environment feedback is exploited within trajectories (Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution) and how trajectories are aggregated across batches (Inter-Trajectory Objective Aggregation). It combines Bayesian Feedback Attribution with Trajectory Mass Normalization to achieve superior performance across ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reinforcement learning methods for LLM agents lack a unified framework for addressing both intra-trajectory feedback exploitation and inter-trajectory aggregation. The authors identify these as two distinct optimization dimensions that need to be properly addressed simultaneously to improve LLM agent training.

Method: BATON introduces two complementary components: (1) Bayesian Feedback Attribution - constructs a feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions within trajectories; (2) Trajectory Mass Normalization (TMN) - assigns equal optimization mass to complete trajectories regardless of their length or sampling properties. The framework was evaluated with GRPO and GiGPO algorithms.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that both axes provide independent performance gains, and their combination consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across different model scales on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA benchmarks.

Conclusion: The dual-axis approach of BATON successfully addresses both optimization dimensions in reinforcement learning for LLM agents, with the combination of Bayesian Feedback Attribution and Trajectory Mass Normalization providing synergistic improvements that outperform existing methods.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning for LLM agents involves two distinct optimization di- mensions: how environment feedback is exploited within a trajectory, and how complete trajectories are aggregated across a batch. We formulate these dimen- sions as Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution and Inter-Trajectory Objec- tive Aggregation, and introduce BATON (Bayesian Attribution and Trajectory Objective Normalization), a dual-axis policy optimization framework. BATON instantiates the first axis with Bayesian Feedback Attribution, which constructs a feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions, and the second with Trajec- tory Mass Normalization (TMN), which assigns equal optimization mass to com- plete trajectories. Experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA show that both axes provide independent gains and that their combi- nation consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across model scales.

</details>


### [275] [MetaRTL: Meta-path Attention Enhanced Relational Table Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19832)
*Ken Zhong,Weichen Li,Zheng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MetaRTL is a two-stage framework for scalable and expressive relational table learning that addresses the computational limitations of deep GNN/HGNN approaches by using lightweight pre-training followed by non-parametric message passing with attention-based meta-path aggregation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing relational table learning methods rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, which lead to high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases. There is a need for a more efficient approach that can capture rich relational semantics while maintaining high scalability.

Method: MetaRTL uses a two-stage approach: (1) Lightweight pre-training to obtain initial table embeddings; (2) Non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module called MetaAttn. This design shifts computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation.

Result: Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Conclusion: MetaRTL successfully captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency by combining lightweight pre-training with efficient meta-path aggregation via the MetaAttn module.

Abstract: Relational table learning has gained increasing attention with the widespread use of relational databases. Existing methods typically rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, leading to high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases. We propose MetaRTL, a two-stage framework for scalable and expressive relational table learning. In the first stage, MetaRTL obtains initial table embeddings via lightweight pre-training. In the second stage, it performs non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module, MetaAttn. By shifting computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, MetaRTL captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

</details>


### [276] [A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19843)
*Haya Halimeh,Sascha Kaltenpoth,Kevin Bösch,Oliver Müller*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to both automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, but reasoning configuration redirects rather than reduces this susceptibility—reducing vulnerability to default nudges while increasing vulnerability to social influence nudges, with effects scaled by model size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLM behavioral biases are documented, how interface design influences AI agents acting as agents remains unknown. This study addresses whether reasoning capabilities in agents make them more robust to digital nudges embedded in GUIs originally designed for humans.

Method: Randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, testing susceptibility to automatic default nudges and reflective social influence nudges, with reasoning configuration as moderator.

Result: Agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Reasoning configuration moderated effects in opposing directions: reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening susceptibility to reflective social influence nudges. This redirection was systematically structured by model scale.

Conclusion: Extensive reasoning does not make agents more robust to nudges but redirects the route of influence. Interface design becomes a governance concern for organizations delegating decisions to autonomous agents, establishing nudge susceptibility as a key behavioral property of agentic AI.

Abstract: LLM-based GUI agents increasingly act on behalf of users in digital environments that were designed with human users in mind. These graphical user interfaces were designed to support, but also deliberately steer, the behaviour and decisions of users. While behavioural biases in the textual outputs of LLMs are well-documented, far less is known about how such influence operates when models act as agents that perceive interfaces and execute decisions---and, in particular, whether the reasoning capabilities increasingly built into these agents make them more robust to it. Drawing on Dual-Process Theory, we empirically investigate whether LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, and how their reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility. In a randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and a total of 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, we found that agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Crucially, the reasoning configuration moderated these effects in opposing directions, reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening it to reflective social influence nudges. Extensive reasoning therefore did not make agents more robust but redirected the route through which choice architecture takes effect. Exploratory analysis further showed this redirection to be systematically structured by model scale. Beyond establishing nudge susceptibility as a behavioural property of agentic AI, the study positions interface design as a governance concern for organizations that delegate decisions to autonomous agents.

</details>


### [277] [Constraint-Safe Graph-Context Scoring for Stable Point-Feature Labels Under Text-Width and Accessibility-Inspired Profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19848)
*Taimoor Ahmad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LABELSENSE-Pilot is a prototype system for point-feature label placement on interactive maps that uses a multilayer perceptron scorer over graph-context summaries, mixed-integer optimization for layout selection, and achieves 85.62% display yield with only 2.09% flicker while ensuring geometric validity (viewport containment, uniqueness, pairwise clearance). It outperforms a handcrafted-utility integer program in stability while making engineering trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current algorithmic evaluations for label placement collapse complex requirements (geometric validity, display yield, placement utility, stability across camera motion, accessibility, multilingual dimensions) into simple overlap counts, failing to capture the full complexity needed for interactive maps.

Method: The system generates eight compass candidate positions per feature, scores candidates using a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries with a previous-placement bonus, and selects layouts through mixed-integer optimization. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates across 155 countries with multiple stressor conditions (density, camera, text-suffix, preference, enlarged-font).

Result: Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot achieved 85.62% display yield, 2.09% flicker, and zero collisions. Compared to a handcrafted-utility integer program, it sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display but reduced flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, while standard geometry at 1.5x reevaluation violated 52.57% of placements.

Conclusion: The system establishes an auditable engineering trade-off between display yield and stability. The authors acknowledge limitations: human accessibility, multilingual usability, and preference studies are not addressed, and official baselines and participant evidence are required before submission.

Abstract: Point-feature label placement on interactive maps must reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability across camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements further change label dimensions, yet algorithmic evaluations often collapse these concerns into overlap counts. We present LABELSENSE-Pilot, a reproducible prototype that generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores candidates with a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus, and selects a layout through mixed-integer optimization. The executed scorer is deliberately not described as a graph transformer. Every returned layout is checked for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates and names spanning 155 countries, with country-grouped splits and generated density, camera, text-suffix, preference, and enlarged-font stressors. Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62 percent of labels with 2.09 percent flicker and zero collisions. Versus a handcrafted-utility integer program, LABELSENSE-Pilot sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display while reducing flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57 percent of selected placements. These results establish an auditable engineering trade-off, not human accessibility, multilingual usability, or preference. Official recent baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

</details>


### [278] [Reproducibility is not construct validity: LLM measurement of institutionally situated communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19866)
*Veronika Batzdorfer,Carlo Romano Marcello Alessandro Santagiustina*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper challenges the assumption that high LLM annotation reproducibility equates to valid construct measurement. Using European Commission AI Act consultation data, the authors show LLMs can produce highly reproducible annotations (ICC > 0.99) yet fail to capture the constructs they intend to measure, as measured by convergence with survey responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers aim to distinguish between annotation reproducibility and construct validity when using LLMs as measurement instruments. They argue that high reproducibility does not guarantee that LLM-inferred measures actually capture the intended construct.

Method: The study links structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders in the European Commission's AI Act consultation. LLM annotations were generated for free-text submissions, and their reproducibility was assessed via intraclass correlations. Convergence between LLM-inferred measures and survey-reported measures was evaluated. Divergence was analyzed across stakeholder groups using effect sizes (Cohen's d), and spatial autocorrelation was tested using Moran's I.

Result: LLM annotations showed extremely high reproducibility (ICC > 0.99) but limited convergence with survey-reported measures. Divergence varied systematically by stakeholder type: business associations expressed greater AI risk concern in text-based consultations than surveys (g = +1.0), while public authorities and nonbusiness groups showed smaller or negative divergences. Positive spatial autocorrelation was found across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036), indicating stakeholders from neighboring countries held similar text-based stances. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remained strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence. This motivates the need for validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.

Abstract: High annotation reproducibility does not necessarily imply that an LLM-inferred measure captures the construct it is intended to measure. We test this distinction using a dataset from the European Commission's AI Act consultation, linking structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders. LLM annotations of consultation submissions are highly reproducible (intraclass correlations > 0.99), yet show limited convergence with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct they were intended to approximate. Divergence between survey-and LLM-inferred text-based measures varies systematically across stakeholder groups: business associations express greater concern about AI risks in text-based consultations than in survey responses ({g} = +1.0), whereas public authorities and several nonbusiness groups show smaller or negative divergences. Divergences between scores suggest positive spatial autocorrelation across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036), indicating that stakeholders from neighboring countries tend toward more similar text-based stances towards AI safety concerns. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels. These results demonstrate that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence and motivate validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.

</details>


### [279] [Physical knowledge on historical data matters more than enforcing physical constraints on the forecast](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19871)
*Etienne Lehembre,Pascal Audigane,Vincent Nguyen,Christel Vrain,Thi-Bich-Hanh Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PIRNN (Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network) is proposed to predict unobservable intermediate physical variables along with target variables in time series forecasting, enhancing model robustness and interpretability using domain knowledge from physical models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting time series in physical process applications remains challenging. Existing Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand the target behavior.

Method: PIRNN integrates physical equations (from models like Gardenia for groundwater level prediction) into a recurrent neural network architecture. It predicts unobservable variables on both historic data and forecast targets, adaptable to any physical model using multiple equations with their own unobservable variable sets.

Result: PIRNN outperforms other models on 5 out of 12 real-world datasets. The ablation study demonstrates the importance of physical background in time series forecasting. Domain expert assessment confirms the coherence of predicted physical variables.

Conclusion: PIRNN successfully enhances model robustness and results interpretation by leveraging domain knowledge through physical equations. The approach is adaptable to various physical models and provides valuable insights through unobservable variable prediction.

Abstract: Time series forecasting has seen signicant advancements with the emergence of new deep learning models. However, forecasting time series in applications involving physical processes remains a major challenge. Despite the apparition of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINN), recent models do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand the target behavior. To this end, we propose a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) which predicts, along the target, unobservable variables on both historic data and forecast target. This approach enhances the model robustness and results interpretation using domain knowledge. Our method is easily adaptable to any physical model using several equations, each having its own set of unobservable variables, to describe it-self. As a case study, we incorporate physical equations used for groundwater levels predictions by the physical model called Gardenia. This model uses transfers equations between reservoirs, optimized with data assimilation, to simulate the evolution of groundwater levels. Evaluation includes several well known neural network models and the Gardenia model compared on twelve real world datasets. In addition, we study the impact of each component through an ablation study. Our model outperforms other models on ve out of the twelve datasets and our ablation study underlines the importance of having a physical background in our time series forecasting task. Finally, the coherence of the physical variables predicted by our neural network is assessed by a domain expert.

</details>


### [280] [TRACE: Accountable Agentic Retrieval for Source Discovery in Digital Archives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19897)
*Donghan Bian,Marie Puren,Florian Cafiero*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical archives, particularly for French Third Republic documents (parliamentary debates and newspapers). It achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653 on the HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic benchmark, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Historical archives present difficult retrieval challenges due to OCR-degraded documents, genre/source heterogeneity, and the need for strong source traceability for scholarly use. Existing retrieval systems struggle with these characteristics, particularly for French Third Republic parliamentary debates and press materials.

Method: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework that leverages corpus-aware agent design. It was evaluated on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, derived from Bibliothèque nationale de France digitised collections. The system was tested against sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines.

Result: TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.656 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming all baselines. Largest gains are observed on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. The system is economically feasible at approximately $0.02 per question under default hosted inference configuration.

Conclusion: For large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches. The prototype is deployed internally within the DECIDON project, accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions.

Abstract: Historical archives pose a difficult retrieval problem for retrievalaugmented generation systems: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and require strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. We introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. The system was developed in the context of DECIDON, an interdisciplinary project on the circulation of political discourse between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, involving digitised historical collections and institutional use cases. The prototype is currently deployed internally within the project and accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions. We evaluate TRACE on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents derived from Biblioth{è}que nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. At approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, TRACE also remains economically feasible for heritage institutions, laboratories or companies that cannot rely on costly local GPU infrastructure. These results suggest that, for large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches.

</details>


### [281] [From "Who Is This User?" to "What Does This Purchase Mean?": A Deployed Pipeline for Semantic User Profiling at Bank Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19928)
*Ryota Mitsuhashi,Tetsuro Morimura,Hirotake Ito*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a novel approach to reduce LLM inference costs for user transaction profiling by shifting from per-user to per-transaction-pattern inference. The three-phase pipeline (Resolve, Profile, Tag) achieves comparable accuracy to per-user LLM while reducing inference targets by nearly three orders of magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The per-user LLM inference approach scales linearly with user count, becoming prohibitively expensive at applied scale (tens of millions of users). The authors sought to reduce the inference budget from O(users) to O(pattern count).

Method: Three-phase pipeline: (1) Resolve - abstracts item names with optional web grounding; (2) Profile - single LLM call per pattern emits categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates; (3) Tag - clusters free-text attributes into queryable database. The key insight is running inference over patterns rather than users.

Result: On Open e-commerce corpus, the database achieves statistically indistinguishable AUC from per-user LLM across evaluated attributes. Prevalence estimates show discriminative signal between positive/negative users. Deployed at major Japanese bank with ~1000x reduction in LLM inference targets.

Conclusion: Per-pattern LLM inference is a practical solution for large-scale user profiling, achieving comparable accuracy to per-user approaches while dramatically reducing computational costs, enabling deployment at banking scale.

Abstract: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories binds the inference budget linearly to user count, which becomes prohibitive at applied scale. We re-cast attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern. The pipeline runs in three phases: Resolve abstracts item names with optional web grounding, Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern, and Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. In Profile, a single LLM call per pattern emits predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates. Because inference runs over patterns rather than users, the budget grows with the pattern count rather than the user count. On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user's raw history directly in AUC across the evaluated attributes, and the prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. The pipeline is deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling on the order of tens of millions of users, with close to a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/CyberAgentAILab/profiling-agent-open-ecommerce.

</details>


### [282] [Beyond Depth Truncation: Controlled Evaluation of Depth Utilization in Recursive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19934)
*Ha Van Dau,Thanh Tung Khuat,Nguyen Thanh Dung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current depth evaluation methods for recurrent language models conflate three distinct factors (block applications, computation volume, readout position), yielding misleading slopes. The Depth Control Protocol (DCP) is proposed to disentangle these factors through controlled experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard evaluation practice of truncating depth at inference time and measuring quality degradation produces a single slope that is conventionally interpreted as reflecting "depth utilization," but this slope actually conflates three separate model properties changed simultaneously by depth truncation.

Method: The paper proposes the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite with five components: (1) three positive controls that isolate each confounded factor while varying others, (2) a negative control applying identical interventions to dense transformers, and (3) a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The key "linchpin control" runs the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, which is only realizable in weight-sharing architectures.

Result: Not provided in abstract - this is a methodology paper proposing a diagnostic protocol.

Conclusion: The conventional depth evaluation metric is fundamentally flawed because it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties. DCP provides a proper disentangled analysis, with the linchpin control being strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures where repeating a layer yields the same model in an alternative configuration rather than a different model.

Abstract: Depth-recurrent language models iteratively apply a small layer stack, decoupling per-token compute from distinct parameter count. To determine whether such a model genuinely utilizes its depth, both recurrence and layer-pruning literatures rely on a shared evaluation: truncating depth at inference time, plotting quality against retained depth fraction, and reading off the slope. While cheap and training-free, this metric suffers from an unexamined flaw: it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties simultaneously. Depth truncation concurrently reduces the number of block applications, decreases the volume of distinct computation performed, and pushes the readout head onto an out-of-distribution residual stream. The observed slope conflates all three factors, yet is conventionally interpreted as reflecting solely the second.
  We propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite that disentangles these three quantities. DCP comprises three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying the identical interventions to dense transformers to ensure the effect is not an artifact of the measurement protocol, and a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The linchpin control, running the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures, since in a dense network repeating a layer yields an entirely different model rather than the same model in an alternative configuration.

</details>


### [283] [MaSCoD: A Multi-Agent Framework for Structural-Context-Guided Candidate Causal Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19944)
*Yudai Nakada,Yuichiro Nishiura,Jin Michael Splichal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MaSCoD is a multi-agent LLM framework for causal discovery that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. It shows dataset- and backbone-dependent performance, with the Full approach outperforming No Phase 1 in Recall and F1 but with increased false-positive rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based causal discovery methods rarely treat premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a framework that organizes structural information before direct-edge judgment.

Method: MaSCoD organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. The study compares Full (supplies structural hypotheses before judgment) versus No Phase 1 (constructs hypotheses within judgment procedure) across six dataset-backbone settings using GPT-5.4 and GPT-4o on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs datasets.

Result: Full achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1 across all six settings, but also increased false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, but not uniformly. Supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, the retention gap was present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs.

Conclusion: Structural pre-organization should be an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control in LLM-based causal discovery. The study motivates evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment, rather than treating them separately.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to causal discovery, but candidate-graph generation rarely treats premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. We propose MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. We evaluate MaSCoD on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication. MaSCoD exhibits a dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. Across all six dataset-backbone settings, Full, which supplies structural hypotheses before direct-edge judgment, achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1, which instead constructs them within the judgment procedure, while also increasing false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention over all evaluated baselines was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, rather than uniformly across settings. Partial ablations showed that supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, stage-wise analysis showed that the Full-No Phase 1 retention gap was already present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs. These findings support structural pre-organization as an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control and motivate evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment.

</details>


### [284] [Not All AI Agents Are Equal: Characterizing Resource and Performance Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19947)
*Wonmi Choi,Minuk Park,Zhixiong Niu,Yongqiang Xiong,Chuck Yoo,Gyeongsik Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes resource dynamics of LLM-based AI agents across three representative tasks (retrieval-augmented QA, web search, software coding). It reveals that agents exhibit diverse behaviors depending on tasks, and concurrent request processing exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in CPU, disk I/O, and memory. The authors propose CPU-aware optimization techniques achieving 5.4× improvement for CPU-sensitive tasks and 32% average latency reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The current agent ecosystem runs without consideration of resource dynamics, leading to significant waste of precious resources. The execution model involving iterative reasoning and tool execution with remote LLM APIs and local tool containers makes optimization difficult due to inter-mixed latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks across requests.

Method: The authors characterize latency with respect to resource dynamics when processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently. They study three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. Based on observations, they demonstrate optimization opportunities including CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation.

Result: Key findings: (1) Agents have wide range of behaviors depending on tasks; (2) Same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics; (3) Running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in CPU, disk I/O, and memory; (4) Faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Optimization results: CPU-sensitive agent tasks improve ~5.4×, average latency across multiple tasks reduced ~32% compared to native agents.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that resource dynamics are crucial for AI agent optimization. Task-aware resource allocation strategies can significantly improve performance. The proposed CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation techniques effectively address the bottlenecks in concurrent agent processing.

Abstract: LLM-based AI agents process user requests through iterative reasoning and tool execution, often involving the invocation of remote LLM APIs with local tool containers. This execution model can make the optimization of agent serving difficult because latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks inter-mix across requests. However, the current agent ecosystem runs without much consideration of resource dynamics, which results in significant waste of the precious resources. This paper analyzes the resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. To this end, we characterize the latency with respect to the resource dynamics of processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently. Our measurements show that agents have a wide range of behaviors depending on tasks, so that even the same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics. We also find that running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in resource dynamics such as CPU, disk I/O, and memory. Furthermore, we uncover that faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Based on these observations, we demonstrate new optimization opportunities that exploit the resource dynamics of tasks: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation. Our results show that the latency of CPU-sensitive agent tasks improves $\sim$5.4$\times$, and the average latency across multiple tasks is reduced $\sim$32% compared to native agents.

</details>


### [285] [Neuro-Symbolic Agentic AI for Networked Low-Altitude UAVs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19961)
*Yuqi Ping,Tianhao Liang,Nanchi Su,Guangyu Lei,Junwei Wu,Qinyu Zhang,Tingting Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework to enhance reliability and adaptability of networked low-altitude UAVs, addressing challenges of uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity. The approach integrates neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction through a reference architecture, demonstrated in an urban fire-inspection case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Networked low-altitude UAVs face significant challenges including uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity. Existing agentic systems suffer from hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization, limiting their reliability and adaptability for autonomous UAV operations.

Method: The paper develops a reference architecture integrating five key components: (1) task and goal management, (2) neuro-symbolic planning, (3) verification and metacognition, (4) skill execution and network interaction, and (5) shared knowledge and memory. The framework leverages data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer capabilities. An urban fire-inspection case is implemented in LAESim to demonstrate UAV coordination under intermittent connectivity.

Result: The case study demonstrates that a UAV can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse verified image-delivery skills, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before mission completion. The approach shows potential for reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems.

Conclusion: NSAAI offers a promising framework for UAV autonomy by combining neural and symbolic approaches. Key research directions include uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation. The framework addresses critical limitations of existing agentic systems and enables more reliable and adaptive UAV operations in complex environments.

Abstract: Networked low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) need reliable and adaptive decision-making capabilities to operate under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity, while many existing agentic systems remain limited by hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. This article investigates neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework for combining neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction to support more reliable and adaptive UAV autonomy. We first examine its capability foundations in data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer, and then develop a reference architecture integrating task and goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution and network interaction, and shared knowledge and memory. An urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim illustrates how a UAV can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before completing the mission. The results illustrate the potential of NSAAI to support reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems. We further discuss key research directions in uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

</details>


### [286] [Customizable and Jointly Optimized Route Planning: A Deep Architecture Enabling Differentiable Shortest-Path Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19996)
*Rui Zhao,Chao Chen,Longfei Xu,Chenguang Ji,Hengbin Cui,Kaikui Liu,Xiaolong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a deep learning architecture for optimal route planning in navigation and ride-hailing services. The method uses multi-objective Dijkstra to generate Pareto optimal routes, then trains a neural network to emulate shortest-path search in an end-to-end differentiable manner. A novel constrained optimization loss function is used to handle diverse user preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classic graph algorithms lack optimality guarantees when using heuristic cost functions, while prior data-driven approaches suffer from feedback loop problems by equating optimal routes with user trajectories that are influenced by navigation services.

Method: 1) Run multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect Pareto optimal routes as candidate set. 2) Design a neural network that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. 3) Define route preference as constrained optimization and propose a novel loss function optimizing a single objective while keeping others under constraints.

Result: The proposed architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability on real-world datasets.

Conclusion: The joint optimization of cost functions and route-ranking model enables flexible handling of diverse user preferences while maintaining optimality guarantees through the Pareto optimal candidate set.

Abstract: With the widespread use of online navigation and ride-hailing services, achieving optimal route planning for diverse user preferences has recently attracted increasing attention. Classic graph algorithms for pathfinding use heuristic cost functions to define edge weight, thus providing no optimality guarantee of route quality. Prior data-driven approaches equating ground truth of the optimal route with user trajectory, which is however moderately influenced by the navigation service, suffers from the feedback loop problem. To address these issues, we propose a deep architecture that is able to jointly optimize cost functions and route-ranking model towards any route preference. First, we run a multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect the set of Pareto optimal routes, deeming it as the complete candidate set. Exploiting the property of such a set, we design a neural network structure that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Second, we define route preference as a task of constrained optimization of route attributes, and propose a novel loss function that optimizes a single-objective variable, with other variables strictly under constraints. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results show that our architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.

</details>


### [287] [E-AVI: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Assessment for Automated Video Interviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20001)
*Haoshen Wang,Dongbo Che,Zeyi Xie,Yuanjie Du,Shicheng Hua,Xingyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: E-AVI is an evidence-grounded framework for automated video interview assessment that provides timestamped multimodal evidence to support numerical predictions, enabling inspectable evaluation, natural-language feedback, and follow-up question answering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional automated video interview assessment systems provide numerical predictions without sufficient inspectable support, limiting their practical utility and transparency for recruiters and candidates.

Method: E-AVI extracts timestamped multimodal evidence (verbal content, acoustic delivery, visual behavior) and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings. A shared evidence pool supports natural-language feedback generation and QA.

Result: E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation on RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses confirm the predictive contribution, grounding quality, and practical utility of the evidence pathway.

Conclusion: The E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis, advancing the transparency and practical applicability of automated video interview assessment systems.

Abstract: Automated video interview assessment integrates verbal content, acoustic delivery, and visual behavior, yet numerical predictions alone provide limited inspectable support. We present E-AVI, an evidence-grounded framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring. A shared evidence pool further supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering. On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses characterize the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility of the evidence pathway. Together, these results demonstrate that our proposed E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

</details>


### [288] [Geopolitical Divisions Across Languages in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20005)
*Maxim Chupilkin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study investigates whether AI chatbots (GPT, Claude, Gemini) provide different political answers when asked about the war in Ukraine in different languages. Testing 20 statements across 112 languages (67,200 responses), the researchers found that language choice affects the political leanings of AI responses, with patterns correlating to countries' geopolitical positions (public opinion of Russia, UN voting, aid to Ukraine).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses growing concerns about AI systems as news sources and potential vectors for information warfare. The motivation is to investigate whether AI models exhibit language-dependent political biases that could reflect and amplify geopolitical divisions.

Method: The researchers asked three major AI chatbots (GPT, Claude, Gemini) to evaluate 20 statements about the war in Ukraine in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. They grouped responses by countries' official languages and correlated them with public opinion data, UN voting records, and aid to Ukraine.

Result: The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. Responses grouped by countries' official languages correlate with geopolitical positions: more Russia-leaning answers correspond to countries with more favorable views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in UN votes, and less aid to Ukraine. This pattern appears across all three AI models and remains consistent when individual statement pairs are removed.

Conclusion: The findings suggest a potential pathway for information warfare: biases in training data may be reflected in AI outputs, which could then spread geopolitical biases across different language communities. This raises concerns about AI systems as sources of news and political information.

Abstract: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events. But do they receive the same political answers when they ask in different languages? Here we show that the language of a question can change how the same AI systems assess the war in Ukraine. We ask GPT, Claude and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When we group responses by countries' official languages, they follow a pattern resembling worldwide political divisions: relatively more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in United Nations votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The broad pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed. Our findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.

</details>


### [289] [FedeRICo: Federated Region-Influenced Coupling for Traffic Flow Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20026)
*Fermin Orozco,Man Luo,Johan Wahlström*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedeRICo is a federated traffic forecasting framework that addresses client heterogeneity and broken cross-client spatial dependencies through dual-branch architecture with gradient alignment and boundary-aware residual communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban traffic forecasting requires data from multiple stakeholders who cannot share raw data due to privacy/commercial constraints. Existing federated methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) parameter aggregation dilutes client-specific representations across heterogeneous graph domains, and (2) road network partitioning breaks propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries.

Method: FedeRICo employs a dual-branch forecasting architecture: (1) a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimization without destructive parameter interference; (2) a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. Cross-client spatial dependencies are recovered by extracting boundary messages through trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients.

Result: Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

Conclusion: FedeRICo successfully addresses the challenges of federated traffic forecasting by combining gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication, preserving both client-specific representations and cross-client spatial dependencies.

Abstract: Urban traffic forecasting often relies on information distributed across stakeholders who may be unable to share raw data due to privacy or commercial constraints, motivating federated spatial-temporal approaches.
