In such federated settings, each client observes traffic over a distinct sensor subgraph with its own spatial topology and temporal dynamics, leading to significant heterogeneity across clients. Existing federated spatial-temporal methods typically rely on model parameter aggregation and provide limited mechanisms for recovering spatial dependencies across client boundaries. This introduces two key limitations. Specifically, parameter aggregation across heterogeneous graph domains tends to dilute client-specific representations, while road network partitioning breaks the propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose FedeRICo, a federated traffic forecasting framework that combines gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication. FedeRICo employs a dual-branch forecasting architecture in which a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, while a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. The global branch is coordinated through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimisation without destructive parameter interference. To recover cross-client spatial dependencies, boundary messages are extracted through a trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients. Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

</details>


### [290] [Can Data Attribution Filter Out Subliminal Learning? Not Reliably](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20027)
*Moritz Weckbecker,Sweta Jena,Jonas Müller,Ponnurangam Kumaraguru,Sebastian Lapuschkin,Wojciech Samek,Louis Jaburi,Gonçalo Paulo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates gradient-based training data attribution methods (GradCos, contrastive GradCos, and EK-FAC) as a defense against subliminal learning in language models, where models acquire behavioral traits from training data without obvious semantic signals. These methods are compared against divergence tokens, a stronger baseline requiring counterfactual teacher models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Subliminal learning allows language models to transmit behavioral traits through training data that lacks obvious semantic relationships to those traits, undermining content-based filtering as a safety intervention. Training data attribution offers an alternative approach that identifies training examples responsible for model behavior independent of semantic content.

Method: The researchers evaluated three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models, comparing them against divergence tokens as a baseline. They tested both token-level and sample-level filtering approaches to mitigate subliminal learning effects.

Result: Token-level filtering with EK-FAC mitigated a significant portion of the subliminal learning effect, while other methods provided minimal benefit. All methods mostly fell short of divergence tokens. Sample-level filtering was less effective for every method, though EK-FAC often provided a stronger signal than divergence tokens in this setting. Success was inconsistent across methods and settings, with variants working well for some model-preference combinations failing for others.

Conclusion: Gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but reliability varies significantly. Some approximations (particularly EK-FAC) are more reliable than others, but no consistent explanation was found for why certain methods work better for specific model-preference combinations. More research is needed to understand and improve these attribution methods.

Abstract: Subliminal learning allows language models to transmit behavioral traits through training data with no obvious semantic relationship to those traits, undermining content-based data filtering as a safety intervention. Training data attribution offers an alternative: it identifies the training examples responsible for a given model behavior, independent of their semantic content, and so may apply in exactly the cases where semantic inspection fails. We evaluate three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models, comparing them against divergence tokens, a strong baseline previously shown to localize subliminal learning (albeit one that requires access to counterfactual teacher models). Filtering at the token level, EK-FAC mitigates a significant part of the effect, the other methods provide little benefit, and all mostly fall short of divergence tokens. Filtering entire samples is less effective for every method, though EK-FAC often gives a stronger signal than divergence tokens in this setting. Success is inconsistent across methods and settings: variants that work well for some model-preference combinations fail for others, and we do not identify a consistent explanation for these differences. Our results suggest that gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but that some approximations are more reliable than others.

</details>


### [291] [DART: Distillation-Aware Reparameterization for Training-Free LoRA Reuse in Few-Step Video Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20051)
*Shihong Li,Juntao Xu,JinCao,Maowen Tang,Jun Huang,Jintao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DART is a training-free method that addresses the problem of reusing LoRA adapters trained for longer video generation trajectories when applying them to shorter (distilled) denoising schedules. It combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration to preserve functional behavior while improving quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Step distillation reduces video generation costs, but reusing LoRA adapters trained for longer trajectories on shortened schedules can alter functional effects or degrade quality. Existing approaches assume static parameter compatibility, but the authors observe that similar measured geometry can coexist with different adapter behaviors under shortened denoising schedules.

Method: DART combines two components: (1) Low-rank coordinate transport for parameter adaptation, and (2) Target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations. The method requires no source training videos and is training-free. It focuses on joint evaluation through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance.

Result: On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F improves joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and changes macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Component analysis shows calibration accounts for most quality improvement, while coordinate transport provides complementary gains when combined. Adapter-level results show positive functional effects for some adapters and strong attenuation with reduced negative functional effects for others. The same trend holds on two additional targets.

Conclusion: The results motivate evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, without assuming recovery for every adapter. This represents a shift from assuming parameter compatibility to actively measuring and correcting functional behavior.

Abstract: Step distillation reduces the cost of video generation, but reusing a LoRA trained for a longer trajectory can alter its functional effect or degrade target quality. Static parameter compatibility offers one perspective on this problem; our observations show that similar measured geometry can coexist with different adapter behavior under a shortened denoising schedule. We propose DART, a training-free method that combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations and no source training videos. On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F improves the joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and changes macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Component analysis shows that calibration accounts for most of the quality improvement, while coordinate transport provides complementary gains when combined with calibration. Adapter-level results reveal positive functional effects for some adapters and strong attenuation with reduced negative functional effects for others. Evaluations on two additional targets show the same aggregate trend. These results motivate evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, without assuming recovery for every adapter.

</details>


### [292] [MAGMA-GEN: Validated Recovery Supervision from Ambiguous Failures via Counterfactual Re-Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20056)
*Loan Bernat,Matthieu Grard,Ariane Herbulot,Florent Lamiraux*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAGMA-GEN is an on-policy data-generation pipeline for hierarchical robotic systems that converts ambiguous failed rollouts into validated recovery supervision, using a privileged coach to hypothesize decision-level errors and propose corrections, retaining only validated recovery actions through re-execution testing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hierarchical robotic systems executing long-horizon manipulation tasks face ambiguous failed rollouts where poor downstream states may stem from invalid high-level decisions, partial observation, or execution failures. Existing supervised learning lacks recovery state data, while reinforcement learning struggles with sparse rewards and non-local credit assignment.

Method: MAGMA-GEN uses a privileged coach to hypothesize early decision-level errors and propose localized correction or recovery actions. Candidates are retained only if re-execution from the same state under matched conditions improves downstream progress, producing supervised examples from the agent's own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations.

Result: MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities against distillation and trajectory-repair baselines under evolving task constraints, validated in both simulation and real-robot execution.

Conclusion: MAGMA-GEN effectively addresses the challenge of learning from ambiguous failures in hierarchical robotic systems by generating validated recovery supervision from the agent's own failure distribution, enabling improved performance on long-horizon manipulation tasks without requiring human demonstrations.

Abstract: Hierarchical robotic systems executing long-horizon manipulation tasks must make high-level semantic decisions that orchestrate stochastic low-level skills. In this setting, failed rollouts are ambiguous: a poor downstream state may reflect an invalid high-level decision, partial observation, or a valid decision whose physical execution failed. Traditional supervised learning lacks data for such recovery states, while reinforcement learning struggles with sparse rewards and non-local credit assignment. We propose MAGMA-GEN, an on-policy data-generation pipeline that converts ambiguous failed rollouts into validated recovery supervision. MAGMA-GEN first uses a privileged coach to hypothesize an early decision-level error and propose localized correction or recovery actions. Because this diagnosis is fallible, candidates are retained only if re-execution from the same state under matched conditions improves downstream progress. This produces supervised examples from the agent's own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations. Evaluated on interactive long-horizon manipulation tasks, MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities, against distillation and trajectory-repair baselines under evolving task constraints in both simulation and real-robot execution.

</details>


### [293] [WiCleanData: Guaranteeing the Type Consistency of Wikidata by Taxonomy Refinement and Constraint Enforcement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20057)
*Yiwen Peng,Marc Jeanmougin,Thomas Bonald*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WiCleanData is an automated pipeline that cleans Wikidata by fixing taxonomy issues and removing type constraint violations, producing a refined knowledge graph available via web interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wikidata's collaborative nature introduces errors, inconsistencies, and excessive complexity including redundant classes, instance-class ambiguity, wrong taxonomic paths, and type constraint violations. Manual curation is infeasible at scale.

Method: An automated three-stage pipeline: (1) taxonomy cleaning using language model assistance, (2) type constraint simplification via hierarchical aggregation, and (3) fact filtering to remove violations.

Result: A refined version of Wikidata with consistent taxonomy and zero type constraint violations, publicly accessible through a web interface for exploration and downstream applications.

Conclusion: WiCleanData provides a clean, reliable knowledge graph that addresses Wikidata's quality issues at scale, enabling easier exploration and more reliable downstream applications.

Abstract: Because of its collaborative nature, Wikidata suffers from errors, in- consistencies, and excessive complexity, such as redundant classes, ambiguity between instances and classes, wrong taxonomic paths, and type constraint violations. The manual curation of these issues is infeasible at scale. To address these challenges, we introduce WiCleanData, a refined version of Wikidata with a consistent tax- onomy and free from type constraint violations. Specifically, we have designed an automated pipeline that first cleans the taxonomy with language model assistance, then simplifies type constraints by hierarchical aggregation, and finally filters facts accordingly. The resulting knowledge graph, free from any type violation, is made publicly available via a Web interface, enabling easy exploration and downstream applications.

</details>


### [294] [FCA-Guided Counterfactual Explanations for Multi-Modal Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Framework Achieving Perfect Validity with Emergent Sparsity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20067)
*Abdullahi Isa,Souley Boukari,Muhammad Aliyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes FCA-CF, a counterfactual explanation framework for multi-modal breast cancer diagnosis that uses Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) concept lattice as a structural constraint. It achieves superior performance: 100% validity, sparsity of 2.37 features changed, and proximity of 0.900, while being the sparsest and most proximate valid method among benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep learning models for breast cancer diagnosis lack actionable counterfactual explanations. Attribution-based methods (LIME, SHAP) cannot generate alternative instances and thus cannot be evaluated on counterfactual quality metrics. There is a need for genuine counterfactual methods that provide actionable, interpretable explanations.

Method: The FCA-CF framework uses Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) concept lattice as a hard structural constraint on counterfactual search, operating over a multi-modal TCGA-BRCA dataset. It is benchmarked against four genuine counterfactual methods: Wachter-style CF, DiCE, FACE, and NICE, evaluated on 60 benign-predicted TCGA-BRCA instances. Ablation analysis is performed to identify the contribution of different components.

Result: The FCA-CF framework achieves Validity = 1.0000 (100% flip prediction), Sparsity = 2.37 features changed (best among all valid methods), and Proximity = 0.900 (tied with NICE as best). The classifier achieves Accuracy = 0.980, F1 = 0.976, ROC-AUC = 0.9947. Ablation shows the FCA lattice constraint is the primary sparsity driver (removing it increases sparsity by +40%, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.78), while Phase C greedy refinement accounts for +113% sparsity increase when disabled (p < 0.001, d = 5.01).

Conclusion: FCA-guided counterfactual generation achieves a clinically important Pareto-dominant outcome: simultaneously the sparsest and among the most proximate of all valid methods, with perfect validity. The emergent sparsity property arising from lattice topology rather than numerical penalty terms constitutes a structurally novel contribution to the counterfactual explanation literature.

Abstract: Deep learning models for multi-modal breast cancer diagnosis achieve high predictive accuracy but remain clinically unacceptable without actionable, counterfactual explanations. Attribution-based methods (LIME, SHAP) are categorically inapplicable to this purpose, as they generate no alternative instances and thus cannot be evaluated on counterfactual quality metrics. This investigation provides empirical evidence that FCA-Guided Counterfactual (FCA-CF) framework that uses a Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) concept lattice as a hard structural constraint on counterfactual search, operating over a multi-modal TCGA-BRCA dataset. We benchmark against four genuine counterfactual methods: Wachter-style CF, DiCE, FACE, and NICE, evaluated on 60 benign-predicted TCGA-BRCA instances. The FCA-CF framework achieves Validity = 1.0000 (100% of counterfactuals successfully flip the prediction), Sparsity = 2.37 features changed (best among all valid methods), and Proximity = 0.900 (normalised L2-based, matching NICE as joint best). The classifier achieves Accuracy = 0.980, F1 = 0.976, ROC-AUC = 0.9947. Ablation analysis confirms that the FCA lattice constraint is the primary sparsity driver (removing it increases sparsity by +40%, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.78), while Phase C greedy refinement accounts for the largest individual contribution (+113% sparsity increase when disabled, p < 0.001, d = 5.01). FCA-guided counterfactual generation achieves a clinically important Pareto-dominant outcome; it is simultaneously the sparsest and among the most proximate of all valid methods, with perfect validity. The emergent sparsity property arising from lattice topology rather than numerical penalty terms constitutes a structurally novel contribution to the counterfactual explanation literature.

</details>


### [295] [Marginal utility, matrix factorization, and the Key-Value (KV) cache: a unified information-economic framework for sovereign geo-mining inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20068)
*Caroline Gans Combe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper bridges economic marginal utility theory with machine learning (matrix factorization and KV cache in transformers), showing these are mathematically equivalent to constrained utility maximization. It applies this framework to geo-mining document extraction, achieving 90% accuracy with 2.62ms latency using an 11.2M parameter model trained in 5 minutes. A diagnostic reveals a degenerate mode in TIES merging that can be fixed with layer-wise calibrated densities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to unify economic utility theory with machine learning constructs, viewing model compression, cache eviction, and dimension selection through the lens of constrained utility maximization under budget constraints (memory, computational).

Method: Theoretical analysis connecting singular value spectrum to marginal utility schedules, eigenvalue spectra to representation utility, and cache operations to constrained optimization. Empirical validation using an 11.2M parameter hierarchical classifier on uranium-exploration corpus with TIES model merging and layer-wise calibration.

Result: The 11.2M parameter model achieves 90.0% level-1 accuracy (vs 92.0% for proprietary model) with 2.62ms latency vs ~2000ms for API. Uniform-density TIES merging produces a degenerate mode (identical outputs across 5 districts with high confidence), which is corrected by layer-wise calibrated densities.

Conclusion: The marginal utility framework provides a unified allocation rule for dimension retention and cache management. The approach enables efficient extraction with minimal computational cost, though the full-scale benchmark remains projected. The degenerate mode in TIES merging is reproducible and fixable through calibration.

Abstract: This paper builds a theoretical bridge between the economic notion of marginal utility and two machine-learning constructs, matrix factorization and the Key--Value cache of transformer language models. The singular value spectrum of a rating matrix is shown to be a diminishing marginal utility schedule for latent factors, the eigenvalue spectrum of the projected covariance operator to be the marginal utility schedule of a model's learned representation, and cache eviction and low-rank cache compression to be instances of constrained utility maximization under a memory budget. The three collapse into a single allocation rule: retain the top dimensions whose eigenvalue exceeds the shadow price of the binding constraint. The framework is applied to the automated extraction of structured information from geo-mining documents, where it motivates a multi-pass inference protocol, a layer-wise TIES model merging procedure, and a selection policy combining extraction quality, localization drift and energy, scalarized with a Conditional Value-at-Risk term on drift. Two empirical contributions are reported. An 11.2-million-parameter hierarchical classifier, trained in about five minutes on a single GPU, reaches 90.0 per cent level-1 accuracy on a held-out test set from a 973-document uranium-exploration corpus, against 92.0 per cent for a proprietary model on a fifty-document human audit of the same corpus, at a latency of 2.62 ms per card against approximately 2,000 ms for the API and at negligible cost. A diagnostic of uniform-density TIES merging exposes a reproducible degenerate mode in which the merged model returns token-identical outputs across five geographically distinct districts while declaring high confidence; re-executing the merge under layer-wise calibrated densities removes that signature on the diagnostic sample. The full-scale extraction benchmark, including LoRA fine-tuning, is reported as projected rather than measured and remains an empirical extension of this work.

</details>


### [296] [Tailored to you: longitudinal effects of personalising language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20077)
*Canfer Akbulut,Justine Breuch,Arianna Manzini,Lujain Ibrahim,Matija Franklin,Roma Patel,Iason Gabriel,Kristian Lum,Laura Weidinger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study investigates the downstream effects of sustained interactions with personalized vs. non-personalized language models on user behavior, attitudes, and self-perceptions over 5 days with 992 participants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While personalized language models are rapidly developing, the effects of sustained interactions on users' self-perceptions, interpersonal relationships, and behavior outside the immediate human-AI interaction remain poorly understood. This research addresses this critical gap.

Method: A 5-day longitudinal study with 992 participants who completed daily advice-seeking interactions with language models under three conditions: (1) non-personalized baseline, (2) memory-based personalisation (conditioned on prior conversational history), and (3) survey-based personalisation (conditioned on pre-study intake survey information).

Result: Repeated exposure, rather than personalisation itself, drives several changes in human-AI interaction over time. However, personalisation approaches produce distinct effects: memory-based condition led to greater self-disclosure and lower "creepiness" ratings; survey-based condition resulted in higher regret about sharing personal information.

Conclusion: Different personalisation approaches have nuanced and sometimes opposing effects on user outcomes. The findings highlight the importance of responsible design and deployment of personalized AI systems, considering how personalisation methods (memory-based vs. survey-based) impact user trust, disclosure behavior, and regret.

Abstract: Interest in developing personalised language models is rapidly growing. While personalisation is often viewed as a mechanism to better serve diverse user needs, the effects of sustained interactions with personalised models on people's perception of and behaviour toward AI remain poorly understood. Most critically, downstream consequences outside the immediate human--AI interaction loop, such as effects on users' self-perceptions and interpersonal relationships, remain largely unexamined. In this study, we recruited 992 participants to complete daily advice-seeking interactions with language models over the course of five days, comparing outcomes from a non-personalised baseline against two personalisation approaches: memory-based (conditioned on prior conversational history) and survey-based (conditioned on information collected through a pre-study intake survey). We find that several changes in human-AI interaction over time are driven primarily by repeated exposure rather than personalisation itself. However, participants interacting with personalised models experienced differences in advice-seeking and information-sharing attitudes and behaviours: participants in the memory-based condition engaged in greater self-disclosure and rated the model as less creepy, while participants in the survey-based condition reported higher regret about having shared personal information with the AI. We conclude by highlighting the nuanced effects of different personalisation approaches on interaction outcomes, and discussing the implications of these findings for the responsible design and deployment of personalised AI systems.

</details>


### [297] [A Proposal for an Agentic AI Architecture to Support Multi-Domain Decision-Making in the Brazilian Armed Forces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20080)
*Gioliano de Oliveira Braga,Sidnei Barbieri,Ágney Lopes Roth Ferraz,Wagner Comin Sonaglio,Henrique Curi de Miranda e Lourenço Alves Pereira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes an Agentic AI architecture for multi-domain defense operations, enabling autonomous planning, data access, and decision support across Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, Air Force) to address OODA loop bottlenecks in complex operational environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The growing complexity of multi-domain operations (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, EMS) has overwhelmed C2 centers with data volume and velocity, straining the OODA decision cycle. Current AI tools are reactive, isolated, and heavily dependent on human operators for information integration and decision-making.

Method: The paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture with four application fronts: decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion. It outlines data/sensor access requirements and security/permission safeguards for deployment across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.

Result: A conceptual Agentic AI architecture designed for autonomous planning, tool execution, and audible action across all three Brazilian Armed Forces, with defined application fronts and security frameworks.

Conclusion: Agentic AI can transform defense decision-making from reactive to proactive, but requires robust security safeguards and permission controls for responsible multi-domain employment across military contexts.

Abstract: The growing complexity of multi-domain operational environments (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, and electromagnetic spectrum) has increased the volume and velocity of data reaching command-and-control (C2) centers, straining the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) decision cycle. Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems currently employed in defense are, in general, reactive and isolated tools that still rely heavily on human operators to integrate information, assess scenarios, and formulate courses of action. This paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture for AI systems that can plan, access data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously and audibly, aimed at supporting decision-making across the three Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, and Air Force). Four application fronts are discussed (decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion), as well as the data and sensor access requirements and the security and permission safeguards necessary for responsible employment across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.

</details>


### [298] [UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20089)
*Wenjie Liao,Liangjie Zhao,Zehong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UnifiedPlayers is a cooperative framework with three specialized players (Planning, Execution, Evaluation) that jointly adapt trajectory generation and evaluation for tool-using agents, outperforming prior methods by 3.5%+ on mathematical reasoning and 3.9% on general reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-evolving methods for tool-using agents separate trajectory generation from evaluation, relying on static verifiers that cannot adapt to emerging failure modes. This creates a coordination challenge when jointly adapting planning, execution, and evaluation.

Method: UnifiedPlayers uses role-specific rewards to coordinate three players (Planning Player generates tasks, Execution Player produces multi-turn trajectories with Python tool calls, Evaluation Player constructs executable verifiers) under Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Result: Outperforms strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5% on mathematical reasoning and 3.9% on general reasoning tasks across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks. The learned verifier achieves 84.2% adversarial detection accuracy with 2.03× higher per-question variance than self-consistency baseline.

Conclusion: Cooperation among specialized players offers a promising path toward self-enhanced tool-integrated agents, with the adaptive verifier providing more discriminative feedback than static alternatives.

Abstract: Self-evolving methods reduce the need for human-annotated trajectories by allowing tool-using agents to generate their own training data. Yet existing methods typically separate trajectory generation from evaluation, relying on static verifiers that cannot adapt to emerging failure modes or self-consistency signals that may reinforce errors shared across trajectories. Jointly adapting planning, execution, and evaluation offers a promising alternative, but introduces a fundamental coordination challenge: each component continuously changes the data or feedback used to train the others. We address this challenge with \textbf{UnifiedPlayers}, a cooperative framework comprising a Planning Player that generates tasks, an Execution Player that produces multi-turn trajectories with Python tool calls, and an Evaluation Player that constructs executable verifiers. We design role-specific rewards that coordinate the three players toward a shared learning objective under GRPO. Across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers outperforms the strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5\% on mathematical reasoning and 3.9\% on general reasoning tasks. Moreover, the learned verifier achieves 84.2\% adversarial detection accuracy, while its reward signal exhibits 2.03$\times$ higher per-question variance than a self-consistency baseline, providing more discriminative verifications. These results highlight cooperation among specialized players as a promising path toward self-enhanced tool-integrated agents.

</details>


### [299] [Solving Minimum Span Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20091)
*Hieu Truong Xuan,Khanh To Van*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces and solves the Minimum Span Antibandwidth/Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling (MSABL/MSCABL) problems using a unified SAT-based framework. The approach treats these problems as sequences of decision problems and exploits their monotonicity. Two strategies are evaluated: parallel SAT solving (multiple candidate spans concurrently) and incremental SAT solving (progressively restricting label domain). The methods are competitive with CPLEX and Gurobi, with parallel approach best for MSCABL and incremental for MSABL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The traditional perspective on Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth problems focuses on maximizing the minimum distance between adjacent vertices. However, the complementary perspective - fixing a minimum distance and minimizing label span - has received little attention. This paper aims to fill this gap by introducing and solving MSABL/MSCABL problems.

Method: The paper develops a unified Boolean Satisfiability (SAT)-based framework that formulates MSABL/MSCABL as sequences of decision problems, exploiting their monotonicity to accelerate search. Two SAT solving strategies are compared: (1) Parallel SAT solving - examining multiple candidate spans concurrently, and (2) Incremental SAT solving - reusing a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain. Results are evaluated on benchmark instances from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection.

Result: SAT-based approaches are highly competitive in solution quality. The parallel approach performs best overall for MSCABL, while the incremental approach performs best for MSABL. With the no-hole constraint, they remain competitive with CPLEXCP and significantly outperform CPLEXMIP and Gurobi, particularly for MSCABL.

Conclusion: SAT solving is an effective exact approach for MSABL and MSCABL problems. The proposed framework demonstrates that SAT-based methods can compete with and sometimes outperform traditional optimization solvers like CPLEX and Gurobi for these NP-hard graph labeling problems.

Abstract: The Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth problems are NP-hard graph labeling problems that aim to maximize the minimum (cyclic) distance between labels assigned to adjacent vertices. Extensive research on these problems has resulted in a variety of mathematical formulations and computational approaches. However, their minimum span perspective, in which a prescribed minimum (cyclic) distance is fixed and the objective is to minimize the label span, has received comparatively little attention. In this paper, we consider this complementary perspective by introducing the Minimum Span Antibandwidth/Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling (MSABL/MSCABL) problems and developing a unified Boolean Satisfiability (SAT)-based framework for solving them. The SAT-based framework formulates MSABL/MSCABL as a sequence of decision problems and exploits their monotonicity to accelerate the search process. We also consider two SAT solving strategies, parallel and incremental SAT solving: the former examines multiple candidate spans concurrently, while the latter reuses a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain. The proposed approaches are evaluated on benchmark instances from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection and compared with CPLEXCP, CPLEXMIP, and Gurobi. The results show that SAT-based approaches are highly competitive in solution quality, with the parallel approach performing best overall for MSCABL and the incremental approach for MSABL. With the no-hole constraint, they remain competitive with CPLEXCP and significantly outperform CPLEXMIP and Gurobi, particularly for MSCABL. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of SAT solving as an exact approach for MSABL and MSCABL.

</details>


### [300] [Perception, Layout, and Validation: Calibrated Confidence for Reliable Straight-Through Processing of Financial Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20110)
*Yichao Jin,Yushuo Wang,Yuxuan Han,Kwan Ching Yee Sonia,Weiyang Song,Chiu Jin-Chun Kent,Wong Chong Hwee,Wong Tiong Kiat,Kenneth Zhu Ke,Jingyuan Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a decomposed confidence framework for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to enable reliable straight-through processing (STP) of key-value extractions from financial documents. The method uses three interpretable channels (perception, layout, validation) combined with conformal risk control to replace unreliable native VLM confidence signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern VLMs can extract key-value fields from financial documents without human review, but their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and weakly correlate with field correctness. This prevents reliable automated processing (STP) as there is no bounded guarantee on the residual error of auto-approved extractions.

Method: The paper introduces a decomposed confidence layer with three interpretable channels: (1) Perception channel - assesses visual understanding quality, (2) Layout channel - evaluates spatial relationships and document structure, (3) Validation channel - checks consistency and semantic validity. These channels are combined with a final conformal risk control mechanism to provide calibrated probability with bounded error guarantees for the auto-approved tier.

Result: The method was validated on three public datasets (real invoices, synthetic invoices, ad-buy forms) using two VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). The decomposed score consistently improved AUROC from 0.54-0.74 (VLM verbalized signals) to 0.90-0.99. For industrial deployment, native VLM confidence could only clear 0.1%-7.0% of fields under risk control (<10% error target), while the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while maintaining empirical error at or below the target.

Conclusion: The decomposed confidence approach with conformal risk control enables reliable STP for financial document extraction. By breaking down confidence into perception, layout, and validation channels, the method achieves significant improvements in separating correct from incorrect extractions, making industrial deployment feasible with 49-72% auto-approval rates while maintaining error bounds.

Abstract: Straight-through processing (STP) on extracted key-value fields from financial documents without human review requires a calibrated probability together with a bounded guarantee on the residual error of the auto-approved tier. The emergence of modern Vision Language Models (VLMs) provides an out-of-the-box capability for extracting the key-values, but their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and weakly track field correctness. This paper introduces a decomposed confidence layer along three interpretable channels, including perception, layout, and validation. Together with a final conformal risk control, the score can be used for reliable STP of financial documents. The method is validated on three public datasets covering real invoices, synthetic invoices, and ad-buy forms, using two different VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). Our decomposed score consistently improves the separation of correct from incorrect extractions, substantially raising the AUROC from 0.54-0.74 for VLM verbalized signals to 0.90-0.99 with contributions from all three designed channels. Crucially for industrial deployment, this enables usable STP. The native VLM confidence signals could clear only 0.1%-7.0% of fields under risk control at a target error of <10%. In contrast, the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while holding the empirical error of the accepted tier at or below the target.

</details>


### [301] [MTVA-Bench: Evaluating the Language Model Inside Cascaded Voice Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20152)
*Pritish Mishra,Ishaan Kumar,Akshat Mandoli,Sudarshan Kamath*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MTVA-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating language models in cascaded voice agent systems, addressing the gap between end-to-end benchmarks (which mix errors) and LLM benchmarks (which ignore real-world constraints like transcription issues). It evaluates 49 agents across 490 scenarios in 7 languages using deterministic checks and two LLM judges for task completion and conversation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of voice agents are either too broad (end-to-end benchmarks mix ASR, LM, and TTS errors) or too narrow (LLM benchmarks ignore real phone call challenges like transcription issues, voice splitting across messages, and script compliance). There was no benchmark that evaluates the language model under the same conditions it faces in cascaded voice systems.

Method: MTVA-Bench evaluates the language model in cascaded system conditions. The caller is played by an LLM following rubrics, and tool calls are answered by a mock backend that responds to the model's actual arguments. The benchmark contains 49 agents across 490 reviewed scenarios in 7 languages. Scoring combines deterministic checks on tool calls with two LLM judges: one scores scenario-specific rules, and one grades conversation quality without task access. Both judges must cite specific messages. Task and conversation scores are weighted equally.

Result: In a seven-model study, six models select the correct tool within 6.4 points of one another, but their overall scores span 24.4 points. The performance gap mainly comes from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and what the model says around its tool calls.

Conclusion: MTVA-Bench reveals that while tool selection is similar across models, significant differences emerge in execution quality—argument handling, action sequencing, rule adherence, and conversational behavior. The benchmark successfully isolates language model performance in realistic voice agent scenarios, providing a more accurate evaluation than previous approaches.

Abstract: Generally, most voice agents are cascaded systems, i.e., an ASR model transcribes the caller's audio, a language model reads the transcript and decides what to say and which backend tools to call, and a TTS model speaks the reply. Nearly all of the decision making happens in the language model, but existing evaluations measure it either too broadly or too narrowly. End-to-end voice benchmarks score the full pipeline, so recognition errors and model errors mix into a single number. LLM benchmarks isolate the model but they do not evaluate what makes real phone calls hard, such as transcription issues, caller's voice being split across messages and the requirement that replies follow the language and script specified. We introduce the Multi-Turn Voice Agent Benchmark (MTVA-Bench), which evaluates the language model on the same conditions it faces inside a cascaded system. The caller is played by an LLM following a set of rubrics and tool calls are answered by a mock backend which responds to the arguments the model actually sent. The benchmark contains 49 agents working across 490 reviewed scenarios and supports 7 languages. Scoring is a combination of deterministic checks on tool calls with two LLM judges, one that scores scenario specific rules and one that grades conversation quality without access to the task. Both judges must cite specific messages from the transcript. Task and conversation scores are weighted equally, since a call can complete its task and still go badly for the caller. In a seven-model study, six of the models select the correct tool within 6.4 points of one another, but their overall scores span 24.4 points. Most of the gap comes from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and what the model says around its tool calls.

</details>


### [302] [PaGNet: A Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network for Multi-Target Corporate Tax Avoidance Proxy Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20177)
*Wonho Song,Hyungjoon Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PaGNet is a hybrid machine learning model combining LightGBM and neural network branches for forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies from panel data. It uses a per-target validation-optimal blender to produce predictions and branch-reliance diagnostics without trainable fusion parameters. Tested on 1,754 Korean listed firms (2011-2024), it shows improved explained variance (0.08-0.11 gain) for accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) which stably route to the LightGBM branch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies is challenging because predictive signals are distributed across short firm histories and related targets, while screening-oriented applications require transparent model behavior. Existing methods lack explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting and struggle with panel-temporal data structure.

Method: PaGNet uses a two-branch hybrid architecture: (1) LightGBM branch with panel-temporal summaries, and (2) Panel-MLP branch with attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning. A per-target validation-optimal blender produces final predictions and branch-reliance diagnostics without trainable fusion parameters. Evaluated on KoTaP panel of 1,754 Korean listed firms (2011-2024) under leakage-free, shared-hyperparameter protocol across four feature regimes (FS1, FS2).

Result: PaGNet raises explained variance over six baselines by 0.08-0.11 for accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) which stably route to the LightGBM branch. GETR leans toward the neural branch, while CETR shows validation-test branch-selection mismatch. Panel-flatten control shows most accrual gains come from observed multi-year base-panel values, with panel-aware representation adding smaller refinement. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing and identifies far-horizon split where supervised models underperform naive persistence.

Conclusion: PaGNet is best viewed as a proxy-aware panel model that combines competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting, rather than a universally superior tabular learner. It provides transparent model behavior for screening applications while achieving improved forecasting for accrual-related tax avoidance proxies.

Abstract: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies from firm--year panel data is challenging because predictive signals are distributed across short firm histories and related targets, while screening-oriented use requires transparent model behavior. We propose PaGNet (Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network), a two-branch hybrid that combines a LightGBM branch using panel-temporal summaries with a Panel-MLP branch using attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning. A per-target validation-optimal blender produces both the final prediction and a compact branch-reliance diagnostic without trainable fusion parameters. On the KoTaP panel of 1{,}754 Korean listed firms from 2011--2024, PaGNet is evaluated under a leakage-free, shared-hyperparameter protocol across four feature regimes. In the direct-proxy-lag-excluded FS1 regime and the tax-history-augmented FS2 regime, accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) route stably to the LightGBM branch, where PaGNet raises explained variance over the strongest of six baselines by roughly $0.08$--$0.11$ on the primary split. GETR often leans toward the neural branch, while CETR exposes a validation--test branch-selection mismatch rather than a stable branch assignment. A panel-flatten control shows that most accrual gains come from observed multi-year base-panel values, with PaGNet's panel-aware representation adding a smaller but directionally consistent refinement. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing, bounds ETR diagnostics to split-specific behavior, and identifies a far-horizon split where supervised models underperform naive persistence. PaGNet is therefore best viewed not as a universally superior tabular learner, but as a proxy-aware panel model that combines competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting.

</details>


### [303] [Sequential Contextual Fit Predicts Human Behavioural and Neural Dynamics Across Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20179)
*Kun Sun,Rong Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study introduces Sequential Contextual Fit (SCF), an embedding-based metric measuring how well current information matches its recent context. Applied across diverse domains (language, music emotion, EEG, gambling, activity recognition), lower SCF predicted longer processing times, larger transitions, and stronger neural changes, even after controlling for established predictors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human perception, action and decision making unfold in sequences, but existing computational predictors are often domain-specific. The authors aimed to develop a универсальный (universal) measure that can bridge different domains and modalities to predict processing dynamics.

Method: The study computes SCF using a recency-weighted similarity kernel applied to embeddings from various modalities (words, sounds, visual scenes, affective states, choices, actions, neural representations). Six datasets were analyzed: language processing, music-evoked emotion, audiovisual emotion EEG, gambling decisions, human activity recognition, and decision-related EEG. Multiple regression controlled for established predictors including surprisal, RL prediction error, acoustic/visual/sensor change.

Result: Lower contextual fit predicted: (1) longer processing times, (2) larger affective/behavioural transitions, (3) stronger neural-state changes. These effects remained significant after controlling for surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change, and sensor change.

Conclusion: SCF provides a computational measurement layer for relating contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics. It offers a domain-general approach that works across multiple modalities and task types.

Abstract: Human perception, action and decision making unfold in sequences, but computational predictors are often domain-specific. This study computes and tests sequential contextual fit (SCF), an embedding-based measure of how well a current information state matches its recent context. The metric uses a simple recency-weighted similarity kernel and can be applied to words, sounds, visual scenes, affective states, choices, actions and neural representations. Across language processing, music-evoked emotion, a subset of audiovisual emotion EEG data, gambling decisions, human activity recognition and decision-related EEG, lower contextual fit predicted longer processing times, larger affective or behavioural transitions and stronger neural-state changes. These effects remained after controlling for established predictors including surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change and sensor change. SCF therefore provides a computational measurement layer for relating contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics.

</details>


### [304] [JointMatch: A Unified Heterogeneous Graph Neural Solver for Large-Scale Ride-Sharing Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20200)
*Kun Zhao,Xu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JointMatch is a learning-based framework that jointly optimizes request pairing and vehicle assignment for ride-sharing on a single graph, outperforming traditional two-stage approaches (Blossom heuristic and two-stage GNN) in both revenue and speed, achieving 20x faster dispatch at city scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The dominant academic approach decomposes ride-sharing dispatch into two sequential matching problems (request pairing first, then vehicle assignment). This decomposition is computationally convenient but loses revenue and scales poorly because the first stage commits to ride bundles before knowing available vehicles.

Method: JointMatch uses a graph neural network (GNN) on a spatially-sparsified graph where edges are created based on spatial proximity, resulting in linear rather than quadratic scaling with fleet size. The GNN scores all candidate decisions in a single forward pass, handling both request pairing and vehicle assignment jointly.

Result: On NYC Yellow Taxi data, JointMatch exceeds both the classical Blossom heuristic and a faithfully-trained two-stage GNN baseline, often by a wide margin. At city scale (10,000 vehicles), it runs more than 20x faster per dispatch epoch than either baseline. A supervised training stage closes most of the remaining revenue gap, and policy-gradient fine-tuning aligns the model with realized revenue.

Conclusion: Joint pooling and assignment in a unified GNN framework significantly improves both solution quality and computational efficiency compared to sequential two-stage approaches. The linear scaling property enables city-scale deployment with substantial speedup while maintaining or improving revenue outcomes.

Abstract: Ride-sharing platforms must continuously decide which open requests to bundle into shared trips and which idle vehicles should serve them. The dominant academic approach decomposes this into two sequential matching problems -- request pairing first, then vehicle assignment -- and applies a separate solver to each. This decomposition is convenient computationally but loses revenue and scales poorly because the first stage commits to ride bundles before the available vehicles are known. We propose JointMatch, a learning-based framework that handles request pairing and vehicle assignment together on a single graph. The graph is sparsified by spatial proximity so that its size grows linearly rather than quadratically with the number of vehicles and requests, and a graph neural network scores all candidate decisions in one forward pass. On the New York City Yellow Taxi data, the framework already exceeds both the classical Blossom heuristic and a faithfully-trained two-stage GNN baseline -- often by a wide margin -- and at city scale (fleet 10000) it runs more than $20\times$ faster per dispatch epoch than either. A supervised training stage closes most of the remaining revenue gap, and a policy-gradient fine-tune aligns the trained model with realised revenue.

</details>


### [305] [When AI Agents Commit: Cognitive Serializability Across Data, Evidence, Policy, and Authority](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20261)
*Jun He,Deying Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents TCT (Typed Cognitive Transactions), a system for ensuring consistent transaction processing in autonomous agents by combining immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-derived authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation. The system addresses the challenge of maintaining valid mutation-derivation relationships when inputs may change during reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses the problem of ensuring a common valid point for database mutations and their derivation inputs when autonomous agents derive mutations from database reads, retrieved evidence, policy, beliefs, and delegated authority that may change during reasoning. Current database isolation and transaction processing approaches cannot guarantee this consistency.

Method: The paper proposes TCT combining: immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-derived authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, post-seal envelope- and witness-bound grants, co-committed receipts, idempotent grant finalization, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation. It introduces strict Cognitive Serializability (where committed effects admit a serial order and a logical event at which every value exposed to derivation is unchanged) and the weaker Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission (which recertifies an effect against current dependency vector and policy without claiming to serialize the original stochastic derivation).

Result: The corresponding results give serializability conditions and an observational-equivalence boundary for zero-error soundness and positive progress. A falsification suite tests the implementation obligations: the prototype prevented all injected anomalies and added 3.22 ms mean commit overhead.

Conclusion: The TCT system successfully provides serializability guarantees for autonomous agent transaction processing. Complete registered footprints and a single growing phase induce an acyclic lock-point order over local guards and incompatible external reservations, enabling zero-error soundness with positive progress.

Abstract: Autonomous agents derive concrete mutations from database reads, retrieved evidence, policy, beliefs, and delegated authority. Those inputs may change while reasoning is in progress. Database isolation orders the submitted transaction; agentic transaction processing determines whether a proposal satisfies an executable contract. Neither guarantee establishes a common valid point for the mutation and its derivation inputs unless the contract represents the relevant predicates. Typed dependency tokens distinguish content integrity from applicability, and trusted mediation captures the values exposed to reasoning. Under strict Cognitive Serializability, committed effects admit a serial order and a logical event at which every value exposed to derivation is unchanged. The fences last until the runtime event that realizes the sealed durability domain. The weaker Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission recertifies an effect against a simultaneously held current dependency vector and current policy without claiming to serialize the original stochastic derivation. TCT combines immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-derived authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, post-seal envelope- and witness-bound grants, co-committed receipts, idempotent grant finalization, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation. Complete registered footprints and a single growing phase induce an acyclic lock-point order over local guards and incompatible external reservations. The corresponding results give serializability conditions and an observational-equivalence boundary for zero-error soundness and positive progress. A falsification suite tests the implementation obligations: the prototype prevented all injected anomalies and added 3.22 ms mean commit overhead.

</details>


### [306] [AI-Driven Real-Time Relay Optimisation in Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimise Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20271)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Emiliano Pallotti,Simone Angelini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes an AI-driven Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X networks. The framework models vehicular networks as graphs and trains an edge-aware GINE model using optimal MILP solutions as supervision, achieving near-optimal connectivity with 100x speed-up compared to traditional MILP approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable and low-latency communication is essential for smart city services and Industry 4.0 applications. However, limited RSU deployment and complex urban propagation conditions prevent CAVs from maintaining stable connectivity, necessitating efficient multi-hop relay selection strategies.

Method: The paper models the vehicular network as a graph (nodes = CAVs and RSUs, edges = radio-link characteristics), formulates an offline MILP for optimal relay decisions, and trains an edge-aware GINE model using MILP solutions as supervision for real-time inference.

Result: The proposed approach achieves near-optimal connectivity performance, recovering up to 11.3% connectivity gain while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude (up to 100x speed-up) compared to MILP on realistic urban datasets.

Conclusion: The L2O framework enables scalable and real-time network control, making it suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 deployments where low-latency and reliable V2X communication is critical.

Abstract: Reliable and low-latency communication is a fundamental requirement for smart city services and Industry 4.0 applications enabled by NR-V2X networks. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) deployment and complex urban propagation conditions often prevent Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable connectivity. This paper proposes an AI-driven Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X systems. The vehicular network is modelled as a graph, where nodes represent CAVs and RSUs, and edges encode radio-link characteristics. An offline Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation provides optimal relay decisions used as supervision for training an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE). Extensive experiments on realistic urban datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves near-optimal connectivity performance, recovering up to 11.3% connectivity gain, while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude (up to 100 x speed-up) compared to MILP. The framework enables scalable and real-time network control, making it suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 deployments.

</details>


### [307] [JEPA-WAM: Connecting Generated Visual Instructions to World Action Models through JEPA Latent Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20277)
*Tianbin Liu,Jian Zhu,Taiyi Su,Jianjun Zhang,Chong Ma,Zitai Huang,Yi Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JEPA-WAM addresses limited instruction-following in World Action Models by augmenting text instructions with stochastically generated visual instructions (image goals), using V-JEPA 2.1 encoder for semantic representation and achieving state-of-the-art results on a real-robot instruction-following benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current WAMs show limited instruction-following ability when conditioned solely on text instructions due to structural imbalance in robot-learning data: rich visual-action trajectories paired with sparse/repetitive language annotations, allowing policies to rely on visual context rather than grounding instructions.

Method: 1) Use off-the-shelf text-to-image generator to sample multiple task-completion images conditioned on text instructions (no generator training needed). 2) Encode these generated images with frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to extract task-level semantics beyond appearance. 3) Compress dense goal representations into compact goal tokens. 4) Condition both video and action experts through cross-attention using these goal tokens.

Result: JEPA-WAM achieves 87.3% (in-distribution), 74.5% (OOD scene), and 80.9% (OOD instruction) success rates, outperforming π0 by at least 10.0 percentage points and Fast-WAM by at least 27.3 percentage points.

Conclusion: Augmenting text instructions with diverse visual instructions using pretrained V-JEPA encoders significantly improves robotic instruction-following, particularly in out-of-distribution settings. The approach demonstrates that visual goal representations can effectively complement sparse language annotations in robot learning.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have demonstrated strong robotic manipulation capabilities by augmenting pretrained video generative models with action experts. However, current WAMs still show limited instruction-following ability when conditioned solely on text instructions. We argue that this limitation stems in part from a structural imbalance in robot-learning data: rich visual-action trajectories are often paired with sparse and repetitive language annotations, allowing policies to identify tasks from visual context and motion regularities rather than grounding the instruction itself. To address this limitation, we introduce JEPA-WAM, which augments each text instruction with a bank of stochastically generated visual instructions, providing diverse visual cues for instruction following. Specifically, JEPA-WAM uses an off-the-shelf text-to-image generator to sample multiple task-completion images conditioned on the text instruction, without training the generator. Although these generated images may differ from the current visual scene in appearance and layout, they remain semantically aligned with the instruction and serve as visual goal references. To focus on task-level semantics beyond appearance, we encode these references with a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. The resulting dense goal representations are compressed into compact goal tokens that condition both the video and action experts through cross-attention. We further construct a real-robot instruction-following benchmark covering in-distribution, out-of-distribution scene, and out-of-distribution instruction settings. On this benchmark, JEPA-WAM achieves success rates of 87.3%, 74.5%, and 80.9% in these three settings, outperforming π0 and Fast-WAM by at least 10.0, 27.3, and 14.5 percentage points, respectively.

</details>


### [308] [AgentPProf: Semantic Profiler for Long Horizon AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20301)
*Yusheng Zheng,Chaokun Chang,Yu Mao,Tianyuan Wu,Yuxi Huang,Tao Ma,Wenan Mao,Shuyi Cheng,Andi Quinn,Wei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentPProf is a profiler for AI agents that aggregates trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles, enabling flame graph visualization and hierarchical attribution of resources and problems across long-running agent executions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent observability tools focus on per-execution debugging and tracing, but lack cross-run, long-term profiling capabilities. Developers need to identify failure points, unsafe triggers, and high-cost tasks, but cannot do this efficiently at scale without profiling similar to systems software.

Method: The paper proposes a semantic operation stack model that represents all agent activities as uniform operations, with operation stacks replacing runtime call stacks. It introduces recursive operation segmentation that splits trajectories at task boundaries. AgentPProf aggregates trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles for flame graph analysis.

Result: AgentPProf achieves 0.764 B^3 F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, profiling raises MAP by up to 56%, effectively attributing resources, locating problems, and helping optimize token cost at practical profiling cost.

Conclusion: Agent profiling is feasible and valuable. The semantic operation stack model and recursive segmentation enable hierarchical attribution at different granularities, making it practical to identify hotspots, optimize costs, and improve agent quality, safety, and efficiency at scale.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly orchestrate long-running activities with users, tools, and system resources for days and weeks. To improve agent quality, safety, and cost efficiency, developers need to determine where failures happen, what triggers unsafe effects, and which tasks consume the most budget, then optimize those tasks. In systems software, profiling answers similar questions by aggregating resource consumption and attributing it to responsible code paths to identify hotspots. Yet existing agent observability tools focus on per-execution debugging and tracing rather than cross-run, long term profiling, making these questions difficult to answer at scale. Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging, but profiling agents is challenging: the responsible entities are task intent like diagnose authentication, compare branches rather than code paths, and lack stable identifiers for aggregation. We propose a semantic operation stack model that adapts profiling to agent trajectories. Uniform operations represent all activities, and operation stacks replace the runtime call stack, enabling hierarchical attribution at different granularities. We observe that an agent's task occupies a contiguous span and decomposes into subtasks, so we introduce recursive operation segmentation, which recursively splits trajectories at task boundaries. AgentPProf is a profiler that aggregates agent trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles, enabling flame graph visualization and analysis. AgentPProf reaches 0.764 $B^3$ F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, the profile raises MAP by up to 56%, demonstrating that it effectively attributes resources, locates problems, and helps optimize token cost at practical profiling cost. AgentPProf is available at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentsight.

</details>


### [309] [Diagnose, Recover, Certify: Task Readiness under Hidden Dynamics Changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20304)
*Nguyen Viet Tuan Kiet,Huynh Thi Thanh Binh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of detecting and recovering from actuator effectiveness loss in deployed control policies when the fault doesn't affect the current task but may impact future unknown tasks. The authors introduce "task readiness under dormant dynamics drift" and propose "Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport," a Bayesian intervention-based method that couples fault localization with actuator effectiveness estimation using a shared matched-response representation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that actuator degradation can go unnoticed when the current control policy doesn't excite the affected actuator, yet this dormant fault becomes critical when future tasks requiring that actuator are later specified. This creates a challenge where: (1) the fault is invisible during normal operation, (2) limited interaction budget constrains diagnosis, and (3) the downstream task identity is revealed only after diagnosis must be completed.

Method: The proposed method "Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport" is a Bayesian intervention-based procedure that: (1) uses a shared matched-response representation to couple fault localization with actuator effectiveness estimation, (2) preserves diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty, (3) propagates uncertainty to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, and (4) enables explicit trade-offs between expected performance, confidence, and fallback use.

Result: The method was evaluated on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks across multiple simulators using a protocol that separates diagnosis from capability recovery, scoring deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, interaction cost, and return. The evaluation identifies fault regimes where transported evidence is decisive.

Conclusion: The framework successfully enables an agent to identify dynamics changes, characterize them with limited interactions before task identity is revealed, and provide either a recovered policy with calibrated performance bounds or an abstention decision to a safe fallback. This addresses the fundamental challenge of maintaining task readiness under dormant dynamics drift with limited task-agnostic interaction budget.

Abstract: A deployed control policy can conceal consequential dynamics changes: an actuator may lose effectiveness without affecting the current task when the policy rarely excites it, despite being critical for a future task that has not yet been specified. We introduce task readiness under dormant dynamics drift, a decision problem that unifies active change diagnosis and post-change control recovery under a limited, task-agnostic interaction budget. An agent must identify whether and where local dynamics have changed, use a small number of informative interactions to characterize the change before downstream task identity is revealed, and subsequently provide each candidate task with either a recovered policy and a calibrated lower bound on its achievable return or an abstention decision to a safe fallback. We propose Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport, an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that couples fault localization with estimation of actuator effectiveness through a shared matched-response representation, thereby preserving diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty. This uncertainty is propagated to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, enabling deployment decisions that explicitly trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use. We evaluate the resulting framework on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks spanning multiple simulators, under a protocol that separates diagnosis from capability recovery, scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, and interaction cost as well as return, and identifies the fault regimes in which transported evidence is decisive.

</details>


### [310] [NeuSOGA3D: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Explainable 3D Geometric Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20323)
*Qingde Li,Qingqi Hong,Zihan Li,Jie Tian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NeuSOGA3D is a hybrid neuro-symbolic framework for 3D reconstruction from unorganized point clouds that combines neural perceptual priors with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning, producing CAD-compatible geometric representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Three-dimensional reconstruction from unorganized point clouds is challenging in computer vision and CAD. Existing neural implicit methods achieve good accuracy but use latent representations that limit interpretability and reuse in engineering workflows.

Method: NeuSOGA3D projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations, and fuses them through shape-preserving CSG operations to generate a coarse visual hull. Additional detail is recovered through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.

Result: Experiments on all 40 categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrate the framework's ability to recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations.

Conclusion: The results highlight the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence, enabling interpretable and reusable geometric representations in engineering workflows.

Abstract: Three-dimensional reconstruction from unorganized point clouds remains a challenging problem in computer vision, geometric modeling, and computer-aided design. While neural implicit methods achieve impressive reconstruction accuracy, geometry is typically encoded in latent representations that limit interpretability and reuse within engineering workflows.
  We present NeuSOGA3D (Neuro-Symbolic Geometric Abstraction in 3D), a hybrid framework that combines learned perceptual priors inherited from NeuSOGA with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning. The method projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations from the resulting observations, and fuses them through shape-preserving constructive solid geometry operations to generate a coarse visual hull. Additional geometric detail is recovered through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.
  Unlike conventional neural implicit approaches, NeuSOGA3D progressively transforms observations into explicit symbolic entities, including control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, and volumetric lofts. Experiments on all forty categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrate the ability of the framework to recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations. The results highlight the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence.

</details>


### [311] [Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation: From Natural-Language Traffic Rules to PROLOG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20334)
*May Myo Zin,Wachara Fungwacharakorn,Ken Satoh,Katsumi Nitta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of translating ambiguous human-written traffic regulations into precise Prolog logic for computational reasoning. The study proposes S4L→Prolog, a four-stage legal translation framework that performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt. Evaluation on 20 real-world traffic rules shows S4L→Prolog achieves 75% accuracy, outperforming NL→Prolog (60%) and LE→Prolog (55%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traffic regulations are written for human interpretation, relying on shared background knowledge and flexible phrasing. This introduces ambiguity, context dependence, and semantic underspecification, which conflicts with the precision required by computational reasoning engines like Prolog that demand explicit logical structure.

Method: The study evaluates three translation approaches: (1) Natural Language to Prolog (NL→Prolog), (2) Logical English to Prolog (LE→Prolog), and (3) the proposed Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation (S4L→Prolog). The S4L framework performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt. A benchmark of twenty real-world traffic rules was used to evaluate each approach in terms of syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness.

Result: S4L→Prolog achieves the highest accuracy at 75% (correctly formalizing 15 out of 20 rules), while NL→Prolog reaches 60% and LE→Prolog reaches 55%. Qualitative analysis shows that S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than the baselines.

Conclusion: Structured reasoning prompts can substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation for legal and safety-critical applications. The S4L framework demonstrates that integrating semantic role extraction and scene completion into a single guided prompt enables direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention.

Abstract: Traffic regulations are written for human interpretation and therefore rely on shared background knowledge and flexible phrasing, which inherently introduce ambiguity, context dependence, and semantic underspecification. These linguistic characteristics conflict with the precision required by computational reasoning engines such as Prolog, which demand explicit logical structure. This study evaluates two baseline translation approaches, Natural Language to Prolog ($NL\rightarrow Prolog$) and Logical English to Prolog ($LE\rightarrow Prolog$), and introduces a new reasoning-guided translation framework called Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation ($S4L\rightarrow Prolog$).
