The proposed S4L framework performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt, enabling direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention. A benchmark consisting of twenty real-world traffic rules was used to evaluate each approach in terms of syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness. $S4L\rightarrow Prolog$ achieves the highest accuracy, correctly formalizing 75 percent of the rules, while $NL\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 60 percent and $LE\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 55 percent. Qualitative analysis further shows that S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than the baselines. These results demonstrate that structured reasoning prompts can substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation for legal and safety-critical applications.

</details>


### [312] [A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349)
*Abhishek Jaiswal,Zoe Falomir*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a hybrid qualitative reasoning model for "Camelot Jr.", a block-puzzle game that trains spatial reasoning skills in children. The model combines qualitative reasoning with mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to enable AI agents to provide human-like tutoring and interpretable feedback to players.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatial reasoning abilities strongly correlate with STEM performance, and games are effective for training these skills in children. However, creating AI agents that can provide human-like tutoring and player guidance requires commonsense inferences from spatial events, which current systems lack.

Method: The researchers developed a hybrid qualitative model that integrates mathematical center-of-mass stability logic with qualitative reasoning (QR) frameworks. The model was designed for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game where players build multi-level bridges to connect two avatars on separate towers while ensuring platform stability, path planning, and using all provided blocks.

Result: The paper introduces a hybrid qualitative model capable of handling the precise physics required for the domain, enabling the translation of game states into interpretable feedback for player guidance.

Conclusion: This work contributes to spatial skill training in puzzle games and advances the development of human-centric, explainable game-playing agents that can provide human-like tutoring through symbolic reasoning representations.

Abstract: Spatial reasoning abilities correlate strongly with performance in STEM fields. Games offer a compelling medium for training these critical skills in developing children who have a natural proclivity for play. However, to facilitate human-like tutoring and player guidance, these games require an AI agent capable of making commonsense inferences from spatial events. Qualitative reasoning (QR) models appear to be a suitable framework for these application domains. As these models reason in symbolic representations, they can seamlessly translate game states into interpretable feedback for human-like player guidance. This paper introduces a hybrid qualitative model designed for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game that requires constructing multi-level bridges to connect two avatars stationed on separate towers. The game poses a challenge for the player, who must make platforms stable, plan their path, and ensure they use all the provided blocks. To handle the precise physics required by the domain, we integrate a mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to guide our qualitative solver. Our work facilitates spatial skill training in Camelot Jr. and contributes to the development of human-centric, explainable game-playing agents.

</details>


### [313] [Generating Heterogeneous 3D Geological Microstructures from 2D Images via a Stable Diffusion-Adversarial Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20358)
*Ali Aouf,Eric Laloy,Bart Rogiers,Christophe De Vleeschouwer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a hybrid deep learning approach for generating 3D microstructures of clay and cementitious materials from 2D images. The method combines denoising diffusion models with adversarial loss (since no 3D ground truth is available) to overcome limitations of SliceGAN in capturing complex heterogeneous microstructures. The model generates microstructures with minimal artifacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Characterizing physical properties of clay and cementitious materials is important across materials science and geological waste disposal. Traditional 3D imaging is expensive and technically limited. While SliceGAN has shown good results for homogeneous systems, it struggles with complex heterogeneous microstructures, necessitating an alternative generative framework.

Method: The authors introduce a hybrid approach combining denoising diffusion models with adversarial loss. Since no 3D ground truth is available, they replace the standard denoising loss with an adversarial loss to ensure stable training. This approach leverages the stability and generation quality of diffusion models while adapting them for the unavailable 3D ground truth constraint.

Result: The resulting model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artifacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.

Conclusion: The proposed hybrid diffusion-adversarial approach successfully addresses the limitations of SliceGAN in capturing fine details of complex heterogeneous microstructures, providing a viable method for 3D microstructure reconstruction from 2D images.

Abstract: Characterizing the physical properties of clay and cementitious materials matters across many fields, from materials science to geological waste disposal. Property simulation typically calls for 3D imaging, which is expensive, not always accessible, and technically limited for certain materials. Recent progress in deep generative models offers a way around this, reconstructing 3D volumes from the more easily acquired 2D images.
  Among GAN-based methods for 3D microstructure generation, SliceGAN has shown strong results for homogeneous isotropic and anisotropic systems. It struggles, however, to capture the finer detail of more complex heterogeneous microstructures, which motivates alternative generative frameworks.
  We introduce a hybrid approach that draws on the stability and generation quality of denoising diffusion models. Since no 3D ground truth is available, we replace the standard denoising loss with an adversarial loss, which yields a stable training process in our experiments. We show that the resulting model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artefacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.

</details>


### [314] [The Organization of Inference: Information, Resource Constraints, and AI Production](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20449)
*Yukun Zhang,Kemu Xu,Yishen Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies how the economic value of AI inference depends on organizing capacity and task information across different production stages. Using controlled experiments on software-engineering tasks, the authors find that direct execution maintains a constant 59.6% success rate regardless of token budget (12K or 24K), while planning-assisted execution improves from 36.2% to 51.2% as capacity increases. At higher token budgets, planning outperforms direct execution by 29.6 points, demonstrating that workflow structure and information access fundamentally shape productive value beyond raw scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers aim to understand how the distribution of computational capacity and task information across AI production stages affects economic value. This addresses a fundamental question in AI system design: should resources be allocated to direct execution or to planning/reasoning stages? The study seeks empirical evidence on these "organizational margins" using controlled experiments.

Method: The authors conducted controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. They compared two resource panels (12,000 and 24,000 logical-token ceilings) across two execution modes: (1) direct execution and (2) information-constrained planning. They also tested a strict read-only planning campaign varying whether the planner had access to task issues. Success rates, binding rates, and token utilization were measured across conditions.

Result: Direct execution achieved identical 59.6% success at both token ceilings. Planning success improved from 36.2% to 51.2% as tokens increased from 12K to 24K, narrowing the gap by 15.0 percentage points (95% CI: 4.2-25.8). At 12K tokens, issue access improved planning success by ~16 percentage points over issue-hidden planning. Task-informed planning lagged direct execution by ~10 points at 12K tokens but exceeded it by 29.6 points at 24K tokens. Planning's binding rate dropped from 46.2% to 0.8%, while downstream execution accounted for 89.9% of total token use increase.

Conclusion: Scale determines the capacity available to a system, but workflow and information structure fundamentally shape the productive value of that capacity. At low token budgets, direct execution outperforms planning; at higher budgets, planning becomes superior. The findings suggest that optimal resource allocation depends on both available scale and how information is structured across production stages.

Abstract: The economic value of inference depends on how capacity and task information are distributed across stages of AI production. We study these organizational margins using controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. In two matched resource panels, direct execution records the same success rate of 59.6 percent at logical-token ceilings of 12,000 and 24,000, while success under information-constrained planning rises from 36.2 to 51.2 percent. The planning disadvantage narrows by 15.0 percentage points (95 percent task-cluster bootstrap interval: 4.2 to 25.8). A strict read-only planning campaign varies whether the planner sees the task issue. At 12,000 tokens, issue access raises success by about 16 percentage points over issue-hidden planning. Compared with direct execution, task-informed planning is about 10 points lower at 12,000 tokens; at 24,000 tokens, it shows a 29.6-point advantage. In the resource panels, direct execution uses substantially less than either ceiling, while the planning workflow's binding rate falls from 46.2 to 0.8 percent and downstream execution accounts for 89.9 percent of the increase in total use. Scale determines the capacity available to a system; workflow and information structure shape the productive value

</details>


### [315] [SkillAA: Attribution-Guided Skill-Graph Updating with Targeted Validation and Rollback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20455)
*Ziqiao Shang,Ling-Yue Ge,Lan-Zhe Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillAA (Skill Abductive Attribution) is a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models that uses a unified graph representation to support skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. It routes candidate repairs from failed rollouts to specific graph objects and uses Local and Big Gates for validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for editing skills in frozen language models lack structured routing from observed failures to editable locations. Current skill graphs underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation.

Method: SkillAA represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph. It contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only selected local structures, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment.

Result: With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA achieves 81.5% on SearchQA, 66.7% on LiveMath, and 91.2% on DocVQA, attaining the highest observed mean in every main setting.

Conclusion: Attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation are effective for skill optimization in frozen language models. The unified graph structure successfully enables skill selection, targeted repair, and validation.

Abstract: External skills provide domain procedures without parameter updates, but existing methods often edit skills directly from failed rollouts without structured routing from an observed failure to an editable location; existing skill graphs also underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation. We introduce SkillAA (Skill Abductive Attribution), a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models. It represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph, allowing the same structure to support skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. SkillAA contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only the selected local structure, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment. With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and attains the highest observed mean in every main setting. These results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation.

</details>


### [316] [How Do Agent Harnesses Create Value? Planning Information and Release Control in Stateful LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20474)
*Yukun Zhang,Kemu Xu,Yishen Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pre-written task-specific plans improve oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points over sham controls, with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks, and a read-only verifier rejects 61% of invalid episodes while withholding 17% of correct ones at minimal cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research investigates how three agent components—supply planning guidance, execution organization, and completion checking—affect success rates, erroneous acceptance, and cost in real-world scenarios.

Method: Two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in τ²-bench were conducted across 265 matched cells, comparing Fixed (prewritten task-specific plans) with Sham (shuffled policy text matched in word count) to isolate the contribution of guidance content. A read-only terminal verifier was also evaluated.

Result: Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90% CI: 1.15--13.36), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. The verifier rejects 61% of oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17% of correct ones, at less than one cent additional cost per episode. The relative importance of planning vs. verification depends on liability levels: at low liability, planning gains dominate; at high liability, the verifier's avoided false passes dominate.

Conclusion: A standalone verifier captures nearly all false-pass benefits of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost, making it particularly valuable in high-liability scenarios.

Abstract: Agent harnesses supply planning guidance, organize execution, and check completion. We study how these components affect success, erroneous acceptance, and cost in two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in $τ^2$-bench. The primary comparison pairs prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) with shuffled policy text matched in word count (Sham), isolating the contribution of guidance content. Across 265 matched cells, Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90\% task-clustered bootstrap interval, 1.15--13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. A read-only terminal verifier rejects 61\% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17\% of correct ones, at less than one cent of additional cost per episode. Which component matters more depends on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance: at low liability the planning gain dominates; at high liability the verifier's avoided false passes dominate---and a standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost.

</details>


### [317] [SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20519)
*Haozhe Liu,Tian Ye,Sensen Gao,Qihang Cao,Yitong Li,Mingchen Zhuge,Duomin Wang,Ruihua Zhang,Ping Luo,Jiawang Bian,Lei Zhu,Ligeng Zhu,Enze Xie,Song Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents SoL-Pi, a system that improves token efficiency in coding agents by 44.7-49.0% while maintaining performance comparable to Pi, resulting in significant cost savings ($4.36-$13.50/hour) across different harness implementations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As coding agents evolve from supervised code completion to continuous, unattended exploration with long reasoning trajectories, token efficiency becomes critical for scaling recursive self-improvement. The goal is to reduce token traffic and API costs while maintaining performance across increasingly numerous and diverse environments.

Method: The researchers apply an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across diverse environments. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi: action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading. The system is evaluated on EdgeBench with 51 tasks.

Result: SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. Estimated hourly savings are $8.75-$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and $4.36-$5.71 relative to Pi.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates that token efficiency can be significantly improved through harness-layer optimization without sacrificing performance. The four mechanisms spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading effectively reduce token usage while maintaining comparable results, making automated harness discovery more viable for production-level outcomes.

Abstract: As coding agents move from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration, their work expands from isolated predictions into long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. Token efficiency therefore becomes important for scaling recursive self-improvement. We take an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments for harness rollouts. At this scale, the process yields reusable improvements that transfer beyond their development setting, moving automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi, spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading. On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. In other words, estimated hourly savings are \$8.75-\$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and \$4.36-\$5.71 relative to Pi.

</details>


### [318] [FreqCondNorm: Towards Cross-domain Predictive Maintenance through a Frequency-Conditioned Transformer Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20535)
*Zaynab Raounak,Camille LHermine,Zhiguo Zeng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses poor transferability of deep learning predictive maintenance models across machines and operating conditions, particularly with scarce labels and signals spanning 1 Hz to ~100 kHz. The proposed FreqCondNorm Transformer architecture uses FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization to unify heterogeneous time-series. Pretrained on 5 datasets using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning, it achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, but fails to improve RUL prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labeled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). This limits practical deployment where models must generalize across different machines and conditions.

Method: FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture with FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. Pretraining uses masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling on five public datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS).

Result: On fault diagnosis: 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 percentage points over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life (RUL) prediction.

Conclusion: FreqCondNorm effectively addresses cross-domain fault diagnosis with heterogeneous sampling frequencies through frequency-conditioned normalization and contrastive pretraining. The limitation in RUL prediction suggests a fundamental mismatch between pretraining objectives (fault diagnosis) and downstream RUL tasks, warranting future investigation into alternative pretraining strategies or task-specific fine-tuning.

Abstract: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labelled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). We propose FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture that introduces a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. The architecture is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling. On fault diagnosis, the model achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life prediction, suggesting a mismatch between pretraining and RUL objectives that warrants future investigation.

</details>


### [319] [Refuse, Decompose, Refresh: A Claim-Safe Protocol for Closed-Loop AI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20538)
*Peiying Zhu,Sidi Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical problem in AI evaluation: that evaluations can be reproducible but still support wrong claims, especially in closed-loop systems where policy determines observable states and failure traces. The authors propose a "claim-safe protocol" with three components (Refuse, Decompose, Refresh) to ensure valid claims. They instantiate this in a simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, and two fault-mask families, testing on 1,440 heldout cases. Results show only 55/72 units were reference-admitted, stable false admission was 0/20, and clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction by 0.1264 nats per row.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that AI evaluations can be perfectly reproducible yet still support incorrect claims. This risk is particularly acute in closed-loop systems where policy determines which states are visited, which components are observable, and which failures leave measurable traces. The authors aim to create a protocol that ensures claims are supported by actual evidence rather than just reproducible measurements.

Method: The authors propose a "claim-safe protocol" with three actions: 1) Refuse - abstain when clean reference streams or matched runtime comparisons lack support; 2) Decompose - report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as a single PASS/FAIL; 3) Refresh - treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute reference maps rather than fault evidence. They instantiate this protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development/heldout seeds. The preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows.

Result: Only 55 out of 72 regime-component units were reference-admitted, and 54 out of 55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0 out of 20 represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows that "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, while only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that rather than using a universal threshold, they contribute an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims. The protocol ensures that claims are properly supported by evidence and that abstention is treated as a valid outcome when evidence is insufficient.

Abstract: An AI evaluation can be perfectly reproducible and still support the wrong claim. This risk is acute in closed-loop systems: policy determines visited states, observable components, and which failures leave a measurable trace. We propose a claim-safe protocol with three actions. Refuse: abstain when a clean reference stream or matched runtime comparison lacks support. Decompose: report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as one PASS/FAIL label. Refresh: treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute a reference map, not as fault evidence. We instantiate the protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds. The preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows. Only 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows why "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, while only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference. Rather than a universal threshold, we contribute an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims.

</details>


### [320] [Language-model groups overstate consensus when replaying human deliberation on a reasoning task](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20543)
*Tengfei Shao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines whether LLM agent groups can simulate human group deliberation on a Wason task. The authors find that agent groups achieve much higher consensus rates than human groups (gaps of 34-44 percentage points), but this consensus does not track collective accuracy. Belief-anchored agent groups are biased estimators of human group outcomes, raising concerns about using simulated groups to study collective cognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-consensus rates are often used as indicators of collective cognition, but different operationalizations of participation and final states can yield vastly different estimates. The authors wanted to compare LLM agent groups directly with human groups using identical scoring methods.

Method: The authors replayed 100 human Wason groups with matched LLM agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer. They scored both agents and humans with the same code across multiple definitions. They conducted several sensitivity analyses: submit-based comparison (n=98), participation-matched comparison (n=45), removed early stopping, and reparameterization removing the memorizable answer.

Result: Human consensus rates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0% depending on scoring definition. About 20% of human participants never posted, while agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual, with gaps of 34.0-43.9 percentage points for chat mode and 34.1-44.4 points for reasoning mode. Reasoning-mode groups agreed nearly unanimously but mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy.

Conclusion: Belief-anchored agent groups are biased estimators of human group-outcome distribution in this setting. The analyses provide a scoring-explicit basis for assessing simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes, cautioning against using LLM agents as proxies for human collective cognition without careful validation.

Abstract: Full-consensus rates are often treated as indicators of collective cognition, yet depend on how participation and final states are operationalized. We replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched large language model (LLM) agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer and scoring agents and people with the same code. Across human scoring definitions, estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0%; about one fifth of participants never posted, whereas agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual in two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses: the submit-based comparison (n = 98) yielded gaps of 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points for chat and reasoning modes, and the participation-matched comparison (n = 45) yielded gaps of 34.1 and 44.4 points. These complementary routes reduced different measurement asymmetries yet converged within 0.5 percentage points. The gap persisted without early stopping and under a reparameterization removing the memorizable answer; reasoning-mode groups then agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution in this setting. These analyses provide a scoring-explicit basis for assessing simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes.

</details>


### [321] [Limits of Confidence in Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20581)
*Russ Webb,Amitis Shidani,Alice Bizeul,Dan Busbridge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes discrete diffusion models (remasking and uniform-state samplers) that write multiple token positions per step. The authors prove theoretically that these methods cannot capture dependencies between tokens in the target distribution, and demonstrate empirically on a synthetic task (ScanAndAdd) that the generated distribution diverges significantly from the target.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current discrete diffusion methods assume positions being written are conditionally independent given already-fixed tokens, but for real-world domains (pixels, phonemes, words) there are inherent dependencies between tokens that this assumption fails to capture.

Method: The authors provide theoretical analysis proving that: (1) a step matches the training distribution only when written positions are conditionally independent given fixed tokens; (2) no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group; (3) per-position distributions don't determine whether a group is dependent (two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals but differ in which value combinations occur). They empirically verify on ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task with closed-form joint distribution.

Result: On ScanAndAdd: every group of 2+ undetermined positions written by a confidence ranking is dependent; the generated distribution measures 29× the sampling-noise floor total variation; per-sample metrics are 1.0 (indicating complete failure to capture dependencies).

Conclusion: Discrete diffusion methods using per-position distributions cannot capture token dependencies inherent in real-world domains. This represents a fundamental limitation requiring new approaches to model dependent groups in discrete diffusion.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion, including remasking and uniform-state samplers, generate a sequence by writing multiple token positions per step, drawing each from a per-position distribution and choosing which positions to write from those same distributions. For domains of general interest (pixels, phonemes, or words) there are inherent dependencies between tokens. We show that a step matches the training distribution only when the positions it writes are conditionally independent given the tokens already fixed, that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and that per-position distributions do not determine whether a group is dependent: two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals while differing in which combinations of values occur. On ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task whose joint distribution is available in closed form, we verify that every group of two or more undetermined positions a confidence ranking writes is dependent, and measure the generated distribution to be $29\times$ the sampling-noise floor total variation while per-sample metrics are $1.0$.

</details>


### [322] [PAA: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra: A Generative and Complete Probabilistic Extension of Allen's Interval Relations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20634)
*Julian Eggert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper extends Allen's interval algebra to handle uncertain temporal relations by modeling intervals with Gaussian distributions, deriving relation probabilities from boundary distributions rather than scoring, and recovering crisp Allen relations as a special case when tolerance vanishes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Allen’s interval algebra uses crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries, which is inadequate for uncertain temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories where expressions like "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning.

Method: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra (PAA) models time points as Gaussian distributions, intervals as Gaussian midpoints with truncated-Gaussian durations. Relation probabilities are computed as multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and the thirteen relations form a true partition under a single tolerance that recovers crisp Allen as tolerance vanishes.

Result: The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it, with coarse predicates being unions of leaf relations whose probabilities are leaf sums. The hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points (13→5→3 relations). Each relation decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions like "shortly before" from contact relations. Results are Monte-Carlo validated.

Conclusion: The PAA provides a principled probabilistic framework for qualitative temporal reasoning that handles uncertainty, preserves the structure of Allen's algebra in the limiting case, and is implemented as an open-source Python package.

Abstract: Allen's interval algebra is a qualitative calculus for temporal relations, but its thirteen base relations are crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries. This is inadequate for temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories, where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain and expressions such as "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning. We develop the probabilistic Allen algebra (PAA): a generative and complete extension in which relation probabilities are derived from distributions over interval boundaries rather than assigned as scores. Time points are Gaussian; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation is a boundary-ordering predicate in one common probability space: point-point relations reduce to error functions, and point-interval and interval-interval relations to multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and under a single tolerance the thirteen relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen as the tolerance vanishes. The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates such as precedence, overlap, and containment are unions of leaves whose probabilities are leaf sums, and this hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points and thirteen relations reduce to five and then three. Each relation further decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions such as "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated and shipped as an open, tested Python package.

</details>


### [323] [Ownership in AI-Assisted Everyday Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20658)
*Megan Wei,Melanie Subbiah,Audrey Lee,Annya Dahmani,Dave Edwards,Helen Edwards,Ellie Pavlick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: As AI becomes integrated into everyday tasks, this study explores when people feel a sense of ownership over work produced with AI. Through qualitative surveys asking participants about two self-selected tasks (one feeling like their own, one not), researchers found that felt ownership depends on the collaboration process - people retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite, but disown work when they merely approve AI suggestions. Ownership can extend to settings where people own the vision but not execution. Loss of personal voice and lack of comprehension erode ownership. Willingness to disclose AI use is shaped by community norms rather than actual pride.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, there is a need to understand what happens to people's sense of ownership and contribution when machines share in producing what we make. This is increasingly important as AI assistance becomes ubiquitous.

Method: Exploratory qualitative survey where participants described two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not.

Result: Felt ownership depends on the collaboration process: people disown work when merely approving AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can extend to settings where people own the vision but not execution (e.g., tasks they couldn't have completed without AI). Loss of personal voice and lack of comprehension both erode ownership. Willingness to disclose AI use is decoupled from actual pride/ownership and is shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure.

Conclusion: The study proposes several research directions to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

Abstract: When does work done with AI still feel like ours? As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, we must examine what happens to our sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what we make. We report an exploratory qualitative survey in which participants were asked to describe two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. We find that felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration: people disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can also extend to settings where people own the vision for a project but not the execution; respondents reported high ownership on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and a lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Finally, willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, and instead shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure. We propose several research directions as a result of these findings to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

</details>


### [324] [Deep Noir: Autonomous Steering Discovery via Architectural Chronometry in Transformer Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20722)
*Frank E. Bobe,Gregory D. Vetaw,Darshan W. Bryner,Matthew G. Cook,Jose L. Salas-Vernis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Deep Noir is a framework that autonomously discovers optimal steering parameters for LLMs at inference time using Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution, eliminating manual hyperparameter tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where and how strongly to steer remains manual and requires extensive trial-and-error. This paper aims to automate the discovery of optimal steering parameters.

Method: The framework uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously identify optimal intervention points (specific heads and steering magnitudes) across three model scales (1B, 2-3B, and 7-9B).

Result: Deep Noir achieves 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam detection at 1B scale (SD=4.7, 39 runs), 21-42 percentage-point gains at 7-9B across four architectures, and 13.1 percentage-point improvement on SST-2 sentiment with zero code changes. It significantly outperforms RepE without head masking (p<0.01). Additionally, the study reveals that steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface that increases with steering magnitude.

Conclusion: Mechanistic grounding via Deep Noir enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. However, steering introduces security vulnerabilities relevant to agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

Abstract: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where and how strongly to steer remains manual. We introduce Deep Noir, a framework that uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters. Across three scales (1B x 3, 2-3B x 2, and 7-9B x 4), our engine achieves 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam at 1B (standard deviation 4.7; 39 runs), with gains increasing to 21 to 42 percentage points at 7-9B across four architectures. On SST-2 sentiment, it achieves a 13.1 percentage-point improvement with zero code changes. Mechanistic grounding enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. On sentiment, RepE without head masking fails to improve over baseline, while Deep Noir improves all models (p less than 0.01). We further show that steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface whose vulnerability increases monotonically with steering magnitude. This finding is relevant to agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

</details>


### [325] [RAFT: A Stateful Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20754)
*Mingxuan Zhang,Xiaowen Wang,Anupma Sharan,Zhengyi Chen,Chenyu Diana Zhang,Shanshan Yang,Chittibabu Pacharu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAFT is a stateful RAG framework for troubleshooting agents that treats support cases as temporal sequences rather than static documents, retrieving relevant historical cases by matching intermediate states and returning full case trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG systems treat support cases as static documents, failing to capture their multi-stage, stateful nature. This limits their ability to retrieve actionable guidance from similar historical cases during troubleshooting.

Method: RAFT abstracts closed historical cases into directed chains of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level. It surfaces cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returns the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state. An optional case-level graph links cases through configurable similarity representation. Evaluation uses a synthetic benchmark from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation and real Apache Jira issues with duplicate labels.

Result: RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline. Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories.

Conclusion: RAFT successfully addresses the limitation of static document retrieval in RAG systems by capturing the temporal dynamics of troubleshooting cases. The framework demonstrates significant improvements in retrieval accuracy across all case stages, with evidence supporting transfer to real-world scenarios.

Abstract: Effective troubleshooting agents in enterprise customer support depend on retrieving actionable guidance from similar historical cases, yet existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat support cases as static documents and overlook their multi-stage, stateful nature. We introduce RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents), a stateful RAG framework that abstracts each closed historical case into a directed chain of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level, surfacing cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returning the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state; an optional case-level graph links cases through a configurable similarity representation. We evaluate this retrieval layer directly, which, unlike evaluating a full agent system, requires no production deployment. Because public multi-stage troubleshooting data is extremely rare, we pair a synthetic benchmark built from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation with real Apache Jira issues carrying human-created duplicate labels. RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline; the Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories. We release our benchmark, implementation, and the Apache Jira evaluation set.

</details>
